This state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework; legal gender recognition, identity documents, border screening and anti-discrimination law are set nationally and are carried by the national record.

The state/province's anti-violence documentation project recorded 723 LGBTIQ+-hostile incidents in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports, which is a new high for incoming reports. The recorded incidents include insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and on the street. Several inner districts are the most affected, and 58 attacks targeted LGBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. The project states that its figures capture only part of what occurs because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025. One district is named among the worst-hit.

At the state/province's 48th annual Pride event, a vehicle was driven into a crowd, killing one woman and injuring several people; the event was cancelled. The anti-violence project offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, open daily from 17:00 to 19:00.

Ahead of the 2025 parade season, the state/province's Pride organisers urged vigilance with hundreds of thousands of participants expected. A venue owner in one district reported 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.

The anti-violence project assessed that large-city parades such as this state/province's and another large city's in the parent nation were not specifically threatened, and that smaller towns are the hardest to police.

The state/province's nightlife includes venues designated for women, lesbians, intersex, non-binary, trans and agender people, defined by the exclusion of cis male identity and motivated by discomfort with cis men's dominance of many queer venues. Two male-exclusive venues historically admitted only male patrons and turned away feminine men and gender-queer individuals; entry policy has widened since the 2000s, though instances of exclusion still occur.

The state/province's prison service publishes an information page for trans, inter* and non-binary people in custody. It states that legislation has created a basis for considering their situation, that prison staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it sets out gender-segregated placement, intake procedures, and counselling and support offers for detainees in the state/province's prisons, including named facilities.

The 2025 count is lower than the 2024 count while the number of incoming reports reached a new high; the project describes both as an incomplete record because of a high dark figure. No general crime or population denominator for the state/province appears in the sources, so the incident counts cannot be converted into a per-capita comparison.

The source reporting the vehicle attack at the Pride event does not record a stated motive, a charging decision or a court outcome.

National-level matters, including gender recognition, identity documents, border screening and anti-discrimination law, are carried by the national record and are not restated here.

The state/province is a sub-national unit of the country. Identity documents, equality law and the self-declaration route for legal gender change are set nationally; what is specific to this state/province is a political record and one prosecution.

The state/province is one of three sponsors, with two neighbouring state/provinces, of an initiative to the national upper legislative chamber to tighten the national self-determination law, reported by a national news agency on 2 June 2026. The proposal would create an "abuse review" mechanism allowing registry offices to intervene on objective, documentable grounds. It is backed by legislators from a conservative bloc and resisted by another party, while the national family ministry runs a scheduled evaluation of the self-determination law.

The case the initiative cites is a prosecution in the state/province. In July 2023 a district court there sentenced the convicted person, then registered as male, to one year and six months' imprisonment without parole for incitement to hatred, defamation and insult. At the end of 2024 she changed her legal gender from male to female by declaration at a registry office. The chief public prosecutor in the state/province told regional public broadcasting that she would begin the term at a women's prison in a neighbouring state/province, and national outlets questioned whether the change was serious. That case is the trigger for the initiative.

For a trans visitor, the state/province's registry offices are the point of contact with the national self-declaration route, and its government is on record seeking to add a review layer to it. Nothing in the sources documents practice at state/province level in policing, prisons, health services or venues bearing on trans people.

The case's later course ran through other jurisdictions. She was arrested in a neighbouring jurisdiction in April 2026 and, as international reporting noted on 16 July 2026, transferred after extradition to a men's prison in a neighbouring state/province, with the receiving prison's management saying the decision prioritised the safety of women at the women's facility. Whether a registry gender entry can be reversed is still before a court, and that question sits at the centre of the state/province's initiative.

The case's political weight rests on the convicted person's profile as an organiser of far-right demonstrations since 2014, many of them on a central square in a city in the state/province.

The initiative is a joint move with two neighbouring state/provinces, so its fate is decided in national politics rather than by the state/province's government alone.

Residents who have changed their gender entry by declaration at a registry office in the state/province are the group the proposed review mechanism would reach. The state/province's government holds that registry offices should be able to intervene on objective, documentable grounds, and whether an entry can be reversed is undecided in court.

The prosecution in the state/province and the chief public prosecutor's public statement on placement show that a person's gender entry can become a matter of official and press comment in the course of criminal proceedings there.

No rule, practice or incident specific to the state/province is recorded in the sources for policing, prisons, health care, women-protected venues or hate-crime enforcement as they affect trans people. The state/province's documented activity is confined to the initiative and the case.

The outcome of the initiative and of the national evaluation of the self-determination law is not resolved in the sources, and no court has yet decided whether a registry gender entry can be reversed.

The sources do not record how many registry offices in the state/province have processed self-declaration changes, or any guidance issued to them at state/province level.

No state/province-specific statute, ordinance or enforcement series on transgender matters is recorded. This state/province runs no separate legal gender recognition procedure and holds no custody rule of its own on the placement of transgender prisoners, so the position a transgender visitor or resident stands under is set by national law.

An initiative in the national upper chamber to tighten the national self-determination law, brought by three other state/provinces, would apply in this state/province as in every other one. It is a proposed amendment to the national framework rather than a measure of this state/province, and no enforcement action, court ruling or complaint on transgender custody or on transgender visitors is recorded here.

Pressure on the national self-determination law is being generated outside this state/province. The initiative in the national upper chamber comes from three other state/provinces, and no ministry, court or parliamentary group here is recorded as sponsoring or opposing it. If adopted, the change would reach residents and visitors through national legislation rather than through any statute of this state/province.

The absence of a rule at this level means the practical exposures a transgender visitor meets, including custody placement, screening at airports and access to women-protected spaces, are governed by national provisions and by private operators rather than by anything this state/province has legislated.

For people living in this state/province, no statute, ordinance or enforcement series at this level addresses transgender status. Legal gender recognition, custody placement and protection from discrimination are administered under the national framework, and no complaints body, advisory service or publicly funded support structure specific to this state/province is recorded.

Whether the initiative in the national upper chamber will be adopted, and in what form, is unresolved. No date is recorded for a vote, and the sources do not state whether this state/province supports or opposes it.

No data specific to this state/province is sourced on custody placement practice, police or airport screening, access to women-protected spaces, or hate-crime enforcement. The reference entry reviewed for this state/province returned no substantive finding.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation: the constitutional, equality and identity-document regime of the country applies in the state/province, and no sub-national instrument displaces it. The region-specific material available here consists of two incidents in one city concerning public LGBT life.

A local news outlet reported a fire at an LGBT community venue in that city shortly before the city's annual LGBT event, which prompted an investigation by the political police. Neither the circumstances of the fire nor the outcome of that investigation are sourced, and no finding of an anti-LGBT motive has been reported.

A second local news outlet reported on 26 October 2025 that the annual LGBT parade in that city went ahead under a large police deployment with two counter-demonstrations present. Organised counter-demonstrations at the city's principal LGBT public event are the only documented hostility signal in the state/province for that period; no arrest figures, injury reports or trans-specific incidents connected with the parade are sourced.

Neither report concerns sub-national legislation or sub-national policy on gender recognition, custody, health care or sex-separated facilities. On those subjects the national framework governs in the state/province as elsewhere in the country, and the national assessment should be consulted.

Both reports concern public LGBT organising rather than the legal position of an individual trans visitor, so they bear on the safety and visibility of public gatherings in the state/province rather than on legal exposure.

The referral of the venue fire to the political police indicates that authorities in the state/province treat attacks on LGBT premises as politically motivated offences. Whether that produced a suspect, a charge or a motive finding is not recorded.

The 26 October 2025 parade took place with a large police deployment and two counter-demonstrations. No comparison with events in other state/provinces appears in the sources, and there are no attendance or incident figures against which the event's risk level could be measured.

Users of the LGBT community venue in the city have no sourced statement on whether it reopened after the fire or on any prosecution arising from it.

Participants in the annual LGBT event on 26 October 2025 faced two counter-demonstrations alongside a large police presence; no arrests, injuries or follow-up measures affecting participants are reported.

No sub-national measure altering the legal position of trans residents in the state/province beyond the national framework appears in the sources.

The outcome of the political police investigation into the fire at the LGBT community venue is unresolved; no motive finding, suspect or charge is sourced.

No sub-national statute, court decision or administrative practice on gender recognition, prison placement, health care or single-sex facilities is sourced here. How those matters are handled in the state/province remains unverified.

The two items are raw counts: one fire at an LGBT venue and one parade met by two counter-demonstrations. With no per-capita or statewide baseline, they establish no rate and support no ranking of the state/province against others.

Placement for people held in this state/province is set at state/provincial level rather than nationally: prison administration is a state/provincial competence in the parent nation, so the placement rule sits in the state's own correctional act, while legal gender recognition and anti-discrimination law sit in the national framework. Section 17 of the state/provincial correctional act took effect on 1 March 2026 and anchors placement to the legally recorded gender entry. The accompanying exception clause is drafted in general and abstract terms and is available to all prisoners; it is not written specifically for transgender prisoners. A transgender visitor detained in this state/province therefore has the placement decision taken at intake against the gender entry on their legal record, with the exception clause as the only route away from it.

A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 reads this state/province's drafting as the model preferable to the alternative used in other state/provinces, where exception clauses are written to target transgender prisoners specifically, and raises constitutional doubts about that alternative approach. The analysis is legal commentary on the statute and on the drafting choice; it is not a record of how this state/province's clause has been applied.

The state/provincial amendment is one step in a sequence of sub-national corrections to placement rules that had stood unchanged since the 1970s. This state/province is the one whose amendment brought the modernised group past an absolute majority among the state/provinces, so the position in which placement rules were left untouched at sub-national level no longer holds as a general matter.

The rule in this state/province is not affected by litigation over the national self-determination law; that litigation and the accompanying debate over tightening the law concern the national framework and do not alter the state/provincial placement provisions.

Residents of this state/province who are held in its prisons are placed under the state/provincial correctional act by reference to their legally recorded gender entry, in force since 1 March 2026. The exception clause is open to any prisoner rather than restricted to transgender prisoners, so a transgender person in custody in this state/province relies on a provision that is not framed around their situation.

No public record shows how the exception clause has been applied in an individual case in this state/province, and no state/provincial guidance for transgender prisoners appears in the available sources.

How the general exception clause in section 17 is applied in practice in this state/province is unresolved: the sources contain the statutory text and a legal analysis, but no documented case, decision or administrative practice from its facilities.

No state/provincial figures on transgender prisoners, complaints, or facility-level arrangements are available, and no state/provincial prison-service information page for transgender people in custody appears in the inventory.

Prison placement litigation covered in the same source inventory concerns another state/province and the national framework; it yields no finding specific to this state/province.

This state/province stands under the national framework set by the national self-determination statute. It has enacted no trans-specific statute of its own and no prison-placement rule of its own. Prison administration and the civil-registry offices are competences of the state/province, so the layer a trans person actually deals with here is run by state/provincial authorities, applying the national framework without local amendment.

Under the national self-determination statute the legal gender entered in the civil registry is the reference point for prison placement in every state/province, and a provision of that statute permits state/provincial law to override that entry. This state/province has not passed such an override. The placement of a trans person held in a facility here therefore turns on the registered entry rather than on a local exception clause; how intake review is conducted in the state/province's prisons is not documented in the available sources.

Legal gender changes for residents are processed through the state/province's own registry offices. This state/province maintains no separate rule on bathrooms, changing or leisure facilities, or identity documents of its own, so a visitor meets the national framework rather than a local variant.

This state/province has no veto over the self-determination framework it applies. A legislative initiative in the national upper chamber to tighten the national self-determination statute, launched by several state/provinces after the dispute over a prisoner's placement, would take effect here as national law if enacted, with no state/provincial statute required.

Because registry offices and prison administration are state/provincial competences, the practical handling of a trans person's file or custody here depends on state/provincial authorities rather than on a national agency, even where the governing rules are national.

A trans resident of this state/province changes their legal gender entry at the state/province's registry offices; the procedure follows the national self-determination rules rather than a local variant.

Prison placement is a state/provincial responsibility rather than a national one, so any change to placement rules in the state/province's own facilities would have to come from state/provincial legislation. As it stands, there is no state/provincial placement statute to cite, and the registered entry is the governing reference.

No state/province-specific enforcement action, court ruling, or incident involving a trans person appears in the sources. The materials document the position here only as an absence of local legislation, so how the registry offices and prison intake handle individual cases is not sourced.

Placement practice inside the state/province's prisons is not documented in these sources; the question is governed by the national framework together with the absence of a state/provincial exception clause.

No state/province-level statistics on trans people in custody, and no state/province-level breakdown of discrimination complaints under the national equal-treatment statute, are available in the source set.

Prison administration in the parent nation is a competence of the state/provinces, and this state/province is one of them. Placement decisions for transgender people held in its correctional facilities therefore rest with the state/province's own justice administration rather than with a national authority. No case file, official guidance or enforcement account concerning a transgender prisoner in the state/province appears in the sources reviewed for this assessment; the longer contest over how a legal gender entry interacts with prison housing is documented nationally and in other state/provinces, and belongs to the national assessment.

Documentary matters for a trans visitor or resident in the state/province stand under the national framework. Legal gender and first-name changes are made by self-declaration at the state/province's registry offices under the national self-determination law, in force since 1 November 2024, with three months' notice and without a psychological evaluation or a court order. The state/province's own procedural handling of those declarations is not documented in the sources reviewed.

The state/province has a long-established gay commercial quarter, where bars, cafés and clubs operate in the streets adjoining the city's entertainment area; reference material describes it as a principal centre of the gay scene in the subregion. That material records no local dispute over trans access to those venues.

The exposure a trans visitor meets in the state/province divides between local and national layers. Recognition of legal gender, asylum and admission policy, equal-treatment law and airport screening procedure are set nationally; prisons, policing and the licensing of commercial venues sit with the state/province. Where the two layers meet, no position taken by the state/province is documented in the material reviewed, and the disputes over placement and access that exist are recorded at national level and in other state/provinces rather than in this one.

The national argument over trans access to women-protected leisure facilities is carried by the national assessment. No venue, sauna operator or police unit in the state/province is named in any source reviewed as having taken a position on trans access, and no screening complaint or access dispute arising there appears in the material.

Residents file declarations changing legal gender and first name with the state/province's registry offices, which also handle the civil-registry consequences of the change. Trans people sentenced to custody there serve in the state/province's own correctional facilities, administered locally; the sources reviewed do not document how those facilities house a prisoner whose legal gender differs from the birth entry.

No data specific to the state/province on transgender prisoner placement was located. Whether its correctional statute contains any provision on gender identity, and how its facilities have applied it, is unresolved on the material reviewed.

Whether the state/province's registry offices have issued procedural guidance of their own for self-determination declarations, beyond the national law, is not sourced. No local record of venue access disputes, screening incidents or hate-crime enforcement involving trans people was located; the national-level record on those subjects sits in the national assessment.

This state/province stands under the national framework. It has enacted no statute or ordinance specific to trans people, and it has no provision of its own governing where a trans prisoner is held. Placement in a facility in this state/province therefore follows the national rules, with no state/province-level variation layered on top of them.

No trans-specific exception clause of the kind that has drawn constitutional doubt in other state/provinces' prison acts exists in the law of this state/province.

The state/province's own trans-relevant legislative record is a co-sponsored initiative. It tabled a joint motion in the national upper chamber with several other state/provinces for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019.

No material specific to this state/province adjacent to the visitor assessment appears in the inventory. Prison-placement litigation, airport screening complaints and access disputes in the sauna sector are national in scope and are carried by the national record rather than here.

Trans residents of this state/province have no state/province statute or ordinance addressed to them. Legal gender recognition, protection from discrimination and custody placement all run through the national framework, and the state/province has not enacted a placement rule for trans prisoners.

Its trans-related legislative action is the 2019 motion in the national upper chamber on conversion therapy, co-tabled with several other state/provinces and presented in plenary on 12 April 2019.

The inventory holds no enforcement data, incident reporting or prison-service guidance specific to this state/province for trans people, and no finding on gender identity from a state/province anti-discrimination body. Whether the state/province will legislate on trans-prisoner placement is not sourced.

Constitutional doubts raised about trans-targeted exception clauses in state/province prison law are analysed at national level and are carried by the national record; no such clause exists in the law of this state/province to test them against.

The state/province stands under the national framework, and no region-specific signal on trans visitor risk was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment applies.

Custody placement remains the sharpest documented exposure. The state/province's own prison law retains the unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, which operate on a binary men and women housing model. An analysis of 18 March 2026 reports that placement rules in most state/provinces have stood unchanged since the 1970s and are now being revised: since 1 March 2026 a new Art. 17 of a neighbouring jurisdiction's prison law is in force, and three other state/provinces' rules have also recently entered into force, giving a majority of state/provinces revised rules. This state/province is not named among them.

The same analysis argues that no constitutional duty exists to anchor placement to the registered gender entry, since a prisoner self-declaration would intrude less on the right to gender self-determination. Only one state/province's law explicitly references the gender entry; other state/provinces do so implicitly.

How placement is applied in practice has gone both ways. A July 2026 report concerns a convicted far-right extremist holding a legally recognised female gender entry who was transferred from a women's prison to a men's prison after public outcry. The transfer indicates that placement follows the civil-registry entry and that exceptions permitting placement contrary to that entry are invoked inconsistently.

This state/province's prison law sits within a national landscape in which a majority of state/provinces have recently revised their placement rules while a minority, including this one, retain the 1970s-era text. A trans visitor's exposure in custody therefore depends on which state/province's facilities hold them.

Residents held in this state/province's prisons are subject to the state/province's unrevised 1970s-era placement rules, which do not expressly reference the registered gender entry. The analysis notes that only one state/province's law explicitly references the gender entry, with other state/provinces doing so implicitly or not at all; this state/province is not named in that mapping.

Whether this state/province has any pending revision of its prison placement rules is unresolved in the source inventory. The inventory does not document any state/province-specific incident of trans prison placement, nor any state/province-level guidance, complaint procedure or oversight body for trans prisoners here.

The state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework on legal gender recognition, identity documents, relationship recognition and anti-discrimination, and that layer is carried by the national record. What follows is specific to the state/province.

A prohibition on gender-neutral language forms took effect in the state/province on 1 April 2024. It bars such forms in schools, universities and all regional administration, implementing a government declaration of December 2023 together with a cabinet decision amending the language rules that govern public authorities. Critics dismiss the measure as symbol politics while pointing out that it reaches every public counter, registry office and classroom in the state/province. A trans visitor dealing with a registry office, town hall or university there therefore deals with offices operating under an official register from which gender-neutral wording has been excluded.

The state/province has co-sponsored an initiative in the national upper chamber with three other state/provinces to tighten the parent nation's self-declaration law, an organised attempt by subnational governments to make the nationwide self-ID route stricter. The contested ground behind the initiative was the law's treatment of children's gender entry: the upper chamber's criticism of 20 October 2023 held that the draft allowed parents to decide changes for under-14s "without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare". The state/province government's posture toward self-declaration is therefore openly restrictive, even though the procedure itself remains the national one.

The language ban is one of two organised interventions by the state/province government in the national gender-recognition debate; the other is the four-state/province upper-chamber initiative, in which it acts alongside three other state/provinces. No source in the inventory records comparable legislative activity by the state/province on documents, facilities, healthcare or custody.

The ban's critics and its authors agree on its reach and disagree only on its value: the government treats gender-neutral language as a matter for regional language rules, while opponents characterise the measure as symbolic. The disagreement does not change the practical scope, which covers administration, education and public-facing counters alike.

For people living in the state/province, the language restriction binds schools, universities and the entire regional administration. Public-sector employees and students must use a prescribed register of the language, and the rules were adopted through the state/province cabinet rather than by a vote of the regional legislature.

The state/province executive has made restriction of the national self-declaration procedure a position it carries into the national upper chamber, joining three other state/provinces in seeking tighter conditions on legal gender change. Residents are subject to the national procedure in force, but the state/province government's stated objective is a stricter version of it.

Unresolved: whether the four-jurisdiction initiative produced any amendment to the national procedure, or any change in how local registry offices apply it, is not sourced here.

Unresolved: no information in the inventory addresses whether the language prohibition affects how local registry offices record, display or speak about a changed gender entry or name on documents issued in the state/province.

Not sourced: state/province-specific reporting on prison placement, airport or transport screening, access to gendered facilities, healthcare refusal, hate-crime incidents or protection machinery. The national record carries that material; no local figure or case appears in this inventory.

This state/province has no documented statute, ordinance or placement reform specific to transgender people. Legal gender recognition here is governed by the national self-determination act, which applies in this state/province as in every other state/province.

The state/province is the site of a July 2026 regional court ruling that ordered a prisoner held in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change. That decision is the documented flashpoint in this state/province for how the national self-determination act interacts with custodial placement.

Placement under the framework analysed in a legal analysis published on 18 March 2026 follows a prisoner's legal gender entry unless the state/province's correctional law provides otherwise. The analysis separates exception clauses written in abstract terms from clauses aimed at trans prisoners specifically, and treats the drafting choice as decisive for the outcome in practice.

For a trans visitor, the documented exposure in this state/province is custody. A person detained here cannot assume that a completed legal gender change will determine where they are held. No state/province-level rule on identity documents, facilities access or healthcare specific to trans people is documented.

The regional court decision is the only placement ruling documented in this state/province. No other adjudication, administrative guidance or legislative response at the state/province level is recorded.

The ruling sits inside a framework-level contest over how correctional statutes draft exceptions to placement by legal gender entry, a contest that runs across the state/provinces rather than being specific to this one.

Trans people held in this state/province's prisons are subject to the placement question decided in the July 2026 regional court ruling. No state/province-level placement policy or correctional-act amendment on gender-diverse prisoners is documented.

Whether this state/province's correctional act contains an exception clause permitting placement by something other than legal gender entry is not stated in the sources.

The regional court ruling is reported without the court's reasoning, the facility involved, or whether the decision was appealed. The outcome for the prisoner concerned is not documented.

No enforcement action, hate-crime prosecution or facility-access dispute involving trans people in this state/province is recorded.

This is a state/province of the parent nation. National law on identity documents, legal gender recognition and prison placement applies here as it does elsewhere in the country; the material below is the state/province-specific layer.

That layer is configured by the legislature elected on 1 September 2024. The party classified as right-wing extremist by the state/province's domestic intelligence service took 32.8% of the vote. A centre-right party followed at 23.4%, a newly formed populist party at 15.8% in its first election, a left party at 13.1% and the social democrats at 6.1%. The centre-right party, the populist party and the social democrats formed the state/province's first three-party minority coalition under the minister-president, a cabinet without its own legislative majority. Institutional hostility to gender policy in this state/province rests on this configuration.

Nothing in the sources reviewed documents a trans-specific safety incident, police practice or refusal of service in this state/province. What is recorded for the state/province is legislative and party-political, with no state/province-level enforcement or violence record to assess.

On 2 June 2026 this state/province co-signed an initiative brought by two neighbouring state/provinces to tighten the national gender-recognition law. The proposal followed a widely reported case, and its anti-abuse amendments were presented alongside measures for stronger recognition of trans and intersex people. The initiative concerns the national statute rather than state/province law; this state/province's role is a co-signature, not a separate recognition regime.

The largest party's fraction in the state/province legislature has moved that the existing ban on gender-inclusive language in schools be consistently implemented, arguing in its motion that schools must not be a socio-political experimental field. The same fraction has proposed dismantling the state/province's equality machinery. These measures bear on residents: pupils, teaching staff and anyone who uses state/province anti-discrimination structures.

No source in the inventory records trans-specific violence, policing or prosecution in this state/province, so no state/province-level risk assessment of that kind can be made from this material. Whether the co-signed initiative to tighten the national gender-recognition law advances, and in what form, is unresolved. The coalition's lack of its own legislative majority leaves the passage of the school-language measure and the proposed dismantling of the equality machinery open.

This state/province has no trans-specific statute of its own. Its state/provincial constitution was amended in 2011 so that its anti-discrimination provisions explicitly include sexual orientation and gender identity, one of five state/provincial constitutions to carry such a clause. The consequence for a visitor is that transphobic hate speech is prohibited under this state/province's constitution, while hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity is not banned nationally.

Prison placement in this state/province is governed by the national framework because the state/province has enacted no placement statute of its own; the legal gender entry is the default basis for placement unless a state/provincial law provides otherwise. A constitutional-law analysis published on 18 March 2026 cites this state/province's single-cell accommodation with en-suite shower as a positive practice model for trans inmates. The same analysis records that constitutional law does not oblige authorities to follow the legal gender entry, so the default here is a practice rather than an enforceable guarantee.

This state/province's protection against discrimination on gender identity rests on its constitution rather than on trans-specific legislation. Legislative activity on trans prison placement in other state/provinces has not been matched here, which has no placement statute.

This state/province was among the state/provinces that tabled the joint motion in the national upper chamber for a ban on conversion therapy, presented in plenary on 12 April 2019. The ban that followed was enacted nationally rather than by this state/province.

The 2011 amendment to this state/province's constitution makes sexual orientation and gender identity explicit grounds in its anti-discrimination provisions. The clause binds state/provincial authorities and is the basis for the prohibition of transphobic hate speech here.

People held in this state/province's prisons are accommodated under its single-cell-with-en-suite-shower model, cited in the March 2026 analysis as a positive practice for trans inmates.

No record specific to this state/province of enforcement of the constitutional prohibition of transphobic hate speech was identified: no prosecutions, complaints or court decisions from this state/province appear in the sources.

The single-cell accommodation model is cited in a legal commentary rather than in a court ruling or a statement by the state/provincial prison service, and no account of its application to an individual trans prisoner here was identified.

No statute, ordinance or administrative rule specific to this state/province on trans prison placement was identified; the state/province's position is defined by the absence of such a rule.

Police-registered offences hostile to LGBTIQ people in the state/province have risen in each year since 2022: 33 offences that year, 83 in 2023, 135 in 2024 and 141 in 2025, a more than fourfold increase across four years. The state/province interior minister called the development alarming in answers to inquiries from opposition members of the state/province legislature and attributed part of the responsibility to far-right forces.

The 2024 figure, given in the interior ministry's answer to an August 2025 inquiry, was 52 higher than the previous year and comprised 16 cases of dangerous grievous bodily harm, seven of bodily harm, 13 of property damage and 26 of insult. Suspects were identified in 46 of the 2024 proceedings, and six convictions resulted.

Physical attacks form part of the record. The interior minister cited a January 2026 incident on a tram in a city in the state/province in which a male couple was insulted, threatened and spat on for homophobic motives.

An international airport in the state/province produced a documented complaint by a transgender traveller. On 23 November 2024 a transgender woman was refused a search by a female officer during screening, and the male officer handling her told her she was 'not a woman'. The state/province is a constituent unit of the country. Criminal law, policing, prisons and family law are devolved to its legislature, while legal gender recognition and equality law are set at national level; the findings below are specific to the state/province.

Trans people in the state/province change their legal gender under the national gender-recognition statute of 2004. A gender-recognition reform bill was introduced to the state/province legislature in March 2022 and passed in December 2022 by 86 votes to 39, applying only within the state/province. The national government blocked the bill under a statutory power in the state/province's devolution legislation while it awaited royal assent, the first time that power has been used to overturn state/province legislation, so the reformed procedure the legislature legislated for is not in force.

Hate crime in the state/province is governed by its 2021 hate-crime act, passed by the legislature in March 2021 by 82 votes to 32, given royal assent a month later and in force on 1 April 2024. It lists gender identity as a protected characteristic. Earlier state/province legislation enacted in 2009 provides penalty enhancements where an offence is motivated by the victim's gender identity.

The state/province prosecution service's report 'Hate crime, 2025-26', issued 30 June 2026, records 7,115 hate-crime charges in total, up 17% on 2024-25 and the highest since 2003-04. Transgender-identity aggravation accounted for 104 charges, up 21% from 86 the previous year and the highest level since the 2021 act took effect. Sexual-orientation aggravation accounted for 2,062 charges, the second commonest category.

The state/province police service recorded 8,538 hate crimes in 2024-25, according to a government report published 17 February 2026, the first annual report under the 2021 act. The highest rates per a small population were in the two largest cities, at about 32.25 each. Sixty-two per cent of recorded hate crimes carried a race aggravator and just over a quarter a sexual-orientation aggravator; the report gives no per-resident rate for the transgender-identity category.

The state/province police service published interim guidance on 25 June 2025 providing that searches involving the removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex, in both custody and stop-and-search contexts. Where a person's lived gender differs from their sex at birth, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

On 19 June 2026 a judge of the state/province's highest civil court, in a challenge brought against the state/province prison service, struck down that service's non-statutory guidance on trans custody as unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis. The guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in establishments matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The case was heard in February 2026, when the court was told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as flexible; the claimant was challenging a policy of holding only biological females in the women's estate.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in the state/province since 16 December 2014 under legislation passed by its legislature on 4 February 2014 by 108 votes to 15 and given royal assent on 12 March 2014, with the first ceremonies on 31 December 2014. No religious organisation or celebrant is obliged to perform such marriages.

The two hate-crime series measure different things over different periods. State/province policy ambition and the legal position diverge. The Action Plan's stated goal sits alongside national rules on gender recognition and single-sex spaces that apply in the state/province and that the devolved administration cannot alter.

England stands under the parent nation's national framework, which the national record carries.

The definitions that govern services, searches and detention allocation in England were fixed by the national supreme court's unanimous judgment handed down 16 April 2025 in litigation over the statutory definition of a woman. "Woman" and "sex" in the national Equality Act 2010 mean biological woman and biological sex, so a gender recognition certificate does not entitle a trans woman to the Act's sex-based protections. A judge on the bench stated that the ruling should not be read as reducing the Act's protection against discrimination for transgender people.

The national equality and human-rights commission, the body enforcing the Equality Act 2010 in England and a neighbouring jurisdiction, updated its code of practice on 20 May 2025 in response to that judgment. The code advises that services and businesses may ask a person for a birth certificate where there is "genuine concern" about biological sex, and that trans people may be excluded from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety. This is the operative guidance a trans visitor encounters at venues, transport and services.

Prison and custody decisions in England are governed by the same national ruling, under which Article 8 of the applicable human-rights convention confers no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex. In argument on 5 February 2026 in a judicial review testing how far that ruling reaches into prison accommodation, government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while the petitioning campaign group called the identity-based policy "Orwellian".

The national interior department's statistics for England and a neighbouring jurisdiction, published 9 October 2025, record 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025. The transgender strand fell 11% and the sexual-orientation strand 2% against the previous year. The bulletin cautions that recorded figures understate prevalence, giving a national crime survey estimate of about 176,000 hate-crime incidents a year, and that a February 2024 recording-system change at the capital city's police force means earlier years over-counted.

A regional LGBTI rights organisation's comparative scoring places the parent nation first in the region in 2015 with 86%, ninth in 2020 with 66%, and 22nd in 2025 with 45%, the third steepest drop in the region; its 2020 executive expressed concern about a hostile climate on trans rights fuelled by opposition groups. These scores are parent-nation-wide rather than England-specific, so they describe the regional climate rather than any England-only measure.

The hate-crime figures are raw counts for England and a neighbouring jurisdiction with no population denominator in the source, and the transgender strand is reported only as a year-on-year percentage change. Neither figure supports a per-capita comparison with other jurisdictions, and the February 2024 recording-system change at the capital city's police force means comparisons against earlier years rest on a different counting basis.

Residents of England are covered by the national Equality Act 2010 as interpreted from 16 April 2025: sex-based protections follow biological sex, and a gender recognition certificate does not alter that position, while the bench judge's statement preserves the Act's discrimination protection for transgender people.

The national equality and human-rights commission is the enforcing body for residents, and its code of practice of 20 May 2025 binds service providers, businesses and associations. Its two operative provisions permit a birth-certificate request on "genuine concern" about biological sex and permit exclusion from single-sex sport "when necessary" for safety.

Residents held in custody in England are allocated by biological sex, Article 8 conferring no automatic right to accommodation with the opposite biological sex. Government lawyers argued on 5 February 2026 that a blanket rule to that effect would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, and no outcome of that hearing is documented in the sources used here.

For residents reporting hostility, the official baseline is the national interior department's bulletin for England and a neighbouring jurisdiction of 9 October 2025: 115,990 police-recorded hate crimes in the year ending March 2025 against a national crime survey estimate of about 176,000 incidents a year, with the transgender strand down 11% year on year.

The outcome of the judicial review heard on 5 February 2026 is unresolved in the sources used here; no English court decision on prison accommodation for trans prisoners is documented.

The interior department's bulletin supplies only a percentage change for the transgender strand. No trans-specific hate-crime count or rate for England and a neighbouring jurisdiction appears in this record, so the strand's absolute size cannot be stated.

Whether the equality commission code's "genuine concern" standard has been tested in court, and how venues and transport operators apply it in practice, is not sourced here.

A regional police force's searching and biological-sex policy, released under freedom-of-information law, could not be retrieved at research time, so its terms for trans people in custody are unresolved.

The occupied parts of the region run under occupying-state-appointed authorities applying the occupying state's federal law — an all-audiences "propaganda" law, a 2023 transition ban, and an "extremist" designation of the LGBT movement — plus wartime arbitrariness with no rule of law. The self-proclaimed entity's first "constitution" expressly provided that "perverted unions between people of the same sex are prosecuted by law"; the clause was removed but persecution continued.

Documented practices go beyond the statute: a respondent reported a gay man shot and buried behind a checkpoint; people were brought to a notorious informal detention site for intimidation, ransom and forced labour. A 2022 assessment records that when the military or occupation administration learns a person is LGBT, they face insults, violence, extortion, restriction of freedom and threats to life. A documentation project found occupying military specifically searching for LGBTIQ+ people, with 81 known victims of detention/violence. UN reporting places LGBTQ+ persons at acute risk of sexual violence in detention.

Transgender people are specifically trapped: appearance-document mismatch prevents them from leaving through checkpoints, and discrimination blocks work, services and housing. Almost all openly LGBT residents have fled; those remaining cannot express identity, and no public support can be voiced. No monitor, remedy or protective institution operates.

Under occupation by a neighbouring state since 2014, the peninsula is governed by the occupying state's full legal regime: a "propaganda" law extended to all audiences, a 2023 ban on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming medical care, and a supreme-court designation of the "international LGBT movement" as an extremist organisation, with participation or financing punishable by up to twelve years in prison. Local courts fine people tens of thousands of currency units for "propaganda" — books, images and social-media posts — with penalties exceeding the average local wage.

The occupation leadership has openly threatened LGBT people, promising that "self-defense forces and police will react" to any gay street presence; a militia threatened to "pack and post" LGBT people out of the peninsula. No public LGBT event has taken place since the occupation began. International monitors are barred from entering.

An interview-based human-rights report documents a foreigner lured via a fake dating profile into an apartment where five men stripped and beat him, forced him to lick a toilet, filmed the assault and published the video — a documented visitor-facing predation pattern with no police recourse. A 2025 assessment reports violent attacks on LGBT people and those perceived as LGBT, almost all openly LGBT residents having fled, and those remaining not expressing identity visibly. The occupying state's legal gender-change procedures were unusable in practice under the occupation authorities even when nominally available.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation; it has no statute of its own prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so protection for trans visitors and residents rests on national law rather than on state/province legislation.

An ordinance signed on 28 August 2025 by an appellate judge guarantees transgender people the use of their social name and the use of bathrooms and locker rooms in accordance with gender identity. It is the clearest region-specific rule on gendered facilities in the state/province.

In 2022 a resident became the first person in the state/province to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker. The civil registry had refused the entry for lack of a regulated third-gender procedure, and the marker was secured through a year-long lawsuit brought by a legal clinic at a local university.

On 5 May 2025 the state/province prosecution service, the national prosecution service, the labour prosecution service, the national public defender's office and the state/province public defender's office jointly recommended that the state/province security secretariat and the state/province justice secretariat provide regular training for military police, civil police, firefighters, penitentiary and socio-educational agents on respect for LGBTQIA+ rights and improved service. The recommendation set a response deadline of 20 business days and required a training plan within 60 days covering 2025 and later years. It also requires gender identity, sexual orientation and social name to be recorded in police occurrence reports and prison records, with data protection and privacy safeguards, so that violence against transsexual women and travestis, including domestic and family violence, can be monitored.

Police records in the state/province logged 240 occurrences of anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across 2020 and 2021.

A civil inquiry preceding the May 2025 recommendation found only partial compliance with existing obligations, including no specific courses for firefighters and no adequate computerised registration and confidentiality system in the state/province justice secretariat. The state/province's own prosecution and defender bodies therefore treat the recording and service standards as unmet rather than settled.

The state/province was named in 2022 the worst in the parent nation for public policies for the LGBTQ community. That assessment concerns state/province-level service provision and institutional capacity, not the legal rights that apply uniformly across the country.

A state/province law banned gender-neutral language in schools from October 2021, when the state/province governor signed it on the 19th, until the national supreme court's plenary declared the ban unconstitutional on 10 February 2023; a national supreme court justice had suspended it by preliminary injunction in November 2021. Gender-neutral language is permitted in state/province schools and cannot be prohibited or penalised.

A law passed on 10 July 2026 required parental authorisation for students to attend classes on gender identity, sexual orientation, sexual diversity and gender equality. The state/province assembly president enacted it after the state/province governor neither vetoed nor signed it, and the state/province court of justice struck it down on 17 August 2026.

The source does not state which institutions or premises the 28 August 2025 ordinance covers, or whether it binds private establishments.

No sourced outcome establishes whether the state/province security secretariat and the state/province justice secretariat met the 20-business-day response deadline or produced the 60-day training plan required by the May 2025 recommendation.

The 2022 ranking of the state/province as the worst in the parent nation for LGBTQ public policies is reported without the methodology or the body that produced it.

Whether the state/province has issued further administrative rules on social name or gender markers since 2022 is not established by the sources.

The state/province is in a region of the country; the national framework applies, and the findings below are specific to the state/province.

A national trans association's 2025 dossier records 7 trans killings in the state/province during 2025, placing it immediately behind the leading state/provinces, which recorded 8; a second report identifies those as two other state/provinces. Across 1,261 killings recorded nationally between 2017 and 2025, the state/province ranks third with 97, after two other state/provinces (151 and 107). These are raw counts with no per-capita denominator, and the state/province is among the most populous in the country, so the ranking reflects population size as well as incidence and does not establish that it is more dangerous per resident than smaller state/provinces.

The pattern is not new. The 2022 dossier ranked the state/province seventh nationally for killings of trans people, with 7 killings of travestis in the state/province that year, when another state/province led the ranking.

On the weekend of 6-7 December 2025, an 18-year-old trans woman was choked to death in a municipality in the west of the state/province. The state/province civil police opened a feminicide investigation, treating the killing as gender-based. The suspect, a 19-year-old app driver, drove the victim's body to the police station, confessed and claimed self-defence, and was released.

The state/province was the first in the country to enact an anti-discrimination ordinance, in 1997. On 1 June 2022 the legislature passed, and on 30 June 2022 its president signed, a law banning discrimination on grounds of gender identity; a parallel measure covering sexual orientation was signed the same day.

Transgender people in the state/province have been able to change their name and legal gender since 2008, with gender self-determination permitted since 2018, and the state/province public defender's office works with other agencies on joint efforts to facilitate document rectification. A decree signed by the then state/province governor on 23 May 2017 gave travesti and transexual people the right to use their social name and have their gender identity recognised across the state/province's direct and indirect public administration; the social name must appear alongside the legal name on official documents, and minors require guardian authorisation. On 11 May 2022 the state/province court of justice allowed a third gender option on documents, and on 26 December 2024 the state/province governor sanctioned a law exempting the cost of protest certificates so that document rectification is free of charge for transgender people.

In 2008 a travesti club dancer won a seat on the capital's city council with 12,861 votes and, on taking office, insisted on a feminine wardrobe and on using the women's restroom.

Against these protections, on 17 December 2025 the capital's city council approved a bill banning the teaching of gender identity in schools, signed into law on 26 March 2026 by the capital's mayor.

The state/province sits in the top band of state/provinces in the annual trans-killing dossiers without leading it: third in the 2017-2025 cumulative count behind two other state/provinces, and just behind two others in 2025. Its record combines a high raw count with early protective legislation, including the first state/province anti-discrimination ordinance in the country in 1997 and notarial recognition of marriages between people of the same sex from November 2012, ahead of nationwide recognition in 2013.

The state/province's protective measures and the capital's school restriction point in opposite directions: the gender-identity discrimination law and the 2017 social-name decree operate across the state/province, while the capital city council's ban on teaching gender identity, signed in March 2026, applies within the capital's school system.

A homophobic attack on a teenager in a municipality in 2022 drew national attention and prompted state/province authorities to act; the sources do not record it as trans-specific.

Notaries in the state/province have recognised marriages between people of the same sex since 26 November 2012, before nationwide recognition. The homosexual stable union book is recognised by the national social-security institute for inheritance sharing and pension receipt, with 30 reported legal cases in the state/province, including a surviving spouse receiving a pension after a companion's death. On 9 March 2010 a court in the capital authorised the adoption of a child by a lesbian couple.

A preventative STD/AIDS programme for travesti sex workers in the state/province produced a booklet, folder and poster in realistic language and images, ran weekly safe-sex workshops, and recorded 900 interventions and the distribution of 14,400 condoms over six months.

The dossier counts are raw totals; the sources provide no per-capita rate for the state/province or for the state/provinces it is compared with, so the ranking cannot be read as a measure of risk per resident.

No state/province-specific rule, unit or documented case on the placement of trans prisoners in the state/province prison system appears in the sources; the national framework governs, and the state/province prison administration's practice is not documented here.

The 2004 list compiled by a state/province-based LGBTQ organisation naming 159 murdered LGBTQ people is a national count and is not disaggregated to the state/province.

The effect of the capital's school law on transgender students, and any legal challenge to it, is not yet documented.

The state/province's 1989 Constitution, Article 10, item III, prohibits discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation and obliges the state/province to implement measures ensuring no one is harmed or privileged on account of birth, race, colour, sex, marital status, nature of work, age, religion, sexual orientation, political or philosophical belief, disability, or any other particularity or condition. A state/province decree published in the official gazette on 12 March 2021 guarantees travestis and trans people in the state/province the right to use their social name before state/province public offices. The name is accepted on badges, cards and identification documents, state/province employees may register it in internal records and systems, and official publications are barred from using a person's civil name without consent.

The state/province recorded 3 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the twelfth-highest raw count among the country's state/provinces in a national dossier that tallied 80 such killings across the country, and 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people in the state/province since 2017. The source supplies no per-capita rate for the state/province and no state/province homicide denominator, so the ranking reflects the size of the count rather than a measured level of risk against other state/provinces.

A jury in the state/province sentenced a businessman, 44, to 13 years and 6 months in prison for the feminicide of a trans woman, who was found dead with knife wounds in January 2024 on a rural property beside a state/province highway in a municipality. On 1 November 2025 a 39-year-old trans woman was expelled from a pizzeria in a municipality after using the women's restroom, following complaints from staff and customers. The owner was taken to a police station for gender-identity discrimination and released on 2 November 2025 after a custody hearing subject to precautionary measures. The case was under judicial secrecy and civil police investigation, monitored by the state/province public prosecutor's office, as of 16 September 2026.

A city in the state/province prohibits trans athletes from women's sports. A city councillor introduced a bill on 4 February 2025 to make biological sex the sole criterion for participation in city competitions; the city council passed the prohibition on 19 August 2025, the mayor signed it, and it was published in the official gazette on 15 September 2025. An LGBTQIA+ pride parade association and the state/province public defender's office sued to overturn it and sought 600,000 reais in damages for moral harm; a court for collective actions dismissed the action on 30 October 2025, and the association said it would appeal to the state/province court of justice.

On 30 July 2025 a professor left a municipal conference of the public health system in a city in the state/province after the mayor interrupted her for using gender-neutral language. Health organisations, women's rights groups and Black rights organisations condemned the interruption.

The state/province's courts have repeatedly struck down local measures restricting discussion of gender and sexuality, and the pattern bears on the legal climate a visitor moves through rather than on any rule aimed at travellers. On 10 November 2022 the state/province court of justice granted preliminary relief holding unconstitutional a municipal law of March 2022 that prohibited the distribution, exhibition and dissemination of didactic material containing "gender ideology" in a municipality's public and private schools. The court found violation of the national constitution and the state/province constitution and an excess of municipal legislative competence; the action was brought by the state/province prosecutor-general's office against the municipal council with the participation of the state/province bar association.

On 21 August 2026 the special panel of the state/province court of justice unanimously declared unconstitutional a state/province law sanctioned in April 2026 that prohibited teaching and dissemination in state/province public schools of content on so-called "gender ideology," gender identity and sexual orientation, including films, music, paintings and other artistic materials. The ruling voided the ban and restored schools' pedagogical autonomy to address gender identity and sexual orientation, on grounds of formal usurpation of the national government's exclusive competence over education guidelines under Article 22 of the national constitution and violation of academic freedom, pluralism of ideas, and protection against bullying and discrimination.

On 4 February 2025 the same city councillor introduced a separate bill to bar minors from a city's pride events; the inventory records the introduction only, and its outcome is not established.

For residents, the state/province's courts have been the main brake on municipal and state/province attempts to restrict gender content. The two rulings above cover the school curriculum in one municipality and across the state/province public school system. Whether the 2021 social-name decree binds private employers and businesses, as distinct from state/province public offices, is not stated in the source.

The prohibition on trans athletes in women's competitions applies to city-level sport, affecting local competitors and clubs; the challenge to it moved to the state/province court of justice after a court for collective actions dismissed the action on 30 October 2025, and the appeal was pending.

The state/province's cumulative count of 43 killings of travestis, trans women, trans men, transmasculine and non-binary people between 2017 and 2025 is drawn from the same national dossier's per-state/province tabulation, which records raw counts without population denominators.

The state/province recorded 7 killings of trans and travesti people in 2025, the second-highest raw count of any state/province in the parent nation in a national trans rights dossier released on 26 January 2026, behind two state/provinces at 8 each, against a national total of 80. On 2 October 2025 a trans woman was shot dead inside her home in an interior town; the Civil Police opened an inquiry to identify the author and motive and no arrests had been reported at publication. The state/province's Civil Police told press that a 22-year-old suspect was lynched by locals at the scene.

The state/province stands under the parent nation's national legal framework, which the parent record carries; the state/province layer adds its own instruments. The state/province legislative assembly's president signed Law No. 18,634 on 13 July 2024, instituting the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People, approved on 4 July 2024. It treats violence based on gender identity, sexual orientation and sex characteristics as structural and incompatible with democratic rule, and requires the state/province to monitor violence data with a compiled methodology, build protection and reception services, map and train public and civil-society reception facilities, and prioritise victims facing rupture of family or community ties and compounded vulnerabilities.

Municipal hostility has been documented and reversed. On 13 December 2017 a municipality in the state/province enacted Municipal Law No. 4432/2017 banning discussion of gender theory or identity in municipal schools, passed 11-to-1 despite a state/province prosecution recommendation to reject it as reinforcing stereotypes and prejudice. On 15 October 2025 the national supreme court struck the law down, lifting the ban on gender-related instruction in the city's schools.

The state/province judiciary has applied national document-recognition rules locally. In 2023, following a 2022 lawsuit by the state/province public defender's office, the state/province court authorised a resident to rectify their birth certificate to register gender as non-binary, the first such recognition in the state/province.

In June 2026 a state/province legislator presented Bill No. 4.092/2026 to create a State Policy for Integral Health Promotion of the LGBTQIAPN+ population within the national public health system. It would reinforce the right to a social name in registration and care, address travestis and transexuais who delay or avoid care for fear of mistreatment, and require training of health professionals and publication of LGBT health indicators under data-protection rules. The bill's status is unresolved in the sources.

The state/province ranking is a raw-count ranking. The state/province's 7 killings place it second nationally, but the sources give no per-capita or population-adjusted comparison with the two state/provinces at 8 or with any other state/province, so the ordering cannot be read as a measure of relative danger for a trans visitor.

The 2021 interior case shows two features at once: a killing of a Black travesti outside the capital region, and the collapse of ordinary process when a suspect was lynched by a crowd before arrest. That pattern of extra-legal violence sits alongside, rather than inside, the state/province's formal protection machinery.

The state/province's own instruments operate on top of a national anti-discrimination and gender-recognition framework that already applies here; the state/province policy adds monitoring, reception services and a prioritisation duty rather than new prohibitions.

Law No. 18,634 obliges the state/province executive to regulate the State Policy for Combating Violence against LGBTQIA+ People and to implement it through reception-service guidelines, emergency support to civil-society services, data collection with research bodies and universities, and partnerships with municipalities, with entry into force on publication.

Residents can invoke the policy's priority categories: victims of identity-based violence or discrimination, people facing actual or imminent rupture of family or community ties, and people with intersecting race, state/province, class, gender, age, religion or disability vulnerabilities.

The state/province court's 2023 non-binary birth-certificate rectification is a state/province precedent available to residents seeking gender-marker recognition, obtained through the public defender's office after litigation rather than by administrative application.

Bill No. 4.092/2026 would bind state/province health facilities on social-name use, professional training and LGBT health data; until it advances, those commitments are not in force at state/province level.

No state/province-specific rule, unit or documented case governing the placement of trans prisoners in the state/province's own prison system is sourced here; the placement framework in force is national and is carried on the parent record.

The sources give no per-capita comparison between state/provinces for trans killings, so the state/province ranking cannot be converted into a relative risk measure.

Implementation of Law No. 18,634 is not evidenced: no regulation, budget line, monitoring report or enforcement action under the policy appears in the inventory.

The legislative status and fate of Bill No. 4.092/2026 after its June 2026 presentation are unresolved in the sources.

This state/province's own legal layer sits on top of the national framework. Law No. 1,417/2009 provides administrative sanctions for discrimination motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation within the state/province public service. A state/province law (No. 2,790/2022) makes discrimination on those grounds a crime, and a further state/province law (No. 2,710/2022) typifies anti-LGBTQ discrimination at state/province sports venues, football stadiums included, as an administrative offence. A 2012 state/province law established a state/province day to combat homophobia, observed each 27 May.

Two state/province bodies carry the protection machinery: a state/province council for combating discrimination and a dedicated LGBTQIAPN+ body, which run awareness campaigns and issue public repudiations of discriminatory acts. The source inventory contains no state/province-level enforcement statistics or case outcomes for these laws, so how they operate in practice cannot be assessed from the material available.

Civil-registry rectification is handled locally. On 19 February 2022 the state/province public defender's office filed the first request in the state/province for name and gender rectification on behalf of a non-binary person, treating the request as legally viable on the same self-determination basis as for transgender people and arguing that the registry should reflect social presentation. The procedure follows the ordinary civil-registry alteration process, and the public defender's office assists applicants. Since 2022 the office has made legal gender change accessible to non-binary people in the state/province.

Gender-affirming care is available through the public health system. On 13 February 2025 the capital city's municipal government opened the state/province's first municipal trans outpatient clinic, at a public specialties centre, running Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 17:00. It offers free multidisciplinary transition care to trans, travesti and non-binary people with no age restriction: general medicine, nursing, endocrinology, gynecology, dermatology, psychiatry, urology, cardiology, psychology, nutrition, social work, physiotherapy, speech therapy, dentistry, laboratory tests, ultrasound, mammography, densitometry, vaccination, rapid tests, Pap smear collection and dressings, with testosterone cypionate and estradiol supplied under clinical protocol. Entry is by referral from a basic health unit or by walking in; the first appointment is a general-practitioner evaluation with onward referral, and clinical demands unrelated to gender transition are excluded. State/province-wide gender-affirming services also run through a national university hospital and a dedicated centre serving lesbian, bisexual, travesti, transsexual and intersex women.

Family formation has drawn judicial attention. In mid-2025 the state/province's high court ran the campaign "Every form of love can also be family" under a national judicial resolution, aimed at ensuring transgender people face no discrimination during the adoption qualification process. Adoption by same-sex couples has been recognised in the state/province since a national ruling in 2010; a couple obtained an adoption in 2016 after six years of proceedings, and in 2017 the state/province legislature considered a bill extending maternity or paternity leave to same-sex adoptive couples on the same terms as heterosexual families.

Marriage equality reached this state/province through a national judicial resolution in 2013 rather than through any state/province act. The state/province had no formal recognition of same-sex unions before that date, although stable unions existed there according to national statistics agency data.

Residents reach the municipal trans outpatient clinic in the capital city by referral from a basic health unit or by walking in. Intake requires an identity card, a tax number and a public health system card. The clinic operates Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 17:00, and does not treat clinical demands unrelated to gender transition.

The state/province public defender's office assists with civil-registry name and gender rectification, which follows the same procedure as any other civil-registry alteration.

A state/province law (No. 1,417/2009) exposes discrimination by gender identity or sexual orientation within the state/province public service to administrative sanctions, and a state/province council for combating discrimination and a dedicated LGBTQIAPN+ body handle awareness work and public repudiation of discriminatory acts.

The 2017 state/province legislature bill on leave for same-sex adoptive couples is recorded as a bill; whether it was enacted is not established in the sources.

No state/province-specific figures for anti-LGBTQ violence, for prosecutions under the state/province law (No. 2,790/2022), or for administrative proceedings under the state/province law (No. 2,710/2022) appear in the source inventory, so the practical enforcement of the state/province's protections is unresolved here.

The state/province's pre-1830 legal history, including the absence of sodomy provisions from the 1830 Imperial Penal Code and the earlier historic-era repeal, is recorded in the sources but bears on no current rule affecting visitors and is not carried into this assessment.

This state/province sits within the parent nation's national framework for LGBTI rights; the national record carries the marriage, identity-marker and hate-crime provisions that apply here, and what follows is the state/province's own layer of law, institutions and enforcement.

Facilities are contested at municipal level. On 6 June 2022 a city council approved a bill banning the installation of unisex restrooms in that city. The source records the council vote but not whether the mayor signed or vetoed the measure, so its current legal force is unresolved.

On 14 April 2024 the state/province legislature approved a bill restricting athletes' participation in competitions according to biological sex. The state/province governor vetoed it on 28 April 2024.

On 21 June 2025 the state/province legislature approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes dealing with LGBTQ topics.
