LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the national supreme court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck the law down in May 2026 by 8 votes to 2; a national supreme court justice stated that it violated the national constitution.

Partner recognition was addressed in this state/province before the national framework was settled. On 3 August 2012 a judge in a city in the state/province authorised registration of a marriage between two women, the first such marriage recognised in the state/province. The state/province prosecution service appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August; on 20 September the state/province court of justice reversed that decision and authorised recognition. On 15 August 2012 the national inspectorate of justice issued a circular letter requiring all civil registries to treat such marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, making this state/province the third in the country to address the question statewide.

State/province institutions have also acted on document recognition. On 22 January 2025 the state/province public defender's office filed suit to secure name and gender rectification for a non-binary person from a city in the state/province, and the court granted the request and authorised the rectification. On 27 June 2025 the state/province legislature and the public defender's office held a free event to help trans, non-binary and travesti people change their name and gender on official documents.

Restriction attempts in the state/province have concentrated on facilities, sport and schooling rather than on criminal law, and none of the measures passed in the current cycle took effect as written. The April 2024 athlete-eligibility bill was vetoed by the state/province governor, and the June 2025 school-content law was struck down by the national supreme court.

Education restriction has a longer local history. In 2015 a municipality in the state/province passed a law prohibiting ideological indoctrination in its schools, a decade before the state/province legislature passed its own school-content measure.

The state/province's own protection machinery runs through its courts and public defender's office rather than through the legislature: the January 2025 rectification suit for a non-binary resident was granted by a state/province court, and the state/province was the third in the country to direct its civil registries statewide on marriage recognition in 2012.

For residents, the practical points of contact with the legal system are document rectification and school policy. Name and gender changes on official documents can be pursued through the state/province public defender's office and through periodic state/province legislature events, most recently on 27 June 2025, which was open to trans, non-binary and travesti people.

Marriage registration practice was standardised for the state/province's registries by the national inspectorate of justice circular letter of 15 August 2012, which required civil registries to treat such marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples.

School content remains contested at local level: the 2025 parental opt-out law passed by the state/province legislature was struck down in May 2026, and the 2015 municipal ideological-indoctrination law remains part of the local record. No state/province-specific count of anti-trans violence or of hate-crime enforcement appears in the sources, so residents' risk cannot be measured against the state/province's general crime picture.

The current status of the city unisex-restroom bill approved on 6 June 2022 is unresolved in the sources: the mayor's signature or veto is not recorded, and no later confirmation of its effect was available.

Whether the veto of the April 2024 athlete-eligibility bill was sustained or overridden is not recorded.

No state/province-level data on anti-trans violence, killings or hate-crime prosecutions appears in the source inventory, so no rate for the state/province can be stated and no comparison with the national figures can be made.

The general claim that larger cities offer more legal infrastructure while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction is not sourced at state/province level and is not treated here as a finding about this state/province.

The state/province is part of the country and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record; the findings below are specific to the state/province and its municipalities.

Access to sex-separated facilities has been contested in the state/province legislature and in municipal councils. In 2021 a state/province representative introduced a bill prohibiting unisex bathrooms statewide and requiring separate male and female facilities. On 16 November 2021 the capital's city council approved a municipal bill of the same kind, introduced by a city councilman. The inventory does not record whether either measure was enacted.

On 4 October 2023 the capital's city council approved, by symbolic vote, a motion of protest against a resolution of the national human rights ministry issued on 19 September 2023, which provided that educational institutions must guarantee use of bathrooms, changing rooms and other gender-segregated spaces according to each student's gender identity and expression, while recommending additional individual-use bathrooms in public spaces. The ministry stated that the resolution has no binding effect and that no school is obliged to adopt it. The motion was to be converted into an official letter to the national government.

Gender markers on documents issued in the state/province are governed by the state/province court of justice. In 2023 that court published a provision guaranteeing inclusion of a non-binary option in the civil registry gender marker, then revoked it in November 2023, limiting administrative replacement of first name and sex to male and female only. In 2025 the same court authorized a third gender option on documents.

Trans participation in sport has produced conflicting rulings between a municipality and the national courts. On 26 April 2024 one municipality enacted a law banning transgender people from competing in sports according to gender identity, with a fine of 10,000 for non-compliance. On 26 February 2026 that municipality's city council approved a motion to bar a transgender athlete from a national women's volleyball cup; the national volleyball confederation filed suit in the national supreme court and a justice issued a preliminary injunction the same day allowing her to compete. In March 2026 LGBTQ rights organizations filed suit against the municipal law in the national supreme court, and on 7 August 2026 the rapporteur justice voted to strike the law down. The inventory does not record a final judgment.

Relationship recognition in the state/province was established before the national rule took effect. On 26 March 2013 the state/province's inspector general of justice ruled that same-sex marriage and the conversion of stable unions to marriage must use normal marriage procedures, and same-sex civil marriage was authorized in all registry offices statewide under the same procedure and documentation as heterosexual marriage, with conversion of a stable union into marriage permitted without judicial authorization. In 2004 the capital recorded the first recognition of a same-sex union in the country: common-law marriage status, previously limited to opposite-sex couples, for a binational couple who had cohabited fourteen years.

State/province courts have granted adoption to same-sex couples. On 14 May 2009 a family court in the capital granted the first gay-couple adoption in the state/province, finding a stable and affectionate union able to raise a child in a healthy environment. On 27 October 2010 a judge in a western municipality authorized irreversible adoption of an eight-year-old child with cerebral palsy by a gay couple together twelve years, under national appellate precedent. On 16 September 2011 justice in a northern municipality authorized adoption of two children by a lesbian couple.

The state/province court of justice moved in opposite directions within two years on the same question: a non-binary civil registry marker was published in 2023, withdrawn in November 2023 in favour of male and female only, and a third gender option on documents was authorized in 2025. The inventory does not reconcile the two positions or state which one governs applications filed today.

The municipal sports ban and the facilities measures are municipal acts that conflict with positions later taken by national courts and with a national ministry resolution the capital's council protested. Enforcement exposure therefore turns on which instrument a given authority applies; the inventory records litigation and injunctions rather than settled outcomes.

The inventory contains no documented incident of violence against a trans or travesti person in the state/province, and no state-level count of such incidents. Nothing in it supports a comparison of the state/province's violence risk with other units.

Residents of the capital live under a municipal prohibition on unisex bathrooms approved on 16 November 2021, and the state/province legislature has before it a statewide bill of the same kind introduced in 2021; the inventory does not record the current status of either measure.

Registry practice for residents shifted twice: name and sex replacement was limited to male and female in November 2023, and a third gender option on documents was authorized by the state/province court of justice in 2025.

Organisers and competitors in the municipality that enacted the sports ban face a law of 26 April 2024 carrying a fine of 10,000 for allowing transgender athletes to compete according to gender identity, subject to litigation at the national supreme court in which a preliminary injunction of 26 February 2026 permitted a trans athlete to compete and a rapporteur vote of 7 August 2026 favoured striking the law down.

Same-sex couples in the state/province have obtained marriage, union conversion and adoption through ordinary state/province procedures since 2013, with adoption rulings in the capital and in two other municipalities on record.

Unresolved: whether the 2021 state/province bathroom bill and the 16 November 2021 municipal ordinance were enacted, and whether either remains in force. The inventory gives their introduction and approval dates only.

Unresolved: whether the 7 August 2026 vote by the rapporteur justice to strike down the municipal sports law produced a final judgment. The inventory records the vote and the earlier preliminary injunction, not a concluded case.

Unresolved: how the state/province court of justice's 2025 authorization of a third gender option interacts with its November 2023 revocation of the non-binary registry provision; the inventory does not state which controls.

Not sourced: any region-specific figure for violence against trans people in the state/province, any account of custody or placement practice in the state/province's own detention facilities, and any account of access to gender-affirming care, public facilities or screening in the state/province's airports and institutions. The national assessment is carried by the parent record.

The state/province sits within the country's national framework for LGBTI people; national rules on marriage, legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination and custody placement apply there. The findings below are those specific to the state/province.

The state/province's own statutory layer is Ordinary Law No. 5,431, signed by the governor on 29 December 2004, which bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. The source does not record gender identity among the grounds it covers.

State/province Law No. 5,916, enacted on 10 November 2009 and published on 12 November 2009, guarantees travestis and transexuais the right to be identified by their social name on registrations, forms, medical records and related documents when using the services of all direct and indirect state/province public administration bodies. The law defines the social name as the name by which they recognise themselves and are recognised socially, requires it to appear first and prominently with civil identification below, directs the executive to designate within 60 days the body responsible for registration and issuance of social-name identification, and retains use of the civil name where public interest or third-party rights require.

On 20 July 2021 the state/province judiciary granted civil registration as a non-binary person to a young person, the first recognition of a non-binary gender marker in the state/province.

On 14 December 2012 the state/province court began granting marriage licences to same-sex couples through all notaries statewide, without the need for a judge's approval; the change was published in the official gazette on 17 December 2012. In 2012 a judge of the 1st Children and Youth Court granted adoption rights to a lesbian couple living together in a stable union since 2007.

The capital city restricts facilities. On 17 June 2026 its city council approved by 12 votes to 5, with one abstention, a bill prohibiting transgender women and travestis from using women's public restrooms, and on 30 July 2026 the city's mayor signed it into law after LGBTQ rights activists protested that it is unconstitutional. The measure governs the capital only; no statewide facilities law is recorded.

Violence risk in the state/province is documented only in aggregate. A 2015 report by a rights organisation listed the state/province as the second state/province with the highest risk of LGBTQ people being murdered. That ranking is LGBTQ-wide rather than transgender-specific, and the source supplies no per-capita rate and no transgender-specific breakdown, so it does not establish a separate trans-specific risk level.

The capital-city measure is a municipal instrument, so it does not govern restrooms outside the capital, and the state/province has no recorded statewide rule on facilities. Its validity is contested by LGBTQ organisations on constitutional grounds; no court ruling on that question appears in the sources.

The state/province's own record runs in two directions. Its 2009 social-name law and its 2021 non-binary registration place it among the earlier movers in the country on identification, while the 2026 capital-city restroom law is a restrictive measure adopted at municipal level.

The 2015 ranking is a comparative risk assessment rather than a count, and its age and methodology limit what it says about present conditions.

For residents using state/province services, Law No. 5,916 sets the display rule: the social name appears first and prominently, with civil identification below it. The executive was directed to designate, within 60 days, the body responsible for registering and issuing social-name identification. Use of the civil name is retained where public interest or third-party rights require it.

Marriage for same-sex couples has been available at notaries across the state/province without judicial approval since the state/province court's December 2012 order, published in the official gazette on 17 December 2012.

Adoption by a same-sex couple in a stable union was recognised by the 1st Children and Youth Court in 2012, in a case where the couple had lived together since 2007.

Non-binary civil registration is obtained through the state/province judiciary; the first such entry was granted on 20 July 2021.

Whether the capital city's law is being enforced, and the outcome of any constitutional challenge to it, is not sourced.

No state/province-specific rules on gender-affirming care, insurance coverage or custody placement appear in the inventory; those matters are governed by national rules and by the practice of national bodies.

The 2015 ranking by a rights organisation does not specify its methodology, and it is not clear from the source whether it reflects per-capita risk or raw counts.

Whether Law No. 5,431's prohibition reaches gender identity, as distinct from sexual orientation, is not stated in the source.

The state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework on legal gender recognition, marriage, anti-discrimination and custodial placement. Within the state/province, homosexual conduct is not criminalised.

The principal restriction a trans visitor can encounter is municipal and applies in the capital. In March 2026 the city council approved by 13 votes to 11 a bill prohibiting transgender women from using women's public restrooms, and the mayor signed it into law on 22 April 2026. The ordinance is confined to the capital and does not extend to the rest of the state/province.

The law was reported to the state/provincial prosecution service on 28 March 2026, and on 29 April 2026 the state/provincial public defender's office opened an investigation into it. On 5 May 2026 a national legislator denounced the ordinance to the national prosecution service.

On 2 April 2013 the state/provincial court authorised marriage between same-sex couples in the state/province, the state/provincial-level decision under which partners of trans visitors marry before its civil registries.

The state/province was among the first state/provinces in the parent nation to write a ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation into its constitution, adopting the provision in 1989 alongside a neighbouring state/province.

The passage of the capital's ordinance was narrow, with the city council dividing 13 votes to 11, and the three challenges to it run through separate channels: the state/provincial prosecution service, the state/provincial public defender's office and the national prosecution service.

The state/province's constitution has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 1989.

On 18 July 2026 the state/provincial public defender's office announced that non-binary people could change their documents to reflect their gender identity through court decisions, giving people registered there a judicial route to a corrected record.

Whether the capital's ordinance is in force, suspended or under judicial review, and how it is being applied in practice, is not established by the sources reviewed; the investigation opened by the state/provincial public defender's office and the referral to the state/provincial prosecution service had not produced a reported outcome.

No information specific to the state/province was identified on custodial placement practice, gender-affirming care provision or hate-crime prosecutions. The procedure and timeline for the document change announced by the state/provincial public defender's office on 18 July 2026, including whether it requires residence in the state/province, are not detailed in the sources.

No other municipality in the state/province is recorded as having adopted a restroom or comparable facilities ordinance.

This state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation for LGBTI people; the national rules on gender recognition, anti-discrimination, health care and custody placement apply in the state/province, and this entry covers only what is specific to it.

A national trans association's ninth annual dossier, reported in January 2026, records 5 trans and travesti people killed in this state/province during 2025. The figure is a raw count with no population denominator for the state/province, so it establishes a number of deaths rather than a rate, and it does not show that this state/province is more or less dangerous than one of different size. The national totals and the world-ranking comparison published in the same dossier are not specific to this state/province.

The same association's 2024 dossier, reported in January 2025, recorded that many of the trans and travesti people killed that year came from the subregion that includes this state/province, and that the victims were mostly young Black women. That is a regional pattern rather than a state/province-level measurement, and it carries no per-capita figure for this state/province.
No rule specific to this state/province on identity documents, gender-affirming care, or custody placement was identified in the source inventory; those matters are set by the national framework.

No prison placement practice, custody data or enforcement record specific to this state/province was identified. The prison-related sources in the inventory are national in scope, and the general overview consulted records no trans-prisoner housing policy specific to the parent nation, so no conclusion about custody conditions in this state/province can be drawn from them.

The state/province stands under the national framework set out for the country; the findings below are those specific to the state/province.

Recorded lethal violence against trans people and travestis places the state/province among the highest-counting state/provinces. The 2024 dossier compiled by a national trans association recorded 12 trans killings in the state/province, second nationally behind one state/province with 16 and ahead of another with 11, with a cumulative total of 100 between 2017 and 2024. The 2025 dossier recorded 8 killings, tied with another state/province for the highest count, within a national total of 80. Both sets of figures are raw counts published without a per-capita denominator, so they rank state/provinces by volume rather than by rate.

A study published on 1 July 2024 by a national university and the state/province public prosecutor's office found that 60% of deaths involving trans people and travestis in the state/province resulted from violence, and that 74% of the victims were Black or of mixed race.

On 15 July 2026 the state/province court of justice, working with the national council of justice, launched an incident-reporting mechanism for LGBTQ violence in the state capital.

Bathroom access has been fought out in the courts rather than settled by statute. A municipal ban on unisex restrooms, approved on 12 September 2022 and enacted on 7 October 2022, was declared unconstitutional by the state/province court of justice in 2024, after a 2023 lawsuit by the state/province public defender's office. A law in the state capital signed on 20 November 2023, which authorised religious institutions to bar transgender people from restrooms matching their gender identity, was suspended by preliminary injunction in August 2025. In August 2026 the court of justice ordered a shopping mall in another municipality to pay 2,000 in local currency in compensation to a trans woman denied access to a women's restroom in a 2019 incident in which a guard demanded proof of "sex change"; the ruling reversed a lower court decision that had denied the claim for insufficient evidence.

Prison housing for trans people in the state/province is governed by a 2014 national portaria of a national human-rights secretariat, which applies to the state/province prison system: transsexual men and women are to be sent to female units, gay and travesti prisoners held in male prisons are to be offered specific conviviality spaces, and LGBT inmates may use their social name, recorded at admission, and choose male or female clothing. The instrument provides no sanctions for non-compliance, and no state/province-specific implementation, wing, segregation practice or individual case is documented.

The state/province's recorded totals sit inside a national picture. The 2025 dossier counted 80 trans killings across the country, and the 2024 dossier placed one state/province first with 16 and another third with 11. A 2017 assessment cited in the state/province's rights record ranked it second-highest nationally for violence against LGBTQ people. Rankings of this kind use raw counts, which track population size; the sources publish no per-capita figures for any state/province.

The state/province's anti-discrimination framework is layered: state/province statutes of 2002 and 2007 sit on top of the national provisions, and several municipalities maintain their own prohibitions, so the protection a person can invoke depends on where in the state/province they are.

Decree No. 47,306 of 15 December 2017 created a social-name card for travestis and transexuais in the state/province, under Decree No. 47,148 of 27 January 2017. The social name is defined as the designation by which the travesti or transexual person identifies and is socially recognised. The card is issued by the civil police through its identification institute, with model, requirements and specifications set by resolution of its chief, and is valid for nominal treatment and identification within the state/province public administration. The social name cannot be altered after issuance, and applicants must already hold civil identification in the state/province identity registry. Regulation and the start of issuance were required within 120 days, with the decree entering into force on publication.

Since 2023 the state/province public defender's office has run free Pride Month initiatives assisting non-binary people with name and gender-marker changes. One individual changed documents on 29 May 2025 through a public-defender lawsuit; non-binary people still face obstacles in the process.

State/province law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation under Law No. 14,170 of 15 January 2002, and Law No. 16,636 of 3 January 2007 established 17 May as a state/province day against homophobia. Municipal prohibitions on gender-identity discrimination apply in three municipalities (laws of 12 May 2000, 11 September 2001 and 12 December 2007). Municipal sexual-orientation discrimination bans include two laws in the state capital of 29 January 2001 and 11 December 2003, one in another municipality of 10 January 2002, and the three municipal laws above; a further municipal law of 18 May 2009 established a municipal day of struggle against homophobia.

No state/province-specific implementation of the 2014 national prison-housing portaria is documented, and the instrument carries no sanctions for non-compliance; how the rules operate in the state/province's units is unresolved in the sources.

Non-binary people in the state/province continue to face obstacles in changing name and gender markers despite public-defender assistance; the sources do not specify the nature or extent of those obstacles.

The 2024 and 2025 trans-killing counts are raw totals published without per-capita denominators, and the sources do not state whether the state/province's rate differs from the national background homicide rate.

This state/province stands under the country's national framework, which the parent record carries in full. Two instruments specific to this state/province appear in the sources. State/provincial ordinance No. 1,797/2023 addresses homophobia. On 9 August 2023 a measure published in the capital's official gazette, approved by the capital's mayor, prohibited transgender athletes from competing in sports according to their gender identity.

No further region-specific signal on policing, custody placement, health-care access or violence against trans people was identified. On those questions the national assessment applies unchanged.

The capital's measure is municipal, so it governs within the capital's jurisdiction rather than across the state/province. The state/provincial instrument, ordinance No. 1,797/2023, is framed around homophobia rather than gender identity, and the sources do not state whether it names trans residents expressly or what it provides beyond its stated purpose.

The capital's measure of 9 August 2023 falls on trans residents competing in local sport in the capital rather than on visitors passing through. State/provincial ordinance No. 1,797/2023 is the state/provincial-level instrument residents can cite against homophobia; the sources do not record which state/provincial body receives complaints under it, what penalty it carries, or any case in which it has been applied.

No record of enforcement, court challenge or repeal of the capital's measure was identified, and whether it remains in force is unresolved. The sources contain no state/province-specific data on custody placement, health-care access, hate-crime enforcement or violence against trans people. The only geographic differentiation they offer is a national-level contrast between major cities and smaller or rural areas, which does not name this state/province.

This state/province sits within the country's national legal framework, which applies in full here. What follows is what the sources establish at state/provincial and municipal level.

A chamber of the state/provincial high court upheld a moral-damages award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing. The first-instance decision, at a municipality in the state/province, had set compensation at 4,000 in local currency. Commercial refusals of service therefore carry documented financial exposure in the state/provincial courts.

The municipal council of the capital city's parliamentary inquiry into violence against trans and travesti persons issued a final report containing 189 recommendations.

An investigation published in May 2024 found that drink-spiking robberies known locally by a colloquial name were victimising LGBTQIA+ people in the capital city, as it prepared for a Pride event expected to draw thousands of tourists. The reported risk attaches to venues and nightlife rather than to street crime generally.

The documented state/provincial material is judicial and municipal: one second-instance ruling on refusal of service, one council inquiry, one city nightlife investigation. No state/provincial statute, agency rules or state/provincial-wide enforcement statistics on gender recognition, care access, custody placement or facility use appear in the sources. National law supplies those areas, and this record does not restate them.

The harms reported are concentrated in the capital city and its metropolitan area, and the sources make no finding about conditions in the interior of the state/province or in smaller municipalities, where the reach of the state/provincial court and the municipal council does not extend.

Residents of the capital city have two documented institutional channels. The municipal council's 189 recommendations set an agenda for the city's response to violence against trans and travesti people, and the state/provincial high court has upheld damages for a trans woman refused entry to a nightclub while wearing women's clothing.

Nightlife districts in the capital city are the setting for the reported drink-spiking robberies, which the investigation links to LGBTQIA+ patrons, and the reporting places them in the period when the city was preparing for a large Pride event.

Unresolved: whether any of the 189 recommendations has been implemented; what became of the nightclub case beyond the award upheld at second instance; and whether the May 2024 drink-spiking investigation produced further findings or arrests.

Not sourced: the proportion of anti-discrimination complaints or prosecutions that reach a court outcome, the number of trans and travesti people held in the state/province's prison system, and whether custody placement practice in that system follows the applicable national rules. State/provincial-level facility-access rules and state/provincial-level gender-affirming care policy are likewise absent from the sources; the sources record only national provisions on those subjects.

The state/province stands under the country's national framework, and adds its own layer of protection. state/province Ordinary Law No. 3079 of 12 September 2006 prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity across employment, housing and other areas, and a provision in force since 2 August 2006 prohibits the manufacture, sale and distribution of symbols inciting discrimination, prejudice, hatred or violence on gender-identity grounds.

Non-binary recognition is not available in practice through the state/province's registries. In 2022 a resident became the first non-binary person in the state/province to obtain recognition, doing so only after a rectification in another state/province and an intervention by the state/province Public Defenders Office in the capital, where no gender-neutral marker existed. Non-binary recognition in the state/province remains decided case by case.

Facilities are a live exposure in the state/province capital. On 18 October 2022 the mayor of the capital signed a municipal law prohibiting unisex or multigender restrooms, and a global equality index records that bathroom access in the state/province carries no explicit legal protection.

Access to gender-affirming care is contested on two fronts. On 10 June 2025 the governor of the state/province signed Law 7552 banning gender-affirming care for minors under 18. In the opposite direction, in November 2023 the State Public Defenders Office opened a collective procedure to monitor public health services for trans and travesti people, covering hormone treatment, outpatient services and the refusal of authorisation for transsexualising surgeries including sexual reassignment surgery; after an October 2023 meeting, municipal health officials committed to dispensing standardised medications on a public ambulatory prescription for hormone therapy and to designating reference primary-care units in each zone of the capital, and the state health secretariat was required to report on gaps in equitable care and hormone therapy. In August 2024 a national prosecutors' office recommended that the state/province formally enable outpatient and hospital transsexualisation services, including sexual reassignment surgeries, with deadlines for approval and for presentation to the national health ministry.

Recorded violence against LGBTQ people in the state/province is thin and structurally undercounted. Research published in a national public security journal finds that cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state/province are underreported, and a national public security forum has registered 43 cases. For 2021-2022, crimes reported in the capital and the interior involving homosexual, lesbian, bisexual and transsexual persons accounted for 0.36% of all reports, with homophobia and transphobia motives and the categories of gender, sexuality, race and intersectionality absent from the records; LGBT victim data were few and poorly structured, victims were not infrequently recorded as perpetrators because of failures in police occurrence reports, and public agents were unprepared to handle these demands. On 5 July 2025 a man was beaten and killed in the capital after reacting to homophobic insults, with residents reporting that he had been bullied by other young people in the region.

state/province and municipal law also restricts LGBTQ expression and public presence. state/province Ordinary Law No. 6463, enacted 10 October 2023, expressly prohibits the use of neutral language, non-binary dialect or any expression departing from standard Portuguese in curricula and teaching materials of public and private educational institutions and in official documents of educational institutions and public agencies throughout the state/province. State Law 6469 of 2023 prohibits the participation of children and adolescents in pride parades, with fines of up to 10,000 reais for non-compliance. On 17 October 2024 the state/province legislature enacted a law prohibiting reproduction of digital media using children linked to homosexuality; it was amended on 13 December 2025 to remove the term homosexuality and instead prohibit reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media.

Protection machinery exists at state level alongside those restrictions. In 2021 the State Public Defenders Office created the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group, focused on human rights violations and on training security agents. In August 2024 the state/province Court of Justice released the booklet Home is a Right, aimed at LGBTQ youth expelled from their homes, which states that conversion therapies are prohibited and ineffective and points readers to the Specialized Human Rights Public Defender's Office. In November 2012 a judge of the state/province Court of Justice authorised the state/province's first adoption by a same-sex couple.

An international LGBTIQ organisation reports that the country's legal advances for sexual and gender minorities face repeal pressure in a conservative national legislature, so protections relied on in the state/province are not politically settled at either level.

A legal guide for expatriates notes that enforcement is uneven in practice: major cities present established legal infrastructure and broader social acceptance, while smaller cities and rural areas may carry more social friction despite identical legal rights. Within the state/province that distinction falls between the capital, where the Public Defenders Office, the Court of Justice and the municipal health commitments operate, and the interior, where the state/province's own crime records show the same provisions applied without motive categories.

The state/province's violence figures are raw counts without a denominator and without a trans-specific breakdown, so they cannot support a comparison with other state/provinces or a statement about relative risk to trans residents.

Residents of the state/province are covered by Ordinary Law No. 3079 of 12 September 2006 in employment, housing and other areas on gender-identity grounds, and by the 2 August 2006 prohibition on producing or distributing symbols that incite discrimination, prejudice, hatred or violence on those grounds.

The State Public Defenders Office runs the Sexual Diversity, Gender Identity and Citizenship Working Group, created in 2021 to address human rights violations and to train security agents, and its health unit holds the collective procedure opened in November 2023 on hormone therapy, outpatient services and refused surgical authorisations. Capital primary-care coverage includes designated reference units per city zone and standardised hormone prescriptions under the public ambulatory arrangement agreed in October 2023.

Residents face state-level restrictions on expression and public life: Ordinary Law No. 6463 of 10 October 2023 bars neutral language and non-binary dialect from curricula, teaching materials and official documents of schools and public agencies; Law 6469 of 2023 bars children and adolescents from pride parades with fines up to 10,000 reais; and the legislature's 17 October 2024 media law, as amended on 13 December 2025, bars reproduction of sexual content linked to children in cultural and artistic media.

LGBTQ youth expelled from home can use the state/province Court of Justice booklet Home is a Right of August 2024, which states that conversion therapies are prohibited and ineffective and directs them to the Specialized Human Rights Public Defender's Office.

Whether the age thresholds for gender-affirming care cited for the state/province from 2 October 2025 (puberty blockers and hormones prohibited under 18, surgery from 21) derive from state Law 7552 alone or from national professional-council rules applied in the state/province is unresolved in the sources; Law 7552 itself is dated 10 June 2025 and covers under-18s.

The 43 registered cases of violence against LGBTQ people in the state/province are recorded as LGBTQ-general, with no stated disaggregation for transgender victims, and the 0.36% share of total reports for 2021-2022 carries no population denominator. No source states a finding on societal tolerance of transgender people in the state/province specifically.

The figure of a 59% rise in registry gender changes by 2024 appears in a source discussing the state/province but its geographic scope is not stated, so it is not attributed here to the state/province.

Whether the capital's 2022 unisex-restroom prohibition has been enforced against any establishment, and whether any challenge to it is pending, is not sourced.

The state/province stands under the country's national framework; the national provisions on identity documents, marriage and partner recognition, hate-crime law and custodial placement apply there and are set out in the national record.

Facilities access is the sharpest change at state/province level. On 14 July 2026 the state/province governor signed a law authorising religious temples and schools to restrict bathroom use on the basis of biological sex. Before enactment the national prosecution service recommended a veto, arguing that the measure would violate the rights of transgender people and the principle of secularism. On 15 July 2026 a political party announced it had filed a lawsuit against the law.

Documentation. On 21 June 2025 a resident became the first person in the state/province to obtain a birth certificate carrying an X sex marker, through an action brought by the state/province public defender's office after a local registry office refused rectification. The registry relied on a provision of the national judicial council, which does not provide for a third gender option, and refused a first-name change without stated legal justification. The public defender's office argued that documentation which does not reflect a person's gender identity is a source of suffering and anguish and a violation of human dignity.

State/province law layer. A 2007 amendment to the state/province constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and a decree of 8 April 2024 created a state/province council for sexual diversity within a state/province secretariat for racial equality and human rights.

Violence. The national trans advocacy tally for 2025 records five of that year's killings of trans and travesti people in the state/province. The figure is a raw count taken from a national tally and is not accompanied by a state/province population denominator, so it does not by itself establish the state/province rate or rank it against other state/provinces.

The state/province's symbolic layer consists of a state/province day of observance against homophobia, established by a 2009 law, and a state/province day of bisexual visibility, established by a 2024 law. Both are observances rather than rights-conferring provisions.

The July 2026 facilities law reaches religious temples and schools; it does not by its terms cover all public accommodations in the state/province.

A state/province education secretariat order issued 10 April 2008 guarantees travesti and transsexual students in the state/province public school system the right to use their social name in enrolment, class records, attendance lists and other internal school documents.

The state/province's position in the 2024 national count of trans and travesti killings cannot be fixed from the audited sources; only the 2025 state/province count is available.

The first X-marker birth certificate issued in the state/province on 21 June 2025 rests on a single action by the public defender's office. Whether registries elsewhere in the state/province now grant the marker as a matter of course is not sourced.

The operational status of the July 2026 facilities law while the challenge filed on 15 July 2026 proceeds is unresolved in the sources.

This state/province operates inside the parent nation's national legal framework; the findings below are those the sources record as specific to the state/province. Its own instrument on the subject is state/province Decree No. 9,755/2020, which sets out guidelines on violence motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity and defines that violence to include discrimination, bullying and cyberbullying.

Access to public facilities is restricted in at least one municipality of this state/province. A municipal law enacted in 2015 bars transgender people from using public restrooms in accordance with their gender identity. After a challenge by a national trans advocacy organisation, a justice of the national supreme court ordered the municipal government to explain the law and set 11 June 2024 as the deadline for that explanation.

Violence figures for the state/province come from a national count. A national trans advocacy organisation's ninth annual dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, records 80 trans and travesti people killed in the parent nation during 2025, five of them in this state/province. The dossier publishes no population breakdown for the state/province-level figure; raw counts of this kind track population size rather than per-resident risk, so five deaths in this state/province does not by itself establish that it is more or less dangerous per resident than others.

On 24 August 2022 the state/province legislature approved a bill prohibiting gender ideology in schools in the state/province, a measure aimed at the same subject matter its own education administration treats differently, as the board of education rule in force since 3 July 2014 continues to permit transgender and travesti students to use their social names.

Municipal education restrictions in this state/province have not survived national review. On 25 April 2020 the plenary of the national supreme court unanimously struck down a municipal law of 2015, which had banned gender-diversity content and references to gender ideology in municipal schools and required prior vetting of all teaching materials. The ruling held that the municipality had usurped the national government's exclusive competence over national education bases and had violated gender equality, plural and democratic education, and secularism. It followed a 2017 challenge by the national public prosecution service and a suspending injunction issued by a justice of that court.

The same municipality produced both the education law struck down in 2020 and the restroom law now under constitutional challenge, and both reached the national supreme court.

Since 3 July 2014, under a board of education rule of this state/province, transgender and travesti students may use their social names in schools.

Registry and document procedure in this state/province has required litigation. In one case, a non-binary person's public defender's office filed a rectification request in February 2020; registry offices refused it, and the state/province's high court granted document rectification on 28 August 2023.

In a second case, begun on 29 January 2025, a court in a municipality of the state/province authorised the name change but refused the gender-marker change, citing the absence of a specific law providing for non-binary recognition. On appeal by the public defender's office, the state/province's high court authorised the gender-marker change on 12 December 2025.

The status of the municipal restroom law after the national supreme court's 11 June 2024 deadline is unresolved in the sources, which do not state whether the law remains in force while the constitutional challenge proceeds.

What accompanies state/province Decree No. 9,755/2020 is not sourced: the inventory records that it establishes guidelines and defines violence motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity, but not what penalties, if any, attach to it or which body enforces it. No state/province-level prosecution or conviction statistics for such violence appear in the inventory.

Reporting on the second registry case carries dates the sources do not reconcile, with a 2023 account of a municipal ruling on the gender marker and a separate appellate decision of 12 December 2025; the sequence of the first-instance and appellate outcomes is therefore not fully established.

No state/province-wide public-facilities rule is documented; the only restroom restriction recorded is the municipal law. No state/province-specific documentation of custodial placement practice or of LGBTI-specific detention units was identified, and no state/province-level source addresses it.

On 27 January 2020 the state/province government installed signage in the women's restrooms of state/province government offices stating that use follows gender identity, and installed unisex restrooms.

A state/province law enacted on 19 December 2002 prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation. The statute does not name gender identity as a protected ground.

Enforcement of anti-discrimination rules in commercial venues is unsettled. On 28 September 2025 a court in the state/province ordered a bar to pay 10,000 in local currency in compensation for denying a trans man access to the men's restroom. On 28 May 2026 an appellate court overturned that decision, acquitting the nightclub of the transfobia allegation on the ground that the evidence did not show the man had been barred from the restroom.

In August 2021 a national culture official publicly criticised the state/province culture department's women's restroom, which was designated as inclusive of trans women and travestis, describing the measure as posing risks to children. The criticism came from a national official against a state/province-level facility policy.

State/province measures affecting trans people have been adopted and then reversed within short periods: a civil-registry route opened in April 2022 was revoked in December 2023, and a first-instance restroom ruling in September 2025 was overturned on appeal in May 2026.

On 22 April 2022 the state/province judiciary authorised non-binary people to change their first name and gender directly at civil registry offices in the state/province, without judicial authorisation. In December 2023 the state/province court revoked that provision.

The sources do not record the reasoning behind the state/province court's December 2023 revocation of the non-binary civil-registry provision, nor whether any administrative route for a non-binary entry remains open in the state/province.

Whether the 28 May 2026 appellate ruling in the restroom case is subject to further appeal is not stated in the sources.

No source records the current status of the 2020 restroom signage in state/province government offices, or whether the policy has been extended, narrowed or withdrawn since the August 2021 criticism.

This state/province has no law of its own prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, a gap recorded by its own public defender's office. A trans visitor in the state/province capital or in the interior depends on the parent nation's national framework, which applies without sub-national variation, and on national enforcement machinery rather than any local statute.

The bodies that have acted on trans documentation are the state/province public defender's office and the state/province judicial inspectorate. On 29 January 2026 the public defender's office published an article explaining how trans people change names and gender markers on documents.

Rectification is administrative and rests on self-declaration. A trans man, trans woman, travesti, non-binary or queer person may apply at the civil registry where the birth was recorded, with effect on the birth certificate and on all official documents, without medical or psychological reports and without proof of surgery or hormone treatment. The service is free where the applicant proves inability to pay, and a court is involved only if the registry refuses the request.

The exception is a change to a non-binary or unspecified marker, which the public defender's office states requires a judicial decision. In August 2022 that office asked the judicial inspectorate to allow "non-binary" entries in civil registry records, and in 2023 the inspectorate published a resolution authorising non-binary individuals to change their documents to include a third gender option. Whether an administrative route to a non-binary marker is open in practice is unresolved.

Local politics in the state/province capital have been hostile to discussion of gender. A municipal law article there prohibiting the teaching of gender and sexuality in schools was suspended on 27 August 2018 by a national supreme court justice, which allowed such teaching to continue.

Legal guidance for foreigners notes that reception varies within the parent nation: major urban centres have established legal infrastructure and are broadly welcoming, while smaller cities and rural areas may apply identical rights amid greater social friction. This state/province has one metropolitan centre and a large interior, the setting that guidance describes.

A resident applies at the civil registry office where the birth was registered. The request is granted on self-declaration, without medical or psychological reports and without proof of surgery or hormone treatment, and the change carries into the birth certificate and all official documents. The service is free where the applicant proves inability to pay. A court is involved only if the registry denies the request; a change to a non-binary or unspecified marker requires a judicial decision.

On 31 January 2023 the state/province judicial inspectorate issued an administrative order consolidating extrajudicial service norms. It sets out civil-registry procedures for birth registration where a parent is transgender and for the annotation of an altered prenome and sex for transgender and non-binary persons.

The 2023 inspectorate resolution and the 2026 public defender's office guidance conflict on whether a non-binary marker can be obtained administratively; no source in the inventory resolves which controls.

No state/province-specific record of enforcement action, complaints, prosecutions or court awards under the national anti-discrimination framework was found.

No local provision on bathrooms, facilities, custody placement or health-care access was identified; those matters are governed by national rules.

The current status of the municipal school law after the 2018 suspension is not sourced, and no state/province-specific data on violence against trans people was found.

The state/province stands under the country's national framework; the national record carries the national law, passport and marker rules, health-system rules and custodial resolutions. What follows is the state/province-level layer.

The state/province recorded 11 killings of trans people in 2024, the highest count of any state/province in its subregion and the third highest nationally, according to a national trans advocacy dossier reported on 28 January 2025. The state/province has about 9.2 million residents, which the source puts at roughly 0.12 killings per a small population. The state/province's general homicide rate is not in the source inventory, so the two cannot be compared here, and the national ranking is by raw count, which tracks population size rather than risk. The ninth such dossier, reported on 26 January 2026, recorded 8 killings in the state/province in 2025, level with another state/province at the top of the ranking, or about 0.09 per a small population on the source's own figures. Both counts come from a dossier that compiles media-reported killings.

A state/province law, sanctioned by the state/province governor and published on 19 May 2021, requires public and private establishments in the state/province, from 90 days after publication, to display a notice of at least 50 cm by 50 cm on the exterior or at an entrance stating that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is expressly prohibited, and listing the phone number of the state/province's LGBT public-policies office for complaints, clarifications and reports. No enforcement actions, penalties or compliance data under the law are sourced.

On 7 March 2013 the state/province's general attorney issued a decision obligating all notaries in the state/province to accept same-sex marriages, effective 15 March 2013. For a trans visitor whose relationship or identity documents are read under birth-sex status, that notarial obligation is the operative state/province-level guarantee; no state/province-specific rule on how a notary handles a trans partner's documents is sourced.

On 22 May 2024 the state/province's high court authorized a resident to rectify documents to reflect a neutral gender, the first non-binary person in the state/province to obtain such a rectification. On 29 May 2024 the state/province was reported to be issuing its first birth certificate recognising a person as non-binary. Whether the two concern the same person is not stated.

On 16 November 2006 the state/province governor signed a law requiring educational material on sexual orientation to be included in the training of the state/province's civil and military police, published in the official gazette on 26 November 2006. How the requirement is applied today is not recorded.

On 12 December 2017 a municipal chamber in the state/province approved a municipal bill, introduced by a councillor, prohibiting pedagogical activities that reproduce the concept of "gender ideology" or any discussion of gender diversity in all municipal and private schools in that municipality. It passed by majority with a single opposing vote and was sent to the mayor. Whether it was signed or vetoed is not recorded.

The state/province's protective measures and its killing counts sit in the same record without an explanation of the gap. The state/province has a signage duty on premises, a notarial access decision from 2013, a police-training requirement from 2006 and a court route to document rectification, while the national trans advocacy dossier places it at the top of the 2025 ranking by raw count. No prosecution, conviction or compliance data for the state/province appears that would show how the protective measures operate in practice.

Raw-count rankings are the only comparison the inventory supports. The state/province's 8 killings in 2025 are level with another state/province, but no population denominator for that other state/province is given, so the two cannot be compared per capita; the state/province's own per-capita figure is supplied by the source, and its general homicide rate is absent, so the trans-specific rate cannot be set against the background rate.

The municipal bill runs against the state/province-level direction: a municipal chamber moved to bar discussion of gender diversity in schools in the same state/province that requires anti-discrimination notices in establishments. The outcome of that bill is not recorded.

Residents of the state/province have a state/province reporting channel for discrimination: the state/province's LGBT public-policies office, whose phone number the 2021 law requires establishments to display. The duty falls on public and private premises, so it applies to businesses residents use day to day, not only to venues visitors frequent.

Document rectification runs through the state/province's high court. The 22 May 2024 authorization for a neutral gender entry was the first of its kind in the state/province, and the state/province was issuing its first non-binary birth certificate within the same week.

Notaries in the state/province have been bound to accept same-sex marriages since 15 March 2013 under a decision of the state/province's general attorney. No state/province-level guidance is sourced on how a notary should treat a trans person's documents where the record and the person's presentation differ.

Police training in the state/province has been required to include material on sexual orientation since a law signed on 16 November 2006. Whether the requirement is currently enforced, and what the training covers on gender identity, is not recorded.

School policy is contested at municipal level. A municipal chamber approved a bill in December 2017 barring discussion of gender diversity in municipal and private schools; whether the mayor signed or vetoed it is not recorded.

The fate of the municipal bill is unresolved: it was forwarded to the mayor on 12 December 2017 and no sanction or veto is recorded.

Whether the 22 May 2024 neutral-gender rectification and the 29 May 2024 non-binary birth certificate concern the same person is not stated.

No state/province-specific custodial or prison-housing practice for trans people appears in the inventory. The material available on that subject is national in scope, is internally inconsistent between sources, and is carried by the national record.

No enforcement, penalty or compliance data for the 2021 state/province law is sourced, and no general homicide rate for the state/province is in the inventory, so the trans killing counts cannot be compared with the background rate for the state/province.

The trans advocacy counts rest on media-reported killings; no state/province-specific methodology note or undercount assessment is given.

A national trans advocacy organisation's ninth annual dossier, reported in January 2026, attributes two of the 80 trans and travesti people killed nationwide in 2025 to this state/province. The figure is a raw count. The inventory supplies no population denominator for the state/province and no general homicide rate for it, so the count cannot be converted into a per-capita rate, cannot be ranked against other state/provinces, and cannot be measured against the state/province's background homicide level. It stands as two documented killings and nothing more precise.

This state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework, which the parent record carries in full. The inventory documents no state/province-level variation on identity documents, entry, public facilities, gender-affirming care, partner recognition, hate-crime enforcement or police and custody practice. No court ruling, government measure, police operation or civil-society incident report specific to this state/province appears in the sources reviewed.

The only sub-national breakdown available is the dossier's table of killings by state/province, which places this state/province at two deaths for 2025. No state/province-level data on non-lethal violence, robbery, harassment or police response accompanies it, so the wider safety picture for trans visitors here is not documented.

Resident-facing information specific to this state/province is absent from the inventory. Nothing is recorded on local policing of anti-trans violence, on access to the public health system's trans-specific services within the state/province, on local custody arrangements, or on municipal-level protection measures. Trans residents are covered by the national legal and protection framework described in the parent record, and no state/province-specific gap or addition to it is sourced.

The 2025 figure of two derives from a national count compiled from reported killings, and the inventory gives no methodology note for the state/province line item. Whether the count is complete, whether it includes deaths of residents occurring elsewhere, and how the state/province's population size compares with other units are all unresolved. A comparison against the state/province's general homicide rate cannot be made from these sources.

A second report on the same dossier was filed from a national news outlet's local desk but reported only the national total of at least 80 killings; it adds no state/province-level detail and is not treated here as evidence about the state/province.

State/province courts and police have acted in cases involving trans women. In February 2026 the state/province court ordered preventive detention of a man accused of exploiting trans women in a city there; the suspect had been a city-hall employee until January 2026, and pre-trial custody was confirmed in the extortion case. In April 2025 the state/province tourism police arrested two trans women in flagrante for extorting a tourist from a neighbouring jurisdiction in a beach district.

A peer-reviewed census study of travestis and transgender women in the state/province prison system interviewed 138 self-declared travesti or trans-woman inmates across eleven units classified as masculine in the metropolitan region between April and June 2021, drawing on the state/province prison administration's own database. It documents that travestis and trans women in that system are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and characterises placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. A 2015 state/province law grants them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics.

National totals for trans and travesti homicides are carried by the national record. The state/province-level count is not above the jurisdiction's general background rate and is not treated here as a trans-specific risk signal.

For trans and travesti residents in the state/province prison system, the 2015 state/province law's parity provisions apply only in women's units; the 2021 census study found that most trans and travesti inmates in the metropolitan region were held in units classified as masculine, where the parity guarantees do not reach.

No region-specific source in the inventory documents enforcement of the 2015 state/province parity law in women's units, nor any state/province-level programme addressing the placement gap identified in the 2021 census study. The state/province's trans homicide count is not broken down by municipality or compared against the state/province's general homicide rate in the available sources.

The state/province's own constitutional layer is older than most in the parent nation: in 1989 it was among the first to write a ban on sexual-orientation discrimination into its constitution. On 17 December 2025 a constitutional amendment, proposed by a state/province legislator, amended a constitutional article to guarantee protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, with violators subject to punishment by law, effective on promulgation. The state/province is the first in the parent nation to write gender-identity protection into its constitution.

The state/province's judiciary has its own marriage provision. On 5 July 2012 it issued a judicial provision regulating same-sex marriage throughout the state/province. Since 2025 the state/province has allowed individuals to change their gender marker on documents to non-binary.

Court facilities in the capital are explicitly gender-neutral. From 28 August 2025 the state/province's high court provides operating gender-neutral bathrooms on the ground, first and eighth floors of a courthouse in the capital, usable by any person regardless of gender identity. The same measure directs that in all judiciary units male and female bathrooms be used respecting each person's gender identity, under human-rights and non-discrimination principles, and requires that all new constructions and renovations be planned with gender-equity demands.

Institutional access has widened at a national university in the state/province. On 17 November 2025 it approved affirmative-action quotas for trans people in undergraduate courses.

A counter-current sits in the state/province legislature. On 1 December 2020 a state/province legislator tabled a bill to prohibit the use and teaching of gender-neutral language in public and private schools and in state/province public offices, requiring traditional language in schools, official notices and public offices.

The 2025 amendment places the state/province ahead of the others on constitutional gender-identity protection; its 1989 sexual-orientation clause was shared at the time with only one other state/province. Both are state/province-level constitutional texts rather than general public-accommodation rules.

The measures with the most concrete physical effect are institutional in scope. The gender-neutral bathrooms and the directive on use of male and female facilities apply to judiciary units, and the trans quota applies to a national university in the state/province; neither governs private commercial premises, hospitality or transport in the state/province.

Trans residents hold a state/province-constitutional anti-discrimination guarantee: a constitutional article, as amended on 17 December 2025, covers sexual orientation and gender identity and makes violators subject to punishment by law. The 1989 sexual-orientation clause it builds on was one of the first in the parent nation.

State/province documents allow a non-binary gender marker as of 2025, and the judiciary's 2012 provision regulates marriage for same-sex couples throughout the state/province.

A national university in the state/province reserves undergraduate places for trans students under quotas approved on 17 November 2025.

Court users in the capital have gender-neutral bathrooms at a courthouse, and judiciary units across the state/province are directed to let people use male and female bathrooms according to their gender identity.

A 2020 bill by a state/province legislator would bar gender-neutral language in schools and public offices, requiring traditional language in teaching, official notices and public administration.

The legislative status of the December 2020 bill on gender-neutral language is not recorded in the sources; whether it was enacted, rejected or remains pending is unresolved.

No state/province-specific enforcement data, violence statistics or police practice appears in the inventory. The state/province-level protections are recorded as law and institutional policy, not as documented enforcement outcomes.

The scope of the non-binary document marker, including which state/province documents and agencies offer it, is not detailed in the sources.

Whether the December 2025 constitutional amendment has accompanying implementing regulation is not sourced.

The state/province stands under the country's national framework, and its own record shows a state/province legislature moving against trans and LGBTIQ people while the courts have narrowed the state/province's own protections.

The state/province constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, but as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Two state/province statutes that did cover gender identity have been stripped back: a state/province law of 4 April 2003 was repealed on 8 October 2015 by a complementary law, and a complementary law of 28 December 2010 was partially overturned on 11 October 2018 after a 2015 Supreme national Court challenge on labour-law grounds. What remains of that complementary law penalises private entities and, where applicable, state/province public servants who promote, permit or tolerate discriminatory acts based on gender or sexual orientation, covering violent, coercive or vexatious acts, refusal of entry to places of free public access, denial or surcharging of lodging and property transactions, and prohibition of affectionate expression permitted to others, punishable by a fine of 2,500 reais rising to 5,000 on repeat, a 30-day licence suspension or revocation, and up to 30 days' suspension for state/province servants; complaints go to the state/province secretariat of public security, with fines paid into the state/province civil police improvement fund. In October 2018 the Supreme national Court unanimously declared two items of that law formally unconstitutional.

Legislative hostility is documented in volume. From January 2019 to June 2025, state/province deputies introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills against 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills, including proposals to prohibit neutral language in official government communications and to bar minors from hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care; 4 of the anti-LGBTQIA+ bills were archived and none were enacted. As of 2025 the legislative assembly had 19 anti-LGBTQ bills on record with 11 authored by one political party. A 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights, about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme national Court. A separate report covering January 2015 to October 2025 found the legislative assembly and its 295 municipal chambers approved or advanced at least 271 laws, bills and normative acts already declared unconstitutional by the Supreme national Court, 41% attacking gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIA+ people, 36% already in force and only 11% judicially annulled, concentrated in one subregion and accelerating in the last five years.

Restroom access is contested. In January 2026 the governor signed a state/province law requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms; from June 2026 the state/province national university installed signs indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 case in the state/province capital where a trans woman was denied access to the women's restroom, a lower court ordered 15,000 reais in compensation for pain and suffering, the state/province Court of Justice overturned it, and in June 2024 the Supreme national Court dismissed her appeal pending since 2014 by an 8-3 vote, withdrawing its recognized general repercussion on procedural grounds that the original claim pleaded only consumer-law damages rather than constitutional provisions, thereby issuing no binding constitutional ruling on trans bathroom access; in August 2025 an extraordinary appeal was filed with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts.

Education policy has also been restricted. A decree of the state/province governor on 15 June 2021 banned gender-neutral language in state/province schools until it was overturned in May 2025 by the Supreme national Court, and a municipal law of December 2021 banned it in public office until struck down in August 2022 by the state/province Court of Justice. In October 2025 the Supreme national Court struck down a 2015 municipal law that had prohibited teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools. In April 2026 the governor signed a law allowing parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics. In December 2023 the Constitution and Justice Committee of the legislative assembly approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of August 2026.

Document and registry practice in the state/province runs through the courts rather than a state/province statute. The Army provides that any person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and considered exempt from mandatory military service for not meeting national Constitution, Military Service Law, implementing regulations and the 2024 General Conscription Plan requirements.

In September 2026 the Court of Justice ordered the parents of a gay teenager in one municipality to pay 100,000 reais in compensation after kicking him out and exposing his sexual orientation on social media.

Law 2389, enacted 30 December 2020 and in force from 5 January 2021, prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity in the state/province capital and reaches conduct a visitor is likely to meet: refusing entry or stay in any public or private establishment open to the public, selective service not required by law, denying or surcharging hotel, motel or pension lodging, denying or surcharging the rental, purchase or lending of property, restricting access to buses and taxis, refusing school enrolment, and inciting discrimination or violence through any medium. Individuals and legal entities are liable. Penalties run from a warning and a fine set by municipal regulation to suspension of activities or operating licence for up to 30 days and interdiction or loss of licence, graded by gravity, recidivism and economic capacity. Law 3,355 of 18 December 2017 guarantees the nome social in all acts, registrations, records and forms of the state/province's direct and indirect public administration. Registration and attendance must record both the civil-registry first name and the chosen social name; public servants must address the person by the indicated name in written acts, with the civil-registry name confined to internal use alongside the social name; pejorative expressions are prohibited; official letters, summons and notifications must carry both names; servant training is mandated; and non-compliance is a functional infraction carrying administrative liability and sanction.
