The state/province maintains a sub-national transgender policy and welfare architecture that predates and runs alongside the national framework. In November 2015 it adopted the country's first government transgender policy, providing for identification as male, female or a third-gender category, equal access to social and economic resources, equal treatment under law, and non-discrimination on grounds of sex. The state/province was reported to the national legislature in December 2021 as one of the state/provinces that had constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under the relevant provision of the 2019 rules.

Transition-related care is nominally subsidised but unevenly available. In March 2016 the state/province social welfare department proposed free sex-reassignment surgery in government hospitals, at least in medical colleges, from the following financial year; the state/province later provided reimbursement for gender-affirming surgeries. Training gaps mean many government hospitals cannot perform the procedures, pushing patients toward costlier private institutions, and reimbursement requires patients to raise funds before they are refunded. A government medical college hospital opened a clinic exclusively for transgender patients in 2017, operating twice a month with a specialist panel and also serving sex workers, after a district legal aid body's proposal prompted by reports that transgender people feared approaching hospitals and relied on self-medication; the same body proposed separate public toilets for transgender people to a district official. Another government medical college hospital completed the state/province's first sex reassignment surgery in January 2017. The suicide of a transgender woman after alleging a botched gender-affirmation procedure prompted protests and led the state/province to appoint an expert committee on transgender health-sector issues and to begin steps toward free surgeries in government hospitals.

The clinic issues health cards denoting transgender status, a documentation practice a visitor should expect to encounter at state/province facilities. Welfare measures include scholarships for transgender students in the lower secondary classes, a district budget allocation for employment and skill training, and a 2017 social welfare department workshop with around 30 transgender representatives covering identity cards, pensions for those over 60, skill development, scholarships, educational loans and driving lessons for employment as ride-hailing drivers. A transgender-owned and operated taxi service was launched to provide livelihood and public visibility. A transgender school opened in 2016 to prepare students for school-leaving board examinations and vocational training for ten students aged 25 to 50; it ceased operating as a school after three months and became a hostel for transgender metro staff. A gender-equality park opened in February 2016.

Policing is the sharpest risk area. Reports describe a spate of killings of transgender people with inadequate police investigation, and a rise in police harassment when transgender people approach stations to file complaints, which produced a direction from the state/province police chief that grievances be received without delay. In October 2023 an annual pride march in one district was attacked by a mob and police carried out a lathicharge. In December 2023 the state/province high court described cyber attacks against the LGBT+ community as a serious issue and directed authorities to act. The suicide of a transgender bodybuilder, described by a state/province minister as a martyr, drew attention to transphobic groups rooted in religious fundamentalism, with the minister attributing it to cyberbullying and media transphobia.

Recorded cases under the national transgender rights statute are few nationally and concentrated in a small number of state/provinces. This state/province accounted for 2 of the 7 national cases in 2021 and 4 of the 11 in 2023, joint-highest with a neighbouring jurisdiction. These are raw counts against very small national totals, and the reporting itself attributes the low figures to bias in police registration rather than to low incidence; they are not a per-capita measure of risk and do not establish that this state/province is more dangerous than a less populous one.

Community infrastructure is comparatively developed. One organisation campaigns on sensitisation of healthcare, curricula and workplace policy; another runs a 24-hour helpline for members in distress; a third serves female-born LGBTIQA+ members. An annual queer pride event has been held since July 2010, and annual walks since 2017 focus on sensitising police and media. An estimated small population of transgender people lives in the state/province, around 81 per cent of whom wish to transition and 76 per cent of whom conceal their identity for fear of non-acceptance; societal discrimination in employment and housing and implementation gaps in state/province schemes remain documented problems.

The state/province's early policy lead and its delivery record diverge. A visitor relying on state/province-subsidised transition care should expect private-sector costs and delay.

What the state/province's sources document is checkpoint and transport-hub enforcement in which gender presentation is treated as a possible concealment method. On 2 August 2024, police at a highway checkpoint in the northern part of the state/province stopped a bus bound for a major city elsewhere in the country via a city in a neighbouring state/province and detained seven nationals of a neighbouring jurisdiction, two of them transgender and five described by police as disguised as third gender; the case was registered as one of fraudulent documents and border crossing.

A separate report of the same period records 15 nationals of a neighbouring jurisdiction, seven of them transgender, apprehended in separate incidents within 24 hours, carrying fraudulent identity and tax documents. The two accounts differ on the number detained at the checkpoint and on how many of them were transgender.

On 9 November 2024 a joint 24-hour operation detained 12 nationals of a neighbouring jurisdiction, among them minors and transgender people. Six, including three transgender persons, were held after midnight while travelling to a major city elsewhere in the country; a second group of six, including three children from a district in the neighbouring jurisdiction, was held at a railway station. A local facilitator was arrested for moving them.

The state/province shares an 856-km border with a neighbouring jurisdiction, and these checkpoints sit on the highway and rail routes running from that border towards the rest of the country. Under the national framework binding this state/province, a 2025 law restricts trans people's use of public restrooms. The congressional committee unanimously approved a dictamen merging two bills, introduced by two congressmen, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, required medical attention, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over gendered restroom labels at a national airport. An LGBTIQ activist called the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would depend on security staff's personal judgment, including ID checks, and noting there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions. A national human-rights institute's legal analysts argue this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of the Constitution and the regional human-rights convention. They state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Separately, an April 2025 child-protection law mandates that public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their identity; its vague child-protection articles enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and the obscenity minimum sentence rises from three to four years. A international human-rights organisation states child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating. The national human-rights institute states the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks; the institute cites an advisory opinion of the regional human-rights court, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

The bathroom-restriction measures stand alongside other national turbulence affecting LGBTIQ organising: an April 2025 NGO foreign-funding law lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order' or 'security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising, and in July 2025 a constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. Public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination.

On 19 December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. The judgment, issued after years of litigation, is the country's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per a national news service, the regional human-rights court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the subregion's history, reaching the Court via the regional human-rights commission.

Opinion polls show age-based variation: 18 to 24-year-olds (66%) were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals than the population overall (49%), and younger people showed higher approval of same-sex marriage (8.3% approval among the population in 2010, higher among younger respondents).

Transgender residents may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November 2016, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the national health ministry revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. In June 2024 the country's health authorities also removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by a international human-rights organisation as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In May 2024 the health ministry reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases. Conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals, a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and not a voluntary choice. Pride marches have been held annually since 2002, with the oldest recorded march in 1984.

Both sit under the national framework on legal gender recognition carried by the national record; what follows is the state/province's own layer.

Article 1 of the 2017 statute sets the law's purpose as guaranteeing an adequate normative framework for gender self-determination for people whose felt gender identity differs from that assigned at birth, and public bodies of the state/province must treat people according to their felt gender identity. The duty reaches the public administration, health and education services a visitor may deal with.

The 2018 equality statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, provides access and admission rights (article 56), reverses the burden of proof (article 57), and establishes a regime of administrative infringements and sanctions for discrimination against LGTBI people (articles 58 to 66). A complaint about being refused service or admission can shift the evidential burden onto the respondent, and the state/province's administration can fine discriminators.

Its courts have handled gender-identity-motivated offences. A provincial court convicted over a June 2022 incident in a park in one of the state/province's cities, where an 18-year-old and several minors insulted, chased, filmed and mocked a trans woman solely because of her gender identity. The adult accepted six months' imprisonment, suspended for two years on condition of committing no offence, plus a 720-euro fine and 1,000 euros in moral damages to the victim; two minors had already been sentenced to supervision measures. The specialised hate-crime prosecutor handled the case.

The inventory of state/provincial gender-identity laws lists two statutes for this state/province where most of the ones it covers list one. This state/province stands under the national framework. Its sanctioning ladder runs from a warning or a fine of up to EUR 3,000 for minor breaches, through EUR 3,001 to EUR 20,000 for serious breaches, which cover degrading remarks or incitement to violence against LGBTI people or their families in the provision of services, to EUR 20,001 to EUR 45,000 for very serious breaches, with accessory penalties that include exclusion from regional public aid for up to one year. Multiple discrimination raises the grade of the infraction.

This state/province was among eight state/provinces that approved LGBTI and trans equality laws in the 2010s, and the 2016 statute remains the operative regional instrument. Implementation of the national trans-equality law falls to the regional government.

The regional statute's remedies are administrative rather than criminal, so a refusal of service or a degrading remark in this state/province runs through the regional sanctioning regime and the observatory rather than a prosecution.

The protected grounds include sex characteristics alongside gender identity and expression, and the serious-breach tier names the families of LGBTI people, which reaches a trans visitor travelling with a partner or relatives.

The statute's scope is public and private activity in the state/province, which covers service providers, employers, healthcare and housing rather than only regional public bodies.

For residents, the 2016 regional statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics in employment, healthcare, housing, education and the provision of services in the state/province, and bars any demand that a person prove a declared gender identity by psychological or medical report.

The regional observatory against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is the regional consultation body for these questions, with LGBTI organisations represented on it.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note carries this state/province's own row in its Shari'a penalties table covering twelve state/provinces (section 8.4.3), confirming that the Shari'a layer extends criminalisation to acts between women, leaving the state/province's code broader in scope and harsher than the national statute for Muslim defendants.

An overview of LGBTQ rights in the country places this state/province inside the northern Shari'a block, where same-sex acts carry penalties ranging from imprisonment to capital punishment and where lesbianism is punishable by imprisonment or caning in most state/provinces, with death penalties applied only in two of them. On that account this state/province falls in the lashing-and-imprisonment tier for women's conduct rather than the capital tier, consistent with its own statute, while its sodomy provision for men remains capital. The same source records a cross-dressing layer in the northern block: prison or a fine for men who dress or behave as women, illustrated by a 2025 one-year imprisonment sentence in a neighbouring jurisdiction. No housing, segregation or placement rule for trans prisoners is documented for this state/province or elsewhere in the country.

The national Criminal Code, which applies alongside this state/province's Shari'a layer for non-Muslim defendants, punishes sex acts between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency between men with up to 3 years, while lesbianism carries imprisonment or caning in most state/provinces and death in two of them. Cross-dressing is penalised in some state/provinces, with one allowing up to one year's imprisonment or a fine for men who dress or behave as women. A visitor's exposure therefore depends on both the national statute and this state/province's own Shari'a penal layer, which for Muslim defendants carries the harsher and broader penalties.

The academic literature on Shari'a implementation in northern state/provinces, from which this state/province's statute details are drawn, is an annotated legal compilation rather than an enforcement record; it documents what the enacted text says, not how often or how the state/province's courts apply it. The secondary characterisation placing this state/province in the lashing-and-imprisonment tier for women's conduct and the capital tier for men's conduct is consistent with the statute but not an independent enforcement finding.

For Muslim residents of the state/province, its Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 supplies the operative penalties: stoning to death for sodomy, and 50 lashes with up to six months' imprisonment for lesbianism. The statute was signed and brought into operation on 1 December 2000 and gazetted on 31 December 2000, and it remains the state/province's enacted text as recorded in the sources.

The state/province's Shari'a courts hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, a jurisdictional feature identified in 2004 as shared only with the other northern state/provinces that adopted criminal Shari'a by 2002. No trans-prisoner housing, segregation or placement rule is documented for this state/province or elsewhere in the country in the available sources.

Whether the state/province's stoning provision for sodomy has been carried out, and how frequently its courts impose the lashing and imprisonment penalties for women's conduct, is not sourced in this inventory; the sources document the enacted statute, not enforcement practice in this state/province specifically.

The state/province stands under the national framework, and its own criminal law adds two layers that a visitor has to read together. The national home office's June 2025 country note records that the state/province separately adopted its own secular Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' (sodomy, lesbianism and bestiality) with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, a ceiling above the national 14-year maximum.

Running in parallel, the state/province's Sharia Penal Code Law 2002 applies to Muslims. It was signed into law and came into operation on 21 June 2002, published in the state/province gazette of 4 July 2002, and bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code. A human rights organisation's 2004 report traces the wave of adoption back to a neighbouring state/province's Sharia Establishment Law of 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, after which twelve northern state/provinces had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002; those twelve remain the only sub-units where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, this state/province among them.

The home office's June 2025 note carries this state/province's own row in its twelve-state/province Sharia penalties table: death by stoning as the maximum for liwat (sodomy), and same-sex acts between women punishable 'at the discretion of the qadi (Sharia court judge)'. An annotated legal volume records that this state/province is one of only three whose statute provides without qualification that 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', with no unmarried/married graduation, while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir, discretionary punishment. A trans visitor read as Muslim therefore faces a capital ceiling on men's same-sex acts under the state/province's own promulgated code, alongside the 21-year secular ceiling that applies regardless of faith.

The state/province's two-layer structure is harsher than the national baseline on both tracks: the state/province's secular Section 259 ceiling of 21 years exceeds the national 14-year maximum, and its Sharia layer carries the twelve-state/province bloc's capital maximum for sodomy, stated in the enacted text without the unmarried/married distinction that appears in two of the other three state/provinces with the same wording.

The home office table derives from an international LGBTI organisation's documentation, and the qadi-discretion formulation for same-sex acts between women means the outcome for a woman or a trans woman read as a woman is set by an individual judge rather than by a fixed tariff.

For residents of this state/province, the practical exposure combines the 2017 secular Penal Code and, for Muslims, the 2002 Sharia Penal Code, with the Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction here. The secular statute alone reaches 21 years' imprisonment plus a fine for 'unnatural offences'.

The Sharia layer's stoning-to-death provision for sodomy is enacted text, not a maximum that requires a further legislative step, and the lesbianism provision is discretionary with the qadi.

The inventory does not document any state/province-specific enforcement incident, arrest, prosecution or killing under either statute; the enforcement record cited in the national framework concerns other sub-units. Whether the 21-year secular ceiling or the Sharia capital provision has been applied in any recent case here is unresolved on these sources.

How the two layers interact for a non-Muslim charged under Section 259, and whether the Sharia layer's jurisdiction over Muslims is limited by offence or by the accused's stated faith, is not sourced here.

This state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework, including a 2014 national statute prohibiting same-sex marriage, which applies here as it does elsewhere in the country.

This state/province lies outside the Shari'a regime. The death-penalty exposure for male same-sex conduct that applies in twelve states/provinces in the north of the country does not reach here. No anti-discrimination protection exists for LGBTI people in this state/province.

Dating applications carry an entrapment risk that is not confined to any one city. The documented cases and the underground scene described are based in a major city elsewhere in the country, and the sources extend the same risk to gay and transgender app users here. Victims seldom report to the police, because making a report carries its own risk of arrest or assault.

Exposure here sits below the Shari'a states/provinces. Twelve states/provinces in the north of the country apply Shari'a law under which male same-sex conduct carries a maximum of death, and this state/province is not one of them. The maximum a visitor faces here is the 14 years available under the criminal code and the national statute.

Enforcement of the national statute has been documented mainly as mass arrests at parties and social venues and as police profiling and extortion of people perceived as gay. No operation of that kind in this state/province appears in the sources, so its own enforcement record is not separately visible.

The criminal code offences in force here apply to residents as well as to visitors, and no anti-discrimination protection exists for LGBTI residents in employment, housing or services.

No LGBTI organisation, health service or support network based in this state/province is documented in the sources, and no state/province-level body addressing the safety of LGBTI residents appears in them.

No arrest, prosecution or violent incident in this state/province is documented in the sources. The national enforcement record is not disaggregated by state/province, so the frequency of enforcement here cannot be stated.

The dating-application extortion cases documented by the investigative reporting are based in a major city elsewhere in the country; the sources extend the risk to app users here without recording a case in this state/province.

Whether the criminal code offences here are applied to transgender and gender-nonconforming people specifically, as distinct from gay men, is not documented in the sources.

The state/province stands under the parent nation's national legal framework. Its own documented record is one of mob violence against people accused of same-sex conduct, and it contains no instance in which police protected the person accused.

In February 2008, in a remote community in the state/province, police declared a man wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner were found together. A mob beat both men for desecrating the community; the wanted man escaped before police arrived and police arrested his partner for interrogation. A local newspaper reported the wanted declaration on 15 August 2008.

On 10 June 2010, the same newspaper reported from the state/province capital, in a local government area, that a man narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was found with his partner in the partner's rented apartment. A neighbour raised the alarm; he fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, and the crowd then, in the newspaper's words, 'unleashed terror' on his partner. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution appears in the report, and his whereabouts were still unknown when it was filed.

In May 2018, in a town in the state/province, a mob lynched one of two men found together while the other escaped. The report presented the killing as an 'abominable act' against traditional heritage, treating it as community redress.

For a visitor, the documented exposure comes from community perception rather than from a prosecution: in these accounts it is neighbours, not patrols, who raise the alarm, and the single police action documented across the three cases was taken against the couple rather than against those who beat them. The cases reported involve men accused of same-sex conduct, and the source inventory holds no case in the state/province in which a report identifies the victim of violence as a transgender person. Risk to a trans visitor therefore has to be read from the way accusations of sexual and gender nonconformity mobilise a crowd, not from a documented attack on a trans person there.

The 2018 killing in a town in the state/province was reported under a traditional-heritage framing, with the attack presented as a response to an 'abominable act'. Violence that is locally legible as community redress shapes whether it is reported and whether it is investigated as a crime.

The documented incidents are separated by a decade and by geography. They occurred in the state/province capital in a local government area, in a town in the state/province, and in a remote community, so the record does not tie the exposure to a single locality or to the urban part of the state/province alone.

The 2008 file is unusual in the record for producing formal police action, but that action ran against the accused: a wanted declaration for one man and the detention of the other for interrogation, with no step taken against the crowd that had beaten them.

In the recorded cases the alarm came from neighbours and community members rather than from officials, and discovery happened in private or residential settings: a couple found together in a remote community in 2008, and a rented apartment in the state/province capital in 2010.

Residents accused in these circumstances have no example of protection in the record. The 2008 case ended with one man beaten and fleeing and his partner held for interrogation. The 2010 case ended with one man escaping the neighbourhood and the other left to the crowd, with no arrest or prosecution recorded. The 2018 case in a town in the state/province ended with one man dead.

A national rights organisation's 2024 human rights violations report, published in January 2025, records 556 violations affecting 850 victims based on real or perceived SOGIESC across the parent nation. The figures are national and carry no breakdown for this state/province, and the organisation states they represent only a fraction of the true scale, so no rate or magnitude for the state/province can be derived from them.

No general homicide or violence rate for the state/province appears in the source inventory, so the count of documented incidents there cannot be compared against the level of background violence.

The outcome for the man left to the crowd after the 2010 attack is not recorded, nor is the outcome of the 2008 detention or the disposition of the wanted declaration. No prosecution of any mob is documented in the 2008, 2010 or 2018 cases.

The three incidents rest on reports by a single local newspaper. Incidents reported through other channels, or not reported at all, would not appear in this record.

The state adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation in 2000 under its governor, as part of a 1999-2002 wave of northern state/provinces that created a parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction. A 2004 human-rights report lists this state/province among the twelve that had done so by 2002, the only state/provinces whose Shari'a courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond national law.

The state/province's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, so the Shari'a penal code's personal scope covers most people there, residents and visitors alike. A visitor who is not Muslim falls outside that code's personal application, but practical exposure is shaped by a security environment in which identification as LGBTQ+ has been used as grounds for detention regardless of the code's formal personal scope.

The national immigration department's country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (Version 4.0, June 2025) records that Shari'a penal codes in the twelve northern state/provinces apply to Muslims, with death the maximum for men in all twelve and penalties for acts between women ranging from death in a minority of state/provinces to flogging and imprisonment. The same note records public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023 and observes that few secular cases reach court.

The national criminal code, which also applies here, penalises same-sex male conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment (3 years for attempts) and is silent on women. A trans visitor therefore faces exposure under both the national layer and, if Muslim or identified as such, the state Shari'a layer.

This state/province's Shari'a jurisdiction sits within a national pattern of twelve northern state/provinces with parallel religious-criminal courts; the national immigration department's note (June 2025) treats these twelve as a distinct category for risk assessment, with harsher maximum penalties than the national code.

The enforcement section of that note (June 2025) documents public flogging of persons cross-dressing in 2023, indicating that gender presentation, not only sexual conduct, has been the stated basis for corporal punishment in the northern state/provinces.

The state/province's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, so the Shari'a penal code's personal scope covers most residents. Shari'a law was established here in 2000 under its governor, within the 1999-2002 wave that created the state/province's parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims.

Residents who are Muslim fall under the Shari'a penal code for criminal matters; the maximum penalty for men in all twelve northern state/provinces, including this one, is death under the June 2025 assessment.

The state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework. The death penalty attached to same-sex conduct under religious-law provisions operates only in twelve states elsewhere in the country and has no application here.

Enforcement in the state/province has taken the form of raids on private hotel gatherings. In June 2018 police in the state capital arrested more than 100 people attending a party at a hotel on charges that they were gay and lesbian, and by July 2018 the group was facing homosexuality-related charges in court.

The raid of 27 August 2023 in a major city is the most detailed incident in this inventory. At around 9 pm, officers from a police division in one local government area raided a hotel on Refinery Road and arrested 67 people at what police described as a same-sex wedding between a 22-year-old groom and a 20-year-old bride. The state police command spokesman said the operation followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival, that 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and ceremonial wedding clothing were recovered. The 67, publicly known by the number charged, were taken to court, and the spokesman said efforts continued to arrest those who fled.

Accounts of that night differ. A foreign government's 2023 human rights report records that police raided a 'white party' organised by the local LGBTQI+ community in the state/province on 27 August 2023 and detained more than 200 individuals, that police alleged the event was a same-sex wedding, and that some civil society representatives disputed that description. One of the 67 arrested alleged that he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated.

Reporting from the state/province indicates that the law suppresses complaints as well as enabling arrests. A human rights lawyer based in the city told a foreign government's country-policy note that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault and extortion — under-report for fear of prosecution under the same statute. A visitor who uses dating or hook-up applications in the state/province faces the same luring and blackmail pattern documented across the country, in which the threat of disclosure is the leverage.

The state/province's documented enforcement consists of two mass arrests on single nights, in June 2018 in the state capital and on 27 August 2023 in a major city. These are raw arrest totals from individual operations, not incidence rates, and no per-capita or population comparison is available for the state/province; they should not be read as a measure of how often such operations occur.

The two accounts of the August 2023 operation differ in scale and in characterisation: 67 people charged after an alleged same-sex wedding, against more than 200 detained at an event described by organisers as a 'white party'. The discrepancy is unresolved in the sources, and the police framing of the event is contested by civil society representatives cited in the same reporting.

Charges in the state/province have been framed alongside drug allegations and, in the police account, alongside a cross-dresser's confession about a gay club. Gender presentation and association, not conduct alone, are stated triggers for the operation.

The most recent incident in the state/province in this inventory is dated 27 August 2023. No later state/province-specific arrest, prosecution or violence incident is documented here, and the absence of later records is not evidence that such operations have stopped.

The 67 people arrested at the hotel on 27 August 2023 were charged to court, and the state police command stated at the time that suspects and exhibits were in custody and that efforts to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution were continuing. The group arrested in the state capital in June 2018 was facing homosexuality-related charges in court by July 2018. No outcome, dismissal or conviction in either case is recorded in this inventory.

The state police command's publicity around the August 2023 operation named the alleged ceremony, the recovered items and the cross-dresser's confession, indicating that the state's own account of the raid is a matter of public record and that suspects' identities were circulated through official channels.

Unresolved: whether the 67 prosecutions and the state capital prosecutions have concluded, and with what result. The inventory records the charges and no disposition.

Unresolved: whether the 67 people charged and the more than 200 individuals detained are the same operation counted differently, or two separate actions on 27 August 2023. Both sources give that date; the counts and the description of the event do not match.

The state/province stands under the country's national framework, and its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests independently on the state/province's own legislation. The state/province's statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities was signed by the state/province's governor on 10 December 2000 and gazetted in a state/province gazette (No. 42, Vol. 26) on 18 October 2001. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state/province. Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction over the statute's offences to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts.

The state/province enacted a second, parallel layer of its own. A human rights organisation's 2004 report lists the state/province among twelve states in one region of the country that had adopted Shari'a into their criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond national law. The sourcebook of enacted Shari'a Penal Codes records a state/province Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified; the state/province text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why this state/province is not among the individually annotated codes. The parallel Shari'a layer therefore rests on a state/province-specific enactment rather than on national or umbrella coverage.

A foreign government's immigration department, in its country-of-origin information note of June 2025, states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in those twelve states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve, and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police. A visitor therefore faces two state-level regimes, one secular and one Shari'a-based, each of which independently reaches same-sex conduct, and the secular statute's own jurisdiction clause routes those cases to Shari'a and Area Courts as well as to Magistrate Courts.

The state/province's exposure is set by two enactments made by the state/province itself rather than by the national statute alone: the 2000 morality law, gazetted in 2001, and the Sharia Penal Code Law signed on 3 March 2003. Both are state/province-specific, so the death penalty available here does not depend on how the national framework is applied locally.

The hisbah, the local morality police, is named in the June 2025 foreign immigration note as a body whose attitude forms part of the enforcement picture for Shari'a provisions across the twelve states. Enforcement of the state/province's morality statute is assigned to Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts, so the forum a case lands in is determined by the statute's own jurisdiction clause.

The inventory contains no state/province-specific arrest, raid, prosecution or killing of a transgender or gender-nonconforming person, and no documented execution under either local statute. The 2000 statute's Section 7 death penalty applies on its own terms to same-gender intercourse, and Section 3 reaches lesbianism, a homosexual act, prostitution and pimping as state/province offences. Section 4 closed all brothels on commencement of the statute.

The hisbah operates as a morality police in the state/province, and the June 2025 foreign immigration note treats the attitude of the hisbah as part of the enforcement environment for Shari'a provisions. The state/province's Sharia penal code remains in force. A foreign government's country policy and information note of June 2025 confirms it, and death by stoning is the penalty provided under Section 133 of the state/province's Sharia penal code law of 2001 and Section 134 of the state/province's penal law of 2001.

On 28 June 2022 a Sharia court sitting in a local government area sentenced three men to death by stoning for homosexuality, among them a 70-year-old man. The prosecution was brought by members of a local morality-enforcement group through a private complainant, who told the court the three were arrested at a village in the same local government area on 14 June 2022. The presiding judge held that they had violated Section 134 of the state/province's penal law of 2001 and granted a 30-day appeal window. Relatives of the convicted men said the judgment had not been carried out at the time of reporting. A news agency described the sentence as the first time the death penalty had actually been imposed for homosexuality in the country.

The foreign government's note records that the 2022 sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state/province's governor, and that a further report placed a death-by-stoning sentence for homosexuality from a Sharia court in the state/province in May 2024.

Earlier convictions in the state/province were reversed on appeal. One man was convicted on 25 September 2003 under Section 133 of the state/province's Sharia penal code law of 2001 and sentenced to death by stoning; the state/province's upper Sharia court quashed the sentence for denial of counsel and a defective confession. Another man's conviction was quashed on 14 November 2003. An international human rights organisation recorded a number of cases in which convictions and sentences to death were quashed on appeal.

In 2007 police in the state/province arrested eighteen men and charged them with sodomy for dressing as women, an offence under the Shari'a penal code. The charges were later reduced to vagrancy, and the men were held in jail for several years awaiting trial; the pre-trial detention dissolved by the end of 2011.

Persons perceived as trans-feminine in the state/province have been arrested and held in custody under Shari'a charges for years.

The 2022 sentence could not be carried out until ratified by the state/province's governor, and relatives said it had not been carried out at the time of reporting. No stoning sentence in the state/province is recorded as having been carried out.

At a sodomy trial in January 2014 at an upper Sharia court in the state/province, an angry mob stormed the premises demanding a death sentence.

The reversals recorded in the state/province turned on procedural defects, denial of counsel and a defective confession, rather than on the lawfulness of the offence itself.

Prosecutions in the state/province's Sharia courts have been brought by a local morality-enforcement group through individual complainants.

The 2007 arrests show charges reduced from sodomy to vagrancy while detention continued for years: the downgrade of a charge did not shorten custody.

The state/province stands under the national framework, and no variation from it was identified in this inventory: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and the criminal provisions it reinforces apply in the capital as they do elsewhere, and the national layer is carried by the parent record.

The state/province's documented trans-specific killing is that of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known by a public pseudonym. National news reporting dated 9 August 2024 states her beaten and bruised body was found along a highway in the capital on Thursday 8 August 2024, hours after she posted a final video, having previously expressed fear for her life. A police statement described the victim as "a man fully dressed in female clothing with no means of identification". The capital's police chief ordered a "thorough and discreet" investigation.

Follow-up reporting in 2025 states that six months after the killing, no suspects had been charged despite that promised investigation. The country is an independent jurisdiction with its own criminal law; the assessment below is national.

Article 25 of the Refoundation Charter, adopted in March 2025, criminalises all lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex and asexual acts or practices, expressly including transgender acts or practices. The February 2026 penal code punishes LGBTQIA+ acts or practices with 5 to 10 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 100 million CFA francs, and the punishable practices expressly include changing or attempting to change one's birth sex. Same-sex sexual relations carry the same 5 to 10 year term and fine, covering same-sex sexual activity and public announcement of a romantic relationship with a person of the same sex.

Creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment and a fine of up to 500 million CFA francs. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences cannot be applied to these penalties.

Since March 2025, Article 24 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Since June 2026, marrying a person of the same sex and officiating, organising or bearing official witness to a same-sex wedding is punished with 10 to 20 years' imprisonment.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. Article 95 of Law 2022-59 punishes collecting and processing data revealing sexual life or sexual orientation with three months to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; Law 2015-36, which had prohibited discrimination including on grounds of sexual orientation, was repealed in 2023 with convictions expunged.

Same-sex sexual activity was explicitly outlawed in 2025 and penalised in 2026. Before that change the age of consent stood at 13 for heterosexual acts and 21 for homosexual acts.

After the 2026 code took effect, dozens of people were arrested across the country and some imprisoned, including military officials, and LGBTQ people went into hiding. Organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working, ending access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP.

Documented enforcement includes two men caught naked in a parked car arrested for public indecency and fined; two young women in a southern town in 2022 prosecuted for lesbianism and acquitted for lack of legislation but imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act; and two young women reported as lesbians in the capital in 2025 prosecuted for public indecency but acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, with the judge allegedly sanctioned for leniency. As of 8-9 December 2022 the country had no specific law criminalising same-sex relationships, and a lawmaker from that southern town had presented to the Speaker of Parliament a proposal backed by nearly all MPs to criminalise same-sex relationships, with punishment unspecified and no debate scheduled.

No violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity was reported and no documented cases of discrimination in employment, housing, education, health care or statelessness on those grounds were recorded, though stigma or intimidation probably prevented incidents from being reported. Two gay rights organisations operated in secret, partly because they were not formally registered.

Asylum seekers from three neighbouring countries who held LGBTQ public demonstrations in the capital in 2022 were denied refugee recognition, hindering relocation, and faced shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers.

Gay men and lesbians face strong pressure to conform to societal norms, leading many to lead socially acceptable lives in public while seeking LGBT relationships privately. The 2025 acquittal of two women prosecuted for public indecency caused widespread debate ranging from approval to outrage. The only official cultural-values statement in the record concerns LGBTQ practices generally: "all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be (...) are not in line with our social and cultural values". The record contains no statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

The country's legal system layers a Sharia criminal track over the ordinary Penal Code. A 2004 human-rights survey listed twelve northern state/provinces of a neighbouring country having adopted Sharia criminal provisions, including this state/province, a wave traced from a Shari'a Establishment Law promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force from 27 January 2000. The provisions remain in force.

The state/province's own instrument, the Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, was signed into law on 22 February 2000, came into operation on 4 May 2000 and was gazetted on 9 March 2000. It amends the Penal Code Law so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts a section under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment, with amputation added to the caning paragraph, while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies.

A national country policy note from a neighbouring government (version 4.0, June 2025) sets out the hybrid legal system, the twelve-state/province Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women, and the limits of the available arrest data.

Changing or attempting to change one's birth sex is itself a punishable practice under the 2026 code. Same-sex marriage and officiating or witnessing such ceremonies carry 10 to 20 years' imprisonment since June 2026.

The state/province criminalises same-sex conduct under its own Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 23 November 2001. The enacted statutory text covers conduct by men and women and reaches beyond the parent nation's national criminal code. An international human rights organisation's 2004 report on Shari'a implementation lists this state/province among twelve state/provinces in one region of the country that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond the national code.

The penalties set by the state/province statute are severe and gendered. Unmarried men convicted of sodomy face caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment, and married men face stoning to death (rajm). The lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. The state/province's own formulation defines gross indecency as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour.

A foreign government's country-of-origin information note of June 2025 states that Islamic law applies to Muslims in twelve state/provinces in one region of the country, which include this one, and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women. It records the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' between men as death in all twelve, with penalties for 'lesbianism' ranging from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and on the attitude of the morality police (hisbah).

Enforcement in this state/province is documented through a single mass operation. In October 2023 the state/province command of a national law-enforcement and civil-defence corps raided a gathering at a roadside plaza on a highway in the state/province that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. A command spokesperson told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, and that 17 females were present at the scene; the command stated that the detainees would be charged in court for a crime of social vice in the state/province.

A national newspaper of 23 October 2023 independently confirmed the operation, reporting that the arrests followed a tip-off about a same-sex birthday party and planned marriage. The corps' state/province commandant confirmed the arrests; the spokesperson said the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and officers voiced concern over the participants' ages. Detention therefore reached people present at a gathering rather than only those alleged to have engaged in conduct. The most recent documented enforcement action in this record is this October 2023 raid; no later instance is documented.

The state/province's sodomy offence is not a local drafting accident. The identical provision, 100 lashes plus one year for unmarried men and stoning for married men, appears in three other state/provinces in the same region, which points to a shared statutory template across four of them rather than an isolated local measure.

The October 2023 raid was carried out by a state/province command of a national security and civil-defence corps, not by a Shari'a court, and the charge announced was framed as social vice. Moral-crimes enforcement here thus runs through ordinary criminal procedure as well as through the Shari'a courts, which widens the range of agencies a visitor can be processed by.

Women were drawn into the same operation: 17 females were detained at the scene and were characterised by the command as invited guests and onlookers. The gendered reach of the statute's lesbianism offence is matched in practice by the detention of women who were not alleged to have committed anything.

This state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation, which applies in full across all the country's states and provinces. The parent nation presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has hardened since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the national Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" statute criminalises public expression that, explicitly, "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government warnings state/province this directly to LGBT travellers.

The national refugee-authority country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment section updated 11 June 2025) records that same-sex activity is not criminalised in the parent nation, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. No discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

Penalties applicable in this state/province are substantial. 'Gay propaganda' offences carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court 'extremist' designation of the international LGBT+ movement makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws. a human rights organisation reported on 30 June 2025 that national courts had issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation, approximately 98 administrative and three criminal. The assessment finds that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those held in the parent nation's autonomous nation are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and affirms that LGBT+ people in the parent nation constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention.

Two foreign-government advisories bear on visitor exposure. One rates the parent nation Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers, and states that official support is 'very limited' in parts of the country.

The Supreme Court ruling of November 2023 entered into force in January 2024 and, according to the same human rights reporting, opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. In 98 court cases, 81 people were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles, while repeat displays are punishable under the criminal code by up to four years. On 15 May 2025 investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an accusation carrying up to 12 years.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. a news outlet reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the parent nation's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million roubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. Another outlet documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in the national capital, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night. a third outlet reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in the parent nation through 2025, and carried a resident's description of herself as "a second-class citizen" after the designation. a wire service reported in December 2024 that a man detained on extremism-related charges over a LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented independently of court process. a broadcaster reported on 27 July 2024 on "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. The human rights organisation has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing the parent nation.

Displaying symbols of the designated "international LGBT movement" has produced 98 administrative cases and 81 guilty findings with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and a repeat display becomes a criminal matter carrying up to four years. Participation in the designated movement is punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years. Between December 2022 and March 2024 at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws nationally.

An international human rights organisation documented a February 2017 police purge in which men believed to be gay were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. In late March and early April 2017, the organisation recorded security forces under that head rounding up dozens of men suspected of being gay and subjecting them to detention, torture, humiliation, enforced disappearance and severe beatings, with at least three deaths.

A newspaper reported that more than 100 men were detained across the main city and other settlements in late March 2017, among them religious officials and television presenters who had concealed their orientation; at least three detainees were killed and further killings were alleged. Detainees were held in a secret prison and in multiple detention centres, where they were beaten and tortured with electric shocks; at least three and reportedly up to 20 were beaten to death. Men who were released fled the state/province, and users abandoned LGBT messenger groups and closed social-media accounts.

The purge reactivated within two years. A renewed campaign beginning in December 2018 detained around 40 people, including gay men and women, with two killed; by May 2019 police had resumed unlawful detentions, beatings and humiliation of men presumed to be gay or bisexual. In January 2019 the newspaper learned that warnings were circulating through a social-media platform's LGBT-group administrators telling those still at large to leave the state/province; a spokesperson for the head of the state/province denied the reports. The newspaper's April 2017 investigation into the torture and killings produced no criminal case.

A rights monitoring organisation's investigation recorded a mass wave of unlawful detentions in which people were seized over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse and forced to sign contracts; families sometimes had to recruit two "volunteers" to secure a detained relative's release.

A national human-rights organisation's state/province-by-state/province tracker of legal gender recognition, dated March 2025, records this state/province among the units that have legislated an administrative procedure, and records the 2024 reform as the one that expanded access to minors and non-binary people following the supreme court's June 2023 ruling.

A national newspaper reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform approved by the state/province congress allows minors to change their gender and chosen name on birth certificates, and that the administrative processes are described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children. That pattern describes the neighbouring state/province, not this one, but it indicates what a non-reforming state/province's trans residents face.

National impunity conditions bear on any visitor's expectation of protection. The national travel advisory advises travellers to exercise a high degree of caution across the country because of high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with an avoid non-essential travel advisory covering this state/province and the northwestern mainland coast. This is a general-country advisory rather than a trans-specific one.

The national advisory's avoid non-essential travel designation names this state/province directly, but it is issued on criminal-activity and kidnapping grounds rather than on any trans-specific risk, and it applies to all travellers regardless of gender history.

Impunity for homicide nationally is documented at above 95% for 2022, a figure that shapes how much protection a formal legal right is likely to deliver in practice, including in state/provinces that have legislated recognition.

An academic analysis of 22 November 2024 found that the country's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, and that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the analyst cautioned explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture. The country has no single national procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set separately in each state/province. Whether the state/province or any of its districts has issued its own morality or public-order regulation is not sourced here; the inventory documents that subnational regulation varies by district in the parent nation but supplies no example for this state/province.

The state/province operates no provincial criminal law reaching sexual conduct or gender expression. It stands under the national framework without local additions, and no regency-level regulation on dress, public morality or gender presentation is documented in this inventory.

Security-force conduct is the province's defining documented risk. A report published on 22 July 2025 by a regional solidarity network recorded 138 acts of torture or other ill-treatment by police and military against people in detention in two highland areas of the state/province through early 2025, with most victims male and under 24, seven female, and seven minors aged 15 to 17; the report's framing is 'impunity, secrecy and silence', indicating near-total absence of accountability. Any visitor to the state/province, including a visibly gender-nonconforming one, stands in this security-force environment.

A national human-rights monitor's Q3 2025 quarterly records a notable increase in military deployments and operations in the state/province's highland regions since August 2025. In one city, police arrested over a dozen protest participants in August 2025. On 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in a town in one regency, alongside ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous residents. No trans-specific finding accompanies this pattern, but it amplifies exposure for a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

Provincial document practice follows the national pattern: since June 2021 the national home affairs ministry has conducted outreach to issue transgender residents with identity cards, including residents of the state/province, but the card recognises only 'male' and 'female' with no third gender or X designator, and prints gender at birth unless a court recognition is obtained. Families' disapproval can block the documentation process, which officials cite as leaving some residents undocumented and unable to access work or social services.

Legal gender recognition is available nationally after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which the person may marry someone of the opposite legal gender. The judicial system has recognised trans status: one woman was the first trans resident legally recognised as female, and there are documented cases where perpetrators of hate crimes against the transgender community were arrested and prosecuted.

National law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment. A national religious council ruled that transgender persons must live in the gender they were born with, stating that if they are 'not willing to cure themselves medically and religiously' they must be willing 'to accept their fate to be ridiculed and harassed'. This religious-body position sits alongside the judicial system's contrary practice.

Targeted enforcement documented against trans people at national level includes a January 2018 police arrest of twelve transgender women in one northern province, during which their hair was forcibly cut, they were compelled into men's clothing, and beauty salons were closed. A social agency in the national capital declared waria socially dysfunctional and conducted regular raids and incarceration in city-owned 'rehabilitation' centres alongside homeless people, beggars and buskers, requiring documentation and a signed pledge before release; officials stated this was intended as a deterrent against being transgender and warned that continued violations would result in jail time.

Discrimination in employment is documented: transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it challenging to maintain legitimate employment and are frequently pushed into prostitution and other informal or illegal activity to survive, with discrimination and harassment described as not uncommon though violence as quite rare. The source also notes that gays in jails are often sexually abused because of their orientation and do not report it, due to trauma and fear of return.

The control environment includes a 2006 national law against pornography prohibiting presentations suggesting same-sex relations and carrying a fine or up to seven years' imprisonment; a March 2016 broadcasting commission policy banning programmes that make LGBTQ behaviour appear 'normal' and discouraging effeminate, transgender or cross-dressing figures; bans on sites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ terms including a major dating app; and widely practiced, openly advertised conversion therapy, including rehabilitation-centre treatment with de facto legalisation by some city governments after a Family Resilience draft bill was rejected by 5 of 9 factions.

Care context: a 2012 national health ministry estimate put the number of transgender women at around 31 thousand. A transgender health organisation founded 1998 provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers at a free health clinic, operating amid a lack of school sex education and a historical movement focus that led the public to believe AIDS was a 'gay disease'.

Cultural context: transgender identity, also called waria, has long been part of the country's culture and society, and some public tolerance is given to transgender people working in beauty salons or the entertainment industry. The source states that while transgender people in the country are generally more accepted than gays, lesbians and bisexuals, they have in recent years faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting religious groups, which have become more popular.

Military service context: in 2021 a service member became the first in the country's military to legally change gender from female to male, though the case involved an intersex person assigned female at birth and raised as a girl.

The state/province's documented risk profile is dominated by general security-force violence rather than trans-specific harm. A July 2025 regional solidarity network report and a Q3 2025 national human-rights monitor quarterly describe military and police conduct affecting the population broadly; no trans-specific incident is recorded in this inventory for the state/province.

Comparatively, the national picture carries documented trans-specific enforcement (a January 2018 arrest of twelve transgender women in one northern province, capital-city social agency raids) that the state/province itself does not reproduce in this inventory. A visitor's exposure here is therefore shaped more by the general security environment and by national-level document and recognition rules than by provincial trans-targeted policing.

Racial tension affecting indigenous residents, recorded alongside displacement in the Q3 2025 quarterly, is a further axis of exposure for a visitor who is both gender-nonconforming and read as an outsider.

Transgender residents can access the national legal gender recognition route: sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval permits a change of gender on official documents and thereafter marriage to someone of the opposite legal gender. Since June 2021 the national home affairs ministry has conducted outreach to issue identity cards to transgender residents including those of the state/province, but the card carries only 'male' or 'female' and prints gender at birth absent court recognition.

Residents face the national control environment: a 2006 anti-pornography law, a March 2016 broadcasting commission policy, website and app bans, and openly advertised conversion therapy with de facto local-government legalisation in some cities. A national religious council's position that transgender persons must live in their birth gender, and its statement that those unwilling to be 'cured' must accept ridicule and harassment, shapes the local social climate.

Employment discrimination pushes trans residents who do not conceal their identity out of legitimate work and into survival economies including sex work. A transgender health organisation founded 1998 provides HIV/AIDS counselling and free condoms to transgender sex workers through a free health clinic.

Protection machinery available to residents is limited: a 2015 police circular to process hate speech related to sexual orientation and gender identity, a 2009 national police regulation stipulating a duty to protect minority groups' special rights including sexual orientation, and theoretical constitutional and human rights law guarantees against employment discrimination on any ground. No specific law protects citizens from discrimination or harassment based on gender identity as of 2019.

Whether the July 2025 regional solidarity network report's 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment include any trans or gender-nonconforming victims is not stated in this inventory; the victim breakdown given is by age and sex only.

The state/province-specific content in that source is the identity of the actor, a regional morals-and-order force rather than a national agency, and the form the detention took: transfer between two public facilities and hosing down while an officer filmed.

The documented targets in this state/province are trans women there, not visitors. The raid, the detention at the force's office and the hosing at the firefighter building were carried out against people the force encountered within its own jurisdiction; no source records whether any foreign or visiting trans person has been detained by the force.

The analysis of this state/province's regional regulations covers district as well as state/province level, so the restrictive rules are treated as operating in more than one tier of local government rather than as a single state/province-level instrument.
