The state/province stands under the country's national legal framework; the national layer is carried by the parent record. The region-specific layer is a provincial sharia criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and the provincial sharia criminal code enacted in 2014 (Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat) has been enforced since 23 October 2015. It is the country's only state/province that criminalises same-sex relations and enforces Islamic law in addition to the national criminal code.

Article 63 of the code defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by sex at birth. Each offence carries up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than presentation or legal gender marker, a trans visitor whose documents, presentation or partner's sex are read as same-sex conduct falls within the provision and faces caning, imprisonment or a fine.

Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences. On 23 May 2017 an Islamic court in the provincial capital applied the 2014 provisions for the first time, ordering two men caned 82 times each before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque; in 2017 two further men, aged 20 and 23, were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations.

The most recent documented enforcement in this record is from 2025. Two men aged 20 and 21 were sentenced on 11 August 2025 to public caning for kissing, after an April 2025 arrest in which police broke into a toilet; national news reporting on 26 August 2025 stated that two men were publicly caned in the province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing. No later enforcement incident in this state/province is documented in this record.

Trans people in the province have faced targeted enforcement. In January 2018 police in a northern district arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. In a separate parlour raid in January 2018 police tortured detainees, shaved the heads of transgender women, removed their shirts and bras, and paraded them through the street forcing them to shout that they were to become men.

A university human rights research centre reports that transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ people in the country, but its scope is country-wide rather than specific to this state/province, and it supplies no local figure or measurement period; it also covers the January 2018 detention of twelve trans women, the incident described in the summary.

Local legal scholarship engages directly with waria as a law-enforcement question: 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement' (QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture, doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405), by scholars at a local Islamic university, analyses the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens, indicating that local academic discourse frames transgender presence as a matter for policing rather than protection.

Country-wide reporting notes that transgender people have in recent years faced growing discrimination and rejection, mostly from sharia-supporting Muslim groups, which have become more popular in the country; this state/province is where that tendency is written into enforceable criminal law.

The sharia criminal code's special-autonomy authority was granted for Muslim residents, so the layer is framed as applying to the Muslim population of the state/province; the sources do not state how the provision is applied to non-Muslim residents.

The national identity-document outreach running since June 2021 to issue identification papers, including a national ID card, to transgender residents covers nine other state/provinces; this state/province is not among the listed ones. The programme recognises only male and female descriptors, with no third gender or X option, and prints gender at birth unless court recognition has already been obtained.

Transgender residents may change legal gender on official documents after sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, after which they may marry a person of the opposite legal gender. National law does not explicitly protect transgender people from discrimination or harassment, and transgender people who do not hide their gender identity often find it difficult to maintain legitimate employment.

Beauty salons run by transgender people have been a specific target of enforcement in this state/province: the January 2018 action in a northern district closed salons alongside the arrests.

Whether the 2014 provincial sharia criminal code is applied to non-Muslim visitors, or to conduct occurring outside the state/province, is not resolved in the sources; only the 2005 grant of authority framed in terms of Muslim residents is documented.

No figure for violence against trans people specific to this state/province, with a denominator and a general homicide rate for comparison, is available in this record, so no trans-specific rate for the region can be stated.

The record contains no enforcement incident in this state/province dated after 26 August 2025. Whether caning or arrest has continued since that date is not sourced here, and the absence of a later documented case is not evidence that enforcement has stopped.

Entry, visa and airport-screening treatment specific to this state/province, and any local document-marker flagging beyond the national ID outreach noted above, are not sourced in this inventory.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent country, and the penal code, morality provisions, documentation rules and protection gaps that apply nationally apply there. No law, regulation, enforcement action or raid specific to the state/province appears in the sources reviewed.

An international human rights organisation's mapping of the parent country's national laws and sub-national regulations examines eight focus state/provinces. This state/province is not among them. The mapping finds substantial overlap between those state/provinces in the discriminatory regulations they carry, alongside significant variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear, and its authors state that the findings apply beyond the focus set. No sub-national regulation of that kind is documented for this state/province in the source, and a neighbouring state/province was covered while this one was not; its absence from the mapping reflects the study's scope rather than a documented absence of such rules.

Research by a provincial university published in a cultural-studies journal on 23 December 2024 describes same-sex life in the state/province's capital city. Gay groups there describe same-sex orientation as partly converted into an economically valued 'profession', and men report becoming more introverted and careful about expressing their feelings to others after identifying as gay. Same-sex communities in the city live discreetly. The study reports no enforcement incident, no raid and no local regulation.

The sub-national layer matters when moving between state/provinces. The mapping's finding that dress codes, curfews and appearance restrictions vary by state/province means rules documented for one cannot be read across to this one, and the authors' statement that their findings extend beyond the eight focus state/provinces does not identify which additional ones carry such regulations.

A neighbouring state/province was among the eight the mapping examined; this state/province was not, so a traveller crossing between the two moves from a jurisdiction covered by a published regulatory review to one that is not.

Same-sex communities in the state/province's capital city live discreetly, according to the study by a provincial university published on 23 December 2024. Men interviewed for the study say that after identifying as gay they became more introverted and careful about expressing their feelings to others, and that same-sex orientation has partly been converted into an economically valued activity they describe as a profession.

The study records no sub-national regulation, no raid and no enforcement incident in the city.

No source in the inventory documents this state/province's own sub-national regulations directly. The state/province is absent from the mapping's eight focus state/provinces, and the authors' statement that the findings apply beyond the focus set is not itemised unit by unit, so the presence or absence of dress codes, curfews or appearance restrictions there is unresolved on the available material.

The capital-city study addresses gay men rather than transgender residents, reports the absence of enforcement rather than documenting enforcement practice, and gives no information on policing, detention conditions, healthcare access, facilities or violence affecting transgender people in the state/province. No trans-specific violence data for it appears in the inventory.

The state/province stands under the national framework. The source inventory records no ordinance, raid, protection measure, facility or support service specific to the state/province, so the national assessment applies.
No turbulence, adjacent finding or comparison point specific to the state/province appears in the sources consulted.
No sub-national measure affecting trans residents, whether a regulation, enforcement action, service or protection, was identified in the sources consulted.

Whether the state/province's sub-national regulations add morality provisions beyond the national framework is unresolved; no such regulation was located in the sources consulted. No incident, prosecution or enforcement record specific to the state/province was found.

This state/province is one of two in the parent nation that criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national morality provisions; an international human rights organisation's country profile records the provincial offence. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship faces a provincial criminal exposure that does not exist across most of the parent nation.

The provincial capital's city government is preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT people. The mayor announced the move on 19 July 2026 in a mosque courtyard, presenting it as local follow-through on the national defence policy that lists the spread of LGBTQ culture among non-military threats. The regulation is in preparation; no penalty has been specified and no enforcement has been documented.

An international advocacy organisation's mapping of discriminatory regional regulations across eight state/provinces of the parent nation includes this one, placing it inside the regional bylaw belt that drafts such as the capital's extend.

News reporting on 15 August 2026 documents 10 attacks on trans women in another state/province between 30 March and 15 July 2026, with 45 victim-survivors counted in advocacy group data; victims were punched, kicked and some stripped. The reporting links the attacks to the national defence policy that the capital's draft regulation also cites. The incidents occurred in a different state/province, not this one. An official quoted in the same reporting insists the policy is a broader defence measure not aimed at LGBTQI people.

Residents of the provincial capital face a municipal regulation drafted to reject LGBT people, announced by the mayor as local implementation of the national defence policy; the text, penalties and enforcement are not yet documented. This state/province's inclusion in an international advocacy organisation's mapping of discriminatory regional regulations across eight state/provinces of the parent nation means local LGBT residents live under bylaw-level restrictions that operate alongside the provincial criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity between men and between women.

The content of the capital's draft regulation, whether it has been enacted, and any penalty it carries are not sourced; the announcement is the only documented step. No trans-specific violence or police operation in this state/province appears in the source inventory, and the August 2026 attack reporting concerns a different state/province. An international human rights organisation's account of this state/province's provincial offence is carried without the text of the provision or its penalty.

The state/province comprises two large land areas. The official mid-2025 estimate puts its population in the millions. National religious-affairs ministry data for 2022 records 96.88% of residents as Muslim, and Islam was the official religion of the state/province's historic-era rulers.

The state/province's recorded character is conservative and religious, and its economy depends on tourism. The predominant local community maintains strong traditions, among them a locally rooted form of religious practice influenced by local beliefs.

No state/province-specific bylaw, enforcement action, raid, arrest or incident targeting transgender people is recorded, and no state/province-level protective legislation has been enacted. The state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework, and the national assessment applies to visitors here.

The state/province's economy depends on tourism, which places foreign visitors in sustained contact with a population whose recorded religious adherence is near-universal. A visitor-facing economy and a conservative religious public character coexist in the same state/province.

Islam was the official religion of the state/province's historic-era rulers, and the predominant local community's traditions are locally rooted rather than derived from the national framework. The state/province's two main land areas are the settings in which these conditions apply.

No state/province-level legislation protects residents from discrimination or harassment on grounds of gender identity. Any protection available to trans residents comes from the national layer.

The state/province's recorded religious composition and conservative public character are the local conditions trans residents live within; the tourism-dependent economy is the main source of outside contact.

No state/province-level enforcement record is sourced: no court ruling, police operation, or reported incident targeting transgender people. The absence of reported incidents is not evidence that none occurred.

The population figure is an official mid-2025 estimate and the religious composition is national religious-affairs ministry data for 2022. No sourced material separates the state/province's two main land areas, or its urban from rural districts, for trans visitors.

The state/province stands under the national framework on gender identity and documentation. Since June 2021 the national home affairs ministry has conducted outreach to issue identity papers, including the electronic identity card, to transgender residents, and this state/province is named among the nine where this has operated.

The stated reasoning for the outreach was that many transgender people in these provinces were undocumented, particularly where families did not approve of their transition. For a trans visitor in this state/province this bears on document status and enrolment: it is one of the nine where identity-document issuance for transgender residents has been carried out since mid-2021.

An August 2026 feature reports growing repression against the country's transgender community nationally, which sets the wider climate in which this state/province's document-outreach programme operates.

Transgender residents of this state/province have been within the scope of the national home affairs ministry's identity-document outreach since June 2021, one of nine provinces covered. The programme was directed at transgender people who lacked documentation, including those whose families did not approve of their transition.

The source inventory does not document how many transgender residents of this state/province have actually received identity papers under the outreach, nor whether the programme is ongoing or concluded. No state/province-specific enforcement incidents, provincial regulations, or facility-access rules for trans visitors were identified in the inventory.

This state/province sets its own civil, health-care and criminal law within the national framework of the parent nation; national rules on passports, visas, entry screening and national custody are fixed nationally and are not restated here. On the matters a trans visitor encounters at state/province level, the law runs in a protective direction.

State/province legislation enacted in 2023 declares that gender-affirming health care as defined in the Act "is against the public policy of this state/province and must not be enforced or applied" in pending cases, and amends provisions on warrants, arrests and extraditions that arise from other jurisdictions' laws on gender-affirming health care. The lower chamber passed the bill 68-62 on 24 March 2023 after a late-night debate, and the state/province governor signed it. It followed a March 2023 executive order directing the state/province health department to summarise the scientific literature on the safety and effectiveness of gender-affirming care and confirming that providers could bill insurance for such care.

The shield reaches process from another state/province. State/province authorities may not enforce subpoenas, arrest warrants or extradition requests issued elsewhere over gender-affirming care that is legal in the state/province, and may not comply with court orders from another state/province to remove children from parental custody for having obtained such care. Families travelling to the state/province for treatment fall inside that protection.

Anti-discrimination law covers gender identity. The state/province has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity since 1993 in employment, housing, public accommodations, insurance, goods and services, contracts, health benefits and hospital visitation rights, and in that year became the first state/province to outlaw discrimination based on sexual orientation in the same fields. A May 2023 omnibus community justice bill protected "gender identity" as a category separate from sexual orientation and repealed exemptions for nonpublic service organizations, effective immediately. The same act repealed residual statutory language stating that the state/province "does not condone homosexuality or bisexuality" and did not authorise its promotion in educational institutions.

Hate-crime law has provided additional penalties for offences committed because of gender identity since that category was added in 1993; sexual orientation was added in 1989. The trans panic defence was abolished by the omnibus justice reforms signed on 29 May 2024 and effective 1 August 2024, which passed the upper chamber 34-33.

Identity documents are relatively open at state/province level. Changing the gender marker on a birth certificate does not require sex reassignment surgery: it requires a physician's letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a court order for gender change, plus a notarised Birth Certificate Application and a fee, and the previous certificate is kept confidential. The state/province licensing agency updates a driver's licence or state/province ID on individual request with no documentation required, and since October 2018 licences and state/province IDs offer M, F or X on request, with no documentation needed for intersex, non-binary and ambiguous-sex applicants. Birth certificates carry no X option.

Care coverage is written into state/province policy. The public health insurance programme covers transgender-related care, and state/province law bars health insurers from excluding transgender-specific coverage or discriminating against transgender patients. Gender-affirming services were protected by the March 2023 executive order and codified by the legislation signed in April 2023. Conversion therapy is banned for minors and vulnerable adults under a law signed by the state/province governor on 26 April 2023 and effective 1 August 2023, following a July 2021 executive order and city bans beginning with one city in November 2019. Practitioners may not advertise LGBTQ identities as a mental disease, disorder or illness or promise to change sexual orientation or gender identity; violations are subject to discipline by health licensing boards, and insurers and health plans may not pay for conversion therapy.

Private consensual conduct between adults is not criminalised. The state/province's sodomy statute, which punished voluntarily engaging in or submitting to sodomy by the anus or by or with the mouth with up to one year's imprisonment and a fine of up to $3,000, was declared unconstitutional on 15 May 2001 as applied to private, consensual, non-commercial acts of adults, on privacy grounds under the state/province constitution, in an unappealed class action decided two years before a national supreme court ruling on such statutes. The prohibition had been carried since the historic-era adoption of a neighbouring jurisdiction's law in 1849 and the 1851 code, was raised in 1909 to 20 years' imprisonment, was expanded in 1921 to include fellatio, and was reduced in 1967 to a misdemeanour punishable by up to one year in jail or a $1,000 fine; a 1973 repeal attempt failed 46-69 with 19 abstentions, and formal repeal came in May 2023 through an omnibus judiciary and public safety bill signed by the state/province governor.

Marriage is recognised for relationships read locally as same-sex. Same-sex marriage became legal in the state/province on 1 August 2013, after lower chamber passage 75-59 on 9 May and upper chamber passage 37-30 on 13 May, signed by the state/province governor on 14 May, following the defeat of a constitutional ban by 51.5% to 47.5% on 6 November 2012. A trans visitor married to a partner of any birth-sex configuration is recognised on that footing.

Custody placement practice has been documented along birth-sex lines. A transgender woman pleaded guilty to second-degree manslaughter and was sentenced on 4 June 2012 to 41 months; her attorneys acknowledged there was "no way" she would be sent to a women's prison and "really no history of transgender people being placed according to their gender identity" in the state/province. The state/province corrections department placed her in an adult male facility after a state/province gender assessment concluded she would be held in a men's facility, and although she was later transferred to a second facility she remained quartered with men throughout her imprisonment. She was held in segregated custody while awaiting trial. In May 2012 a fellow inmate attacked her with a glass, causing a wound that required eleven stitches; the attacker pleaded guilty in April 2013 to third-degree assault and received six months' jail time plus probation. A petition filed during her imprisonment led the department to administer the correct hormone regimen.

An independent legal-risk assessment published in July 2026 places this state/province in its most protective tier alongside several other state/provinces, the strongest category the assessment uses.

The protective posture sits alongside litigation over contested policies, including the challenge to its high school transgender athlete policy and the abolition of the trans panic defence, which passed the upper chamber by a single vote.

Attorneys representing three school softball players have challenged the state/province's high school transgender athlete policy in court.

Family formation law treats same-sex couples as adoptive and legal parents in practice. The state/province's gender-identity law is protective. A 2014 state/province nondiscrimination law, effective 1 October 2014, prohibits discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations throughout the state/province; before that date protection existed only in a handful of cities and counties. Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited throughout the state/province since a 2001 state/province antidiscrimination law took effect on 21 November 2001.

The hate-crime statute adds penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, listed as a separate category by an amendment effective 1 October 2021. A state/province law effective the same date abolished the common-law gay and trans panic defence.

A 2024 law declaring the state/province a sanctuary jurisdiction for the protection and defence of transgender individuals passed its upper chamber 33-13 and its lower chamber 97-38 and was signed by the state/province governor, effective 1 October 2024. It followed a June 2023 executive order protecting unimpeded access to gender-affirming healthcare and an insurance law effective 1 January 2024 described in comparative rights research across state/provinces as the most transgender healthcare friendly in the country.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation. Passport and visa sex markers, national facility rules, immigration detention and national custody are governed nationally, not by the state/province.

State/province-level identity documents are accessible but not complete. Since 1 October 2015 a birth-certificate gender marker can be changed without surgery or sterilisation on certification from a licensed healthcare provider confirming gender identity; the X marker remained unavailable on birth certificates as of 2023. Motor vehicle agency IDs and voter registration have allowed X since 1 October 2019 without legal or medical documentation, and a state/province university will add X in 2026. A state/province law effective 1 October 2021 repealed the 1971 requirement to publish a name in a newspaper before a legal change on a birth certificate.

Facilities and student access run in favour of transgender people. In March 2018 a national court ruled that transgender students may use restrooms and locker rooms consistent with gender identity, striking down one county's policy; one county adopted gender-neutral bathroom requirements by a 9-0 vote in July 2022 and one city does so by ordinance. A February 2022 county report records that transgender athletes may participate according to gender identity without proof, documentation, or medical or legal transition, after bills in 2022 and 2023 that would have restricted teams by biological sex failed.

Violence against transgender people in the state/province is documented. On 11 September 2026 a 27-year-old Black trans woman was found shot in a neighbourhood of one city and died; she was the second Black trans woman shot to death in that city within ten weeks.

Protection machinery includes one county's unanimous October 2020 LGBTIQ+ bill of rights ordinance, a 15-member state/province commission on LGBTIQ+ affairs created by a state/province law effective October 2021 and expanded to 21 members in April 2023, and a state/province law effective 1 October 2022 that automatically restores honorable discharges retrospectively to LGBT individuals who lived in the state/province at the time.

Marriage between people of the same sex has been legal in the state/province since 1 January 2013 under its civil marriage law, approved 72-67 in the lower chamber on 17 February 2012 and 25-22 in the upper chamber on 23 February 2012, signed 1 March 2012 and approved by 52.4% of voters on 6 November 2012, after a 1973 ban; domestic partnerships have existed since 2008 and marriages from outside the state/province have been recognised since 2010. A trans visitor whose relationship the state/province's law reads as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry there.

An analysis plotting recorded anti-trans incidents against each state/province's law score places this state/province in its safest band on the source's law scale, with a low recorded-incident count, while another state/province records both the worst laws (24.7) and 11.6 recorded incidents. The analysis's finding is that protective law floors do not by themselves predict recorded incident counts. The figures are state/province-level totals; the material reviewed supplies no per-capita denominator, so rankings of this kind track population size as well as risk and should not be read as a comparison of individual danger.

The state/province's sexual-practices statute has its own enforcement history. Court rulings in 1990 and in October 1998 invalidated the prohibition on private consensual oral sex, and a 1999 settlement covered anal sex. Legislative repeal of the anal-sex provision took effect 1 October 2020 and repeal of the oral-sex ban passed in 2023 and took effect 1 October 2023 without the state/province governor's signature. In July 2021 several men were arrested for conduct that was not criminalised when engaged in heterosexually, under an older sexual-practices statute, which remained on the books because the 2020 amendment in one chamber left the oral-sex ban intact after a 2022 repeal attempt died in committee.

Residents have broad public coverage for gender-affirming treatment. The public health programme explicitly covers sexual reassignment surgery for eligible residents over 18 under a law passed in March 2023, signed in April 2023, and effective 1 January 2024. A state/province health equity bill sponsored by a state/province legislator passed the lower chamber as of 20 May 2024 to extend public coverage of gender-affirming treatment and awaited action in the upper chamber.

Conversion therapy by licensed practitioners on minors has been prohibited since 1 October 2018, after passage in April 2018 and signature in May 2018; a national constitutional challenge was dismissed in September 2019.

No documented state/province rule on housing transgender prisoners, no dedicated unit and no named case appears in the sources reviewed, so how the state/province places transgender people in custody is unresolved here.

The sources give no general homicide rate for any city or for the state/province, so whether the two killings in ten weeks exceed the background risk in the city is not established; the ten-week count is a raw figure without a denominator.

The upper chamber's outcome on the health equity bill is not recorded in the sources, and whether the 2024 sanctuary law extends its protections to non-resident visitors is not sourced.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the country for passports, entry screening and national identity documents; the findings below are specific to the state/province.

A national anti-trans legal-risk assessment dated July 2026, built from five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric scoring the most severe bills, lists the state/province among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults, and among the states that prohibit any change to birth certificates. The assessment states that this prohibition forces transgender people to disclose their status when presenting documents.

Birth-certificate gender markers are effectively closed. A national equality research organisation's identity-document tracker records that the state/province's 2023 law bans all gender-marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states, and marks the state/province a negative-law jurisdiction. The regulations accompanying the 2023 statute were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation.

Driving licences and state/province ID cards follow a separate and lower threshold: the state/province motor-vehicle agency updates the gender marker on receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating that the applicant has completed a permanent gender role transition.

State/province statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Employment discrimination is addressed nationally under a supreme court ruling of 15 June 2020, and city-level protections exist in one city for municipal employees and applicants and in rental housing from 2013. An April 2021 state/province law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students.

Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023.

Two bills signed into law in April 2023 ban individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and in higher education respectively. A 2021 bill to the same effect passed the lower chamber 69 to 25 and the upper chamber 27 to 20 but was vetoed by the governor on 21 April 2021.

An April 2023 law, effective 1 July, explicitly allows restriction of transgender individuals' public bathroom usage in many state-run facilities.

A 2023 transgender-student bill, an act relating to preferred pronouns and accommodations to a transgender student, carried a penalty provision and an emergency clause, was signed by the governor, and had its last official action recorded on 9 May 2023. The corresponding May 2023 law, effective 1 July, forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use and requires disclosure of transgender students to parents in state-run schools. A March 2023 bill requiring parental and administrative approval for preferred pronoun use in state-run schools and classrooms had been vetoed.

The state/province's hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, while national prosecution for crimes motivated by gender identity has been available since the national hate-crimes statute of 2009. A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counsellors.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 26 June 2015 under a national supreme court ruling, following prior constitutional and statutory restriction to one man and one woman; related state/province proceedings were suspended in January 2015. A tribal nation within the state/province legalised same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020.

The July 2026 assessment's placement of the state/province among the worst states is derived from a legislative rubric applied to bill tracking, not from per-capita or population-adjusted incident data, so the ranking indicates the volume and severity of enacted measures rather than a measured rate of harm.

A 2022 national survey institute poll found 78 percent of residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, with 22 percent opposed.

In July 2020 delegates of one major party voted for the state/province's election platform opposing any civil-rights protections for LGBTQ people and accusing transgender people of preying on women and LGBTQ people of recruiting children. Many delegates condemned the platform, and the governor opposed it as divisive, stating that all residents deserve to be treated equally and live free of discrimination.

A March 2023 bill that would allow businesses to refuse service on any grounds based on religious objection alone passed the legislature and awaited gubernatorial action; the sources do not record its final disposition.

Residents have no state/province/statutory protection against gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations; the practical floor is the national employment statute as interpreted in June 2020, supplemented by municipal rules for city employees and applicants and rental housing in one city from 2013.

Adoption is permitted with no express statutory ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, but state/province law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate on the basis of sincerely held religious belief. A 1980s supreme court ruling had made parental sexual orientation decisive in custody cases because of societal prejudices; that precedent was reversed in 2003.

Family-law provisions available to residents include recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status, express permission for gestational surrogacy for intended parents whether same-sex or different-sex, and prohibition of traditional surrogacy.

Conversion therapy is banned for social workers, psychologists and counsellors under a June 2021 committee regulation, while the state/province hate-crime statute still excludes gender-identity-motivated violence.

Several tribal nations within the state/province maintain distinct traditions of gender-nonconforming roles, including third-gender people also called two-spirit, with recorded traditional terms in several indigenous languages. The sources state that perceptions of gender and sexuality within these communities differ from those of residents of the region, both historically and at present.

Unresolved: the sources do not state whether the 2008 regulation requiring a sex conversion operation remains the operative birth-certificate rule alongside the 2023 statute, given that the accompanying regulations were rejected. Both instruments are described, and their relationship is not sourced.

Unresolved: whether the 2023 transgender-student bill and the May 2023 pronoun and disclosure law described in the record are the same enactment is not established by the sources; they are reported separately here.

Unresolved: no enforcement instance of the 2023 bill's penalty provision is documented in the inventory, and no dated incident of violence against a transgender person in the state/province appears in the sources, so no incident-level risk statement can be made.

Unresolved: the final disposition of the March 2023 religious-refusal service bill is not recorded in the sources.

A 2023 statute, enacted on 29 March 2023 after the state/province legislature overrode the governor's veto, carries the state/province's restriction on which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools alongside its ban on gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. It is the single 2023 statute containing the school facility restriction, and a national equality map lists it among state/province-level bans on transgender people using public facilities according to gender identity. The facility provision is written for public school students; the sources reviewed identify no state/province-wide rule governing adult use of bathrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Responsibility for carrying out the school restriction sits with local districts. The state/province education department issued guidance in April 2023 for districts implementing the 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to proceed cautiously with the bathroom provisions.

The care ban took effect on 14 July 2023, when a national district judge lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, barring transgender minors from puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law, and a civil-liberties organisation described the ruling as a temporary setback. On 28 September 2023 a national appeals panel allowed the ban to remain in force while challenges proceed. Minors already receiving care were given no phase-out.

Birth certificates can be amended only for post-operative applicants: a doctor's letter stating that gender-affirming surgery has been performed goes directly to the state/province vital statistics office in the capital. A court order was previously required for a person born in the state/province.

School sport is closed to transgender girls under a 2022 statute, which passed the legislature in March 2022, was vetoed by the governor in April 2022 on constitutionality and vagueness grounds, and was enacted over that veto the same month with immediate effect. A further 2023 bill, carrying the minors' care ban among other provisions, advanced on 2 March 2023 and passed on 17 March 2023, was vetoed, and was overridden on 29 March 2023 by simple majority votes; police arrested 19 capitol protesters for criminal trespassing that day.

Employment protection derives from national appellate and executive sources rather than from statute. On 7 March 2018 a national appeals court covering the state/province held that national employment law bars firing an employee for being transgender or for transitioning, because it penalises failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes, and that a national religious-freedom statute does not permit a private employer to dismiss a transgender worker on religious grounds. The case arose from a funeral director dismissed in 2013 after disclosing her planned transition. A June 2008 executive order barred hiring or firing state/province employees on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, restoring protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006. Nineteen municipalities maintain local non-discrimination ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations.

The state/province's hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation and expressly exclude gender identity, so bias-motivated violence against a transgender person falls outside the hate-crime enhancement. The sexual-orientation provision was used in the April 2011 beating of a man in a state/province park, which produced arrests on 15 March 2012 by the state/province police working with a national law-enforcement agency and guilty pleas from two defendants after advocacy by a local organisation.

Conversion therapy on minors has been illegal state/province-wide since the governor's executive order of 18 September 2024, following municipal bans in three cities between March 2020 and May 2021.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the state/province supreme court struck down the sodomy statute in 1992 on state/province constitutional grounds, a result reinforced by a national supreme court ruling in 2003. The unenforceable statute remains on the books; it formerly punished specified sexual acts as a misdemeanour carrying up to 12 months in jail and a $500 fine, with solicitation punishable by up to 90 days and $250.

Religious-exemption and service-access rules cut against those protections. A 2013 religious-freedom statute requires the state/province to show clear and convincing evidence before burdening a sincerely held religious belief; the governor vetoed it over vagueness and the risk of overriding local non-discrimination ordinances, and the legislature overrode him 79-15 in one chamber and 32-6 in the other. A 2017 statute allows religious student organisations use of school facilities and control of their internal affairs. In August 2020 a district court held that a Christian photographer, as a public business, could not be compelled to photograph same-sex weddings because the photographs are art and speech protected against compulsion.

The state/province's protections are a patchwork rather than a floor. Employment protection rests on a national appellate ruling and an executive order limited to state/province employees, while the hate-crime statute omits gender identity and the 2013 religious-freedom statute gives religious claims a statutory route around local ordinances.

Coverage of the local non-discrimination ordinances is municipal, not state/province-wide. Outside the 19 listed municipalities there is no local public-accommodations protection on gender identity, and the state/province-wide non-discrimination guarantee for public employment does not reach private employers.

The 2018 appellate holding governs the state/province along with the other jurisdictions in that circuit, so the workplace position turns on national appellate and supreme court litigation rather than on action by the state/province legislature.

Amending a birth certificate in the state/province requires a doctor's letter confirming gender-affirming surgery, sent to the state/province vital statistics office in the capital; a court order is no longer the route for a person born there.

Minors cannot obtain puberty blockers or hormone therapy in the state/province, with no phase-out for those already in treatment, and the ban has stayed in force through appellate review since September 2023.

State/province employees are protected against hiring or firing discrimination on gender identity by executive order dating to 2008. Private-sector employees in the 19 municipalities with local non-discrimination ordinances have local recourse in employment, housing and public accommodations; elsewhere they rely on the national appellate holding under national employment law.

Bias crimes against transgender residents are not covered by the state/province hate-crime statute, which lists sexual orientation but not gender identity.

Conversion therapy on minors is barred state/province-wide by executive order since September 2024.

Transgender students in public schools are restricted to facilities matching their birth-assigned sex under the 2023 statute, with compliance left to district-level decisions guided by the April 2023 education department advice.

Whether the appellate status of the 2023 care ban has changed since September 2023 is not established by the sources reviewed.

No source in the inventory quantifies enforcement of the school facility provision, records exclusionary or disciplinary incidents under it, or reports trans-specific violence statistics for the state/province.

The scope of national employment-law protection as applied in the state/province following later national litigation is unresolved in these sources.

Whether the surgery requirement for birth-certificate amendment has been litigated or administratively revised is not sourced.

No source addresses how the 2013 religious-freedom statute has been applied to transgender-specific service refusals in the state/province.

The state/province sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, compiled by applying a rubric to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking's authors describe the laws of this tier as having gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

State law effective 1 July 2003 prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership. The public-accommodations limb is the one a visitor interacts with directly: it covers restaurants, hotels, shops and other places serving the public. The 15-or-more-employees exemption was repealed effective 1 July 2019, and 2023 legislation explicitly extended coverage to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under an emergency clause; the state/province's largest city amended its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024 to align.

Since 1 November 2019 transgender people may change legal gender without surgery. Legislation passed 26-13 in the lower chamber and 33-14 in the upper chamber and signed by the governor repealed the 1984 surgery requirement and provides male, female and X neutral designations on birth certificates, driver's licences and government IDs. An applicant submits a Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with fees, with parental consent for minors, or a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for licences and IDs. This replaced a prior requirement for a perjury statement from an institution or physician attesting surgical change plus a certified name-change order.

Since 1 July 2019 businesses and public facilities with single-occupancy restrooms must mark them gender-neutral and available to any person regardless of gender identity or sex, under legislation passed 54-12 in the lower chamber and 23-15 in the upper chamber and signed by the governor. The state/province has no law prohibiting transgender girls' sports participation; eligibility is determined by birth certificate, original or amended, and the state/province school-sports body has issued no further guidance.

Gender-affirming care is protected rather than restricted. In March 2023 a house bill codified protection for gender-affirming care and sex-reassignment surgery for adults on request without restrictions, including for interstate travellers, and is cited as establishing the state/province as a refuge for transgender youths. A national equality-research organisation's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists the state/province as holding a shield law or 2023 executive order: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal here but banned in the patient's home jurisdiction, which is directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a ban jurisdiction. In 2026 the national health care authority announced use of national funds to maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a national rule moved to exclude it.

Since 2003 the state/province's hate-crime law has explicitly covered violence committed on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity. In February 2022 the legislature passed an omnibus crime bill repealing the common-law gay and trans panic defence, signed 9 March 2022. March 2019 school-bullying legislation protects students on the basis of gender identity and requires districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies, effective 1 July 2019.

Same-sex couples have had the same marriage rights as different-sex couples since the 19 December 2013 supreme court ruling requiring equal marriage rights, making the state/province the 17th jurisdiction in the country to recognise same-sex marriage; statutory codification passed 62-0 in the lower chamber and 39-0 in the upper chamber in March 2019 and took effect 1 July 2019. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore has that relationship recognised here.

The July 2026 ranking's contrast tier shows how far the state/province sits from the worst-law jurisdictions: those carry up to five-year prison terms for gender-identity-related offences in one state/province, or an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use in another. The protective tier holds fifteen states/provinces in total.

The national shield picture around the state/province is uneven. The equality-research organisation's map records 16 states/provinces plus the national capital district, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, as holding shields, while 32 states/provinces and 5 state/provinces, covering 56%, hold none; youth-care bans are tracked nationally with some permanently blocked in court.

Statewide polling shows sustained but dated public support for the statutory framework: 73% supported anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people in 2018, and 64% supported a law covering sexual orientation and gender identity in 2017. The capital city is cited as a gay capital and the largest metropolitan area as a gay-friendly city.

Indigenous gender traditions in the region predate the current legal regime. One nation of the region recognised four gender roles, including a male-bodied person with a feminine nature who was typically chosen for communal and spiritual roles, wore female clothing and did female work, and could have sexual relations with men, which the tribe accepted; comparable recognised roles existed among several neighbouring pueblos and nations. Colonisation eroded this acceptance: the role became a subject of ridicule, and Christian converts among one nation were prohibited from attending a traditional ceremony because male cross-dressing could be observed. A documented writer on the subject notes that the "tolerance or even respect of transgender people" was used by early explorers to argue for colonisation of native peoples and their lands in the name of Christianity. Today LGBTQ members of that nation may find it difficult to be accepted by family.

Residents have a statutory non-discrimination entitlement dating from 1 July 2003 across employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and union membership, with the 15-or-more-employees exemption removed effective 1 July 2019 and 2023 legislation extending coverage expressly to local entities, counties, schools, universities and government-run agencies under an emergency clause. The largest city aligned its Human Rights Ordinance in May 2024.

Legal gender change for residents requires no surgery and no medical evidence: a Request to Change Gender Designation on a Birth Certificate form with the applicable fees, with parental consent for minors, or a Request for Sex Designation Change form to the Motor Vehicles Division for a licence or government ID. Male, female and X designations are available on birth certificates, driver's licences and government IDs. A 2023 bill repealed the requirement to publish a legal name change in a newspaper, which had risked the privacy, safety and lives of transgender individuals.

Students are covered by March 2019 bullying legislation requiring districts to adopt prohibition, reporting, investigation, disciplinary, prevention and staff-training policies on the basis of gender identity, effective 1 July 2019. Sexual orientation change efforts on minors are prohibited under a 2017 bill, passed 32-6 in the upper chamber and 44-23 in the lower chamber and signed 7 April 2017 by the governor, effective 6 July 2017.

Residents retain access to gender-affirming care under the March 2023 house bill, and in 2026 the national health care authority announced that national funds would maintain Medicaid coverage for gender-affirming care after a national rule moved to exclude it. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is also addressed by state law, and enforcement of the state's non-discrimination regime was upheld unanimously by the state supreme court in 2013 in a case concerning refusal to photograph a same-sex commitment ceremony.

No trans-specific violence incidents, homicide counts or enforcement outcomes for the state/province's hate-crime or non-discrimination provisions appear in this inventory; the absence of documented cases is not evidence of their non-occurrence, and no period of observation is given.

How the state/province's X designation on state IDs and birth certificates interacts with national document rules for a resident crossing the border is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The inventory reports that 70% of LGBT youth of one Indigenous nation have attempted suicide without giving a survey date, a sample, a methodology or a trans-specific breakdown; the figure is not carried into the assessment above for that reason.

Whether the March 2023 care statute's "on request" standard applies to non-resident minors travelling for care, and what documentation a visiting minor would need, is not specified in the sources. The state/province school-sports body's silence on further eligibility guidance is recorded as an absence of guidance rather than a stated rule.

Public-opinion figures cited are from 2017 and 2018 and measure support for LGBTQ anti-discrimination legislation generally, not current trans-specific prevalence or attitudes.

The state restricts trans people's use of sex-separated facilities under a women's privacy statute signed by the governor on 22 September 2025 and effective 4 December 2025. Restrooms must match the sex recorded on a person's birth certificate, and the law reaches public schools, universities, prisons and state government buildings. Facilities face a $25,000 fine for a first violation and $125,000 for subsequent violations. The companion gender-placements statute reaches prisons only as to restroom use; it does not govern cell assignment or the housing placement of trans prisoners.

Enforcement began within days of the effective date. On 6 December 2025 state police troopers checked identification at women's restrooms outside the state capitol, and trans women holding female ID markers were admitted. Protests followed at the capitol, the capital city council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and opponents warned that unclear guidelines produce uneven and invasive enforcement.

On 27 April 2026 the national justice department filed a second complaint that escalated the state investigation of the capital-city school district over its bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint. It was the first state/province enforcement inquiry into a school district under the bathroom law.

A national legal risk assessment dated July 2026 places the state in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier for adult trans travellers, alongside three other states. States in that assessment are graded law by law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture using a five-year legislation-tracking methodology.

A statutory definition act passed in May 2025, signed in June 2025 and effective September 2025 defines female as a person who can biologically produce ova and male as one who can biologically fertilize ova, requires people with disorders of sex development to select one binary gender with no third-gender recognition, and applies across all state/province statutes, regulations and laws using gendered terms. The statute explicitly bans any change of sex on state/province driver's licences and birth certificates. Before it took effect, changing the gender indicator on a birth certificate required a court order, with judicial discretion often referencing WPATH Standards of Care and a narrative statement from a doctor or therapist that the change was appropriate and in the person's best interest; on 30 January 2025 the governor separately directed state agencies to recognise only two genders.

Gender-affirming care for minors has been banned in the state since a statute signed in June 2023, which followed a February 2022 opinion from the national justice department classifying such care as child abuse.

The state has no statewide law barring discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations or insurance as of 2021, although state courts recognised the 2020 national employment ruling in March 2021 and several cities prohibit such discrimination. The state hate-crime statute enhances penalties for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, and prosecutions under it are rare.

Custody carries documented harm. A transgender woman incarcerated by the state corrections agency and diagnosed with gender dysphoria was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the agency's official treatment policy excluded the procedure. In the resulting national case the district court denied the state's immunity defences but ruled against her Eighth Amendment claim, and a national appeals court affirmed dismissal on the ground that refusing the surgery was a permissible medical choice, with one judge dissenting on summary-judgement procedure.

Same-sex marriage has been licensed in the state since a national ruling of 26 June 2015, and a 2022 national marriage statute requires the state/province to recognise same-sex marriages lawfully performed in another jurisdiction without obligating the state/province to issue them. The state/province has no statewide recognition of domestic partnerships for same-sex or opposite-sex couples, though the capital and five other major cities provide health insurance to domestic partners of city workers, and an April 2013 opinion from the national justice department held that the constitution bars political-subdivision benefits based on domestic-partnership status.

The state shares the top 'Do Not Travel' tier with three other states in the July 2026 assessment. The grading is law by law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture rather than a tally of incidents, so the tier reflects statutory and enforcement conditions.

Opponents of the women's privacy statute warn that unclear guidelines produce uneven and invasive enforcement. The two documented enforcement episodes in this inventory are the identification checks outside the state capitol on 6 December 2025 and the escalated complaint against the capital-city school district on 27 April 2026; no later instance is documented.

Legislative activity has been sustained. Around fifty bills were filed in early January 2023 to criminalise youth gender-affirming care, reduce adult access, bar sex-marker changes for minors and further restrict sports participation. A prefiled November 2022 bill would expand the definition of sexually oriented businesses to reach any performance where a performer uses clothing, makeup or other markers to exhibit gender variance from birth-assigned sex while singing, lip-syncing, dancing or otherwise performing, which would capture transgender performers in any role as well as cisgender portrayals of diverse or ambiguous genders, and would criminalise minors' attendance at drag shows.

A statute signed in June 2023 effectively bans gender-affirming care for minors. It followed a February 2022 opinion from the national justice department classifying such care as child abuse and governor directives ordering the state family-services agency to investigate parents who facilitate it and imposing criminal penalties for a knowing failure to report. Five district attorneys refused to follow the directives, and a March 2022 temporary injunction blocked them; a state/province appeals court reinstated the injunction after a civil-liberties suit on behalf of providers and a family with a 16-year-old transgender girl on puberty blockers. Investigative supervisor testimony stated that trans-child cases faced different rules, with mandatory investigation regardless of evidence and a prohibition on discussing them by email or text. Earlier legislative efforts included two 2021 bills, one passed 18-13, to revoke the licences of doctors providing blockers to minors, while a further 2021 bill excludes a parent's refusal to affirm a child's gender identity or sexual orientation from the child-abuse definition.

A parental-rights statute enacted June 2025 bars school employees from teaching or discussing gender identity, bans LGBT-related student organisations, mandates deadnaming and misgendering of trans students and expands parental authority over schools.

As of 2021 no state law bars employment, housing, public-accommodations or insurance discrimination based on gender identity, though state courts recognised national employment protections in March 2021. The capital city and four other cities prohibit gender-identity discrimination in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations, with narrower city-employment or public-accommodation protections in ten further cities. A law effective 1 September 2025 explicitly listing banned diversity-programme provisions in schools and certain workplaces for sexual orientation is in effect and under court challenge, and voters passed a constitutional parental-rights amendment in November 2025.

Any adult may adopt regardless of sexual orientation, and legally married same-sex couples can adopt jointly and obtain supplemental birth certificates listing both parents. Lesbian couples may access IVF and assisted insemination, though health-plan IVF coverage requiring fertilisation only with the spouse's sperm restricts access, and even publicly funded adoption agencies may discriminate on religious beliefs.

Domestic-partner benefits are local matters: one county paid $300 per month cash subsidies in October 2012, three other counties allow partner participation, and one school district allows inclusion at full worker cost. A November 2013 voter-approved city measure in the largest city was interpreted to require spousal benefits for legally married same-sex couples, and an April 2013 opinion from the national justice department held the constitution bars political-subdivision benefits based on domestic-partnership status.

Same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised by a 2003 national ruling, but as of 2023 the state remains one of three states retaining a dormant same-sex-only sodomy statute termed deviate sexual intercourse; a 2025 lower-chamber repeal passed that chamber and failed in the upper chamber. The state retains a same-sex-exclusionary Romeo-and-Juliet affirmative defence allowing a defence only if the actor is not more than three years older than a child under 17 or is a spouse and not of the child's same sex, with no published constitutional challenge since the 2015 national marriage ruling.

Other resident-facing measures include a June 2019 statute barring adverse government action for supporting religious organisations that may refuse LGBTQ service, an October 2020 internal policy permitting social-worker discrimination against LGBT clients, the February 2022 removal of a national LGBTQ youth suicide-prevention organisation from state/province resources, and a rule effective in 2025 under which judges refusing same-sex weddings on religious grounds face no punishment.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence or killing figures for the state, so no comparison against the state's general homicide rate can be drawn from these sources.

Guidance accompanying the women's privacy statute remains unclear in these sources; opponents warn of uneven enforcement, and no identification-check episode later than 6 December 2025 is documented here.

The capital-city school district investigation was escalated on 27 April 2026, and no outcome is sourced.

The prefiled November 2022 bill on gender-variant performance has no documented status after pre-filing, and the court challenge to the law effective 1 September 2025 has no documented outcome in these sources.

Whether existing driver's licences or birth certificates carrying a changed gender marker can be renewed or amended after the September 2025 definition act is not sourced here.

The July 2026 risk assessment's tiering has no later update in this inventory.

This state/province is a sub-unit of the country and stands under the national framework carried by the parent record and the parent bundle; what follows is its own law and practice.

A national trans legal risk assessment dated July 2026 places it in a Low-Risk group of nine jurisdictions, defined there as jurisdictions that largely refrain from targeting transgender adults without specialising in their protection.

There is no ban in this state/province on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity; a national equality-mapping project records no such restriction here.

Since 2013, under a state/province anti-discrimination act, discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity has been prohibited in employment, housing, public accommodations and other areas. The bill passed the upper chamber 11-7 on 6 June 2013, passed the lower chamber 24-17 with amendments, passed the upper chamber on amendments 11-9 on 18 June, was signed the next day and took effect immediately.

Since 2013 the state/province has imposed additional penalties for a violent crime motivated by the victim's actual or perceived gender identity.

A 2023 bill that would formally repeal the common-law gay and trans panic defence and ban its use was introduced in May 2023 and passed both chambers of the legislature in June 2023; the source records the governor as having neither signed nor vetoed it.

The state/province allows a change of legal gender marker on state/province-issued identification on the signed statement of a licensed medical provider alone. Since 11 February 2017 sex reassignment surgery has not been an explicit requirement for an amended birth certificate, which instead requires a signed affidavit of surgical, hormonal, psychological or other treatment appropriate for gender transition. As of April 2020 the state/province did not offer a gender X marker on driver's licences.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 July 2013, with civil unions converted to marriages.

State/province-level protection machinery includes an executive order of 11 August 2009 extending anti-discrimination safeguards to state/province employees and applicants on the basis of gender identity, and an executive order signed in January 2025 creating an LGBTQ+ commission for the state/province.

The July 2026 assessment's own definition of the Low-Risk group is relative rather than protective: membership indicates that a jurisdiction largely refrains from targeting transgender adults, not that it legislates affirmatively for them. This state/province's classification should be read against that wording.

The state's core protections date from 2013 and predate the current national posture, so they operate as a state-level layer alongside national rules on travel documents and entry, which the parent record carries.

Two measures were unresolved at the time of sourcing: the 2023 bill on the gay and trans panic defence, passed in June 2023 but recorded without executive action, and the gender X question on driver's licences, for which the inventory supplies only an April 2020 position.

The state/province's anti-discrimination coverage of gender identity extends to employment, housing and public accommodations under the 2013 act, and an executive order of 11 August 2009 separately protects employees and applicants in state/province executive branch departments and agencies.

Since 26 March 2016 the state/province has prohibited discrimination based on gender identity within insurance contracts, including sex reassignment surgery.

A state/province statute introduced 26 April 2017 and signed and effective 23 July 2018 defines conversion therapy to include practices seeking to change gender identity, behaviours or gender expressions, and makes it unprofessional conduct subject to discipline for physicians, nurses, mental health and chemical addiction professionals, psychologists and clinical social workers who perform it on a minor or refer a minor out of jurisdiction for it; the state/province child-welfare department is barred from performing or recommending it for a minor.

A law signed 25 June 2015 and effective immediately allows inmates to access and change the name on birth certificates to reflect gender identity, where previously inmates could change names only for religious reasons.

An LGBTQ+ commission for the state/province was created by executive order in January 2025 under the governor.

The equality-mapping page on bathroom and facilities bans was not retrievable at the archived URL used (HTTP 404); the finding that this state/province has no such ban is carried from the underlying map rather than read off the page itself.

No state/province-specific policy on the placement of transgender inmates in custody here is documented in the inventory; national corrections guidance on this question is carried by the parent record.

The status of the 2023 panic-defence bill after its passage in June 2023 is unresolved in the sources: no signature, veto or later disposition is recorded.

The absence of a gender X option on the state/province's driver's licences is stated as of April 2020 and has not been verified as current.

The inventory supplies no state/province figures on enforcement of the 2013 gender-identity penalty enhancement or on reported incidents of anti-trans violence here.

The state/province restricts restroom and locker-room use by sex assigned at birth in public schools and government-owned buildings. A law introduced on 11 January 2024 and signed by the state/province governor on 30 January 2024 gives effect to that rule. It does not reach private businesses, so hotels, gyms and commercial venues fall outside it. New government buildings must include single-occupant facilities. A person facing a complaint may answer it with documentation: a birth certificate and, where the marker on that certificate has been changed, proof of gender-affirming surgery. The defence rests on records a visitor will generally not carry, and the law provides no alternative route for someone whose documents were issued outside the state/province.

Enforcement runs through complaints rather than police action. A reporting form allows residents to report transgender people in privacy spaces such as changing rooms and restrooms, and complainants may choose whether their own names are included while the state/province investigates each reported violation. A procedure adopted in May 2024 allows officials and individuals to file formal complaints about suspected incorrect bathroom use in schools and government buildings. A civil-liberties organisation opposed the law on the ground that it invites discriminatory enforcement.

In March 2025 the state/province enacted a ban on LGBTQ pride flags in public schools and government buildings. A May 2025 account places the signing on 7 May and describes the state/province as the first to prohibit such flags explicitly, with fines of $500 a day. A major city in the state/province adopted a flag modelled on the transgender pride flag as an official city flag in May 2025. A state/province advocacy organisation's executive director said the state/province leads the country in anti-LGBTQ legislation.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned. The ban passed the lower chamber on 26 January 2023 and the upper chamber 20-8 the following day, and was signed on 28 January 2023 with immediate effect; treatment already under way in January 2023 could continue. Clinicians may provide care to patients under 25, but those patients hold a retroactive right to disaffirm consent and sue. A legislative legal review found the ban potentially unconstitutional for targeting transgender people. A two-year systematic review commissioned under the ban and released in May 2025 concluded that the treatments are effective for mental health and psychosocial outcomes and for body changes consistent with an affirmed gender, and safe with respect to bone density, cardiovascular risk, metabolic change and cancer; the legislature dismissed the findings and kept the ban in force.

State/province-issued identity documents remain amendable. A transgender person may change the gender marker on a birth certificate on submission of a certified court order changing name and gender; surgery is not required, and an X descriptor is available subject to judicial approval. In May 2021 the highest court held 4-1 that judges must grant sex and name changes when the clinical requirements are met.

Nondiscrimination protection is partial. A 2015 statute bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment and housing but not in public accommodations, and exempts religious organisations and their affiliates, including schools and hospitals. The hate-crime statute amended in 2019 covers gender identity, carries enhanced penalties and requires the collection and publication of hate-crime statistics; those amendments passed the upper chamber 18-11 and the lower chamber 64-9, with concurrence 22-3, and were signed on 2 April 2019.

Sports participation has been contested for several years. A 2022 law barring transgender athletes from sports, athletics and the Olympics was vetoed by the governor on 22 March 2022 and enacted over the veto to take effect on 1 July; on 19 August a judge partly reversed it and allowed transgender girls to be considered case by case for girls' sports in 2022-2023. On 3 October 2024 two public universities forfeited matches against another university during litigation over a transgender player's eligibility. In 2024 the state/province also barred transgender students from dormitories matching their gender identity, after a transgender woman was assigned to a women's dormitory at a public university.

Marriage equality reached the state/province on 6 October 2014, after a national appellate court affirmed a lower court ruling of 20 December 2013 striking the ban; that ruling displaced a 1995 non-recognition statute and a 2004 constitutional amendment defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman, which voters approved 65.8 per cent to 33.2 per cent. Adoption follows from the recognition of the marriage. Foster care and adoption are otherwise limited to married or single persons, with cohabiting unmarried couples barred and priority given to married couples under a 1998 statute. For couples using in vitro fertilisation, parental recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational parent follows only from marriage. In August 2019 the highest court held the bar on same-sex surrogacy agreements unconstitutional.

Private consensual sexual conduct is not criminalised. The sodomy statute was invalidated by a national court ruling in 2003 and repealed by the legislature in 2019, following lower-chamber approval 74-0 with one abstention on 29 January, upper-chamber approval 25-2 with two abstentions on 22 February, and the governor's signature on 25 March 2019. Earlier changes had reduced the offence from a felony to a misdemeanour in 1969 and created an exemption for married couples in 1973.

Two neighbouring jurisdictions moved in the same direction on flags, signing comparable bans on LGBTQ pride flags at public buildings in 2025, while a city in one of them made the pride flag an official city flag. The pattern is not uniform across the region, since municipal counter-measures exist inside jurisdictions that restrict the symbol.

Within the state/province the two restrictive instruments differ in how they bite. The flag prohibition carries a financial penalty of $500 a day, while the facilities law operates through complaints filed by officials or private individuals and is supported by a public reporting form, with the documentary defence turning on records held by the person complained about.

The state/province corrections system is a documented site of harm for transgender prisoners. A March 2024 investigation by the national justice department found that the state/province corrections department discriminated against an inmate by denying gender-affirming hormones.

Conversion therapy on minors is prohibited by an executive order issued by the governor on 21 January 2020 and codified by legislation in February 2023. The prohibition covers LGBT minors but exempts clergy, religious counsellors, parents and grandparents unless they are acting as psychologists.

Schools operate under anti-bullying legislation in place since 2006, with parental notification added in 2013 and an administrative rule covering sexual orientation. A public university in the state/province has protected against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in employment since 1991, extended the policy to faculty duties in 1996, to student rights in 1997 and to admissions in 2009, and a major city ordinance adopted in 2009 and 2010 covers employment and housing.
