Two further state/province measures apply to residents. A March 2020 law bars personalised vehicle plates carrying offensive references to sexual orientation, and consumer privacy legislation effective 31 December 2023 explicitly includes sexual orientation.

No data on the number of complaints filed under the 2024 facilities law or through the reporting form, or on their outcomes, appears in the sources for this record; the mechanism is documented, its use is not.

Whether the documentary defence in the 2024 facilities law can be met by a visitor holding documents issued outside the state/province is not addressed by any state/province source consulted. Nor is it established how the state/province's own gender-marker rules interact with national passport and visa marker rules for incoming travellers.

The flag ban is dated inconsistently: one source places a ban in March 2025, another reports the signing on 7 May 2025. Whether the prohibition covers a city's own official flag, including the flag a major city in the state/province adopted in May 2025, is not resolved by the sources.

A legislative legal review found the 2023 care ban potentially unconstitutional for targeting transgender people, and the review's later treatment in litigation is not sourced here. The hate-crime statute requires the collection and publication of statistics, but no gender-identity-specific figures for the state/province were located.

No state/province-specific data on violence against transgender people was identified in the sources used for this record.

The state/province's own anti-discrimination statute prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage in force since 2008 and expanded again by the 2025 legislature, as documented in the legislature's own 2025 summary of gender-affirming-care and transgender legislation. As of 12 October 2026 the state/province's gender-identity policy and overall profile sit in the source's top bands, and a July 2026 national legal-risk assessment lists it among the most protective state/provinces for transgender people.

A 2025 state/province anti-discrimination act, signed by the governor on 16 May 2025 after passing on 6 May, requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, prohibits deadnaming and misgendering in workplaces and schools with immediate effect, and requires schools with dress codes to allow a student to choose from any uniform option. Its provisions simplifying changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences, and changes of name on marriage licences, take effect on 1 October 2026.

Gender markers on state/province documents are changeable without surgery. The state/province's public health board removed the surgical requirement unanimously in February 2019, ending a rule that had applied since 1 January 1984. A change is made by request, using a designation form to the motor vehicle division for licences and IDs and correction and designation forms to the health department for birth certificates. Birth certificates offer M, F, Intersex and X markers; IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus confirmation from a medical or mental health professional.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the state/province's civil rights division ruled that a transgender six-year-old could use the girls' restroom at her elementary school, and in 2023 the state/province implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. The anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

The hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001, with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a jury convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in a case described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The gay panic defence was abolished by a bipartisan bill passed in June 2020 and signed in July 2020, effective immediately.

Gender-affirming care is protected at state/province level but is under direct pressure. Legislation signed in April 2023 was enacted to protect, defend and guarantee gender-affirming healthcare services and to guarantee safe passage of transgender individuals from other jurisdictions. Since the beginning of 2023 basic health insurance coverage must explicitly include sexual reassignment surgery as a basic policy, and a July 2026 assessment counts the state/province among those with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. On 18 May 2026 the state/province's highest court ruled 5-2 that a children's hospital violated state/province anti-discrimination law when it suspended gender-affirming care for transgender youth under national pressure, and ordered a lower court to issue an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy. One justice wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth means the decision denies the petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity; two justices dissented, citing national threats that could shut the hospital system.

Conversion therapy has been banned statewide on minors since a bill signed on 31 May 2019. After the highest court's 8-1 ruling of 31 March 2026 requiring strict scrutiny of that ban, a bill passed on 8 May 2026 redefines conversion therapy as direction toward a pre-determined gender identity or sexual orientation outcome and removes the statute of limitations for claims.

Custody is governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged that the state/province corrections department subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care. The court-approved 2024 consent decree entered in a district court in the state/province's largest city required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing comprising a 100-bed unit at the men's prison and an integration unit at the women's prison, and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. A separate 2019 settlement paid a transgender inmate $170,000 over her safety while held in a men's prison. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief won through consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

Three ballot measures certified for the November 2026 vote would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into state/province law. One would ban transgender children from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex, another would prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics, and a third concerns child sex trafficking. The measures were pushed by conservative activists and signatures were certified by state/province elections officials on 17 March 2026.

Restrictions on transgender students in school sport have been adopted at district level. In April 2025 one school board voted 3-2 to advance a policy banning biologically male students from female sports and the reverse; a second board voted 6-1 in June 2025 for a similar policy, with a third district following suit. In December 2025 an undisclosed lawsuit settlement was reached over the banning of trans individuals from playing on female sports teams within some association governing districts, and the terms of that settlement are not public.

The state/province's protective framework is operating under direct national funding pressure. Its own public health-insurance agency has said that restoring coverage suspended under a national rule will require legislative action, which indicates that state/province-level protection does not by itself hold when national funding conditions change. A visitor assessing this state/province should read its protections together with that constraint rather than as a fixed ceiling on what the state/province can deliver.

The state/province will suspend public health-insurance coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning 13 October 2026, because a national rule finalised in August 2026 blocks national funds for such care for people under 18, and under 19 under a child health programme. The state/province's health-insurance agency said resuming coverage will require legislative action. About 500 youth under 19 received covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25. Patients already taking hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period, and behavioural healthcare is unaffected.

The anti-bullying law requires school districts to adopt prevention policies covering bullying on the basis of gender identity, and schools with dress codes must allow any uniform option under the 2025 act. These are resident-facing obligations on school districts rather than rules a visitor would encounter.

Implementation of the 2025 act's document provisions is dated 1 October 2026, so changes of gender identity on birth certificates and driver's licences and changes of name on marriage licences made before that date proceed under the earlier procedures.

The outcome of the November 2026 ballot measures is unresolved; the sports measure and the surgery measure were certified for the vote but their passage and any subsequent litigation are not sourced here.

The terms of the December 2025 lawsuit settlement concerning trans individuals barred from female sports teams in some association governing districts are undisclosed in the sources, so which districts are bound and on what terms remains unresolved.

Compliance with the 18 May 2026 highest-court order is not sourced beyond the direction to a lower court to issue an injunction; whether the children's hospital resumed puberty blockers and hormone therapy, and whether other hospitals in the state/province altered care under national pressure, is unresolved.

Whether the 2025 act's document-change provisions are operating as written after their 1 October 2026 effective date is not documented in the sources.

The status of the conversion-therapy regime after the May 2026 amendment, including any challenge to the redefined statute or to the strict-scrutiny standard set in the March 2026 ruling, is unresolved.

No state/province-specific figure for killings or violence against transgender people, measured against the general homicide rate, appears in the sources; no such comparison can be made from this inventory.

The national layer, including passport and visa markers, entry screening, national custody policy and national care restrictions, is carried by the parent nation's record and is not restated here.

A July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map places the state/province in its 'Low-Risk' tier, describing it as having enacted fairly robust non-discrimination policies while falling short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity is unlawful in the state/province under its civil-rights act, following a July 2022 ruling by the state/province's highest court that affirmed the national justice department's appeal; the legislature codified the protection in a bill passed in March 2023 and signed by the state/province governor on 8 March 2023. The ruling built on a 21 May 2018 state/province civil-rights commission interpretation adopted 5-0 and on a 7 March 2018 national appellate decision holding that national employment law prohibits employment discrimination against transgender people. Sexual-orientation protection followed the same route, from a December 2003 executive order and a March 2013 marina-loan non-discrimination provision through the May 2018 commission interpretation to the March 2023 codification.

Hate-crime law covers gender identity implicitly within the state/province's 1992 hate-crime statute under the category 'gender', per an August 2021 court declaration. A hate-crime package adding 'gender identity or expression' explicitly passed the lower chamber in June 2023 and the upper chamber in December 2024, was signed in January 2025 and took effect 90 days after signature. Sexual orientation has been recognised for hate-crime data collection since 1992.

The gay and trans panic defence was abolished by a law passed, signed and implemented in July 2024.

Conversion therapy is banned throughout the state/province under a bill passed by both chambers in June 2023 and signed in July 2023, following a June 2021 executive order barring taxpayer dollars or funding for conversion therapy on minors.

Sex on a birth certificate can be changed without sexual reassignment surgery under a 30 June 2021 court ruling that declared the 1978 surgery and physician-statement requirement unconstitutional; the position was certified and codified by a bill passed in December 2024. Changing sex on a driver's licence or state/province ID requires a signed statutory declaration and a fee under the system in place since November 2019.

Marriage between two people of the same sex is legal in the state/province under a national supreme court decision of 26 June 2015. The state/province had barred it by a 1995 statute signed by the governor at the time and by a 2004 constitutional amendment approved with 58.6% of the vote, which also barred civil unions. In litigation over the ban the district court held it unconstitutional on 21 March 2014; more than 300 licences were issued on 22 March 2014 before national appellate stays, and the national appellate court reversed on 6 November 2014.

The state/province's sodomy statute has not been repealed by the legislature even though same-sex sexual activity is legal under a national supreme court decision of 2003. The statute as written applied to both homosexual and heterosexual conduct, and the state/province and one neighbouring jurisdiction are the only ones in its part of the parent nation without statutory codification.

The state/province's highest court announced a September 2023 decision on respecting an individual's pronouns for judges.

In March 2025 the lower chamber adopted a bipartisan resolution urging the state/province high-school athletic association to ban transgender athletes from girls' and women's sports. The measure is advisory and does not change state/province law or the state/province's non-discrimination protections. The association has cited potential conflicts between an executive order and the gender-identity non-discrimination provision of the state/province civil-rights act.

State/province government employment protections cover gender identity under a 2007 extension and a January 2019 executive order that reaches state/province employment, contractors and grantees. Insurance companies and corporations are explicitly barred from discriminating on the basis of gender identity under a bill passed by both chambers in October 2023 and signed by the state/province governor. A state/province commission was established in June 2023.

Local conversion-therapy bans predate the statewide prohibition, including a municipal ordinance of August 2020, punishable by up to 90 days' imprisonment and a $500 fine.

The sources do not confirm whether driver's licences and state/province IDs carry an 'X' gender marker. The marker was announced in January 2020 as forthcoming and was still described as 'soon' in November 2021, with no later confirmation in the inventory.

The risk map's finding that the state/province falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people is stated without state/province-specific detail. No state/province-specific care restriction, custody policy or enforcement incident appears in the inventory.

The scope of the state/province's highest court's September 2023 pronoun decision is not described beyond judges.

The legislature has not repealed the sodomy statute; whether repeal is pending is not sourced.

No state/province-specific data on anti-trans violence or on enforcement statistics was identified in the sources.

The state/province restricts transgender people from using bathrooms, locker rooms and changing areas matching their gender identity in public schools and state/province-owned buildings under a 2025 law signed by the governor on 20 March 2025 and announced the following day. The law took effect on 1 July 2025 and passed the lower legislative chamber 49-21. Its scope covers state/province-run facilities, primarily K-12 schools and state/province colleges, including off-campus activities. It is the first facilities restriction of its kind to be enacted in the state/province, after comparable bills failed in 2016, 2017, twice in 2018 and in 2022.

The law's "reasonable accommodation" clause and the floor debate around it raised the prospect that incarcerated transgender people would be placed in solitary confinement in order to comply.

No statute in the state/province explicitly prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the state/province's hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. National law supplies the only backstop: employment protection as construed in a national court decision of 2020 and national hate-crime prosecution under a 2009 national statute.

Identity documents are closed to gender-marker change. On 5 March 2026 the state/province's highest court ruled that a transgender person cannot amend the sex designation on a birth certificate to reflect gender identity, affirming the denial of a plaintiff's September 2024 petition to change the marker from male to female and holding that a change is permitted only to correct an error made at birth. A legal gender change on a driver's licence or state/province ID remains available by court order or a physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery, and on a birth certificate by court order, photo ID, application and fee.

Gender-affirming care for people under 18 is banned under a 2023 law, passed in February 2023 and signed on 13 February 2023. The law required prior puberty-blocker or hormone treatment to be systematically reduced, ending no later than 31 December 2023, and authorises affected people to sue until age 25 or within three years of discovering an injury.

An advocacy legal-risk assessment published in July 2026 lists the state/province among the worst states/provinces for legislation targeting transgender adults, drawing on five years of daily legislative tracking and a rubric for the most severe bills.

State/provincial institutions have also acted against transgender health provision directly. On 16 December 2022 the state/province terminated a transgender advocacy organisation's $136,000 nationally funded Community Health Worker contract for LGBTQ+ and transgender community health in one municipality. To settle the organisation's discrimination lawsuit, the state/province's health secretary issued an apology letter on 17 January 2024 acknowledging the termination and differential treatment compared with other Community Health Worker contractors, affirming equal treatment under law regardless of race, colour, national origin, religion, disability, age or sex; the state/province paid $300,000 covering attorney fees, committed not to discriminate against the organisation in violation of state/provincial or national law in any services, programmes or activities, and allowed the retention of a community health worker.

Transgender participation in female school sports was restricted by executive order in March 2021, after the governor declined to sign a broader legislative ban over college-sports concerns, and then by statute signed on 4 February 2022 and effective 1 July 2022; a civil-liberties organisation threatened litigation.

Earlier legislative attempts set the pattern. A March 2016 bill requiring transgender students to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching birth sex was vetoed by the governor, and a 2019 bill barring K-7 instruction on gender identity and expression passed the lower chamber on 12 February 2019 but failed in the upper chamber on 29 March 2019.

A March 2021 law signed by the governor allows businesses to deny goods or services to LGBTQ people on the basis of owners' purported religious beliefs, and a 2017 law signed on 10 March 2017 permits taxpayer-funded foster care and adoption agencies to deny services to LGBT people, including qualified LGBT prospective parents, on religious grounds.

Protection below the state/provincial level is patchy. One county and several municipalities provide limited public-employee or, in one municipality's March 2018 ordinance, comprehensive employment, housing and public-accommodations protections; further municipalities also provide limited public-employee protections. In September 2019 a tribal council passed hate-crime legislation protecting LGBT and two-spirit individuals by a 14-2-1 vote.

Marriage between two people regardless of sex has been recognised in the state/province since 26 June 2015 under a national court decision, superseding a November 2006 constitutional amendment and statutes defining marriage as between a man and a woman and barring recognition of other unions. The change followed a national court ruling filed 22 May 2014, in which the judge ruled for the plaintiffs on 12 January 2015, with the ruling stayed pending appeal.

Adoption law does not specify rules for single individuals or married same-sex couples; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation with non-genetic married mothers recognised after donor insemination, and gay male couples may use surrogacy with pre-birth orders, but a 2017 resolution permits agencies to refuse placements that violate their religious or moral convictions.

How the 2025 facilities law is enforced in state/province custody is unresolved: the enacted text does not specify how the "reasonable accommodation" requirement is to be met, and the solitary-confinement prospect was raised in floor debate rather than written into the statute.

Whether the driver's licence and state/province ID gender-change procedure remains operative after the March 2026 birth-certificate ruling is not sourced; the two concern different documents and the ruling addressed birth certificates only.

The document-change procedures described here are drawn from a reference article on LGBTQ rights in the state/province and have not been confirmed against current state/provincial agency guidance.

The July 2026 legal-risk ranking is an advocacy assessment built on a bill-severity rubric, not a legal determination, and its placement of the state/province should be read as a legislative-trend indicator rather than a statement of enforceable law.

In August 2026 a mob beat a transgender couple over restroom use at a public park in one municipality. One of the two, who has a pre-existing spinal injury, and the other, who suffered a concussion and blood pooling, were both charged with disturbing the peace; local law enforcement recorded no arrest of any attacker that day, and a plea deal had not been signed. One of the two was denied hospital care and taken to a men's jail.

That person was held in a men's facility and searched by a male guard even though her driver's licence carries a female marker. The marker on her licence did not determine her housing or her search procedure in custody.

In the same period the municipality voted one of the most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances in the country.

Gender-marker changes on state/province documents require surgical proof. A driver's licence marker change requires a physician-signed statement confirming successful sex reassignment surgery; a new birth certificate requires a certified court order confirming surgical gender change, with proof of a diagnosis recorded as "transsexual or pseudo-hermaphrodite" and of anatomical change.

The state/province's 1997 hate-crime statute provides penalty enhancements for offences motivated by sexual orientation or perceived sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity, so gender-identity bias crimes fall to national prosecution under the national hate-crimes statute of 2009.

Gender-affirming care for minors is banned: the legislature overrode the governor's June 2023 veto in July 2023, and the ban on puberty blockers, hormones and surgery took effect on 1 January 2024.

Marriage is recognised after the 2015 invalidation of the state/province's 2004 constitutional ban on marriage and civil unions and its 1988 and 1999 civil-code provisions; married couples hold full joint adoption and parental rights, following a 2014 state court ruling that granted the state/province's first adoption by a same-sex couple.

The state/province's unenforceable sodomy statute remains on the books, carrying up to five years' imprisonment, a $2,000 fine and sex-offender registration; a repeal bill failed 66-27 in April 2014.

The state/province has no law prohibiting gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations. An equality-index research organisation places both its gender-identity policy and its overall policy in the source's lowest band as of 12 October 2026, leaving national employment-discrimination processes as the main recourse. Two municipalities prohibit gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations; several other municipalities and one parish extend protection only to public employees.

The state/province's sex-education statute prohibits classes from discussing male or female homosexual activity.

A 2017 amendment to the state/province's domestic-violence law removed opposite-sex language, so sentencing no longer differs by the sexes of the parties; it passed 54-42 in the lower chamber and 25-13 in the upper chamber and took effect on 1 August 2017.

The state/province barred transgender girls from public-school sports in June 2022, with more than two-thirds support in both chambers; a 2021 bill passed the lower chamber 77-17 and the upper chamber 29-6 but was vetoed, and the override failed by two votes.

Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black transgender woman serving a life sentence at a state/province prison, was killed on 2 April 2024 in a fight with several other inmates. A national advocacy organisation records her death in its memorial to transgender people killed that year.

Executive orders barring sexual-orientation discrimination in state/province employment, issued in 1992, 2004 and 2016, all lapsed, expired or were struck down and upheld on appeal in March 2018, leaving no protection on that ground for state/province employees.

Transition-related surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy are excluded from health insurance and from the public health coverage programme for low-income residents, so residents pay for care out of pocket.

Two further bills related to the 2023 minors' care ban remained awaiting legislative action when the sources were compiled; their status is unresolved.

A national advocacy organisation states that killings of transgender and gender-expansive people are systematically under- or mis-reported, so the number of such deaths in the state/province is not reliably established.

The plea deal in the August 2026 attack had not been signed at the time of reporting; the outcome of the charges against the two victims is unresolved.

The sources describe a municipal restroom ordinance in one municipality; they do not describe any statewide facilities statute, so the state/province-level position on restroom access is not established by them.

The state/province's care-access law is the most protective element of its own record. In September 2022 the governor signed a state bill making this state/province the first to declare itself a sanctuary for transgender young people seeking medical care. Youth from outside this state/province can obtain hormones and puberty blockers here, and the law shields families from child-abuse investigations or criminal prosecution for seeking gender-affirming care, including families who travel to the state/province for it.

The state/province's prison system is the one documented instance of identity-based placement in this inventory. As of January 2021 this state/province is coded as the single sub-unit allowing transgender inmates to be housed according to their gender identity, with housing assigned identity-based within the general population and no trans-only separate facility documented. In 2015 this state/province became the first sub-unit to fund gender-affirming surgeries for transgender prison inmates, and coverage by a state/province public broadcaster of the state/province corrections department's operational guidelines that year confirms the identity-based care and guidance posture while containing no explicit statement of a trans-only unit or segregation practice. The most recent documented statement of this housing practice in this record is dated January 2021; no later instance is documented.

Recorded hostility sits alongside that protective framework. A national LGBTQ monitoring group documented more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents nationwide in 2025, of which this state/province recorded 198, the highest figure of any state/province. That ranking is by raw count only: the source supplies no population or per-capita denominator, so the count does not establish that this state/province is riskier for an individual visitor than a smaller sub-unit.

A separate analysis of the same 2025 incident data reports a dramatic increase in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports in the state/province's largest city in law-enforcement data covering the same period as the governor's platforming of anti-trans figures.

A July 2026 analysis places this state/province in a top-tier protective-law band with a low recorded-incident count, and argues that even the most protective statutory floors do not eliminate recorded hostility.

The same 2025 national incident count that puts this state/province at 198 records a neighbouring sub-unit at 72, another at 66, and two further sub-units at 50 each. The comparison is between raw counts across sub-units of very different population sizes, and the source provides no per-capita adjustment.

This state/province's prison housing posture is distinguished in the source from another sub-unit, which is described as the one place maintaining separate facilities reserved for transgender people only. The model here is identity-based placement within the general population rather than a dedicated unit.

The July 2026 analysis sets the recorded-incident count against the protective-law rating to argue that statutory protection and recorded hostility coexist, which bears on how much weight a visitor should place on the sub-unit's legal posture when judging day-to-day exposure.

The care-access shield operates for families in this state/province and for families who travel here for care, protecting them from child-abuse investigations and criminal prosecution over gender-affirming care sought for a young person.

Transgender people held in this state/province's prisons are housed according to their gender identity within the general population under corrections-department guidelines documented from 2015, and the state corrections system funds gender-affirming surgery for transgender inmates, a provision introduced in 2015 as the first such funding in the country.

This state/province recorded 198 of the more than 1,000 anti-LGBTQ incidents logged nationally in 2025, and its largest city saw a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ hate-crime reports to law enforcement over that period.

Whether the identity-based prison housing policy documented as of January 2021 remains in force is unresolved in this inventory; no source dated after that point confirms or contradicts it, and no trans-only facility in this state/province is documented either way.

The 198-incident figure for 2025 has no denominator in the sources, so its per-capita significance is unresolved; the ranking of sub-units is by raw count only.

The methodology behind the July 2026 figures of the law rating and the recorded-incident count is not stated in the inventory, including what the 1.9 counts or over what period.

No region-specific information is sourced here on facility or bathroom access, identity-document and gender-marker rules, entry screening, or hate-crime statute coverage; those layers sit in the national record or are not covered by this inventory.

The state/province sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate/driver-licence restrictions and withdrawal of legal recognition. The same ranking places the least protective states at the opposite end, with prison terms of up to five years for youth-care provision and arrest policies for gender-identity bathroom use.

Gender identity and expression have been protected statewide in credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act was signed in January 2019 and took effect in February 2019, building on a 2009 executive order barring gender-identity discrimination in state/provincial employment and Division of Human Rights regulations issued 4 November 2015, effective 20 January 2016, covering transgender harassment and discrimination in those domains. A 2024 constitutional amendment explicitly bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with further anti-bias reform bills signed in November 2022. The gay and transgender panic defence was repealed in June 2019, effective immediately, making this the sixth state/province to abolish it. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned effective 25 January 2019.

Since 2014 transgender adults could change the gender on birth certificates with a notarized medical affidavit verifying surgery or a gender dysphoria diagnosis; this was updated in 2020 to allow self-affirmation, with parental consent required for those under 17. The June 2021 Gender Recognition Act allowed an X marker on driver's licences and eased sealing of name- and gender-change records. An X marker on the state/province's largest city's birth certificates took effect 1 January 2019 and on death certificates from 2 January 2020; X was reported for state/provincial court and jury documents in November 2019 and in healthcare data from August 2020; X on all state/provincial forms was approved in April 2022 for 2023, with some organizations until 2024, alongside updatable marriage certificates. A November 2021 law effective 1 January 2022 requires utilities and municipalities to use preferred names and pronouns.

Shield protections apply. A national healthcare equality map, data as of 27 September 2026, lists the state/province as having a shield law or executive order from 2023: the shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care legal here was banned in their home jurisdiction, which is directly relevant to visitors travelling from ban jurisdictions. Nationally, 16 states/provinces and the national capital district, covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold shields, while 32 states/provinces and five state/provinces, covering 56%, hold none. The largest city issued an executive order on 12 June 2023 barring city resources from being used to detain, prosecute or investigate the provision or receipt of gender-affirming care. A state/provincial law of 25 June 2023, making this the twelfth shield jurisdiction, bars courts from enforcing out-of-jurisdiction laws removing custody over youth gender-affirming care, bars treating such care as child abuse, and bars law-enforcement cooperation with out-of-jurisdiction agencies. A September 2023 municipal ordinance and April 2025 city council bills expanded provider protections.

Former Penal Law Section 240.37, in effect since 1976 and used by police to harass and arrest transgender individuals, was repealed in February 2021, effective immediately. Gender-neutral bathrooms were mandated by a law signed in December 2020, effective 23 March 2021. The anti-bullying law covers gender, including gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying, in all public elementary and secondary schools, with a 2019 loophole closure. A June 2023 law explicitly includes gender identity in drug treatment and addiction programmes, and a November 2020 law requires annual judiciary statistics by gender identity.

One county remains the only county in the state/province banning transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities, with a 2025 ruling finding no clear violation of anti-discrimination laws and a civil-liberties lawsuit seeking inclusion.

Same-sex marriage became legal statewide under a Marriage Equality Act passed 24 June 2011 and effective 24 July 2011, following a May 2008 directive recognizing out-of-jurisdiction marriages. Consenting adult same-sex sexual activity was legalized by a 1980 court decision, with defunct sodomy provisions affecting National Guard employees repealed effective 2000. A 2019 law granted state/provincial veterans benefits to those dishonorably discharged under a 1993–2011 national policy.

On 16 December 2009 the state/province barred state/provincial agencies from discriminating on the basis of gender identity in all state/provincial-employment matters including hiring, termination, retention, appointment, promotion, tenure, recruitment and compensation, defining gender identity as having or being perceived as having a gender identity, self-image, appearance, behavior or expression whether or not different from sex assigned at birth, and ordered equal-opportunity efforts, consistent guidelines and swift confidential complaint investigations, effective immediately.

The state/province's protective posture operates inside a national framework that has moved sharply against trans people since January 2025. National passport and visa rules, national facility mandates, national custody policies and national healthcare funding restrictions apply at the border and in nationally controlled settings regardless of state/provincial law; a visitor's exposure at entry, in national buildings, or in national custody is governed by those national rules, not by this state/province's statutes.

The July 2026 ranking that places the state/province in the Most Protective tier is a rubric over tracked bills and enacted laws, not a measure of incidents or of enforcement on the ground. Its contrast tier identifies one state/province with prison terms of up to five years and another with an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use, which shows the spread of the national picture this state/province sits apart from.

The shield-law count is a national distribution: 16 states/provinces and the national capital district hold shields covering 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, while 32 states/provinces and five state/provinces covering 56% hold none. This state/province's shield therefore protects people who travel here for care, but offers no protection once they return to a ban jurisdiction.

Public-attitude polling cited in the source shows support for discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity rising from 75% in 2017, with 19% opposed, to 82% in 2022, with 14% opposed; same-sex marriage support moved from 69% in 2017 to 75% in 2022. These figures are LGBTQ-general and do not isolate transgender-specific attitudes.

Residents benefit from the full stack of state/provincial protections: the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act's statewide coverage of credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since February 2019, the 2009 executive order on state/provincial employment, the 2015 Division of Human Rights regulations, and the 2024 constitutional amendment barring gender-identity discrimination.

Birth-certificate gender change has been available since 2014 by notarized medical affidavit, self-affirmation since 2020 with parental consent for minors, and the June 2021 Gender Recognition Act added X markers on driver's licences and easier sealing of name- and gender-change records. X markers extend to the largest city's birth certificates (1 January 2019), death certificates (2 January 2020), state/provincial court and jury documents (November 2019), healthcare data (August 2020) and all state/provincial forms approved in April 2022 for 2023, with some organizations until 2024. Utilities and municipalities must use preferred names and pronouns under a law effective 1 January 2022.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with anti-bias reform bills signed November 2022. The panic defence was repealed in June 2019. Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 25 January 2019. Penal Law Section 240.37, used to arrest transgender people, was repealed in February 2021. Gender-neutral bathrooms have been mandated since 23 March 2021.

Shield statutes protect residents and providers: the 12 June 2023 city executive order, the 25 June 2023 state/provincial law barring enforcement of out-of-jurisdiction custody-removal orders and law-enforcement cooperation, a September 2023 municipal ordinance and April 2025 city council bills.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 24 July 2011 under the Marriage Equality Act. Adoption non-discrimination for gay and lesbian applicants dates to 1982, second-parent adoption was protected by 1995 rulings, joint same-sex adoption was allowed by 2004, though an October 2020 district court order allowed religious-affiliated agencies to turn away gay, single and unmarried heterosexual couples. Commercial surrogacy, banned from 1992 to 2020, was legalized effective February 2021, with a February 2021 requirement that insurance cover same-sex couples for IVF, surrogacy and fertility treatments, amid an April 2022 lawsuit by a male same-sex couple alleging only heterosexual and female same-sex couples receive coverage.

One county bans transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities; a 2025 ruling found no clear violation of anti-discrimination laws and a civil-liberties lawsuit has been filed for inclusion.

SONDA, effective 2003, prohibits actual or perceived sexual orientation discrimination and explicitly includes asexuality. The Hate Crimes Act has covered sexual orientation since 1 July 2001. Under a 2012 court decision, labeling someone gay or homosexual is no longer defamation. Parade bans ended in September 2014 in the largest city and November 2024 in one borough. A 1985 law enabling municipalities to close gay bathhouses and saunas remains in effect as of August 2026. Adultery was repealed in November 2024.

The state/province's largest city is home to the largest transgender population in the country, estimated at 50,000 in 2018 and concentrated in two boroughs, within broader 2005 estimates of 272,493 self-identifying gay and bisexual individuals in the city and 568,903 LGB residents in the metropolitan area.

The source's societal-tolerance language — that the state/province has "generally been seen as socially liberal" and that attitudes moved "from general antipathy and hostility to tolerance and acceptance" — refers to the LGBTQ community generally, not to transgender people specifically; the article provides no trans-specific tolerance quote distinct from LGBTQ-general wording. This is unresolved in the inventory.

The inventory does not document any trans-specific violence incident in this state/province, nor any figure that could be compared against a general homicide rate, so no trans-specific violence magnitude can be stated here.

The 2018 estimate of 50,000 transgender residents in the largest city is a population count, not a risk measure, and the 2005 metropolitan LGB figures are two decades old.

Whether the 2025 ruling on the county sports ban will survive the pending civil-liberties litigation is unresolved in the inventory.

The April 2022 insurance-coverage lawsuit by a male same-sex couple over IVF and surrogacy coverage has no documented outcome in the inventory.

How this state/province's shield statutes interact with national healthcare funding restrictions and national enforcement pressure after January 2025 is not addressed in the inventory.

The measure, signed by the governor and effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a transgender person to use a restroom or changing room that does not match the sex assigned at birth. It reaches government buildings and public-facing private businesses, including gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues and hospitals. A first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail. A civil-rights organisation filed suit on 30 April 2026 on due-process, equal-protection and privacy grounds, arguing the law targets no criminal conduct; six transgender residents of the state/province are plaintiffs in the challenge, brought before the effect date. According to that organisation, this is the only state/province law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses, and it carries steeper penalties than other jurisdictions' bans.

This state/province's bathroom statute is the only law of its kind reaching private businesses, and the civil-rights organisation assesses its penalties as steeper than comparable bans. The state/province's continued X option on driver's licences and identity cards diverges from the position on national travel documents, so a visitor may hold a state/province-issued credential that does not match the marker available on a passport.

A 2022 bill that passed the lower chamber and would have imposed felony liability and up to life imprisonment on parents who took their children out of the state/province for gender-affirming care was blocked in the upper chamber. A bill passed by the lower chamber in February 2024 and pending in the upper chamber would recognise only male and female throughout state/province law.

The state/province bars any change of sex on birth certificates, permitting only male or female sex at birth. The 2018 implementation law was allowed into legal effect in January 2026, ending a period from 6 April 2018 when transgender people could change birth certificates to reflect gender identity after a 2017 lawsuit. A 2020 statute that would have reversed that position was ruled moot and unenforceable on 7 August 2020 by a district judge, with $321,000 in attorneys' fees awarded to a civil-rights legal organisation and approved in August 2022.

In November 2019 the state/province health board removed doctor approval for a gender change for transgender minors, retaining parental permission, emancipation or a court order as the routes.

Transgender prisoners may receive hormone therapy under a September 2024 national ruling that nullified a 1997 state/province law banning it.

An April 2024 law bars teachers and education agencies from using pronouns for students that are not based on birth certificates. Transgender athletes are barred from public school and university teams matching their gender identity under legislation signed 30 March 2020. A March 2026 law requires schools, childcare providers and medical professionals to disclose a transgender minor's status to parents within three days of learning it.

Municipal and county ordinances covering gender identity reach about 40% of the population, including employee protection in one county.

Sources differ on the classification of the bathroom offence: a civil-rights organisation describes a first offence as a misdemeanour carrying up to one year in jail, while one encyclopedia entry describes it as a felony. The discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the 16 June 2026 narrowing by a district judge remains in force, and the outcome of the civil-rights organisation's suit, are not established by the sources reviewed.

No record of enforcement action under the measure against a visitor or resident was identified in the sources reviewed.

No state/province-specific data on violence against transgender people that is materially above the general homicide rate was identified in the sources reviewed.

The current litigation status of the 2018 birth-certificate implementation law is not sourced.

Visitors to the state/province face state/province law that regulates gender presentation in public, restricts access to sex-segregated facilities by birth sex, and criminalises some categories of performance. The 2023 adult-entertainment law (SB 3/HB 9) defines "adult cabaret entertainment" to include male or female impersonators and prohibits it on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony with 1 to 6 years and fines to $3,000.

The drag ban has survived challenge. A national judge held it vague and overbroad in June 2023, but the appeals-court ruling upholding the law now stands and the national supreme court declined to hear challenges to it. A separate suit remains ongoing.

Facility use is governed by birth sex. Under a women's safety and protection Act passed in April 2026, transgender people must use only facilities matching their sex assigned at birth, trans women are barred from women's shelters, and transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons by sex assigned at birth. A 2019 statute separately defines a transgender person using the bathroom corresponding with their gender identity as indecent exposure. The 2021 requirement that small businesses post warning signs in such circumstances was struck down in May 2022 on First Amendment grounds and is not in force; the 2021 ban on transgender students using public-school bathrooms matching their identity has been in litigation since August 2021.

Identity documents are effectively closed. Change of sex on an original birth certificate has been prohibited under the state code since 1977, and a 2023 law signed by the state's governor defines sex by anatomy and genetics existing at birth. The state vehicle-licensing agency refused a legally transitioned transgender woman a gender change on her driver's licence, prompting a suit filed by a national civil-liberties group in a county court on 23 April 2024; the outcome of that suit is not sourced here.

Gender-affirming care is barred for minors. A bill signed 1 March 2023 makes it illegal to provide such healthcare to anyone under 18 in state/province or through out-of-state telehealth, banned new care after 1 July 2023 and required existing care to be withdrawn by 31 March 2024, authorises regret suits against parents, guardians and physicians, and permits $25,000 actions by the state's chief prosecutor against providers. The national supreme court upheld it as not violating equal protection on 18 June 2025. A May 2024 law adds civil penalties for adults who help a minor obtain such care, and April 2024 legislation bans the care for inmates.

Violence against trans women is documented at a high rate. A July 2026 national analysis using international monitoring data records 10 killings of trans women in the state between 2008 and 2025, a rate of 7.8 per 100,000 per year, and treats that figure as an undercount floor rather than a complete count; the same analysis places the state in its worst tier for laws passed.

The gay and trans panic defence remains available to lower or eliminate punishment for fatal attacks, and reporting from April 2021 describes police and legal officials turning a blind eye to assaults on LGBTQ people while treating attractions as sin. LGBTQ people in the state are reported to be discriminated against, refused service and beaten.

The hate-crime statute has covered bias based on sexual orientation since 2001 but does not list gender identity. A February 2019 opinion by the state's chief prosecutor concluded that selecting a victim because they are transgender qualifies for enhancement under the state's sentencing provision as a crime committed because of gender. The state criminal-investigation agency recorded 0 anti-transgender incidents in 2019, 1 in 2020 and 2 in 2021; these are raw recorded counts with no population denominator and reflect recording and reporting practices rather than incidence.

Marriage is available on the same terms as elsewhere in the country, but a law signed 21 February 2024 allows government employees to refuse to solemnise marriages that conflict with their personal beliefs.

The state/province's relative position is measured consistently low. A national equality organisation's 2024 index records that the state lacked statewide non-discrimination protections in employment, housing and public accommodations and was among the states most likely to have religious-refusal or other anti-LGBTQ+ laws; a 2024 assessment by the same organisation also classified the state among the lowest-ranking for LGBTQ rights.

The July 2026 national analysis that produces the 7.8 per 100,000 killing rate ranks jurisdictions by state-level tallies of killings of trans women; its own figure for this state/province rests on 10 recorded deaths across 18 years, a count small enough that a single additional year moves the rate substantially.

Drag-law litigation has a longer history than the current position suggests. The 2023 adult-entertainment law was halted before enforcement in March 2023 and declared vague and overbroad in June 2023 by a national judge, with the state's chief prosecutor appealing and oral argument held 1 February 2024. In one county, a district attorney's August 2023 threat against a Pride event was enjoined on 1 September 2023. The national supreme court's refusal to hear challenges left the appellate ruling upholding the law as the operative position, with a further suit still running.

Reporting from April 2021 compared the economic and social effects of the state's bathroom legislation to the 2016 backlash in a neighbouring jurisdiction, where similar laws produced corporate and event withdrawals.

Local protections exist but are narrow. Public-employment ordinances in several municipalities do not reach private employers and are blocked as to them by a state/province preemption statute, and a further bill would bar agencies from considering business anti-discrimination policies for taxpayer contracts. Workplace protection comes through national case law rather than state/province statute: a March 2018 national appeals-court ruling and a June 2020 national supreme court decision hold that firing a person for being LGBTQ violates the national employment statute.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the state/province since 1996, after a unanimous state/province appeals court decision and legislative repeal the same year.

Trans residents have no state/province statutory protection against discrimination in employment, housing or public accommodations; the protections they hold in the workplace derive from national employment-statute litigation. A January 2021 national school-enforcement directive covering gay, lesbian and transgender students was preliminarily enjoined on 15 July 2022 by a national court in the state.

Participation in school sport is restricted by birth sex. Legislation passed 26 March 2021 (upper chamber 27-6, lower chamber 71-16 with 5 abstentions) banned transgender youth athletes, and a 22 April 2022 state law requires proof of gender assigned at birth under threat of loss of funding. Litigation over a student at a town in the state barred from boys' golf produced partial summary judgment on 29 March 2024 and remains unresolved.

Schools must out gender-nonconforming students. A May 2024 law, effective immediately, requires teachers to report to administrators, who report to parents, whenever a child requests a different name or pronoun; enforcement runs through parental complaint and through a legal challenge brought by the national justice department. A 2023 state law shields teachers from suit and discipline for using birth-certificate pronouns.

Prison conditions for trans inmates are set by statute. An April 2024 bill banned gender-affirming care for inmates, and the 2026 women's safety and protection Act mandates placement by sex assigned at birth in addition to the shelter and facility restrictions.

Consequences for families follow the care ban. The 2023 care law authorises regret lawsuits against parents, guardians and physicians, and permits the state's chief prosecutor to bring $25,000 actions against providers; a May 2024 law adds civil penalties for adults who assist a minor in obtaining prohibited care.

Adoption and foster care operate on religious-refusal terms. A 2007 opinion by the state's chief prosecutor allowed adoption by single persons and same-sex couples where in the child's best interest, but a January 2020 law effective immediately allows adoption and welfare agencies to reject LGBTQ parents on sincerely held religious beliefs with liability protection. A foster and adoptive parent protection Act signed by the state's governor in April 2024 eliminated the 10-year dignity-and-respect protection, permitting foster or adoptive placement of LGBTQ children with non-LGBTQ-supportive agencies and, as reported, without a child-preference provision.

Local anti-discrimination ordinances in several municipalities cover public employment only and are preempted as to private employers.

Whether the 2019 indecent-exposure definition has been used in prosecutions against transgender people, and the frequency of any such enforcement, is not sourced in this inventory.

The inventory does not document any arrest or charge under the adult-entertainment law against a transgender person rather than a drag performer; its application to trans visitors' everyday presentation is unresolved here.

The outcome of the April 2024 suit against the state vehicle-licensing agency over a driver's licence gender-marker change is not sourced, and the current status of licence-marker practice for transgender residents is unresolved.

Whether the 2026 women's safety and protection Act's facility and shelter provisions have been challenged, enjoined or enforced since passage is not sourced; the same applies to the April 2024 prison care ban.

The August 2021 lawsuits against the public-school bathroom law and the student sports litigation are recorded as ongoing without a final disposition in this inventory.

The separate drag-ban suit described as ongoing has no status beyond that description, and the recorded anti-transgender incident counts for 2019 to 2021 are raw counts with no denominator or methodology for comparison to other jurisdictions.

The state/province operates within the national framework of the parent nation, and the national layer of exposure is carried in the parent record. State/provincial law protects gender identity across several areas a visitor encounters directly, while its transgender-related restrictions are concentrated in schools and in rules covering minors.

A civil-rights statute passed on 6 February 2020, signed on 11 April 2020 and effective 1 July 2020 prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit. It covers sexual orientation on the same terms and replaced earlier protections limited to state/provincial employment. A law signed 4 March 2020 with the same effective date permits localities to enact their own sexual-orientation and gender-identity protections.

Violence motivated by gender identity falls within the state/provincial hate crime law under legislation signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020, which also added sexual orientation. Legislation repealing the gay and trans panic defence passed in March 2021, was signed by the state/provincial governor, and took effect on 1 July 2021.

State/provincial identity documents are comparatively accessible. The state/province has offered an X gender marker on driver's licences since 1 July 2020, and since 1 September 2020 changing the sex designation on a birth certificate requires only "appropriate clinical treatment", replacing a surgery requirement that had been in force since 1979.

The criminal provisions on private sexual conduct no longer stand. The sodomy statute was struck down on 12 March 2013 and revised to remove the criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations, by a vote of 40-0 in the upper chamber on 7 February 2014 and 100-0 in the lower chamber on 6 March 2014, signed into immediate effect. The lewd-cohabitation statute was repealed in 2013 and the fornication statute was repealed on 4 March 2020. The sodomy statutes had already been rendered unenforceable by a national supreme court ruling in 2003.

Marriage between people of the same sex is recognised in the state/province and has been performed since 6 October 2014, when the national supreme court declined to hear the appeal against the ruling striking down the ban and marriages began at 1 p.m. that day. The statutory ban was repealed on 3 March 2020, and a codifying protection was signed in March 2024, effective 1 July. A constitutional amendment banning such marriages, dating from 2006, remains in the constitution, with repeal resolutions approved in January 2025 and January 2026 awaiting a voter referendum. A designated-visitor statute signed on 26 March 2007 and effective 1 July 2007 extended hospital visitation rights to same-sex couples.

On schools, in 2014 a county school board was held to have acted unlawfully in denying a transgender high school student use of the boys' bathroom, a ruling the national supreme court allowed to stand in 2021. In July 2023 the state/provincial education department adopted policies banning bathroom access and pronoun usage for transgender students, which were intended to be reversed in 2026. The state/provincial high school athletics association barred transgender athletes from girls' sports in February 2025. The state/province prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of minors.

Official posture toward transgender students has moved in both directions through the courts. In September 2021 the state/provincial supreme court upheld the reinstatement of a teacher suspended for speaking against transgender children and declining to use their pronouns on grounds of Christian belief. In May 2024 the state/provincial governor vetoed a bullying-definition bill that would have included gender identity.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places the state/province in its low-risk group of state/provinces, and names it alongside one other state/province as having enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on that assessment's reading of state/province-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

The state/provincial document position does not align with the national travel-document position described in the parent record: a visitor may hold a driver's licence or birth certificate issued by the state/province carrying markers that the national passport regime no longer issues, and the two layers have to be read separately.

The state/province's protections for gender identity were enacted by statute in 2020 and by the panic-defence repeal in 2021. Its restrictions on transgender students, by contrast, were adopted administratively by the state/provincial education department in July 2023 and by the state/provincial high school athletics association in February 2025, and the school policies were intended for reversal in 2026.

Family formation rules matter mainly to residents. Single people may adopt in the state/province with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples adopting, but two bills signed on 9 April 2012 and effective 1 July 2012 authorise adoption agencies to refuse on religious grounds. A bill passed in February 2019, signed in March 2019 and effective 1 July 2019 legalised surrogacy contracts for same-sex couples, and a February 2021 bill barred taxpayer funds from going to religious organisations that discriminate in adoption.

Health-related provisions affecting residents include the prohibition on providers attempting to change the sexual orientation of minors, alongside the ban on attempts to change a minor's gender identity, and legislation signed on 31 March 2021 that decriminalised and modernised the state/province's HIV laws. A bill barring insurance discrimination against PrEP users was vetoed in March 2025.

A state/province-by-state/province list of bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity is attributed in the research to an equality map published by an advocacy research organisation, but the URL cited for it now returns HTTP 404 after the page moved, and the list could not be verified at the cited address.

Several points remain unresolved. Whether the July 2023 education department policies have in fact been reversed is not established in the available sources. Removal of the 2006 constitutional marriage ban depends on a voter referendum for which no date is sourced. The conclusion that the state/province's youth-targeting policies are unlikely to extend to adults is a risk assessment, not a court ruling. No figures specific to the state/province on hate-crime enforcement or on violence against transgender people appear in the available sources.

The state/province falls in the Moderate-Risk group of an advocacy organisation's July 2026 legal-risk assessment, alongside two other state/provinces. That tier is defined as state/provinces that have passed one or two laws aimed at transgender adults, enacted multiple laws targeting transgender youth, or are advancing negative laws quickly. It sits above the assessment's worst-law and do-not-travel tiers and below its protective groupings.

No statewide statute bars a transgender adult from using a public restroom or changing room matching their gender identity, and no statewide law bans gender-affirming care for adults. Pressure has reached the state/province through appointed regulatory boards rather than the legislature. The governor's earlier attempt to limit transgender students' access to single-sex facilities failed, while boards the governor appoints have restricted transgender girls' participation in girls' sports.

The state medical board, whose members the governor appoints, voted unanimously on 22 August 2025 to recommend restricting medical care for transgender youth and approved a draft regulation that would classify providing gender-transition care to anyone under 18 as unprofessional conduct, exposing clinicians to disciplinary action. A board member had proposed the resolution in June 2025. The draft must be vetted by the state/province's law department and then pass a 30-day public comment period before it can take effect.

The state/province's education board voted 7-1 in September 2023 to bar transgender students from female sports and athletics across the state/province. Facilities policy below that level is set district by district. One school district board voted 5-1 on 19 October 2022 to require transgender students to use bathrooms matching their sex assigned at birth or a private alternative such as the nurse's office, replacing guidance that had stood for more than seven years; the policy was described at the time as an apparent first for the state/province. It binds one district's schools and does not extend to adult facilities anywhere in the state/province.

The state/province's nondiscrimination law does not cover gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations, and the 2002 executive order protecting state employees from discrimination addresses sexual orientation only. Four municipalities, home to about 46% of the population, prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, public accommodations and housing. One municipal ordinance passed unanimously in July 2020 and took effect in mid-August 2020. Another passed 9-2 in September 2015 and survived a repeal attempt on 3 April 2018, when voters rejected a ballot measure by 53% to 47%; that measure would have required people in public spaces to use bathrooms and locker rooms matching their sex assigned at birth. In a further city, a February 2019 council ordinance covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations was vetoed by the mayor.

The state/province's hate-crime statute does not list gender identity, so bias-driven violence against a transgender person does not trigger a state-level penalty enhancement. A visitor outside the four municipalities with local ordinances has no state/province or municipal recourse against discrimination in a hotel, restaurant or workplace.

Document changes are available and leave a record. An amended birth certificate with a corrected name and gender marker requires a request form, a photocopy of identification, a letter from a medical or mental health provider attesting appropriate clinical treatment for gender transition, or a certified copy of a court-ordered change of sex, plus a fee. The amended certificate keeps the previous legal name printed at the bottom with a notation that it was originally issued under the former name and amended because of a change of name. Changing the gender marker on a driver's licence requires a letter from a licensed provider attesting clinical treatment, or an already-updated birth certificate or a court order for gender change.

Marriage licences have issued without regard to the sex of the spouses since 13 October 2014, after a district court ruling struck down the state/province's statutory and constitutional bans; the statutory ban had been allowed to become law without the governor's signature in 1996, and a constitutional amendment passed on 3 November 1998. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status can therefore marry in the state/province.

Private consensual sex between adults is not criminalised. The state/province repealed its sodomy law with effect from 1 January 1980; the 1899 statute had punished the crime against nature with up to ten years in prison.

The state medical board's August 2025 agenda carried a statement opposing late-term abortion alongside the resolution on gender dysphoria in minors, placing two unrelated policy questions before the same appointed body in one vote.

Because the youth-care and school-sports restrictions move through appointed boards rather than floor votes, the operative rules can shift with board membership and with the governor who fills the seats, without a legislative session.

The state/province's constraint on adult visitors is thin by statute and heavier at the regulatory edge; the measures that materially affect a visiting adult are document rules, the absence of nondiscrimination coverage across the state/province, and the hate-crime gap, not a prohibition on adult care or adult facility use.

National measures that bind travellers across the country are carried by the national assessment, not by this state/province record.

Residents outside the four municipalities with local ordinances have no state/province or municipal protection against gender-identity discrimination in private employment, housing or public accommodations. Employees of the state/province rely on a 2002 executive order that names sexual orientation only, leaving gender identity uncovered in employment with the state/province as well.

Clinicians and families in the state/province face the draft regulation approved by the state medical board on 22 August 2025, which would make providing gender-transition care to anyone under 18 unprofessional conduct and open providers to discipline. Until the law department review and the 30-day comment period run their course, the board's action is a recommendation plus a draft, not an operative rule.

Family law recognises married couples as adoptive parents. A non-genetic, non-gestational mother is treated as the legal parent of a child born through donor insemination only where the parents are married. Lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation, and while the state/province has no surrogacy statute, courts have generally been favourable to surrogacy arrangements.

One municipality banned conversion therapy on minors in August 2020 by a 9-2 vote, the first such municipal ban in the state/province.

Students in the school district that adopted the October 2022 rule attend school under a requirement to use bathrooms matching sex assigned at birth or a private alternative; the policy applies to that district only.

Whether the state medical board's August 2025 recommendation has been formally adopted, and the final text of the draft regulation after law department review and public comment, are unresolved.

No inventory material records enforcement of the four municipal nondiscrimination ordinances in gender-identity complaints, so the practical reach of those protections is not sourced.

The inventory holds no count of trans-specific violence in the state/province and no general homicide rate for it, so no comparison between the two can be made.

Whether school districts beyond the one named have adopted similar facilities policies is not sourced, and the full reach of the September 2023 education board sports rule across district athletics programmes is not itemised.

Whether law enforcement in the state/province has issued guidance on investigating bias crimes against transgender residents is not in the inventory.

The state/province's rules sit under national law, which applies alongside them. Gender identity has been removed from the state/province's civil rights statutes. The state/province had prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2007; in February 2025 the legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing that category, and the governor signed it with effect from 1 July 2025. The state/province became the first in the country to withdraw anti-discrimination protection from a group that already held it. A 2026 law then barred localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state/province's, after several cities passed their own ordinances, with the capital city's protections dating to 1991. A transgender visitor who is refused service, denied housing or dismissed from a job has no remedy under state/province law on the ground of gender identity.

A July 2026 analysis overlays state/province legal-risk grading on a monitoring dataset of killings of transgender people and finds that legal-risk grades predict how a state/province behaves, not how people behave toward trans people; measured rates do not line up with the map's ordering, and the source states that every count is an undercount. The state/province is not named in that analysis, so its position in the violence data is not established by it. The practical inference is that the state/province's legal-risk tier describes its law and enforcement posture rather than a quantified level of threat from private violence.

The school facilities restriction is unusual in reach because it binds everyone on school grounds, not only students. An adult trans visitor attending a school event or visiting a campus is covered by the birth-certificate rule for multiperson restrooms and changing areas, and the single-person alternative is written as a student accommodation conditional on guardian consent.

Conversion therapy is banned for minors in one city only. That city's council prohibited the practice on minors by an 8-2 vote on 22 April 2020. A statewide ban passed the state/province's upper legislative chamber 26-24 on 17 March 2015 and died in the lower chamber, and in 2016 the state/province's medical and psychology boards declined to prohibit it by rule. Providers elsewhere may lawfully offer it to minors.

Instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity is barred in kindergarten through grade 6 under a law signed in May 2023.

Parentage rules for couples read as same-sex under birth-sex status are comparatively developed. Joint adoption by married couples has been legal since a 2008 state/province Supreme Court ruling, and individuals and married couples may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. State/province courts ordered that married lesbian non-birthing mothers be listed on death certificates (a December 2012 ruling) and on birth certificates (a ruling unanimously affirmed on 3 May 2013), so that support obligations and legal rights attach at birth. Lesbian couples have access to IVF with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised if married, and state/province courts have generally been favourable to gestational and traditional surrogacy although there is no defined surrogacy statute.

A research organisation's equality map lists the state/province among those with an enacted ban on transgender people's use of facilities according to gender identity, but does not place the state/province in the group that defines sex by birth in statute, while a 2025 law imposes an unchangeable binary definition of sex determined at birth. The classification discrepancy is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

No statute of the state/province restricting adult use of public restrooms or changing facilities outside school grounds is documented in the sources reviewed; the enacted facility restriction identified is the school rule.

How the 2025 statutory definition of sex interacts with the state/province's marriage framework, in force since 2009, is not addressed in the sources reviewed.

Enforcement of the school facilities rule against adults other than students, including staff, parents and visitors, is not documented beyond the statute's wording; districts were reported to be scrambling to comply when it took effect in 2023.

No state/province-specific homicide or violence figures appear in the sources reviewed, and the monitoring-data analysis states that all such counts are undercounts.

A state/province law was enacted on 26 February 2026 when the legislature overrode the governor's veto, and it took effect immediately. The law confines transgender people to sex-segregated facilities matching sex assigned at birth in publicly owned buildings, a category recorded as covering schools, universities, airports and government offices. It creates civil and criminal penalties of up to $1,000 for using a non-matching facility and authorises bounty-style lawsuits of at least $1,000 by any private person who claims to have shared a bathroom with a transgender person.

The same law bars the updating of driver's licences and state/province identification cards and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The state/province revenue department has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.
