Reissue is at the holder's expense with no grace period, and surrender letters warn of additional penalties for driving without a valid credential.

Two transgender men filed a lawsuit in a district court within days of enactment, represented by a civil-liberties organisation and a law firm, citing fear of violence under the facility-restriction and identification-invalidation provisions.

The identification rules rest on an earlier statute. An earlier state/province law was enacted in April 2023 by veto override, defined biological sex in state/province law and barred agencies from recognising genders beyond sex assigned at birth. The national justice department then directed that new or updated driver's licences and birth certificates reflect only original sex at birth. A temporary restraining order barred gender-marker changes; an appellate court reversed unanimously on 13 June 2025 for lack of evidence of irreparable harm to law-enforcement identification; and in October 2025 the highest court rejected an appeal, allowing the revenue department to continue the changes.

State/province law has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2020, following a national court ruling and human rights commission action in August 2020 covering businesses with four or more employees. The state/province hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for crimes motivated by sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity; national law has covered both since October 2009.

Marriage for same-sex couples became available after a district court ruled the state/province ban unconstitutional on 4 November 2014, effective 12 November 2014, and became fully legal under a national court ruling on 26 June 2015, with all judicial districts issuing licences by the end of that month. Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal under a national court ruling of 2003, which rendered the state/province sodomy law unenforceable, though the legislature has not repealed its same-sex-only sodomy provisions carrying historic penalties of six months in jail and/or $1,000.

A trans-focused legal-risk assessment published on 20 February 2026 moved the state/province from its "Worst Laws" tier to "Do Not Travel," the first state/province added to that tier in a year, citing the bathroom-bounty law that lets private individuals sue transgender people encountered in wrong-sex facilities. The assessment addresses exposure during interstate travel, meaning a visitor whose route passes through the state/province faces the same facility and identification rules as a resident.

The bounty provision is the operative enforcement mechanism: it does not depend on a state/province agency or prosecutor initiating action, since any private person can sue. That changes the practical exposure for a visitor using a public building, including an airport, during a trip.

The state/province banned transgender athletes from female school sports teams through a veto override in March 2023, effective 1 July 2023, after earlier bans passed in April 2021 and April 2022 were vetoed twice. The state/province high school activities association as of February 2023 left decisions case-by-case to schools.

Gender-affirming care for minors under 18 is banned. The governor vetoed a bill on 12 April 2024 and the override failed by two votes; she vetoed a similar bill in February 2025 and that override succeeded on 18 February 2025. In May 2026 a state/province district judge granted a temporary injunction blocking enforcement in a civil-liberties-backed parental lawsuit.

Three municipalities banned conversion therapy on minors: one in June 2020, one in April 2021 and one in October 2021. In 2022 a county middle-school teacher obtained a partial national preliminary injunction allowing her to use students' non-preferred names and to disclose students' gender identity to parents despite a school preferred-name requirement.

Married same-sex couples may adopt. Lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised only if married. The state/province permits gestational and traditional surrogacy on equal terms for same-sex and different-sex couples, but adoption agencies may refuse placements that violate their religious or moral convictions, and under two court rulings of November 2012 and February 2013 unmarried non-biological partners obtain rights only in limited best-interest circumstances.

Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations has been prohibited since 2020 under a national court ruling and human rights commission enforcement, supplemented by city ordinances and executive orders issued in 2007, rescinded in 2015 and reissued in 2019. Voters in two municipalities repealed local ordinances on 6 November 2012. In March 2024 the legislature passed a law defining content containing "acts of homosexuality" as harmful to minors alongside pornography and requiring government ID-based age verification to access such material.

The outcome of the lawsuit is unresolved; the suit was filed within days of the law's enactment and no ruling is recorded in the sources.

Enforcement data for the facility and identification provisions is not sourced. The number of licence holders who have received invalidation notices, and the number of bounty suits filed, are not recorded.

The state/province hate-crime law's exclusion of gender identity is a statutory gap; whether prosecutors charge such offences under national law is not documented in the sources.

The state's controlling statute on sex and facilities is a senate bill signed by the governor on 12 March 2025 after passage by the senate on 3 March and the house of delegates on 6 March. It defines "woman" as an adult human of the female sex and "man" as an adult human of the male sex, and the law recognises no category beyond male and female; language requiring genital examination was struck before signing. At the ceremony the governor said bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centres "should be kept private for women only."

The statute's stated reach covers locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centres, dormitories and prisons, so exposure runs from a rest stop restroom to any shelter or correctional setting a visitor might enter. The state's facility restrictions are catalogued in a national equality map of state/province bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

An independent anti-trans legal risk assessment published 27 August 2026 places the state/province in its "Worst state/provinces" group, one tier below the four jurisdictions it rates "Do Not Travel," within a national frame it describes as "Worst Policies In Effect."

State/province identity documents remain changeable but the route is narrow. A gender marker on a state/province birth certificate requires a birth-certificate request form with a court order for gender change and fees paid to the state/province vital-records office; a driver's licence or state/province ID requires a gender-designation form signed by a licensed physician, with no surgery or sterilisation required. In July 2020 the state's highest court upheld a circuit court's refusal to allow a marker change even after reassignment surgery, so a court order does not guarantee approval.

A 2021 state/province athletics statute, effective 1 July 2021, restricts transgender athletes from teams aligned with their gender identity by defining male and female solely on reproductive biology and genetics at birth. A national appeals court held the ban unconstitutional in April 2024 in the resulting case, and in July 2025 the national supreme court agreed to hear it, leaving the operative position unsettled.

Gender-affirming care for minors is restricted by a March 2023 law effective 1 January 2024 banning puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery except for severe dysphoria diagnosed by at least two physicians. For adults, a 1997 public health-insurance ban on sexual reassignment surgery was ruled unconstitutional in August 2022 and coverage was required, but a national appeals court overturned that ruling in 2026, holding that refusing funding is not irrational; a pending challenge to the adult exclusion was argued on 9 December 2025 and remains unresolved.

An April 2025 bill passed both houses and awaited gubernatorial action that would require teachers and principals to immediately out transgender, non-binary and intersex students to parents and guardians.

State/province statutes provide no discrimination protection on gender identity, and the only statewide employment protection comes from a 2020 national supreme-court ruling on employment discrimination. Fifteen cities bar gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with further protections for county and city employees in one county and two towns. A 2023 religious-refusal statute lets a person or corporation claim that a state/province or local law or government policy burdens religious belief and claim exemption from compliance, which permits denial of business service, housing and government service on grounds of gender identity, and it carries qualified immunity. On 26 March 2025 the state senate approved by 25 to 8 a bill to nullify all city and county LGBTQ anti-discrimination ordinances, which awaited a house vote.

Marriage for couples the state would class as same-sex has been recognised since 9 October 2014, when the national justice department ceased defending the ban and the governor directed agencies to comply with national rulings, despite a statute defining marriage as between a man and a woman that was never repealed.

The risk tiering in the August 2026 assessment is comparative rather than statistical: this state/province sits in the second-highest of five groups, while a neighbouring jurisdiction was moved up to "Do Not Travel" after enacting a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years, partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. The tiering reflects what statutes are on the books, not measured rates of incidents against visitors.

The legal position in the state is in motion on several fronts at once. The athletics ban is before the national supreme court after a national appeals court struck it down, the adult health-insurance exclusion is under active challenge, and the local-ordinance nullification bill and the student-outing bill were both passed by one or both chambers with their final disposition not established in the available sources. A visitor should treat any single provision here as provisional and check its current status before travel.

The national equality-map page that enumerates the state's facility ban has been moved by the publisher and now returns a 404, so the enumeration is cited from the source inventory rather than verified against the live page.

Residents change a birth-certificate gender marker through a birth-certificate request form accompanied by a court order for gender change and fees filed with the state/province vital-records office, and change a driver's licence or state/province ID through a gender-designation form signed by a licensed physician, with no surgery or sterilisation required. A July 2020 decision of the state's highest court upholding a circuit court denial of a marker change even after sexual reassignment surgery shows the court route can fail.

Fifteen cities maintain ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, and one county and two towns extend protection to county and city employees. These local protections are the only non-discrimination cover available in the state, the March 2025 senate bill would strip them, and the 2023 religious-refusal statute lets a business, landlord or agency refuse service on religious grounds with qualified immunity.

There is no statewide conversion-therapy law. Two cities banned the practice in August 2021 and October 2021, so protection depends on municipal boundaries.

Married same-sex couples may adopt, lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation, state law recognises a married non-genetic non-gestational mother after donor insemination, and gestational and traditional surrogacy are valid with equal treatment of different-sex and same-sex couples. Same-sex couples receive hospital visitation through a designated visitor statute.

Employment discrimination on gender identity is addressed only through national employment-discrimination law as construed by a 2020 national supreme-court ruling, effective 15 June 2020, alongside the fifteen city ordinances and the county and town employee policies.

The national equality-map page cited for this state's facility-ban enumeration now returns a 404 after the publisher moved it; the enumeration could not be re-verified against a live page.

The final status of the April 2025 student-outing bill is unresolved. The sources record that it passed both houses and awaited gubernatorial action, with no record of signature or veto.

The status of the March 2025 bill nullifying local non-discrimination ordinances is unresolved beyond senate approval on 26 March 2025 by 25 to 8; no house vote is sourced.

The pending challenge to the adult health-insurance exclusion was argued on 9 December 2025 and no outcome is sourced. The athletics case was accepted by the national supreme court in July 2025 with no decision recorded here.

No source documents an arrest, prosecution or penalty under the March 2025 facilities statute, nor any specific refusal of service to a trans visitor under the 2023 religious-refusal statute; enforcement patterns in practice are not sourced.

The state/province stands under the national framework and adds a layer a trans visitor meets directly on the ground, most sharply in public facilities. Under the state's 2023 public-facility statute, in force since 1 July 2023, a trans person may not use a restroom or changing facility consistent with their gender identity in buildings owned or leased by state/province or local government: state/province offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons and jails, local immigration detention facilities, state/province parks, toll-road plazas, state/province schools, state/province universities, beaches and airports. The statute purports to cover all schools, public and private. Private businesses are outside its scope.

The statute's mechanics put the decision with an authority figure on site. Gender labels are required, an internal disciplinary procedure applies, and an authority figure may order a person to depart; a non-member who does not leave can be charged with criminal trespass. A state/province civil-liberties organisation advises that refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can amount to criminal trespass and that each situation calls for fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

There is one documented arrest. A 20-year-old trans college student was charged on 19 March 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the state capitol, where she had declared "I am here to break the law" on entering. The misdemeanor trespass charge carried up to 60 days in jail and was described as the first arrest under the state's transgender bathroom restrictions. On 20 June 2025 a county judge threw the case out: as a defendant charged under the statute she had no standing to argue that the law itself was illegitimate, so the statute was never substantively tested. No later arrest under the law is documented in this record.

The restriction reaches higher education through administrative rulings. On 23 August 2023 the state board of education approved firing employees of 28 public community and state colleges who enter the forbidden bathroom, and on 18 October 2023 it voted to apply a similar restriction to private college and university buildings including student housing, with compliance proof due by 1 April 2024. The national appellate rule moved the other way first: an August 2020 ruling by a national appeals court that a high school violated the law by refusing a transgender student consistent restroom use was reversed in January 2023 when the court sided with the district to uphold the ban, which was codified on 17 May 2023.

State/province identity documents diverge from what many visitors hold. In January 2024 the state motor-vehicle agency stopped issuing any driver's licence bearing a gender marker different from sex assigned at birth, treating holders, users and applicants as criminally guilty of fraud, with suspension and revocation of the document. In July 2024 transgender people born in the state/province could not update or change sex on birth certificates despite explicit legislation permitting it. Before that closure, an amended birth certificate required an application, a notarized affidavit and a physician letter confirming appropriate clinical treatment, without requiring surgery or sterilisation; after 2011 a driver's licence or ID name change required a court order alongside a physician statement.

Gender-affirming care is restricted in state law, and the restrictions reach adults as well as minors. On 31 October 2022 the state medical board required a 24-hour waiting period for adults before sexual reassignment surgery; on 4 November 2022 it approved a ban on gender-affirming healthcare for minors, effective 16 March 2023 and codified 17 May 2023, which prohibits hormone replacement therapy for transgender minors and adds adult barriers including a bar on insurance coverage and a requirement that treatment be administered by a physician rather than a nurse practitioner. Minors under 18 cannot receive puberty blockers, hormone therapy or confirming surgeries unless intersex, and a board memo stated that social transition should not be a treatment option. A 2023 state/province bill's Physicians Only provision prohibited nurse practitioners and physician assistants from providing gender-affirming care to transgender adults, which a national LGBTQ advocacy group reported disrupted care for an estimated 80 percent or more of transgender clinic patients, with temporary or permanent suspensions after signing. A May 2023 law allows medical practitioners to refuse treatment on grounds of conscience, religion or belief. Litigation has partly checked these rules: three plaintiffs obtained a preliminary injunction on 6 June 2023 limited to themselves, a national appeals court stayed it on 26 August 2024, and a national judge permanently blocked provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024.

Protection machinery at state level is thin. The state's statutes do not address discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing or other areas, and nursing home and hospital protections in force since 2000, amended in 2007, cover sexual orientation but not gender identity. The state hate-crime law provides harsher penalties for crimes based on sexual orientation but does not cover gender identity. Since February 2021 the state human-relations commission has announced enforcement of a June 2020 national supreme court holding that employment discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination, to investigate employment, housing and public accommodations claims. Counties and cities comprising about 55 percent of the population prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation and gender identity in private and public employment, housing and public accommodations.

Two advocacy organisations have warned travellers directly. On 12 April 2023 a national LGBTQ advocacy organisation took what it called the unprecedented step of issuing a travel advisory on risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to the state/province, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people alongside reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks and book bans and curriculum censorship; it reports events and conferences cancelling. A national LGBTQ advocacy group joined with an updated travel advisory in May 2023, citing recently signed legislation, stopping short of a boycott. Same-sex marriage has been legal in the state/province since 6 January 2015, when a state court ruling held the state's ban unconstitutional.

The state/province's facility law is not isolated. At least 14 state/provinces have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings, and the national advocacy organisation's advisory places the state/province's statutes within a wider set of measures on reproductive health, guns and school curricula that it treats as travel-relevant for reasons beyond LGBTQ policy.

The state/province's approach to trans participation in sport predates the facility statute. A law of 1 June 2021 excluded transgender girls and women, defined as students of the male sex based on sex assigned at birth, from female school sports. In early 2023 the state high-school athletics association recommended that female athletes supply menstrual cycle information to a school-accessible database, a measure speculated to serve both abortion-enforcement and detection of trans women. The national justice department threatened competitions including an Irish step dancing competition and a national beauty pageant for allowing transgender competitors, describing them as deceptive and as depriving women of fair competition.

The national advocacy group's description of the facility statute covers publicly owned or leased airports, government buildings, convention centres, parks, school campuses and stadiums, and imposes criminal penalties on visitors and residents alike who refuse to leave when asked, which is the wording a traveller is most likely to encounter.

Resident-facing exposure extends to custody and to public funding. A 2023 national bill of 17 May 2023 allows child custody modification on the basis that a child received or might receive gender-affirming care, and legislation of April 2023 allowed modifying or nullifying out-of-state/province parental custody agreements where the child is allowed or threatened with access, described by opponents as permitting removal of a child across state/province lines; protests against the measures included trans children being detained and one arrested for disturbing the peace.

Local protections exist but stop at the state/province line in force. Conversion therapy is banned in a number of cities, mainly in one metropolitan area, and those bans have been struck down by a national appeals court. In September 2023 one town became an official LGBTQ sanctuary city. Nine counties, thirty cities and one town offer domestic partnership benefits. The state agriculture department added sexual orientation to its workplace policy in January 2019.

Two further statutes bear on public life. A May 2023 law bans adult live performances anywhere a minor might view them under criminal penalty, which the governor said was about drag shows; it was preliminarily enjoined on 23 June 2023 as not all drag is obscene. A bill passed 23 April 2026 and effective January 2027 prohibits state/province and local funding of or promotion for diversity, equity and inclusion as defined to include gender identity, with lawsuits and removal of officials as remedies; it has been interpreted as barring government support for LGBTQ organisations and events, illustrated by one county denying a national housing grant to repair one LGBTQ organisation's headquarters air conditioning.

Whether the state/province's facility statute would survive a direct constitutional challenge is unresolved in this inventory. The single prosecution was dismissed on standing grounds on 20 June 2025, so the statute was never substantively tested, and no later prosecution is documented here.

The current appellate status of the gender-affirming care provisions is unresolved. The inventory records a preliminary injunction of 6 June 2023 limited to three plaintiffs, a stay by a national appeals court on 26 August 2024, and a national judge permanently blocking provisions banning care for minors and adults in June 2024, without documenting what happened on appeal after that.

Whether the January 2024 driver's licence marker rule or the July 2024 birth certificate practice has been litigated is not sourced here. The inventory also does not document how the facility statute is applied at state/province airports in practice, nor any screening or document check specific to ports of entry here; those layers sit with the national record.

The national advocacy organisation's travel advisory is dated 12 April 2023 and the national group's update May 2023. No later reissuance or withdrawal by either appears in this inventory, so their current status is unresolved.

The state/province's law operates inside the parent nation's framework, which governs passports, visas, entry screening, national custody and nationally funded programmes; those national rules sit above the state/province layer and are not restated here. An independent anti-trans legal-risk assessment placed the state/province in its low-risk tier in a July 2026 update, the category covering state/provinces that largely refrain from targeting trans adults without extending them specific protection.

Discrimination protection is explicit across the state/province. Since June 2023 discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been banned, with sexual orientation covered from the same date, and several municipalities maintain their own bans. The state/province's human relations commission has interpreted the prohibition on sex discrimination in its human relations act to cover gender identity since August 2018, investigating complaints and awarding remedies that include stop orders, training and economic damages. Legally binding regulations signed in December 2022 define sex to include gender identity. State/province employees have held executive-order protection since 2003 and state/province contractors since 7 April 2016. A bill to write gender identity and sexual orientation protection into statute passed the lower chamber 102-98 in April 2023 and awaits a vote in the upper chamber, so the current guarantee rests on commission interpretation and regulation rather than legislation.

State/province identity documents are comparatively open. Since August 2016 a transgender person can change the gender on a birth certificate on a physician's note of appropriate clinical treatment, with no requirement for surgery and a parental request required below age 18; birth certificates carry no X option. Driver's licences and state/province IDs have offered X alongside M and F since 23 July 2020.

The largest city has built a local layer on top of the state/province rules. Ordinances adopted in November 2019 bar youth-serving organisations from discriminating against trans, nonbinary and gender-nonconforming youth, require at least one gender-neutral bathroom in every publicly owned building, and confirm that the city's fair-practice ordinance protects nonbinary and gender-fluid people; in December 2021 X was added alongside male and female in all virtual public schools. On 17 October 2023 the mayor declared the city a sanctuary for gender-affirming care by executive order, prohibiting the use of city resources to investigate or punish residents of the state/province or another jurisdiction seeking such care in the city, deprioritising enforcement of any future restriction at the state/province or national level, and shielding travellers from enforcement originating outside the jurisdiction.

Gender-affirming surgery is lawful in the state/province, and no prohibition on gender-affirming care for adults appears in the sources reviewed.

Violence motivated by anti-LGBTQ bias sits outside the state/province hate-crime statute. A 2002 hate-crime law covering LGBTQ people was struck down in 2008 on the constitutional ground that its content had been inserted into an agricultural terrorism bill; bills to reinstate it have never left committee, leaving no statewide hate-crime provision that reaches anti-LGBTQ violence. In April 2021 a mayoral proposal in one city sought an ordinance explicitly naming gender identity; no enactment followed.

Restrictions on transgender participation in sport have moved through the legislature without becoming law. A June 2022 bill that would have required public K-12 schools and colleges to designate sports as male, female or coed, with female-designated teams restricted to athletes assigned female at birth, passed both chambers but was vetoed on 11 July 2022 by the governor. On 6 May 2025 the upper chamber approved Senate Bill 9, the Save Women's Sports Act, reserving women's teams for "biological females" in K-12 and collegiate sport, and sent it to the lower chamber. On 22 April 2026 the upper chamber passed Senate Bill 1293 under the same title; the governor called supportive lawmakers "extremists", and it was unclear whether the lower chamber would take the bill up. All of these measures concern youth school sport rather than transgender adults or public facility access.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity is legal in the state/province. The sodomy statute was held unconstitutional by the state/province supreme court in a 1980 ruling on equal protection grounds, and the remaining sodomy laws were repealed in 1995. Marriage between two people of the same sex has been recognised statewide since a court struck down the statutory ban on 20 May 2014; before that ruling the state/province recognised no marriages, civil unions or domestic partnerships. The largest city offers life partnerships for long-term committed couples with a city nexus, a second city provides domestic partnerships, and one county defines domestic partnership as between people of the same gender.

Older morality statutes on the books retain reach. In December 2021 an 81-year-old man was jailed for nearly two years without trial under an archaic sexual deviant law over alleged non-consensual oral sex in a nursing home.

Obscenity law has been pruned unevenly. A 1987 municipal ordinance defining sexual conduct to include homosexuality was repealed in full after arguments that public displays could render even a Pride parade obscene. Two legislative votes in May 2021 to remove acts of homosexuality from state/province law failed; in July 2022 the legislature unanimously passed repeal of the two-word references to homosexuality in the criminal code, which the governor signed effective immediately.

In July 2026 the governor signed Senate Bill 45, repealing a 1982 law that allowed felony rather than misdemeanor charges against people with HIV engaged in prostitution.

A 2020 appropriations bill added a prohibition on LGBT pride flags and cannabis flags flying at the legislature.

Conversion therapy on minors is banned by municipal ordinance rather than state/province law, covering a number of cities, the first passed on 14 December 2016 and effective 1 January 2017. Five health boards adopted a ban in May 2024 applying to statewide healthcare policies, and an August 2022 executive order bars state/province government funding for conversion therapy. Statewide bills, including one introduced in April 2015 with 20 sponsors, died without action.

Parentage and adoption rules have been settled largely by the courts. In March 2025 the state/province supreme court held that same-sex couples carry the same legal parentage obligations for children conceived through IVF as heterosexual couples where an established household agreement exists, regardless of marital status. A single person may adopt without regard to sexual orientation, stepchild adoption by a same-sex partner was barred until a 6-0 supreme court ruling in 2002 established the right, and no statute prohibits joint adoption by a same-sex couple.

In October 2024 a district court ruled that a school district must allow parents to opt their children out of lessons or activities about transgender identity.

The lower chamber prospects of Senate Bill 1293 were not stated at the time of reporting, and Senate Bill 9 has sat in the lower chamber since 6 May 2025 with no recorded action.

The bill to codify gender identity and sexual orientation protection has passed only the lower chamber and awaits an upper-chamber vote; whether the legislature will convert the commission's interpretation and the December 2022 regulations into statute is unresolved.

No reinstatement of the struck-down hate-crime provision has been sourced beyond committee referral, and the April 2021 proposal remained a mayoral initiative rather than an enacted ordinance.

The state/province stands under the national framework, and national rules on documents, entry screening, national custody and national health funding apply here as they do elsewhere in the parent nation. The state/province layer is where the facility, identification, care and bias-crime questions are decided.

Facility rules are the subject of live legislative conflict rather than settled prohibition. A 2016 law, passed in an emergency session after the largest city allowed transgender people to use facilities matching their gender identity, required public bathroom use according to the sex listed on a birth certificate and barred municipalities from enacting anti-discrimination ordinances covering gay and transgender people. The birth-certificate bathroom provision was repealed by the state/province legislature on 30 March 2017, and no state/province statute now bars a trans person from using the facility matching their gender identity, nor criminalises facility use. Legislators revived a bathroom bill in the 2025 session, so the position remains open and could change within a legislative term.

Identification documents are narrowing. A national court ruling of 26 June 2022 removed the undefined surgery requirement from the state/province birth-certificate amendment process after a civil-rights legal organisation sued in November 2021. A law enacted over veto on 29 July 2025 and effective 1 January 2026 recognises only male and female sexes and requires an amended certificate to keep displaying the sex originally assigned alongside any change, which means a corrected state/province document still carries the original marker.

Care for minors is closed. Three veto-overridden laws effective 16 August 2023 ended the prescription of puberty blockers and hormone therapy and the provision of gender-affirming surgery to people under 18, and a separate law barred individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletic teams. The 2025 law additionally bars state/province funds for gender-transition care for minors and for people in prison, so a trans visitor held in state/province custody would not obtain transition care at public expense. A trans athlete visiting or competing in the state/province falls under the sports restriction.

Recourse after violence is limited. The state/province hate-crime statute covers neither gender identity nor sexual orientation, so an assault on a trans visitor may not be charged as a bias crime under state/province law even where bias is evident.

Non-discrimination coverage outside public employment is municipal and county-level. A state/province prohibition on local ordinances covering gender identity expired on 1 December 2020; ordinances in the largest city and one county explicitly covering gender identity took effect 1 January 2022, and roughly 30 per cent of the population lives under a local ordinance covering sexual orientation and gender identity. A trans visitor therefore has no statewide protection in private employment, housing or public accommodations, and the answer depends on the particular city or county.

The 2016 law produced a commercial and legal conflict that outlasted it: major companies pledged to pull back business from the state/province, the national justice department called the law state-sponsored discrimination and sued, the state/province filed its own suit, and the legislature repealed the measure on 30 March 2017.

The state/province criminal code retains an offence over sexual conduct that a 2003 national court decision made unenforceable for private consensual adult conduct, and a 2005 state/province appellate decision upheld it on its face only for minors, non-consensual or coercive conduct, public conduct, and prostitution. A trans visitor in a relationship that state/province law would read through birth-sex status faces no live exposure under it, but the provision has not been repealed.

A national judge in January 2021 struck down the state/province exclusion of couples it classified as same-sex from domestic-violence protection, extending the protective-order framework to them. A 2008 hospital patients' rights provision grants visitation through a designated-visitor statute.

Students are governed directly by the 2023 school laws. A parents' rights law took effect 15 August 2023: it bars instruction on gender identity in kindergarten through fourth grade, requires school personnel to notify a parent if a student requests a different name or pronoun in records or in class, and gives parents inspection and objection rights over instructional materials.

Public employment protections for residents rest on an executive order of 12 April 2016 barring discrimination against LGBT state/province employees, including on gender identity, and an October 2017 extension covering state/province contractors. The state/province university system and most of its campuses maintain gender-identity non-discrimination policies for employment and for students.

Conversion therapy on minors may not be publicly funded under an executive order of 3 August 2019. A law signed in November 2021 and effective 1 January 2022 bans sexual-orientation discrimination in foster-parenting placements.

Whether trans residents face lethal violence at a rate above the state/province general homicide rate is not established by the sources available here, and no comparison should be inferred from published counts for the state/province.

The text, coverage and current status of the bathroom bill introduced in the 2025 session are not established by the sources, nor is any enforcement practice by local law enforcement at facilities.

It is not established how county offices are applying the requirement that an amended birth certificate continue to display the sex originally assigned, or whether that display affects driving licence issuance.

The 30 per cent figure for local ordinance coverage is a share of population rather than of geographic area, so it does not tell a visitor whether a given city or county has an ordinance covering gender identity.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the country, which applies in full. The findings below are what the state/province adds, and where state practice differs, on top of that framework.

A legal risk assessment's July 2026 update places the state/province in its "Worst Laws Passed" category, among state/provinces the assessment describes as having legislatively erased transgender people. That grading derives from a five-year legislation-tracking methodology with a scoring rubric.

Facility access is restricted by state/province law. A measure signed 13 May 2024 and effective immediately requires individuals in public schools to use bathrooms consistent with sex "determined solely by birth." An equality-rights research organisation tabulates the state/province as having enacted bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2024 and 2025, and records that state/province statute defines sex by birth.

Identity documents carry an outing risk of their own. The state/province vital records office issues an amended birth certificate with a new name and gender marker on presentation of a certified court order, a medical statement attesting to gender reassignment and a fee, but the certificate lists both the updated and the original information, so the prior marker stays on the document. Driver's licence sex markers could be changed on a Gender Designation Form signed by a physician or psychotherapist from 1 November 2021 until a March 2026 law prohibited markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth.

On 17 April 2025 the state/province supreme court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by a justice of that court, referred to the trans boy as a "minor female" and cited a 2023 state/province statute as the state/province's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest.

Gender-affirming care for individuals under 18 is banned under a state/province statute on adolescent procedures signed 28 February 2023. The state/province's largest public hospital closed its adolescent gender clinic on 30 June 2023, leaving a single clinic in one city operating virtually as the only LGBTQ+-specializing clinic in the state/province.

The state/province's 1994 hate-crime statute does not include gender identity. National prosecution remains available, and the national justice department's regional office reported that a man was sentenced to 49 years in national prison for the bias-motivated murder of a transgender woman in a town in the state/province. That sentence was handed down in 2017; the most recent documented bias-motivated killing of a trans person in the state/province in this material is from 2017, and no later instance is documented.

A 2017 religious-liberties statute, effective after a national appeals court lifted an injunction on 23 June 2017, protects individuals, religious organisations and some businesses acting on beliefs that include that gender is determined at birth by anatomy and genetics, giving providers a statutory basis for refusing service.

State/province non-discrimination law provides no protection based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Four municipalities ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, while three others protect city employees only.

Same-sex marriages are recognised in the state/province under the nationwide rule. The state/province's own instruments, a 1996 executive order, a 1997 statutory ban and a 2004 constitutional amendment approved by 86.01% of voters, remain unrepealed; on 29 June 2015 the state/province's chief legal officer directed clerks to comply with recognition or face lawsuits, after initial resistance in some counties. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is therefore recognised in law while the state/province's contrary instruments stay on the books.

An enacted measure prohibits name changes for people in state/province custody. A 2022 bill that would have permitted them died in committee.

Two restrictive bills died in the 2024 session without a vote. One would have restricted transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories and had earlier backing from a lower-chamber majority; the other would have codified a binary definition of sex determined at birth and curtailed legal recognition of transgender people's gender identities. Both lapsed when the two chambers failed to agree on compromise versions by the 29 April 2024 deadline.

Public opinion in the state/province is measured rather than trans-specific. A 2019 poll by a public-opinion research institute found 68% of residents favoured laws protecting gay, lesbian, bisexual and transgender people from discrimination in jobs, housing and public accommodations, with 23% opposed; the same institute reported that by 2024 support for a statewide anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity reached 67%. The source states that the state/province shows lower support than national averages for same-sex marriage and transgender rights, that opinion gaps have narrowed over time, and that younger residents show significantly higher support than older residents.

Visible community presence exists alongside the statutory picture. A university town held its first pride parade on 24 March 2018 after an initial permit denial, drawing approximately 3,000 participants and becoming the largest parade in the town's history.

State law bars transgender students from school sports consistent with their gender identity under a statute signed 11 March 2021 and effective 1 July 2021. Where an athlete's sex is disputed, the statute requires a physician's statement verifying genitalia, DNA and hormone levels.

A 2024 dress code in a coastal county requiring clothing to match sex assigned at birth led to a transgender girl being threatened with in-school suspension for wearing a dress to a regional band event.

Residents seeking a corrected birth certificate must obtain a certified court order and a medical statement and pay a fee, and the resulting certificate carries both the updated and the original information. Driver's licence marker changes were available between 1 November 2021 and March 2026 and are no longer available under the March 2026 law.

Employment, housing and public accommodations protections on gender identity exist only in the four municipalities with full ordinances and, on an employment basis only, in three others; the remainder of the state/province has no such statute.

The two accounts of the April 2025 name-change ruling in this material do not match. One reports that the state/province supreme court denied the petition outright on 17 April 2025; the other states the court barred the change until age 21 for "lack of maturity." Which formulation reflects the operative holding is unresolved here.

The equality-rights tally places the state/province's facility bans in 2024 and 2025, but the specific 2025 enactment counted, and its scope beyond schools, are not identified in this material.

No enforcement data is sourced on how the facility restrictions are applied to adults, including visitors, in practice. No documented arrest of an adult under the 2024 provision appears here.

The March 2026 law barring licence markers not reflecting sex assigned at birth is not sourced as to its exceptions, transition provisions, or its treatment of licences issued by other state/provinces.

Whether the dual listing on an amended birth certificate appears on the certified copies used to support travel or identity documents is not sourced.

No survey of the state/province's own trans residents' reported experiences in a recent period is present in this material; the opinion figures cited cover the state/province population generally and are dated 2019 and 2024.

The state/province's framework for trans visitors is set by an executive order signed by the governor on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a women's bill of rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state/province agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. The governor was the second in the country to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State/province documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a birth certificate requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state/province ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state/province-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-jurisdiction or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in the state/province or seeking locally issued identification faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in state/province athletics have tightened in stages. The school activities association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 a bill banning transgender athletes from any sports passed the legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by the governor; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in the state/province. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and the governor signed it effective immediately. The state/province supreme court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in the state/province, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to the state/province. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in the state/province's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 a district judge ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. The state/province had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. The state/province's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. National law has covered gender identity under a hate crimes prevention statute since 2009. The state/province supreme court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in the state/province rests on national rulings and municipal ordinances rather than a state/province-wide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under a national supreme court decision of 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the state/province equal opportunity commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. National enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the national fair housing statute's prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with the national housing department accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. One city has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both the public and private sectors since 2012, when the city council voted 4-3 on 13 March to amend the city's anti-discrimination laws to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, with an exemption for religious institutions. Another city passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the state/province college system voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in one city under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of the state/province. State/province-wide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in the state/province as a matter of national law. Same-sex marriage has been legal since a national supreme court decision on 26 June 2015, with the then national justice department directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary state/province laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. The state/province permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals: a district court ruled for the plaintiffs in 2015, the state/province supreme court upheld that ruling in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and in March 2021 it held that state/province adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt.

Sodomy prohibitions in the state/province were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against the then governor.

The practical weight of the state/province's measures depends on how long a visitor stays and what they need from state/province institutions. A short-stay visitor using only national documents and private accommodation encounters the framework mainly through facilities practice and the absence of a state/province-wide gender-identity discrimination statute. A trans person resident in the state/province, or a visitor needing locally issued identification or care, meets the marker requirements, the under-19 care ban and the athletics rules directly.

A trans visitor in a relationship that local authorities would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has full marriage and adoption recognition, so the usual concern about partner recognition in hostile jurisdictions does not arise here. The exposure lies elsewhere: in facilities, in custody if arrested and held in local detention, and in the absence of a state/province-wide hate-crime or anti-discrimination provision naming gender identity.

Enforcement of the 1997 hate crime law is documented in a case the state/province supreme court decided in April 2016 protecting a straight victim in the company of gay friends, which indicates the statute is applied to perceived-association bias, but nothing in the state/province's own law extends that to gender identity. National protection covers gender identity, so a bias-motivated offence against a trans person can be charged nationally even where state/province law is silent.

A trans person changing identification while living in the state/province works through procedures that assume surgical intervention. Birth certificate amendment requires a notarized physician affidavit confirming sex reassignment surgery plus a certified court order changing the name. Driver's licence and state/province ID changes require a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change runs through court paperwork, a hearing date, and newspaper publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors.

Gender-affirming care for anyone under 19 is banned. The 2023 law passed the legislature 33-15, was signed effective immediately, and was upheld by the state/province supreme court 6-1 in July 2024. A resident trans minor, or a parent seeking care for one, has no lawful route within the state/province.

Employment and housing claims on gender identity rest on national law. A national supreme court decision of 15 June 2020 made gender-identity employment discrimination illegal. The state/province equal opportunity commission began investigating housing discrimination claims on sexual orientation and gender identity in August 2020, and from 11 February 2021 the national housing department enforced the national fair housing statute's sex provision to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, accepting and investigating complaints covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. Local ordinances add coverage in one city, which has protected gender identity in employment and public accommodations in the public and private sectors since March 2012, with a religious-institution exemption. Another city's February 2022 ordinance covering employment, accommodation and housing was removed by petition in June 2022. The state/province college system added gender identity to its policy by a 4-2 vote in November 2021.

Conversion therapy on gender identity is prohibited in one city under a 2021 ordinance and lawful elsewhere in the state/province; state/province-wide ban bills in 2021 and 2025 did not pass.

Trans students in state/province school athletics must show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery under the school activities association's rules, and a bill signed by the governor in June 2025 after passing two-thirds of the legislature bars transgender athletes from any sports; ten athletes were identified as affected.

Incarceration practice follows assigned sex at birth. In August 2022 a district judge dismissed a transgender woman's claims of failure to treat dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery and failure to protect her after she was housed among male prisoners and celled with a convicted male sex offender who assaulted her. The ruling treated the assault injuries as no more than de minimis and found no inference of substantial risk from the cellmate's prior sex-offence conviction combined with her vulnerability as a transitioning woman in a men's prison.

A news report on the governor signing the executive order could not be retrieved; the publisher returns a 403 error to automated fetches. Its content is corroborated by the governor's own press release and other coverage, so the underlying facts are not in doubt, but the article text itself was not read.

The inventory does not record measures on bathroom access beyond the executive order's endorsement of single-sex spaces, does not record whether any city or the state/province has adopted a facility-use enforcement provision, and does not record state/province-level statistics on violence against trans people. No figure for trans homicide or assault victimisation in the state/province is sourced here, so none is stated.

Several provisions in the national layer are in litigation or have been enjoined, and the operative position on those national measures should be checked before travel. That layer is carried by the national record.

The inventory does not record the state/province's current rules on gender markers for locally issued documents after the 2023 executive order, so whether any agency has narrowed marker practice beyond the statutory surgery requirements described here is unresolved on the sources reviewed.

The state/province's anti-discrimination law, amended in 2006 to cover gender identity and expression and in 1991 to cover affectional or sexual orientation, bars denial of goods, services, facilities and lodging on those grounds in places of public accommodation, which state/province materials describe as including hotels, restaurants, stores and transportation, as well as in housing and employment. A trans visitor refused service or lodging can complain to the state/province civil-rights enforcement body, which investigates and can grant relief.

Bias-motivated crimes carry enhanced penalties where the bias rests on gender identity or expression, with sensitivity training available as a sentencing condition. A bill extending bias and intimidation protections to gender identity passed the lower house 71-0 in March 2021. A national law-enforcement agency's local division has reported gender X in its data since June 2021, a July 2022 police licensing system carries gender-identity protections, and state/province-run hospital patient records are required to protect sexual orientation and gender identity data.

State/province identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 February 2019 a transgender person may obtain an amended birth certificate with corrected name and sex without surgery or any medical procedure, under three laws signed in June 2018; those laws also created an X marker on official documents and put transgender and intersex people on death certificates. Since February 2020 no doctor's note is required to change the M or F marker on a driver licence or state/province ID, and since April 2021 the X, M and F markers are all available. A November 2022 executive order provides privacy and confidentiality in legal name changes. These are state/province documents; passport and visa issuance is governed separately by national rules.

An April 2023 executive order directs state/province agencies to protect and defend gender-affirming healthcare within the state/province's borders, including access by people travelling in from other jurisdictions.

The state/province has recognised and performed marriages of same-sex couples since 21 October 2013, following a 27 September 2013 court decision whose appeal was rejected on 19 October 2013; the legislature codified the position in December 2021 and the governor signed it on 10 January 2022, effective immediately. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can marry and have that marriage recognised here.

A January 2020 law bars the gay and transgender panic defence, providing that provocation is not objectively reasonable when based on actual or perceived gender identity or expression, including an unwanted non-forcible romantic or sexual advance. The bill passed both chambers 73-0 and 39-0.

A July 2026 legal-risk ranking built from a rubric over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills places the state/province in the fifteen-jurisdiction Most Protective tier, alongside fourteen other state/provinces.

The same ranking places the worst-scoring jurisdictions at the opposite end, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment in one neighbouring jurisdiction and an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use in another. A trans visitor crossing out of the state/province enters a materially different enforcement environment.

The state/province's sodomy statute was struck down in 1978 in a court ruling that found it a violation of privacy and autonomy, and the legislature repealed it the same year. In 1967 an appellate ruling invalidated licence revocations applied to venues serving female impersonators or persons of ill repute; the state/province's chief legal officer issued an official apology in June 2021.

Sex while infected with any sexually transmitted infection, including HIV, was reduced from a third-degree offence for HIV and a fourth-degree offence for other infections to a disorderly persons offence by a 2022 bill, signed 18 January 2022.

The three June 2018 laws, including one named for an activist, removed the proof-of-surgery requirement for birth-certificate changes, made the state/province the seventeenth to allow surgery-free changes and the fourth with a third birth-certificate option after three others, and established a state/province task force of government officials, legal, policy and medical experts and community advocates.

September 2018 state/province school guidance promotes policies on names and pronouns, participation in activities, use of facilities and student records, and the state/province interscholastic athletic association allows participation according to gender identity. In June 2023 three local school boards adopted parental-notification policies that out transgender and non-binary students; the state/province's chief legal office sued to block them, describing the policies as potentially violating discrimination and hate-crime legislation.

Sexual orientation change efforts directed at minors were banned by legislation passed in June 2013 and signed 19 August 2013, upheld in District Court on 8 November 2013 and in the Third Circuit on 11 September 2014, with Supreme Court review declined in May 2015 and again on 15 April 2019 in a national appeals ruling. A county court held that claiming to cure a disorder is fraud.

The July 2026 tier placement is an advocacy rubric over tracked bill counts rather than a measure of enforcement on the ground; no complaint or prosecution statistics for the anti-discrimination law's gender-identity provisions were located in the sources.

The outcome of the chief legal office's suit against the three school boards is not sourced, and whether those parental-notification policies remain in force is unresolved.

The April 2023 executive order's effect on subpoenas or warrants from other jurisdictions seeking patient records from state/province providers is not described in the sources.

Whether the state/province bias-crime enhancements have been applied in any prosecution involving a transgender victim is not documented in the sources.

The state/province's own law and practice diverge from the national layer in ways a trans visitor should weigh. Care for minors is banned by statute, the state/province employee health plan is under a court settlement requiring it to pay for gender-affirming care, and access to adult surgery narrowed abruptly in a coastal city in 2025. Documented violence against transgender women has centred on a major city in the state/province.

A state/province law signed by the governor on 23 March 2023 and in force since 1 July 2023 bars licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or surgery for gender transition to patients under 18. Licence revocation is a possible penalty. Minors who began hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 may continue under the law. A civil-liberties organisation said it would sue.

A settlement announced in October 2023 in a national court in a major city in the state/province requires the state/province public-employee health plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, their spouses and their dependents, after a December 2022 lawsuit alleged the plan illegally discriminated by refusing to pay. The plan's coverage of minors' care can extend to treatment obtained outside the state/province, even though that care is prohibited inside it. The settlement keeps public-employee coverage in place alongside the 2023 ban.

The police in a major city in the state/province said in April 2023 that they were investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, after two Black transgender women were fatally shot a week apart; a January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open. The department described the violence against Black and Brown transgender women as epidemic-level. The sourcing gives raw counts without a denominator for the city's general homicide rate, so the figures establish that these attacks occurred and were under investigation, not that transgender residents face a risk measurably above the background rate of violence in the city.

A hospital in a coastal city in the state/province cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries on 13 February 2025, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man. The hospital cited a responsibility to follow state/province and national laws and regulations, and the cancellation came in the weeks after a January 2025 national order denying public health-care funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. A local advocacy organisation said at least two other area residents were also denied care.

The two care rules pull in opposite directions for state/province employees. The state/province law prohibits licensed professionals there from providing transition-related hormone therapy or surgery to under-18 patients, while the health plan settlement obliges the plan to pay for medically necessary care for dependents, and can require it for minors treated outside the state/province. A family covered by the plan therefore has a payment route for care that cannot lawfully be delivered by a clinician licensed in the state/province.

Adult surgical capacity in the state/province turns partly on funding decisions taken outside it. The February 2025 cancellation cited compliance with state/province and national law and followed a national funding directive aimed at youth transition care, yet the surgeries withdrawn included a procedure for a 24-year-old adult.

Residents under 18 cannot lawfully receive transition-related hormone therapy or surgery from a professional licensed in the state/province; those already on hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023 may continue. Clinicians who provide the prohibited care risk losing their licence.

State/province employees, their spouses and dependents enrolled in the public-employee health plan have coverage for medically necessary gender-affirming care under the October 2023 settlement, a coverage line that survived the 2023 statutory ban.

Residents of one coastal city lost access to gender-affirming surgery when a hospital there cancelled all such procedures on 13 February 2025. A local advocacy organisation said at least two people besides the 24-year-old whose pre-approved double mastectomy was cancelled were also denied care.

The outcome of the litigation a civil-liberties organisation announced against the 2023 state/province law is not established in the sourcing, and the ban's current enforceability should be verified before travel.

The sourcing does not record whether the coastal city hospital's suspension of gender-affirming surgery is permanent, nor whether other hospital systems in the state/province have taken similar steps; that city is the only documented instance of adult surgical capacity contracting.

No per-capita or comparative data on violence against transgender people in the state/province appears in the sourcing, and the outcome of the three investigations reported in April 2023 in the major city is not recorded.

How far the public-employee health plan settlement is applied in practice, including whether the plan pays for minors' care obtained outside the state/province, is not sourced beyond the terms of the settlement itself.

The state/province stands under the national framework; national statutes and the national document regime apply here and are carried at national level. This assessment covers the state/province's own statutes, courts and agencies.

A national anti-trans legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places the state/province in a group of sixteen jurisdictions forming the second-highest of five tiers, beneath the four jurisdictions graded highest risk, under a national frame of "Worst Policies In Effect."

The state/province's facility law, a senate bill titled the "Protect All Students Act," was signed by the governor on 27 November 2024 and took effect 25 February 2025. It requires every K-12 school and every college and university, public and private, to designate bathrooms, locker rooms, changing and shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, and requires students to use the facilities matching their birth certificate. Single-occupancy restrooms with controlled use are exempt. The bill was signed out of public view over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil rights groups; its sponsor was a state/province senator from the conservative party. The statute contains no enforcement mechanism.

State/province identity documents are being narrowed. Amendment of the gender marker on a state/province birth certificate was barred under a 1987 state/province precedent, challenged by four transgender residents in March 2018 and invalidated as unconstitutional by a national district judge in December 2020; corrections have been officially permitted since 1 June 2021, although some counties continue to refuse them. Transgender people can change name and gender on the state/province's driver's licences by court order together with a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist, and an X marker has been available since April 2022. In August 2026 the state/province motor-vehicle agency announced rules allowing only male or female markers and requiring an exact-matching birth certificate or passport.

Care and sport are governed by a house bill, the Saving Adolescents from Experimentation Act, which bans puberty blockers, hormones and surgery for under-18s and bars transgender girls and women from women's high-school and college sports. It passed on 13 December 2023, was vetoed by the governor on 29 December 2023, and was enacted by house override on 10 January 2024 and senate override on 24 January 2024. A court blocked it in April 2024, allowed it to take effect in August 2024 after finding the regulation of transgender individuals a legitimate state/province interest, and a state/province appeals court re-enjoined it on 18 March 2025, with the national justice department vowing to appeal. The operative position on any given provision should be checked before relying on it.

Protection is patchy. State/province statutes do not address discrimination on account of gender identity, but gender-identity discrimination in state/province employment has been barred by executive order since 19 December 2018, and a national appeals court covering the state/province held on 7 March 2018 that discrimination on the basis of transgender status is sex discrimination under national employment law. Thirty-three cities and counties have ordinances barring gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations.

The state/province's placement is one tier below the four jurisdictions graded highest risk in the July 2026 assessment. The tiering reflects statutory text and its status in litigation rather than any measured incident rate, and the sixteen-jurisdiction group is a count of units, not a per-capita measure of risk.

The state/province's facility law carries no criminal penalty and no enforcement mechanism, which distinguishes it from the felony bathroom regimes at the top of the same assessment. Exposure under the facility law is therefore institutional: refusal by a school or college to permit facility use, with no stated penalty attached to the designation duty itself.

Trans civic participation has been targeted. In January 2024 a transgender candidate was stripped from the ballot for failing to disclose her birth name under a seldom-enforced disclosure law, and three of four transgender state/province-office candidates that cycle were challenged or disqualified.

A house bill signed 8 January 2025 requires educators, counselors and other school staff to out LGBTQ students to parents and bans "sexual content," including undefined "gender ideology," from kindergarten through third-grade curriculum with a parental opt-out.

The state/province recognises marriage regardless of the spouses' sex, as it has since a national supreme-court ruling of 26 June 2015, which invalidated a 2004 statute and a 2004 constitutional amendment defining marriage. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry in the state/province and have that marriage recognised.

Proposed adult-care rules issued in January 2024 would have required perpetual psychiatric counseling, an ongoing endocrinologist relationship, bioethicist approval and 30-day reporting of gender dysphoria; they were dropped in February 2024 and are not in force.

The state/province has no statute barring discrimination on account of gender identity in private employment, housing or public accommodations. The protections residents actually hold come from a 19 December 2018 executive order covering state/province employment and from municipal and county ordinances: 33 cities and counties bar gender-identity discrimination across employment, housing and public accommodations.

There is no conversion-therapy law after bills failed in 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2021. Several municipalities ban the practice for minors, the earliest in December 2015, with further bans in 2017, 2018 and 2022.

Changing the gender marker on a state/province driver's licence requires a court order plus a Declaration of Gender Change signed by a physician, nurse practitioner, social worker, therapist or psychologist; an X option has existed since April 2022. The state/province motor-vehicle agency's August 2026 announcement restricts markers to male or female with an exact-matching birth certificate or passport. Birth-certificate corrections have been permitted since 1 June 2021 following a 2020 national district-court ruling, but practice varies: some counties continue to refuse corrections.

A house bill in force from 8 January 2025 obliges school staff to disclose a student's LGBTQ status to parents and removes "gender ideology" from the kindergarten to grade three curriculum, with a parental opt-out for the remaining material.

The operative status of the care and sports bill is unresolved in the sources: a state/province appeals court re-enjoined it on 18 March 2025 and the national justice department announced an appeal, but no later ruling is sourced. Whether the care ban or the sports ban is currently enforceable should be verified before travel or enrolment.

The facility law contains no enforcement mechanism, and the sources document no arrest, citation or reported case brought under it. How schools and universities apply the birth-certificate designation in practice, and whether complaints procedures exist, are not sourced.

The state/province motor-vehicle agency's August 2026 marker rules are reported as an announcement. The final rule text, its effective date, and whether it has been challenged in court are not sourced.

County-level refusal to correct birth-certificate gender markers is reported as continuing after June 2021, but which counties, on what stated grounds, and with what remedy are not sourced.

The July 2026 risk map's tiering methodology is not set out in the sources beyond the tier labels, so the basis on which this state/province was separated from the four highest-risk jurisdictions is unresolved.

Whether any replacement regulation for adult gender-affirming care followed the withdrawal of the January 2024 rules in February 2024 is not sourced.
