State/province law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity or expression in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education opportunity. The protections were added in 2005 and retained after a veto referendum on 8 November 2005, and a 2021 law signed on 17 June 2021 wrote gender identity explicitly into state/province statutes. The state/province hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for offences motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, and the gay and trans panic defence was abolished by legislation passed in June 2019 by 132-1 in the House and 35-0 in the Senate, effective 1 July 2019.

Gender markers on state/province driver's licences and identification cards can be changed without medical provider certification, a rule in place since November 2019, on a completed Gender Designation Form offering male, female and X options. Birth certificates reflecting gender identity, including an X marker, have been issued since July 2020 on notarized affidavit. The X marker on a birth certificate requires a declaration from a licensed physician or mental health provider, and applicants who are minors require parental consent.

The state/province has no law restricting transgender people's use of sex-segregated facilities. Its highest court ruled in January 2014 against a school district that had denied a student use of the bathroom aligned with her gender identity.

A law effective since July 2023 allows 16 and 17 year olds to obtain hormone therapy as gender-affirming care, and an April 2024 law explicitly protects, defends and safeguards gender-affirming healthcare. From 1 October 2026 healthcare facilities in the state/province must mandate and include sexual orientation and gender identity data.

In June 2025 the state/province senate rejected a bill that would have barred transgender women from competing in women's sports in state-funded schools. It was the only one of eight anti-trans bills introduced in the state/province in 2025 to pass the House.

The state/province university system announced on 21 March 2025, with an update on 24 March, that it would comply with national restrictions on transgender sports participation. The announcement followed a national agriculture department's suspension of national funding for research and programmes while it investigated possible sex-based discrimination in nationally funded education programmes.

A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places the state/province in its low-risk group. The same assessment separately flags that its risk has increased because of the state/province university system's capitulation on sports participation.

The state/province's civil-rights protections for sexual orientation, later extended explicitly to gender identity, have survived two repeal attempts by referendum. The state/province human rights act was amended in 2005 to extend protections regardless of sexual orientation, after the 1997 protections were repealed in a people's veto on 10 February 1998 and the 1999 protections were defeated in a referendum on 7 November 2000. The 2005 protections survived the people's veto referendum of 8 November 2005.

The state/province corrections department houses a 27-year-old transgender woman convicted of double murder in the women's facility at a state/province correctional centre, where she had been held for at least a year as of April 2026. The placement follows current gender identity rather than birth sex. On 3 April 2026 another inmate, 41, filed a 30-page complaint against the corrections commissioner, the warden and the transgender prisoner, alleging chronic harassment and assault by the transgender prisoner; the complaint was filed by an attorney and no ruling has been reported. The harassment and assault claims are allegations; the placement of a transgender woman in the women's prison is documented.

Licensed health care providers in the state/province are prohibited from practising conversion therapy on minors under legislation signed on 29 May 2019 and effective 17 September 2019. A 2018 ban bill passed both chambers but was vetoed on 6 July 2018, and the override failed 79-61 on 9 July 2018.

Lawmakers voted unanimously in January 2024 to set aside a bill that would have provided sanctuary protections to transgender minors, following public backlash.

The harassment and assault allegations in the April 2026 complaint against the corrections commissioner, the warden and the transgender prisoner are untested; no ruling had been reported at the time of the source.

The July 2026 assessment's criteria and methodology are not described in the source; its low-risk grouping and its increased-risk flag for the state/province are reported as the assessment's conclusions.

Whether the state/province university system's March 2025 compliance with national sports restrictions remains in force is not established by the sources.

Whether the sanctuary bill for transgender minors has been reintroduced in a later legislative session is not sourced.

The inventory contains no state/province-specific figures on violence against transgender residents or visitors and no state/province-level enforcement statistics for the hate-crime enhancement.

The state/province's bathroom restriction now reaches higher education. Legislation signed by the state/province governor on 15 May 2026 requires transgender students in public schools, colleges and universities to use restrooms matching their sex assigned at birth; the legislature's upper chamber amended the bill before passage. A civil-liberties organisation in the state/province, responding on 18 May 2026, describes it as discrimination against transgender students in both school and higher education. A July 2026 risk assessment covering the country records the expansion to universities as adding campus settings to a pre-existing restriction and places the state/province among jurisdictions with escalating law rather than in the harshest tier.

The state/province is one of four state/provinces operating a freeze-frame policy on prison treatments for transgender inmates, alongside three other state/provinces.

It is the only state/province whose domestic violence statutes cover only opposite-sex couples.

Enforcement of the bathroom law is unsettled in one respect. On 10 September 2025 the national supreme court denied the state/province's 26 August 2025 request to pause a national appellate order requiring a school district to let a transgender student plaintiff use the boys' bathroom while his equal-protection and national education anti-discrimination challenge proceeds. The law is unenforceable against him during the litigation, and the courts have not ruled on its merits.

The state/province governor signed a ban on transgender participation in sports on 17 May 2022.

Budget appropriations for 2024-25 and 2025-26 require students to use bathrooms based on sex at the time of birth.

On 11 March 2020 a national district court struck down a 1988 statutory provision barring discussion of same-sex relationships in public-school health education except in the context of sexually transmitted diseases, holding it unconstitutional under the equal protection guarantee and barring its enforcement.

In April 2016 the state/province governor said he opposed a transgender bathroom-restriction bill then before the legislature and considered it unnecessary.

Local employment protections covering gender identity exist in several municipalities and one county, and for city employees in three further municipalities.

No case or ruling in the state/province is recorded on cell placement, special units, or solitary or segregation for transgender prisoners.

The state/province has enacted no hate-crime statute; the earliest sourced confirmation of that absence is dated 26 March 2007.

The sodomy provision remains unrepealed.

The state stands under the national legal framework of the country and under a state/province constitution whose equal-protection and dignity guarantees state courts have repeatedly applied to block or enjoin anti-trans legislation. In the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, the state is the only one whose standing improved, on the strength of that court record, even though the statutes that would otherwise place it among the most restrictive remain enacted.

A 2023 senate bill, signed in May 2023, codified sex as an immutable male-female binary determined at birth and unchangeable. A district judge struck it down in February 2025, holding that it violated the equal-protection clauses of the state constitution by leaving a gap in sex-discrimination protection. A 2026 senate bill, signed 24 March 2026, codified biological definitions of gender, male, female, man, woman, mother and father based on primary sexual anatomy, provides that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role, and applies across more than 60 sections of state law including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, with applicants for driver's and marriage licences required to list sex as so defined. A state/province representative stated that the bill erases transgender, intersex and Two-Spirit recognition; in April 2026 plaintiffs sought to add it to the ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to the 2023 bill.

Changes to sex markers on the state's identity documents have been blocked in court since 2022. A rule of 9 September 2022 barring changes to sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of data-entry error or a DNA test was blocked by court order on 15 September 2022, which the state health department complied with. A bill of 22 February 2023 prohibiting gender-marker changes on all identity documents, signed 19 May 2023, was stopped by a December 2024 injunction from a district judge; after an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update driver's licences and birth certificates, that judge issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 pending trial on sex-discrimination grounds, which the state's highest court upheld on 15 April 2026, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. A December 2024 district court order also enjoined the 2022 health department rule, the motor vehicle agency policy requiring a birth certificate to change a driver's-licence sex marker, and portions of the 2023 senate bill, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed on the claim that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination under the state constitution.

Facilities access is governed by a statute that is not in force. A 2025 house bill, passed in February 2025, requires bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth; a state/province civil-liberties organisation sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 a district judge issued a temporary restraint, finding the law motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A proposal to forbid trans people from using government-building bathrooms aligned with their gender was voted down by the state house on 3 December 2024, and a 2018 ballot initiative requiring public bathroom use to match birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures.

Gender-affirming care for minors is not prohibited in the state. A 2023 senate bill signed 28 April 2023 banned such care and was described as the most comprehensive prohibition in the country; a district judge preliminarily enjoined it on 27 September 2023, ruling that discrimination against a person for being transgender inherently constitutes sex discrimination under national employment-discrimination precedent and served no compelling governmental interest in protecting minors. The state's highest court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with one justice adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and the district judge permanently struck the ban down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly or to show a change in the stance of major medical organizations.

A 2021 law barring transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued national education funding and signed the following month by the governor, was struck down in September 2022 by a district judge as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the state university system's governing regents.

Protection against discrimination is thinner than the court record suggests. By executive order the state/province prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state/province employment and by state/province contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules, broadened by an executive order in November 2008 and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016; national employment-discrimination protection for gender identity applies in the state, and ordinances in several municipalities and one county prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with the county ordinance covering county employees only. The state's hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to national courts under the national hate-crimes statute. In April 2021 the governor signed legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised in the state since 19 November 2014, when a national judge enjoined the state ban effective immediately, a ruling mooted by the national supreme court's marriage decision of 26 June 2015; the state's highest court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in a decision of 10 December 2019. The state permits adoption with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, affirmed 6-1 in an appellate decision of 7 October 2009, which granted parental rights and set precedent for stepparent adoptions by same-sex couples.

The state's trajectory runs against the national direction recorded in the July 2026 assessment, where national policy shifts and litigation keep the youth-side picture unstable and other state/provinces' standings declined; this state/province is the single exception, improving because its courts have blocked the enacted restrictions rather than because the legislature repealed them.

Official hostility has also been expressed through speech and display rules. A 2025 house bill, debated 6 March 2025 and signed by the governor in May 2025 with immediate effect, prohibits flags representing political party, race, sexual orientation, gender or political ideology on government property and in public schools, thereby banning Pride and other LGBTQ flags, while permitting official historical flags including a revolutionary-era flag, law-enforcement and Thin Blue Line flags, tribal nation, foreign country, military service branch, POW/MIA and official school or government entity flags.

A May 2023 house bill prohibited sexually oriented or obscene performances in public spaces where minors may be present and explicitly barred drag story hours at publicly funded schools and libraries; a public library cancelled a transgender woman's reading in response. A district judge issued a temporary restraining order in July 2023, extended in October 2024, blocking enforcement as vague and overbroad with a risk of disproportionate enforcement against trans, Two-Spirit and gender-nonconforming people. A March 2025 bill defining drag as inherently sexual was defeated with 13 members of the governing party joining the opposition.

State/province employment protection has a longer history than statute: personnel rules of 2000 barred sexual-orientation discrimination, an executive order of November 2008 broadened them, and a January 2016 order extended coverage to gender identity and to contractors. Sexual-orientation discrimination is likewise barred in state/province employment and by contractors by executive order, and by municipal ordinances in several cities and one county in employment, housing and public accommodations. State/province statutes do not directly address sexual-orientation discrimination.

The state/province's hate-crime statutes do not cover sexual orientation either, leaving prosecution to national courts under the national hate-crimes statute of October 2009.

The rules for changing sex markers on resident documents have moved repeatedly. Until December 2017 the state/province required sex reassignment surgery and clinical treatment, after which the surgery requirement was replaced by a correction affidavit, gender designation form, court order and doctor's letter for licences. An April 2021 law reintroducing surgical procedures and a court order was signed effective immediately by the governor and blocked in April 2022 for lack of clear legal definitions; the department then imposed a temporary emergency rule in May 2022 banning updates, made permanent months later. That rule and the associated motor vehicle agency policy are the measures enjoined in December 2024 and upheld on appeal in April 2026, so marker changes remain unavailable pending trial.

The state/province permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised if married, and surrogacy is unregulated, with courts generally favourable to pre-birth parentage orders for genetic relationship and case-by-case orders without a genetic link.

The May 2025 flag law bars official display of flags representing sexual orientation, interpreted as prohibiting Pride flags; one municipality adopted a rainbow pride flag as its municipal flag, a step treated as a loophole effectively exempting it statewide. A May 2021 parental opt-in law requires parental consent before K-12 sex education.

The outcome of the April 2026 challenge to the 2026 senate bill is unresolved in the sources: plaintiffs moved to add it to the existing litigation as identical to the 2023 bill, and no ruling on that motion is documented.

Whether the April 2025 temporary restraint against the 2025 facilities bill has since been converted into a permanent injunction, or the law allowed to take effect, is not sourced; the same applies to the status of the December 2024 preliminary block on identity-document changes beyond the April 2026 appellate affirmance.

No state/province-specific incidents of violence against trans people, and no state/province-level count or rate, appear in the inventory, so no assessment of physical risk in the state/province can be made from these sources. National document, entry-screening, custody and care-funding rules are carried by the country-level record and are not restated here.

This state/province sits inside the national framework of the parent nation on passports, visas, entry screening and national custody, which the country record carries. What follows is the state/province layer.

The state/province motor-vehicle agency's ban on gender-marker changes to driver's licences and identification cards took effect on 1 February 2026. It ended the route residents had used to obtain such a change, which ran through a court-ordered gender change or a physician's statement. The ban completed an administrative rule change the agency initiated; advocacy groups who testified against it said it would forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents whose documents no longer match how they present. A civil-liberties organisation has challenged the policy in court.

An executive order issued by the state/province governor in March 2025 defining sex solely as assigned sex at birth directed the state/province health department to stop updating gender markers, and the agency's 2026 rule extended that prohibition to licences and identification cards. Birth-certificate changes had been available by court order from 2014 until 2025. In May 2023 the state/province supreme court declined in split votes to hear two cases brought by transgender girls seeking amended birth certificates, which left appellate rulings standing that trial courts have no authority to grant a change unless the state/province legislature codifies it. One of those cases involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation her school used to restrict her bathroom access.

The state/province issued an X marker between March 2019 and January 2020, on presentation of an amended birth certificate or a physician's statement confirming permanent gender change. The agency withdrew it after a public hearing, and a March 2020 opinion from the national justice department held that only the state/province legislature could authorise nonbinary designations.

As of April 2026, the law of this state/province places no restriction on transgender people using restrooms that match their gender identity, and two of its cities protect that use by ordinance. Proposals to criminalise it have died in committee since 2021, and in August 2023 a national appellate court upheld a preliminary injunction barring schools from limiting a transgender student's bathroom use while litigation continued.

A bill passed the upper chamber of the state/province legislature 37-8 on 27 January 2026 on a party-line vote and went to the lower chamber. It would define sex and gender by reproductive biology at birth, permanently bar amendments to birth certificates, require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females as assigned at birth, and confine prison housing to a placement matching birth sex. Its author framed the proposal as protecting women's private spaces; opponents including an advocacy organisation warned that a provision allowing anyone directly or indirectly injured to sue a school would encourage harassment-style enforcement. The bill received no hearing in the lower chamber and is not law.

Gender-affirming care for minors is barred. A law passed and signed in 2023 under an emergency clause prohibits physicians from providing gender-transition procedures to anyone under 18 or from aiding such care, with a phase-out for existing patients. It was enjoined on 16 June 2023, took effect on 27 February 2024 after a stay, and was upheld in November 2024. The ban covers surgery, puberty blockers and hormone therapy. A trans visitor under 18 cannot obtain that care here.

The state/province's hate-crimes law, enacted in April 2019, allows harsher sentences where an offence was motivated by a victim's perceived or actual characteristics, gender identity among them. It creates an aggravating circumstance rather than a standalone offence; the state/province had tracked bias crimes without any sentencing enhancement from 2003 until then.

An independent legal-risk assessment published in February 2026 places this state/province among the most restrictive for transgender adults, citing the 2026 identification policy and the facility legislation as the drivers of risk for adults.

Treatment inside the jurisdiction varies by locality. The ordinances protecting restroom use in two of its cities, and the employment protections in several counties and numerous cities, have no counterpart at state/province level, and the direction there runs the other way.

The state/province has recognised and performed marriages between people of the same sex since October 2014, when a national court ruling declaring the ban unconstitutional took effect after a higher national court declined the appeal on 6 October 2014. Annual attempts to amend the state/province constitution to bar such marriages ended then.

No state/province statute lists gender identity or sexual orientation as a protected employment category. Protection for state/province employees rests on executive orders from 2004 and 2005. Ordinances in several counties and in numerous cities prohibit employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression; a few other localities cover sexual orientation only. A national appellate court held 8-3 on 4 April 2017 that employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is sex discrimination under national employment-discrimination law, binding here; that holding addresses sexual orientation rather than gender identity.

A 2023 law bars the use of state/province or national funds for sexual reassignment surgery for incarcerated patients, exempting approvals granted before its 1 July 2023 effective date.

A 2023 law bars classroom instruction on human sexuality in kindergarten through third grade and requires schools to notify a parent in writing when a non-emancipated minor asks to be called a different name, pronoun or title.

A May 2023 law bars city and county governments from enacting conversion-therapy bans by ordinance or executive order, so the practice remains legal across the state/province.

The state/province decriminalised sexual activity between people of the same sex effective 1 July 1977, and the age of consent is 16. The earlier statute carried penalties of two to 14 years and, at an earlier period, death; a legislative committee rejected 6-4 a 1977 proposal to reinstate consensual sodomy as a felony.

A religious-freedom statute signed on 26 March 2015 drew boycott threats and protests over its effect on LGBT people, and a clarification on 2 April 2015 provided that it does not authorise providers to refuse services, facilities, goods, employment, housing or public accommodation.

Whether the April 2015 clarification of the religious-freedom statute covers gender identity or only sexual orientation is stated inconsistently across the sources consulted, so the question is unresolved here.

No enforcement data was found on how often gender-identity bias is charged as an aggravating circumstance under the 2019 hate-crimes law.

The civil-liberties challenge to the motor-vehicle agency's gender-marker ban is pending and its outcome is not recorded.

The sources document restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors in this state/province but say nothing about the availability of such care to adults.

The facility bill passed the upper chamber on 27 January 2026 and received no hearing in the lower chamber; its prospects in a later session are not sourced.

Oklahoma is a state/province within the country, so a visitor stands under the national framework described in the national record. Within that framework, the state/province's own laws are among the most restrictive in the country for a transgender visitor. The Movement Advancement Project's national tracker (25 March 2026) lists the state/province among states banning transgender people from bathrooms and facilities matching their gender identity in K-12 schools, with enactments in 2022 and again in 2025. Senate Bill 615, signed in May 2022, requires transgender students and staff to use school bathrooms, changing rooms and similar facilities matching sex assigned at birth per original birth certificate rather than gender identity; this law is linked to the 2024 death of 16-year-old non-binary student Nex Benedict shortly after being beaten in a school bathroom.

On 1 August 2023 the governor signed an executive order defining male and female as biological sexes assigned at birth for all state/province and legal purposes, expressly applying to bathrooms and changing rooms in state/province-owned facilities, sports, domestic violence shelters, rape crisis centers, incarceration, and statistics collection. The order requires state/province agencies to define female, woman, girl and mother as a person whose biological reproductive system is designed to produce ova and male, man, boy and father as a person whose biological reproductive system is designed to fertilize the ova of a female, restricting legal recognition of transgender people for state/province agency purposes including women's spaces.

Identity documents are tightly restricted. Transgender residents could previously change birth certificates upon court order and driver's licenses upon notarized physician statement of permanent and irreversible transition, and in October 2021 the state/province became the 14th to allow a non-binary birth-certificate option in a court case against the state/province health department, but in November 2021 the governor ordered the health department to block any gender-marker changes, and in April 2022 Senate Bill 1100 limited birth certificates to male or female only and banned any other markers effective immediately. House Bill 1225, requiring a male or female designation on birth certificates and prohibiting changes with very little exception, passed its most recent vote 70-17 and headed to the governor's desk as of 6 May 2026, still pending signature; authors said it is designed to strengthen the existing law being challenged in national court by transgender plaintiffs including a resident of one of the state/province's cities, and the national justice department confirmed the bill clarifies that the state/province never permitted gender birth-certificate changes, while critics called it further discrimination. In October 2026 the state/province supreme court ruled retroactively that changing a birth certificate gender marker was never legal, even to correct a cisgender person's error.

Healthcare access is restricted. An October 2022 law bans government funding to hospitals providing any gender transition services to minors. An April 2023 law signed May 2023 explicitly bans any gender-affirming healthcare practices on minors, making the state/province the 16th restricting jurisdiction with a judge declining to block it in October 2023. Senate Bill 904, passed at the end of the 2026 session (77-14 House, 39-8 Senate) and signed 14 May 2026 effective immediately, prohibits use of public funds, state/province Medicaid coverage or reimbursement, and state/province-owned properties and healthcare facilities for gender-affirming surgeries, puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and other medications to delay puberty or develop secondary sex characteristics when affirming a gender identity different from sex assigned at birth, for both minors and adults. Intentional violations by state/province employees are punishable as a criminal misdemeanor; patients face no penalties. The ban exempts mental health counseling, anxiety and depression medications, precocious puberty treatment, intersex care, treatment of complications from prior gender-affirming care, and emergency treatment to prevent death or major impairment, leaving gender-affirming medical care available only at privately owned facilities paid by private insurance or out-of-pocket without Medicaid. A February 2023 House-passed bill to bar publicly funded entities from providing or allowing gender-affirming care to transgender people of any age and to ban insurance coverage did not pass the Senate and did not become law.

Sports and athletics are restricted: in March 2022 the governor signed a law barring transgender women and girls from women's and girls' athletic teams at public schools and universities, and in 2022 he signed S.B. 2 prohibiting transgender students from playing school sports consistent with their gender identity and excluding all transgender girls from school athletics.

State/province statutes provide no discrimination protection based on gender identity. One city prohibits discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations on gender identity and sexual orientation, while three other cities prohibit it only for public (city) employment. Under a June 15, 2020 national supreme court ruling workplace discrimination based on gender identity is illegal under national law, though practice may continue because the state/province is at-will employment allowing firing without stated reason. State/province hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, but the national hate-crime statute signed October 2009 provides additional penalties for crimes motivated by actual or perceived gender identity prosecutable in national court.

On violence, in 2018 a school in a small town shut down for days after a 12-year-old transgender student received death threats including threats of mutilation, whipping and castration from classmates' parents.

A national anti-trans legal risk assessment map (July 2026) assigns the state/province a per-state/province traveller risk grade alongside the others; the July 2026 edition added a fourth 'Do Not Travel' jurisdiction and tracked changes to the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier, though the specific grade assigned to this state/province is not stated in the source inventory.

The state/province's trajectory mirrors a wider national pattern of state/province-level restriction: a neighbouring jurisdiction enacted a law in March 2026 invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth, which rights groups called a template for other state/province legislatures. The state/province's House Bill 1225, still pending the governor's signature as of 6 May 2026, follows the same template of foreclosing gender-marker changes.

The state/province's K-12 facility ban places it among the 9 states/provinces and 1 state/province covered by state/province bathroom bans applying to trans people in schools, against 29 states/provinces, 4 states/provinces and a national district with no such ban. The April 2025 arrest of a trans student in a women's restroom at a neighbouring state/province capitol, described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state/province bathroom-restriction law, indicates the enforcement direction such laws can take.

The state/province's healthcare restrictions sit within a national picture in which gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states/provinces, and where national measures including an executive order of 28 January 2025 and proposed October 2025 health-department rules barring Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18 compound state/province-level bans.

Transgender residents face cumulative restrictions on documents, facilities, healthcare and sports. Birth-certificate gender-marker changes were foreclosed by Senate Bill 1100 in April 2022, and the state/province supreme court ruled in October 2026 that such changes were never legal even to correct a cisgender person's error. Driver's licence marker changes previously required a notarized physician statement of permanent and irreversible transition; the current status of licence marker changes is not stated in the source inventory.

State/province statutes provide no discrimination protection based on gender identity. One city is the only locality prohibiting discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations on gender identity and sexual orientation; three other cities prohibit it only for public (city) employment. State/province hate-crime law does not cover gender identity, though national prosecution under the national hate-crime statute remains available. A June 15, 2020 national supreme court ruling protects against workplace discrimination under national law, but the state/province's at-will employment regime allows firing without a stated reason.

Senate Bill 904, effective 14 May 2026, bars public funds, state/province Medicaid coverage and state/province facilities from gender-affirming care for minors and adults, with intentional violations by state/province employees a criminal misdemeanor. Gender-affirming medical care remains available only at privately owned facilities paid by private insurance or out-of-pocket. Exemptions cover mental health counseling, anxiety and depression medications, precocious puberty treatment, intersex care, treatment of complications from prior gender-affirming care, and emergency treatment to prevent death or major impairment.

Marriage and adoption: same-sex marriage has been permitted since October 2014 after state/province voters approved a 2004 ballot measure banning same-sex marriage, a 2014 district ruling declared it unconstitutional, the national circuit court upheld in July 2014, and the national supreme court denied appeal in October 2014. The state/province permits adoption by a couple or unmarried adult without regard to sexual orientation, and in August 2007 a national circuit court ordered the state/province to recognize a same-sex couple adoption and issue a revised birth certificate, but state/province law allows agencies to refuse placements violating written religious or moral convictions. Lesbian couples can access fertility treatments and IVF with state/province law recognizing a married non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent, though a 2023 district judge stripped such a wife's rights in favor of a sperm donor where she was not in the donor contract and had not adopted.

The state/province retains a no promo homo law forbidding promotion of homosexuality in schools and requiring HIV education to teach that not engaging in homosexual activity prevents HIV spread, and passed a diversity-training ban in April 2021 signed by the governor effective immediately. A 2021 bill (Senate Bill 1141) proposed to let public-university students avoid courses addressing gender, sexual or racial diversity unless required for their major; the source inventory does not state whether it passed.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the state/province since 2003 under a national supreme court ruling, although the legislature has not repealed its sodomy statutes.

The specific traveller risk grade assigned to the state/province by the July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment map is not stated in the source inventory; only the map's existence and its July 2026 additions are sourced.

House Bill 1225's final status is unresolved in the source inventory: as of 6 May 2026 it had passed its most recent vote 70-17 and was on the governor's desk, but no record of signature or veto is provided.

The current status of driver's licence gender-marker changes in the state/province is not sourced; the inventory records only the prior notarized-physician-statement route and the 2021-2022 closure of birth-certificate markers.

Whether Senate Bill 1141 (2021), which would have let public-university students opt out of diversity courses, became law is not stated in the source inventory.

No state/province-specific incident of violence against a transgender visitor (as distinct from residents or students) is documented in the inventory; the 2018 death threats and the Nex Benedict 2024 case both concern residents.

No state/province-specific data on entry screening, document flagging at airports, or detention conditions within the state/province is present in the inventory; those exposures are carried by the national record.

This state/province sits in a tier of fifteen state/provinces rated 'Most Protective' in a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, an assessment built from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, including youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The ranking finds the laws of this state/province have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

A 2022 shield law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is lawful in this state/province was banned in the patient's home state/province. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state/province that has criminalised gender-affirming care.

Law in this state/province bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in public places, in public and private employment, in governmental services and in the receipt of goods and services; gender identity and expression were added to the statute in 2011. The hate-crime law covers gender identity or expression and carries additional penalties, consolidated and strengthened by legislation signed in June 2026 and effective 1 October 2026.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 1 October 2015, under a 2015 law, a birth-certificate sex marker can be changed without surgery on a notarised affidavit from the applicant plus a notarised affidavit from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist stating that the person has received appropriate clinical treatment such as hormone therapy. That change replaced an earlier surgery requirement, which the legislature voted 32-3 to remove on 1 June 2015. Driver's licences and state/province identification can be changed on request, and birth certificates, IDs and licences offer M, F and X options.

Since 1 July 2018, people in custody in this state/province are treated consistent with their gender identity, including in strip searches and in access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials, and in housing based on recognised gender.

The anti-bullying law prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and expression, explicitly covering cyberbullying and harassment, and applies to all school premises. In April 2021 a national judge dismissed the lawsuits seeking to block transgender female athletes from competing in girls' high-school sports, leaving their eligibility intact.

Conversion therapy on minors was banned with immediate effect after signing in May 2017, following House passage 141-8 on 2 May and Senate passage 36-0 on 10 May. The gay panic defence was repealed after unanimous passage in June 2019, signed by the governor and effective 1 October 2019. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised with effect from 1971, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, having been lowered to 15 in 1975.

The ranking's lowest tier is defined by criminal penalties for bathroom use by transgender people and by multi-year prison terms for providing care, which is the contrast against which the placement of this state/province is drawn. Sixteen state/provinces and one national capital district hold healthcare shield laws, covering 38 per cent of the transgender population aged 13 and over, while 32 state/provinces and five additional state/provinces hold none; youth-care bans are tracked in the same dataset, some of them permanently blocked.

These protections operate alongside a national framework that has moved in the opposite direction on passports, entry screening and national facilities, so a visitor's exposure is split between the state/province layer and the national one.

Residents changing a birth-certificate marker use the 2015 procedure: a notarised personal affidavit plus a notarised statement of appropriate clinical treatment from a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or psychologist. Licence and state/province ID sex designations change on request, and the M, F and X options are available across birth certificates, IDs and licences.

For people in custody, the 2018 policy governs strip searches, housing assignment and access to clothing, commissary items and educational materials according to recognised gender. Students are covered by the anti-bullying statute on all school premises, including online conduct. Workers are covered by the gender-identity and expression discrimination ban in both public and private employment.

Providers and patients resident in this state/province rely on the 2022 shield law when care lawful here is prohibited where the patient came from. The strengthened hate-crime statute takes effect on 1 October 2026.

The June 2026 consolidation of the hate-crime law takes effect on 1 October 2026, so the operative penalty provisions before that date are the earlier ones.

A bill passed in June 2023 to reform the 1991 definition of sexual orientation in the discrimination statute was pending executive action at the time of the source.

The July 2026 ranking is a rubric-based assessment of tracked bills rather than a record of enforcement or incidents, and it does not measure how these protections are applied in practice.

The inventory contains no count specific to this state/province of anti-trans violence or killings, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made.

The state/province is a dependent state/province and stands under the national framework of the parent nation for entry, documents, nationally funded care and national custody; the findings below are the state/province's own law, its own enforcement and its own institutions.

A 2025 law was enacted in July 2025. It bars gender-affirming care for anyone under 21, withdraws public funding for that care, and penalises violations with a fixed 15-year prison term, a $50,000 fine per violation for legal persons, and permanent loss of medical licences for professionals. The operative prohibition is directed at medical institutions and health professionals: none may perform surgical interventions or medication treatments that alter sex biology under the pretext of gender transition or as part of gender-dysphoria treatment.

The definition of the banned chemical and surgical practice is drafted more broadly than the operative clause. It expressly names the use of puberty blockers and sex hormones, including androgen blockers, oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, when used to treat gender dysphoria, and it sets the protected class at anyone under 21. A penalty clause covers any person who violates the law's provisions.

The gap between a definition framed around patient use and an operative clause that restricts only providers leaves an unresolved question. Under ordinary criminal-law principles a successful prosecution of a visiting under-21 trans person for using their own lawfully prescribed hormones, or of a parent accompanying them, would almost certainly fail, and no test case had resolved the question at the time of writing. For an under-21 trans traveller the practical reading is that carrying and using prescribed hormone treatment in the state/province sits inside the law's literal definition of a banned practice, and that enforcement risk is harassment-shaped rather than conviction-shaped: questioning, detention or investigation by hostile officials, with the answer arriving only after the fact. The law's protected class is anyone under 21 and does not on its face reach patients 21 or older.

The law was pushed through non-public hearings and is written with deliberate vagueness, so doctors and affirming parents who facilitate hormone treatment or top surgery risk prosecution, a reach that extends to the accompanying parents of a travelling trans teenager. It mandates campaigns by the education and health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. The health secretary proposed amendments that would have allowed puberty blockers and the continuation of existing hormone treatment; the text as enacted stands as the most restrictive care law in any jurisdiction of the parent nation according to the report documenting it. An LGBTQ+ advocacy federation in the state/province announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

A civil-liberties organisation in the state/province urged the governor to veto the bill, which it said criminalizes doctors and parents and creates two distinct categories of children divided by whether identity aligns with sex assigned at birth. Its policy counsel stated that the bill allows parents to authorise treatment where a child's identity aligns with the sex assigned at birth and prohibits them the same right where it does not. Its executive director said the measure discriminates against transgender people and denies the existence of trans children and youth. The bill was authored by the senate president and a senator, passed both chambers in April, was returned for amendments suggested by the health secretary that the organisation warned did not remedy the rights violations, and was re-approved and returned to the governor on 28 June. Opposition was registered by the state/province's college of physicians and surgeons, its psychology association, its college of social work professionals, its association of professional counselling, its bar association and an LGBTQ+ federation.

The state/province amended its hate crime statutes in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics. The first hate crime charges in its history were brought in 2020, after two men were charged in the murder of two transgender women on 22 April 2020; one of them confessed to the killings. In January 2021 the governor declared a public emergency over ongoing murders, assaults and rape of transgender individuals in the state/province.

Anti-discrimination coverage is partial. The 2013 law that passed, signed 29 May 2013, was amended to apply only to employment discrimination, so public facilities, housing, transit and business transactions are not covered. An earlier bill passed the legislature's lower chamber 43-6 in November 2009 with wider coverage, but the upper chamber held no hearings and took no action after the senate president said it would not be approved.

Marriage recognition for same-sex couples was won through a court of the parent nation rather than local statute. The challenge was filed in March 2014, with intervention from legal advocacy organisations, and in June 2014 four couples joined as plaintiffs, among them a former national guard member and two couples already married in a neighbouring jurisdiction in 2007 and in another jurisdiction in 2012.

Consensual private sexual activity between adults is not criminalised. The state/province's highest court upheld the sodomy ban in 2002; after the parent nation's highest court ruled in 2003 against state/province sodomy statutes covering consensual private acts, the state/province amended its penal code in 2004 to remove private, non-commercial sexual activity between consenting adults from the statute.

Legislative attempts to protect trans residents have repeatedly stalled. In March 2019 a party caucus in the legislature's lower chamber blocked a floor vote on a bill that would have banned conversion therapy for minors, despite passage in the upper chamber and governor support; a senator who co-sponsored it dissented publicly. In April 2019 the governor announced a religious-freedom bill alongside a conversion-therapy ban carrying an exemption for clergy acting in a pastoral capacity. Advocates criticised the pairing as opening the door to refusals of service on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and on 13 June 2019 the governor asked lawmakers to withdraw both measures. A 2017 religious freedom bill that would have allowed public businesses to refuse service to LGBTQ people was vetoed by the governor in February 2018.

The care ban withdraws public funding for gender-affirming treatment, which bears directly on how residents, rather than visitors, obtain care in the state/province.

The law mandates campaigns by the education and health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care, a measure that reaches trans students in the state/province's schools.

A 2013 measure extended domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.

No court has resolved whether the definitional clause of the 2025 law can reach a patient, or whether the statute is void for vagueness. The question is unresolved and no test case had been decided at the time of writing.

No sub-national corrections policy, dedicated unit or ruling on the housing of transgender inmates was located.

Reports differ on the surname of the health secretary who proposed amendments to the bill, rendering the attribution unresolved.

The state/province stands under the national framework on travel documents, and adds its own state/province-level restrictions. A bathroom bill became law on 11 April 2023 as Act 619, making it the fourth state/province to restrict transgender students' use of school bathrooms matching their gender identity; the law was amended and extended in 2025, and an equality-map citations record HB 1156 as a 2023 K-12 facility ban extended in 2025. Act 619 of 11 April 2023 separately creates a misdemeanour for transgender use of public bathrooms, locker rooms or changing facilities where a minor is present, dependent on intent of arousing or gratifying sexual desire.

A July 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessment places this state/province in the 'Worst Policies In Effect' group, one tier below the 'Do Not Travel' designation given to four other state/provinces. The grading reflects the state/province's own body of anti-trans law rather than any national measure.

This state/province was the first in the country, in 2021, to ban gender-affirming healthcare for trans minors, after the legislature overrode the governor's veto. HB 1570, banning puberty blockers, hormone therapy and surgery for under-18s, was vetoed on 5 April 2021 as overbroad and extreme but overridden on 6 April 2021; it was blocked and then struck down on 20 June 2023 by a national judge for discrimination and constitutional violations, before a national appeals circuit overturned that ruling on 12 August 2025 and allowed enforcement, citing a Supreme Court decision. Litigation over the 2021 care ban continues, and a national judge enjoined it for 'irreparable harm' to minors while litigation was ongoing.

Identity documents at state/province level have narrowed. Transgender people have been permitted to amend birth certificates since 1981, when a Vital Statistics Act passed 34-0 in the upper chamber and 92-0 in the lower on 19 February 1981, codifying a surgery-based pathway requiring court order verifying sex reassignment surgery and a name change. Identity documents with an X sex descriptor were available from December 2010, but in March 2024 the state/province finance and administration department rescinded X descriptors for driver's licences.

State/province law does not address discrimination based on gender identity, leaving protection only through a 2020 nationwide court ruling. Several cities and the county bar gender-identity discrimination in public employment, while the comprehensive ordinances in two smaller municipalities are unenforced under an Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act; the state/province supreme court struck down one of those ordinances in February 2017.

The state/province has no hate-crime penalty-enhancement statute, and its civil remedy for intimidation, harassment, violence or property damage covers only racial, religious or ethnic animosity, not gender identity. The April 2021 state/province hate-crimes law, signed effective immediately, excludes sexual orientation or gender identity explicitly or implicitly. National law has covered gender identity since October 2009 under a national hate-crime act.

A bill signed 26 March and effective immediately allows medical practitioners to cite religious beliefs to deny healthcare to LGBT patients. In March 2021 the Legislature passed a ban on transgender athletes in sports, signed 25 March and effective immediately; it prohibits transgender women and girls from competing on school sports teams consistent with their gender identity across K-12 and collegiate sports, and allows a student or school claiming harm to sue a school for violation.

In March 2023 the Legislature passed a gender-affirming litigation bill, signed 13 March 2023, allowing those who received such care as minors to sue providers 15 years after turning 18, versus two years for other care. On 21 March 2023 a law prohibiting trans people from using public school bathrooms matching gender was signed, making this the fourth such state/province in the country.

The state/province's placement in the 'Worst Policies In Effect' tier of a July 2026 legal-risk map sits one level below the 'Do Not Travel' designation applied to four other state/provinces, whose measures include a felony bathroom ban of up to five years and a bounty-hunter civil-suit regime. The tiering is a comparative grading of state/province law, not a measure of incident rates.

The state/province's care ban and bathroom regime are part of a wider national pattern: gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 state/provinces, and state/province bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some jurisdictions, government buildings cover 9 state/provinces and 1 state/province, while 29 state/provinces, 4 state/provinces and the national capital district have no such ban.

The national appeals circuit's August 2025 reversal of the injunction against this state/province's care ban, citing a Supreme Court decision, aligns the state/province's position with the Supreme Court's June 2025 ruling upholding a neighbouring jurisdiction's similar restriction, and rights groups have described another state/province's March 2026 law invalidating non-birth-sex documents as a template other legislatures may follow.

Residents face a state/province regime with no state/province-level gender-identity discrimination protection beyond the national Bostock ban. Local ordinances in several cities and the county bar gender-identity discrimination in public employment only; the broader ordinances in two smaller municipalities are unenforced under the Intrastate Commerce Improvement Act of 2015, which bars cities and counties from adopting protected classifications absent from state/province law.

Birth certificates may be amended on a court order verifying sex reassignment surgery and a name change, a pathway in place since the 1981 Vital Statistics Act. Driver's licences no longer carry an X descriptor following the March 2024 rescission by the state/province finance and administration department.

Residents have no state/province hate-crime protection for gender identity: the April 2021 state/province hate-crimes law excludes sexual orientation and gender identity, and the state/province's civil remedy covers only racial, religious or ethnic animosity. National hate-crime coverage under a national act has applied since October 2009.

Trans students in K-12 schools are restricted to facilities matching their sex assigned at birth under the 2023 law extended in 2025, and Act 619 of 11 April 2023 makes trans use of public bathrooms, locker rooms or changing facilities where a minor is present a misdemeanour where intent to arouse or gratify sexual desire is established. Transgender athletes are barred from school sports teams matching their gender identity under the March 2021 law.

Medical practitioners may cite religious beliefs to deny healthcare to LGBT patients under a bill signed 26 March. Those who received gender-affirming care as minors face a 15-year statute of limitations on suits against providers, versus two years for other care.

The current enforceability of the state/province's 2021 care ban after the national appeals circuit's August 2025 reversal is not fully resolved in the sources: litigation is described as continuing, and the operative position should be checked before relying on it.

Whether this state/province has adopted any analogue to the document-invalidation or bounty-hunter regimes noted in the July 2026 risk map is not sourced here; the inventory records only the March 2024 rescission of X licence descriptors.

The enforcement record for Act 619's misdemeanour provision, including any arrests or charges under it, is not documented in the inventory. The only documented arrest under a state/province bathroom-restriction law cited in the wider record occurred in another state/province in April 2025.

Whether the state/province's K-12 facility ban extends to government buildings or adult public facilities beyond the minor-present circumstance in Act 619 is not stated in the sources.

This state/province is a sub-national unit of the country. Passports, visas, entry screening and national facilities are governed by national law; the findings below concern the state/province layer.

State/province anti-discrimination law has covered gender identity in housing, employment and public accommodations since June 2018. Coverage was extended to health care, public accommodations and jury selection effective 1 January 2020, and to public schools effective 17 September 2019, with the anti-bullying statute reaching gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying. Sexual orientation has been protected in public accommodations, housing and private and public employment since 1998.

Hate-crime penalty enhancements for offences motivated by gender identity took effect on 15 October 2019; sexual orientation has been covered since 1991. The gay and trans panic defence was abolished effective 1 January 2024, following passage in June 2023.

Enforcement of the state/province civil rights statute is documented. On 17 July 2026 a county superior court found that a man in a city had violated the state/province civil rights statute by striking a transgender woman.

An advocacy organisation's 2025 national incident census recorded 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in this state/province, the second-highest raw count of any state/province, behind one other state/province (198) and ahead of others recording 66, 50 and 50. The census ranks by raw count and publishes no per-capita denominator, so the figure does not by itself establish this state/province's incident rate relative to larger state/provinces.

Identity documents are asymmetric. A birth certificate issued here can be changed to reflect a different gender only on proof of sex reassignment surgery, legal in this state/province since 1990, together with a certified court order stating a "sex change," an application form, a photograph and fees. A reform bill was vetoed in July 2019 and the surgical requirement remains. Driver's licences have offered male, female and X markers since 1 January 2020, implemented in August 2021; the X marker is not available on birth certificates.

Care rules for minors have tightened. Laws passed on 18 July 2024 banned gender-affirming medicine for minors and, from 1 January 2025, banned reassignment surgery for transgender minors while retaining it for intersex people and circumcisions. Two bills passed in August 2025 and effective January 2026 ban puberty blockers, hormone therapy and chest surgery for under-18 gender-affirming care, with a grandfather clause for treatment already under way as of 1 January 2026, disciplinary action against providers who violate the ban, and a right to sue. Those August 2025 laws removed access to gender-affirming care for transgender youth even where a physician judged it medically necessary.

The same July 2024 package barred transgender girls from girls' sports in grades 5 to 12 from 19 August 2024, with a birth certificate required to establish eligibility. A fourth bill in that package, which would have permitted discrimination against transgender people including adults, was vetoed. In August 2024 the state/province's highest court ruled 3-1 to protect transgender students in schools on privacy and autonomy grounds, and a judge granted a temporary stay of the sports ban pending investigation and appeals.

Marriage between two people of the same sex has been legal since 1 January 2010, following civil unions from 1 January 2008. An April 2021 ruling by the state/province's highest court recognised adultery in such marriages, reversing a 2003 court rule.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the sodomy repeal of June 1975. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation, and 18 where one party is under the care, guardianship or authority of the other.

A 2022 poll by a polling organisation found that 88% of residents of this state/province supported discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity, with 11% opposed.

An encyclopedia entry on LGBTQ rights in this state/province states that it "became regarded as the least safe state/province in the region for transgender citizens" after the August 2025 care restrictions and other changes to transgender protections. The characterisation is attributed rather than measured.

Two earlier measures failed. A 2022 bill that would have required schools to disclose students' gender identities died after a veto threat, and a 2022 attempt to repeal the conversion therapy ban died in the legislature.

State/province employment and contracting: an executive order of 30 June 2016 prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression in public employment, state/province programmes and contracting. Sexual orientation was explicitly listed in expectation-of-privacy legislation effective 1 January 2025.

Schools: the July 2024 package allows parents to opt their children out of instruction on gender identity or expression. Anti-bullying law covers gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying, and has covered sexual orientation since the 2019 extension.

Health coverage: the state/province's ban on public health insurance coverage of transition surgery was lifted on 20 October 2017. Conversion therapy on LGBT minors has been prohibited since 1 January 2019, after passage in 2018.

The operative status of the sports ban is unresolved in the sources consulted: a judge granted a temporary stay pending investigation and appeals, and the outcome of that process is not recorded.

The incident census ranks by raw count and publishes no per-capita denominator, so the ranking does not establish a per-capita rate for this state/province or for any other.

Whether the 2025 restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors have been enjoined, and their status on any given date, is not established by the sources consulted.

The requirement of surgery and a court order for a birth certificate change is recorded as remaining in force after a July 2019 veto; no later amendment is recorded.

The country stands under its national framework; that layer is carried on the national record rather than repeated here.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places this state/province in its Low-Risk States group, alongside eight other jurisdictions, describing that group as jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults. The same assessment names this state/province alongside one other as having enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies judged unlikely to be extended to adults.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity is prohibited through 2020 national Title VII rulings, reinforced by a January 2023 gubernatorial executive order banning gender-identity discrimination in state/province employment and contracts and a June 2023 national justice department affirmation that state/province sex discrimination includes gender identity. Municipal ordinances in nine cities enacted between February 2013 and June 2021 ban gender-identity discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations, with exemptions for religious organizations, expressive groups, government agencies, private clubs and small businesses.

The state/province's hate-crime statute does not include gender identity, though the national hate-crimes statute has covered gender identity since October 2009. A gay and trans panic defence remains available under common law, with reform bills lapsing without action.

Gender-affirming care for minors is restricted. A March 2022 law signed by the Governor banned sex reassignment surgery on transgender children effective March 2023, with an exception permitting surgery on intersex children. A 1982 state/provincial regulation bars Medicaid coverage of sex reassignment surgery; that ban was challenged in August 2020 by two transgender teenagers with civil-rights co-counsel as unconstitutional, following 2019 lawsuits seeking to void it. A June 2023 executive order granted state/provincial government employees over age 21 full Medicaid access and insurance coverage for gender-affirming healthcare and services. Conversion therapy was banned in one county in August 2017 by a 3-2 vote with fines up to $2,500, alongside a June 2023 executive order barring government funding for conversion therapy.

The state/province Supreme Court ruled on 25 April 2019 that family courts may determine care for a transgender child with gender dysphoria only in limited circumstances when divorced parents reach impasse, authorized to decide disputed parenting-plan elements narrowly tailored on evidence of imminent harm. In March 2023 the state/provincial Department of Education introduced a hotline to report schools exposing children to topics including gender ideology for investigation. In June 2023 the Governor vetoed legislature-passed anti-trans bathroom and classroom pronoun-usage bills and an April 2023 bill targeting LGBT safe spaces in schools.

A second March 2022 bill signed by the Governor legally bars transgender children from female sports, athletics and Olympic competition, effective 30 days after enactment.

Birth certificates and driver's licences carry distinct rules. In November 2020 three families with transgender children sued the state/provincial Department of Health Services to permit birth-certificate gender change without sex reassignment surgery; litigation was ongoing as of August 2023 with all resident transgender individuals joined, and an August 2024 national judge order permitted change without surgery. Driver's licence and state/provincial ID gender change requires a signed physician statement attesting the applicant is irrevocably committed to the gender-change process, without requiring surgery.

Same-sex marriage has been recognized since a national district court decision on 17 October 2014 ended enforcement of statutory and constitutional bans, though those bans remain textually in the constitution and statutes as unenforceable under the national marriage precedent and, for out-of-state recognition, the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act. Voters rejected a 2006 ballot measure banning marriage and approved a 2008 measure banning recognition, prompting four cities to enact domestic partnerships or civil unions.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal after a 2001 state/provincial act repealed sodomy laws. Adoption carries no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoptions, though primary consideration goes to married couples unless in the child's best interest or no married couple is available; the state/provincial Supreme Court ruled unanimously in September 2017 that same-sex spouses have equal parental rights to list both names on birth certificates, with October 2020 appeals implementation. Surrogacy contracts are unenforceable though a 1994 court decision allows pre-birth orders for biological parents requiring second-parent adoption for a non-biological same-sex parent, and an April 2022 emergency law allows religious organizations to legally discriminate against same-sex couples seeking to adopt or foster.

On 3 June 2026 a news outlet reported that Pride events in the state/province's second-largest city were cancelled in January and the organizing body effectively dissolved, citing a political and financial environment that made supporting queer events nearly impossible; the city was grouped with two cities in other jurisdictions as affected.

This state/province's position in the July 2026 national assessment's Low-Risk group reflects relative restraint in targeting transgender adults, but the same assessment notes it has enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies judged unlikely to be extended to adults — a distinction that may not hold if legislative priorities shift.

The cancellation and dissolution of Pride organizing in January 2026, reported on 3 June 2026, signals a deteriorating environment for visible LGBTQ organizing in the state/province's second-largest city, even where formal legal protections remain in place. The city was grouped with two cities in other jurisdictions as affected.
