The state/province stands under the national framework carried by the national record; the findings below are specific to the state/province. A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places the state/province in its low-risk group, alongside a set of other state/provinces, describing jurisdictions that have largely refrained from targeting transgender adults while not taking extraordinary steps to protect them.

No statewide law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and gender identity is not a protected class under the state/province hate-crime statute, though sexual orientation is. Prosecutors have sometimes used perceived sexual orientation as the route to charge crimes motivated by a victim's gender identity. Local protection is patchwork: as of 29 May 2025, 21 per cent of the population lived in the ten cities with full employment, housing and public-accommodation ordinances covering gender identity, and 12 per cent in cities with partial ordinances. Several counties and cities ban gender-identity discrimination; two further cities extend protection only to transgender municipal employees. An executive order issued 7 January 2019 prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression in state/province employment, state/province contracting and the provision of state/province services, and directs state/province agencies to adopt and enforce nondiscrimination policies.

The state/province has no law barring transgender people from using government-building bathrooms or facilities consistent with their gender identity, no law defining sex to exclude transgender people, and no restriction on drag performance. Its equality-map profile, current to 29 May 2025, records no ban on best-practice medical care for transgender youth and no shield law protecting providers or patients from out-of-state action.

Identity documents are the main friction point. Gender-marker change on a driver's licence is permitted only in limited circumstances, and change on a birth certificate is restricted: a person born in the state/province who has completed sex reassignment surgery may amend the birth certificate on documentation of the surgery and a name change. Neither licence nor birth certificate offers an X gender-neutral option, and the name-change process is restrictive.

State/province law does not ban gender-affirming care for minors. The governor vetoed a bill on 6 December 2023, blocking a legislature-passed ban on gender-affirming health care for people under 18; the governor had earlier vetoed a June 2023 budget provision that would have barred public health insurance coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming care for all individuals regardless of age. Care access nonetheless contracted under national funding pressure: two major hospital systems each announced on 13 January 2026 that they would pause gender-affirming pharmacologic care for patients under 18 after the national health department said it would deny public health insurance payments to hospitals providing such care to minors. Mental and behavioural health services continued. The state/province's justice department joined a multistate coalition seeking to block the national health department's declaration. The pause follows national funding pressure on hospitals in the state/province rather than any state/province ban.

Marriage between two people regardless of sex has been recognised since 6 October 2014, when the national supreme court declined an appeal and a lower court's stay was lifted. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can expect that marriage to be recognised. Parenting rules allow individuals to adopt without regard to sexual orientation and married couples to adopt; access to IVF and artificial insemination is permitted, with recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother only if she is married. A September 2016 national court ruling required both parents to be recorded on birth certificates, and since 1 July 2021 birth certificates offer gender-neutral 'spouse' and 'parent 1'/'parent 2' options.

Private, non-commercial sexual conduct between consenting adults has been legal since 1983, when the state/province's sodomy provisions were repealed; the repealing legislation stated that the state/province did not approve of sexual conduct outside marriage.

A city police department stopped listing the gender of crime victims in September 2023, alongside race, in order to avoid misgendering transgender people.

Bills restricting gender-affirming care and transgender sports participation have been introduced repeatedly. A 2021 bill barring transgender women from teams aligning with their gender passed the lower chamber on party lines but was never voted on in the upper chamber; it was re-introduced in 2023, and a bill passed by the legislature in 2024 was vetoed by the governor on 2 April 2024. The bill's sponsor called the veto 'disgusting'. The governor had promised the veto since the bill was introduced, and the opposition did not have enough votes to stop its passage in the legislature. On medical care, a 2021 bill prohibiting insurers from covering gender-affirming care procedures for minors failed in committee; a re-introduced bill passed the lower chamber on 12 October 2023 and the upper chamber on 17 October 2023 and was vetoed on 6 December 2023.

Public hearings in October 2023 on bills to ban gender-affirming care for transgender youth, including model legislation, and to restrict transgender sports participation were marked by misinformation, with lawmaker questions indicating gaps in basic knowledge. The state/province and national athletic associations retained their own policies addressing transgender athletes.

A 2017 poll found 73 per cent supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity, with 20 per cent opposed; 66 per cent supported marriage between same-sex couples, with 26 per cent opposed and 8 per cent unsure.

In October 2023 the governor, speaking to 'LGBTQ folks, especially our trans kids', said he would veto any bill that makes the state/province a less welcoming, less inclusive and less safe place to be who you are. Introductions of the transgender athlete and medical-care bills sparked significant backlash from state/province and national advocacy organisations.

People in prison are entitled to hormone therapy. A 2005 statute denying hormone therapy to prisoners undergoing sex reassignment was ruled unconstitutional unanimously by a national appellate court on 5 August 2011, and the national supreme court denied the state/province's appeal on 26 March 2012.

Sex reassignment surgery was explicitly included in public health insurance for state/province employees from January 2019 and was ordered extended to non-government employees in May 2019 under constitutional equal-protection guarantees. A June 2023 budget bill passed by both chambers banning public health insurance coverage of sexual reassignment surgery and other gender-affirming healthcare for all individuals regardless of age was vetoed under line-item veto power. Private insurance and public health insurance were barred from excluding transgender-specific care.

Persons on the state/province's sex offender registry are not allowed to change their names, with no exception for transgender people.

Discrimination based on sexual orientation has been banned statewide in employment, housing, education, credit and all public accommodations since 1982, making the state/province the first in the country to do so; sexual orientation is a protected class in the hate-crime law and under a 2001 law prohibiting sexual-orientation discrimination in schools.

Conversion therapy on minors is banned in 14 communities, with ordinances adopted from March 2018 onward and further bans adopted through 2020. One ordinance carries a maximum fine of 1,000 dollars plus costs, up to 90 days in a county jail and possible suspension of driving privileges for up to five years. A June 2021 executive order barred state/province taxpayer funds from supporting conversion therapy on LGBT minors. Statewide ban efforts were blocked in June 2020 and January 2023, and in July 2025 the state/province supreme court ruled 4-3 that such bans can be enacted by regulation and executive order.

The July 2026 assessment's criteria and methodology are not published in the source; the low-risk grouping is a comparative label, not a statement of legal protection. The equality-map profile is current to 29 May 2025 and does not capture later legislative changes. Whether the January 2026 pause on pharmacologic care for under-18s at the two hospital systems remains in force is not sourced. The specific documentation standard for the limited driver's licence gender-marker change is not stated. The number of municipalities with conversion-therapy bans is given as 14, but the source names 13. Whether prosecutors' use of perceived sexual orientation to charge gender-identity-motivated crimes is systematic is not documented with case counts. The status of the multistate challenge to the national health department's declaration is unresolved.

This state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation. It is the national seat rather than an ordinary state/province, so national law applies directly within its boundaries and the national legislature retains authority over its local legislation and budget.

This state/province has no bathroom ban of its own. The facilities restriction in force there was attached by the national legislature, and on 5 December 2024 transgender-rights activists protesting that measure at the national legislature building were arrested. The ban originates with the national legislature rather than with the locally elected legislature, so it is not something the local council can repeal.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment places this state/province on its low-risk list alongside eight other state/provinces, while cautioning that it may no longer warrant its reputation as the most protective jurisdiction, because its law can be overridden by the national legislature and by national executive orders.

The low-risk placement comes from a legal risk assessment, which tracks enacted law and litigation rather than conditions on the ground. That distinction carries more weight for this state/province than for the other state/provinces ranked with it, since the national legislature and the national executive act on the jurisdiction directly and a favourable ranking can be overtaken without any change in local law.

The other state/provinces listed alongside it are not exposed to the same override by the national legislature. A ranking shared with them therefore does not describe the same degree of durability, and the assessment's own caution about the jurisdiction's protective reputation is the part of the placement that bears on a visitor's expectations.

Residents elect a local government whose legislation and budget remain subject to the national legislature. The bathroom ban attached to this state/province is an override of that kind operating now, and its enforcement record includes the arrests at the national legislature building on 5 December 2024.

For residents who rely on local law for facilities access and other protections, the July 2026 assessment's caution is the operative finding: those protections can be narrowed through national action rather than through the local council, and the jurisdiction's standing as the most protective is no longer treated as settled.

The source inventory holds no jurisdiction-specific information on gender-marker change procedures for locally issued identity documents, on local hate-crime law or its enforcement, on local police practice, or on conditions in local custody. These are unresolved here rather than assessed.

The scope of the bathroom ban the national legislature attached to this state/province is not specified in the available source. Which buildings it covers, how it is enforced beyond the December 2024 arrests, and whether it reaches visitors as well as employees are not sourced.

The July 2026 assessment's criteria and method are not described in the inventory, so the basis for the jurisdiction's low-risk placement cannot be verified from the material available.

The state/province sits in the fifteen-jurisdiction "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, among them youth care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's licence restrictions, and measures removing legal recognition. The rubric describes the laws in this tier as having gone beyond baseline safeguarding of trans rights.

Statewide anti-discrimination law covers the settings a visitor uses daily. A state/province equality law, signed 9 May 2007 as a 2007 bill and in force since 1 January 2008, prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services on the ground of gender identity. Sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether a person's identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from what is traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. The protections apply uniformly across the state/province and do not depend on the locality; religious employers, organisations and institutions are exempt.

Bias-motivated violence carries enhanced penalties: state/province hate-crime statutes add punishment for crimes committed because of the victim's gender identity. A 2021 law, passed and signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively accessible. The driver-licensing agency has offered an X marker for neutral or non-binary identity on licences and state/province IDs since 1 July 2017, and X is also available on birth certificates. Sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on a birth certificate by request since 2014. Legislation in May 2017 abolished the 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex. A court ruling on 10 June 2016 allowed a resident to change gender to non-binary, which a legal advocacy group believed was the first ruling of its kind in the country. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state/province agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option X; legislation signed in June 2021 updated the 2008 definition of gender identity.

Care is shielded for people arriving from jurisdictions that have banned it. The state/province's shield law, signed by the governor on 13 July 2023, protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges or investigation when care that is legal in the state/province was prohibited in the patient's home jurisdiction. The legislature's lower chamber passed the bill in May 2023; the upper chamber passed a version with amendments after a boycott by an opposition party.

Partner recognition does not turn on the parties' birth sex. A national district judge struck down the 2004 constitutional amendment banning marriage for same-sex couples on 19 May 2014, marriages of same-sex couples performed elsewhere have been recognised since 16 October 2013, and gender-neutral marriage was codified effective 1 January 2016. Domestic partnerships have been available since 4 February 2008.

The July 2026 ranking assesses enacted legislation against a rubric; it does not measure enforcement or day-to-day treatment, so the state/province's placement reflects its statutes rather than documented policing practice. The same tier includes several neighbouring jurisdictions.

National pressure on state/province institutions is active. In June 2025 the national education department announced an investigation under a national education civil-rights law into the state/province education department over its allowance of transgender women competing in women's sports.

Public coverage of gender-affirming care is established. A January 2013 discrimination settlement committed the state/province to full medical insurance coverage of gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatment for people on public employee health plans, and in August 2014 officials announced that the public health insurance programme would cover gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming care.

Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 1 July 2015, under a bill signed 18 May 2015 after legislative votes of 41-18 and 21-8; the state/province was the third in the country to enact such a ban.

Residents' records have been corrected by statute. Legislation signed 6 May 2019 amended a 1951 mental health law that equated transvestites with paedophilia, passing the lower chamber 58-2 and the upper chamber 29-0.

A transgender-inclusive public schools policy survived challenge: the trial court ruled against the plaintiffs on 24 July 2018, a national appeals court affirmed on 12 February 2020, and the national supreme court denied review in December 2020. The anti-bullying law covers harassment, including cyberbullying, in all public schools.

Adoption and family formation are open to same-sex couples, married or unmarried, who may apply to adopt; lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction such as in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised as legal parent if married; surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted and courts are generally favourable. In July 2025 a national appeals court held unconstitutional the state/province's requirement that prospective adopters respect, accept and support a child's gender expression and sexual orientation, after the state/province human services department prevented a woman seeking to adopt.

No state/province-specific data was located on police stops, searches, custody treatment or airport screening of trans travellers, or on how the public-accommodations law is enforced in practice against venues that exclude trans patrons.

Hate-crime statutes provide enhanced penalties for gender-identity bias, but charging and prosecution statistics for such crimes in the state/province were not found in the sources.

The 2023 shield law reached the upper legislative chamber in amended form after a boycott by an opposition party; which categories of care remain covered by the narrowed text is unresolved in the sources.

The practical effect of the July 2025 adoption ruling on the state/province human services department's practice is not yet documented.

National rules on passports, visa markers, entry screening and national facilities apply in the state/province but belong to the national record and are not restated here.

The state/province stands under the national framework carried at the country level.

Facility access is the most immediate state/province-level exposure. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records the state/province as enacting bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2022 and 2024. House Bill 322, signed 8 April 2022 as Act No. 2022-290 and codified by the Board of Education in September 2022, requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with the gender recorded on their birth certificate. A March 2024 bill would extend this to ban university bathroom use not aligned with sex assigned at birth, and a July 2026 legal risk assessment records that the state/province's education bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, placing it in the assessment's worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions. Senate Bill 79, signed February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and allows separate single-sex spaces where biology, privacy, safety or fairness are implicated.

Gender-affirming care for minors is criminalised. Since 8 May 2022 the Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act (SB 184), signed 8 April 2022, makes it a Class C felony punishable by 10 years in prison for a medical provider to give puberty blockers, hormones, or surgeries to anyone under 19. The national appeals court allowed enforcement from 21 August 2023, and the ban remained in force after plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025.

Identity documents carry a surgery requirement. The state/province permits amendment of birth certificates and driver's licences to current sex only with documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" and a name change. In Corbitt v. Taylor a January 2021 national ruling invalidated the surgery requirement, but the national appeals court reversed this, leaving the requirement standing; on 20 September 2024 the same court ruled that refusal to issue accurate licences did not violate the national constitution, rehearing was denied 13 November 2024, and judgment was entered 10 December 2024. A national civil-liberties organisation states that most transgender people therefore cannot obtain an accurate licence and must carry daily ID showing the wrong gender, exposing them to harassment and violence in ID checks.

Sports participation is restricted by sex assigned at birth. Since 1 July 2021 public schools must assign single-sex sports teams by "biological sex," and House Bill 391, enacted April 2021 after passing the lower chamber 74-19 with two abstentions and signed by the governor, requires all K-12 athletes to compete based on the gender listed on their birth certificate. House Bill 261, signed 30 May 2023, prohibits college and university competition on a team differing from sex assigned at birth even after gender-affirming hormone therapy, except in co-ed sports.

No statewide nondiscrimination protection exists. State law provides no prohibition on discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment and bullying; there is no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare and no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees. Only two municipalities (since September 2017 and April 2018) prohibit all such discrimination, while three other cities provide public-employment protections. As of 2025, statewide polling places the state/province among the lowest-support states for transgender-inclusive nondiscrimination and access policies, leaving trans visitors without statewide public-accommodations recourse and exposed to denial of care for accompanying minors, exclusion from gendered facilities and sports, and ID incongruence in ID checks.

Hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. The state/province's hate-crime law since 1994 covers only race, color, religion, national origin, ethnicity, or physical or mental disability. Gender identity has been applied to sex under employment law in this appeals circuit since 2011, and the national hate-crime statute of October 2009 bans gender-identity hate crimes.

Marriage recognition has improved on paper. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, but eight counties still refused all marriage licenses by 2017, until the Legislature in May 2019 required recording of marriage certificates and all counties began recording for all couples including same-sex couples on 29 August 2019, leaving prior executive, statutory and constitutional barriers unenforceable.

Adoption is permitted for same-sex couples, though the state/province's high court in 2002 held homosexual conduct created a strong presumption of parental unfitness, and a May 2017 statute signed by the governor protects faith-based agencies refusing placements on religious beliefs.

The state/province's regime sits within a national pattern of tightening state-level restrictions. A July 2026 legal risk assessment places it in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, alongside other states flagged for bathroom bans and document restrictions.

The national appeals court's rulings in Corbitt v. Taylor and its September 2024 decision upholding refusal of accurate licences reflect a broader appellate posture in this circuit that differs from other national circuits on trans document rights.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since the 2003 Lawrence v. Texas decision striking down sodomy laws, and Senate Bill 320, passed by the lower chamber 23 May 2019 by 101 yes with 3 absent and by the upper chamber 28 May 2019 by 32 yea with 3 absent, repealed the state/province's ban on "deviate sexual intercourse" effective 1 September 2019; the age of consent is 16 with a within-2-years exception extended to same-sex contact in 2019.

From 1992 to 2021 state law required sexual education to emphasize "that homosexuality is not a lifestyle acceptable to the general public and that homosexual conduct is a criminal offense," repealed in April 2021 after the governor signed repeal of archaic references to homosexuality and HIV/AIDS.

Residents face a Class C felony, punishable by 10 years in prison, for a medical provider to supply gender-affirming care including puberty blockers, hormones, or surgeries to anyone under 19; the ban has been enforceable since 21 August 2023 and remained in force after plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025.

Changing the gender marker on a birth certificate or driver's licence requires documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" plus a name change; the national appeals court's 20 September 2024 ruling, rehearing denied 13 November 2024 and judgment entered 10 December 2024, left this surgery requirement in place, so most trans residents carry daily ID showing the wrong gender.

State law provides no prohibition on discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment and bullying, no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare, and no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees. Local ordinances are the only protections: two municipalities (September 2017 and April 2018) prohibit all such discrimination, while three other cities provide public-employment protections.

The state/province's hate-crime law since 1994 does not apply to crimes based on gender identity, covering only race, color, religion, national origin, ethnicity, or physical or mental disability. Gender identity has been applied to sex under employment law in this appeals circuit since 2011, and the national hate-crime statute of October 2009 bans gender-identity hate crimes.

Public school students must use bathrooms consistent with the gender on their birth certificate under HB322 (Act No. 2022-290, signed 8 April 2022, codified September 2022); a March 2024 bill would extend this to universities. Senate Bill 79, signed February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth.

Sports teams are assigned by "biological sex" in public schools since 1 July 2021, K-12 athletes must compete by birth-certificate gender under HB391 (April 2021), and HB261 (signed 30 May 2023) bars college athletes from competing on a team differing from sex assigned at birth even after hormone therapy, except co-ed sports.

State law does not address discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment and bullying; sexual orientation has been applied to sex under employment law since 2020, and the state/province's hate-crime law does not cover sexual orientation after a 2009 bill failed in the upper chamber and later bills in 2016 and 2017 failed, though the national hate-crime statute applies.

Same-sex couples may adopt, though the state/province's high court in 2002 held homosexual conduct created a strong presumption of parental unfitness, and a May 2017 statute signed by the governor protects faith-based agencies refusing placements on religious beliefs.

A July 2026 legal risk assessment's grouping of the state/province as a legislatively-erasing jurisdiction is a third-party assessment; the underlying education bill text and its precise campus-bathroom provisions are not reproduced in this inventory and remain unverified here.

The March 2024 university bathroom bill's final legislative status is not stated in the inventory; whether it was enacted, amended, or failed is unresolved.

The inventory does not document any specific incident of violence against a trans person in the state/province, nor any trans-specific crime rate for it, so no comparative violence risk can be stated.

Whether the May 2019 legislative requirement that all counties record marriage certificates has been fully complied with in every county since 29 August 2019 is not independently verified beyond the source's statement.

A July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment map lists the state/province among its 'Most Protective' state/provinces for gender-identity nondiscrimination. The national human rights body's recognition of the deceased and the renewed calls for an anti-discrimination bill that followed her death were national processes; no legislative response at state/province level is documented.

No breakdown at state/province level exists for the national survey data on transgender discrimination, and the sources reviewed record no figures specific to the state/province on enforcement, healthcare access, school facilities or violence.

The state/province's documented trans-specific record is confined to the March 2021 death and its aftermath; no more recent incident, enforcement action or policy change in the state/province is recorded.

The state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework, which carries the parent nation's criminal law, legal gender recognition rules, document policy and protection machinery. The state/province's own documented signal concerns students rather than visitors. Its student human-rights ordinance, enacted on 10 July 2020, contains Article 15, covering gender identity and sexual orientation. The provincial council voted to repeal the ordinance on 24 April 2024. The provincial education authority, which enforces the ordinance, challenged the repeal at the highest court on 13 May 2024 and obtained suspension of execution on 30 May 2024, so the ordinance remains in force while the case proceeds. The authority argues that the repeal violates the constitution and international human-rights treaties.

The ordinance's status is contested between sources. A reference article records that the state/province's ordinance was revoked in 2024, matching the 24 April 2024 council vote, while the national government's submission to a United Nations special-procedures mechanism, dated 21 February 2025, states that the suspension of execution keeps it in effect. No rule specific to the state/province on restroom access, healthcare, policing, hate-crime enforcement or violence was identified; for those matters the national assessment applies.

The state/province's ordinance belongs to a set of student human-rights ordinances adopted by provincial and metropolitan education authorities, in which the provisions on gender and sexual diversity have been the most contentious items. Repeal campaigns against such ordinances have been pursued through provincial councils and tested in the courts.

For students in the state/province's schools, the ordinance remains operative pending the highest court's decision, and the provincial education authority is both its enforcing authority and a party to the dispute. The ordinance prohibits discrimination of students by gender, religion, nationality, disability, race and sexual orientation, with Article 15 addressing gender identity and sexual orientation. A repeal upheld by the court would remove those gender-identity and sexual-orientation protections from the state/province's student-rights framework.

Sources disagree on whether the ordinance is currently in force: a reference article records revocation in 2024, while the government's February 2025 submission to a United Nations special-procedures mechanism states that the 30 May 2024 suspension of execution leaves it in effect. The outcome of the highest court's ruling in the repeal dispute is unresolved in the available material. No documentation specific to the state/province was identified on restroom access, healthcare access, hate-crime enforcement or violence. The same United Nations submission also addresses a parallel dispute in a different jurisdiction, which is not specific to the state/province.

No state/province-specific ordinance, enforcement action or documented incident in this field appears in the source inventory. The national framework of the parent nation governs visitors to the state/province, including national court rulings on public restroom access and on removing the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change; neither source records an incident within the state/province.

The two sourced developments bearing on the state/province are national court rulings whose effect reaches the state/province rather than state/province-level events. No protest, enforcement action or institutional dispute specific to the state/province is documented in the inventory.

No resident-facing fact specific to the state/province is sourced. Trans residents of the state/province rely on the same national legal framework as the rest of the parent nation, and the inventory records no state/province-level service, facility or enforcement practice.

The inventory does not establish whether the state/province maintains its own ordinance or local administrative practice in this field, and no state/province-level incident data is sourced. State/province-specific enforcement and facility practice remain unresolved.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation. No ordinance, sub-national directive, police practice, court decision or documented incident specific to transgender people in the state/province appeared in the available sources.

Two national decisions are final and apply in the state/province. An appellate court finalised an award of 300,000 won against the state, on a claim of 3 million won, over police advice given to a woman who had obtained court approval for an official gender-marker change in 2020 telling her to avoid the women's public restrooms; the court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The advice the court condemned is a general police practice rather than an incident confined to one locality, so the ruling reaches officers in the state/province, though no comparable complaint there has been documented.

In May 2024 a regional court approved a registered-sex change from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery. It held that gender change cannot be determined by surgery, that court guidelines requiring surgery are reference material rather than criteria, and that every person has the right to live according to their gender identity. Applications in the state/province proceed on that footing; the sources record no applicant there and no court ruling on the question.

The rulings that shape a trans visitor's position in the state/province were issued elsewhere in the country. Their reach rests on general applicability rather than on any local instrument, and no court in the state/province has ruled on restroom access or on a registered-sex application.

The damages award is symbolic: 300,000 won against a claim of 3 million won. Its effect is declaratory, so deterrence of the restroom advice depends on officers and venue staff knowing the decision rather than on the size of the penalty.

No district-level or sub-national breakdown of national survey evidence on restroom avoidance was identified, so the frequency of that problem in the state/province cannot be stated.

No sub-national ordinance, local office policy or transgender-specific service appeared in the sources. Residents depend on the national framework for registration, restroom access and remedies against officials or businesses.

A resident applying to change registered sex does so through the courts on the footing set in May 2024, when a regional court held that surgery cannot determine gender change and that guidelines requiring it are reference only; five applicants who had not undergone surgery were approved.

Where police or a business tell a resident to avoid the restroom matching their gender, that advice has been held to infringe personal rights, with compensation of 300,000 won in the case that was finalised. The remedy is real but small, and no resident of the state/province has been documented bringing such a claim.

Whether the state/province has any sub-national provision addressing discrimination on grounds of gender identity, and whether its police force has issued internal guidance on restroom advice or on the treatment of transgender detainees, is not sourced.

National survey figures on restroom avoidance are not broken down below the national level, and no rate for the state/province can be derived from them.

No incident, complaint or damages claim specific to the state/province concerning a transgender person was located in the sources reviewed. The absence of a documented case is not evidence that none has occurred.

The state/province has no separate legal regime of its own; the national law of the country governs. What is documented there runs through a court seated in the state/province and through a cemetery. On 7 October 2021 a district court in the state/province ordered the cancellation of the military's discharge of a transgender soldier, the first known legal case involving a transgender service member. The court held that the military should have treated her as female following her legal sex change, that the loss of genitalia was not a valid ground for dismissal, and that a fitness-for-service review must weigh basic rights. The decision upheld the appeal pursued on her behalf after her death.

On 24 June 2024 the soldier was buried at a national cemetery in the state/province; she was the country's first known transgender soldier. Around 60 activists protested at the burial, arguing that it was marred by discriminatory treatment. The ceremony was conducted as an official state honour there.

The two findings for the state/province are both attached to one person's case and to institutions seated there rather than to any local law. The district court's holding that the loss of genitalia is not valid grounds for dismissal was directed at the basis the military had used to end her service, so the ruling's reach is defined by the national framework it applied rather than by anything local.

The official state honour conferred at the burial coincided with an activist protest over discriminatory treatment in how it was carried out, and the classification the military had applied to her post-surgical status was the basis the court rejected.

For residents of the state/province, its district court is the forum where the discharge of a transgender soldier was reversed, and a national cemetery in the state/province is where she is buried. Around 60 activists attended the June 2024 burial to protest discriminatory treatment in its handling.

The court's reasoning on fitness review and on the irrelevance of genitalia loss is recorded at district court level there; no separate policy of the state/province on transgender matters appears in the sources.

Whether the district court's holdings have been applied in later military fitness or discharge cases is not sourced. No statute, ordinance, police practice, school restroom policy, healthcare rule or hate-crime enforcement record specific to the state/province appears in the inventory.

The inventory for the state/province rests on two news reports, one dated 7 October 2021 and one dated 25 June 2024; no court document or official transcript is cited.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the country. The source inventory records no state/province-specific law, court ruling, enforcement action, incident, or institution. The two legal standards it documents, the restroom-access damages ruling and the removal of the surgical prerequisite for a registered sex change, are national in scope and are recorded as applying in the state/province with no state/province-specific case attached to either. A trans visitor to the state/province therefore faces the national legal position with no documented state/province-level variation.

The standards that reach the state/province were set by courts elsewhere in the country, in the capital and in other state/provinces, rather than by any court in the state/province; the inventory records no ruling by a bench in the state/province on restroom access or on registered-sex change. The state/province's position on these questions is derived from national litigation rather than from local adjudication, and no authority in the state/province is recorded as having contested, narrowed, or extended that position.

No state/province-specific measure appears in the inventory. No ordinance, school policy, hospital protocol, or police guidance issued by authorities in the state/province on restroom access, registered-sex change, or the accommodation of transgender patients is documented. Residents of the state/province depend on the national framework for these questions, and the inventory records no institution in the state/province acting on them.

No state/province-specific incident, enforcement action, or court ruling is documented; whether any exists is unresolved in the source inventory.

The national survey data in the inventory is not disaggregated by state/province, so no state/province-specific figure can be derived from it.

Whether authorities in the state/province have issued any guidance on restroom access, gender-marker change, or hospital accommodation for transgender patients is not sourced.

The state/province's visitor-relevant signal is concentrated in its annual queer culture festival, held every June since 2009 without interruption and described as the parent nation's second-largest LGBT event: a pride parade and film festival running a week or two, usually in late June. The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation for criminal law, legal gender recognition, documents and healthcare; the findings below are those specific to the state/province.

Opposition is organised, annual and large. A conservative-Protestant umbrella body covering the state/province and the surrounding region convened its 17th annual "National Assembly Against Queer" in response to the festival, gathering roughly 3,500 believers from about 1,600 churches at a central transit station and along a 450 m stretch toward a nearby intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans. An estimated 28 religious and right-wing groups have formed a "gay issue countermeasure committee" in the state/province to block LGBT events, and that opposition has kept the festival off an outdoor stage on a popular central street.

Court bids to stop the festival have failed each year. An opposition countermeasure committee sought an injunction against the 2025 edition; the court dismissed it, as it had dismissed the bids for 2022, 2023 and 2024. In 2023, under the then-mayor, municipal officials physically blocked the road. Police again restricted the 2025 march to a single bus-only lane. Organisers framed the event as resistance to "hate and discriminatory politics".

The dispute continued into the 2026 edition. An opposition countermeasures headquarters, made up of a parents' alliance, a Christian council and a merchants' association, filed a collective petition with the national human rights commission demanding a change of venue, arguing the event is likely to infringe public welfare. The group says about 34,000 signatures were collected, which it calls unusually large for a single commission petition. The petition cites the state/province's district court's dismissal of the festival committee's injunction request, a ruling that found the police notice restricting the event legitimate because the road in question is a key urban traffic artery and one lane must be secured for public welfare. It responds to the festival committee's January petition against the national police commissioner and the national assembly speaker over article 12(1) of the assembly and demonstration act.

The counter-mobilisation is organised at the scale of the state/province and the surrounding region rather than the city alone: the umbrella body draws churches from the surrounding region as well as the city, and the 2025 assembly was billed as a national gathering. The venue dispute has been routed through national institutions, the national human rights commission, the national police and the national assembly, rather than settled locally.

The festival is the second-largest LGBT event in the parent nation, so the annual pattern of injunction bids and police route limits is a comparator for visitors planning around other pride events in the parent nation, though the specific restrictions described here are the state/province's own.

For residents, the festival and its counter-assembly recur on a predictable June calendar in the city centre, around a central arterial road and a central transit station, with police route restrictions on the march and a single bus-only lane allocated to it. A merchants' association representing businesses in a central commercial district is a named party to the opposition petition.

Injunction bids against the festival have been filed and dismissed each year since at least 2022, so the legal challenge is a recurring annual event rather than a one-off.

The size of the counter-mobilisation and of the petition rests on the organisers' own figures: the 3,500 participants, 1,600 churches and 34,000 signatures are not independently verified in the sources. The outcome of the 2026 petition before the national human rights commission is not sourced, and the sources do not detail whether police route restrictions differed in years other than 2025.

No data specific to the state/province was identified on violence against transgender people, healthcare access, document or marker practice, or facilities such as restrooms; those matters are carried by the national record for the parent nation. National attitude survey figures cited alongside coverage of the festival are country-level and belong to the national record.

Visitors to the state/province stand under the national framework of the parent nation. Entry rules, identity documents, legal gender recognition, criminal law and the national protection and health-care layers are set nationally and are recorded in the parent nation's own dossier. The material identified at region level concerns one state/province and, in narrower form, another.

The regional council of the state/province passed motion n.340 at its 178th public session in the regional capital on 3 July. Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 approved that motion, committing the regional government to a mandatory 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejecting the aims of gender-awareness content in schools. The official regional government bulletin carries the primary-source text of the deliberation. The most recent documented instance of this instrument in this record is 14 October 2014; no later amendment, repeal or successor measure is documented here.

The measure operates through the school calendar and regional policy statements. It creates no criminal offence, no penalty and no restriction on entry, documents or movement, and it does not alter the national rules on legal gender recognition or anti-discrimination protection.

Regional anti-discrimination statutes in the parent framework cover one state/province (2019) alongside eight others in the country, giving part of the region a region-level discrimination statute while another state/province's documented regional instrument runs in the opposite direction, committing its regional government to a mandatory 'Natural Family Day' school observance and to rejecting gender-awareness content. Two further state/provinces in the region have no regional statute listed in this inventory.

The deliberation is a policy and school-observance instrument rather than an enforcement power; comparisons with criminal law or border measures are not apt, since those sit entirely at national level.

For residents of the state/province, deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 binds the regional government to hold the 'Natural Family Day' observance on the last school day before Christmas, and records the regional council's rejection of the aims of gender-awareness content. The obligation falls on the regional administration and the school system, not on individuals.

Residents of the state/province with the 2019 statute are covered by that region's anti-discrimination instrument, which is a regional measure distinct from the parent nation's national employment-discrimination rules.

No region-specific detention findings for facilities in the state/province are sourced here. The national detention material in this inventory, including a July 2025 institute report and a 2026 psychiatric-journal analysis of trans prisoners, is not broken down by region, and the documented prison cases all sit outside this state/province. Whether trans detainees in local facilities face the same placement and hormone-access problems described nationally is unresolved in this record.

No region-specific incidents of violence against transgender people in the state/province are documented in this inventory, and no region-level survey of trans residents' experiences is sourced. The absence of such material is not evidence of their absence.

Whether motion n.340 or deliberation n.92 has been implemented, funded or observed in practice since 14 October 2014 is not sourced here.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation; no state/province-specific legal regime governing gender identity or sexual orientation was identified in the sources, and the national assessment applies.

On 26 April 2025 three young men were beaten at a fast-food restaurant in a city in the state/province because they were gay. The local prosecutor's office reconstructed a sequence of insults and threats that preceded the physical assault, and video of the attack circulated publicly.

A local outlet's follow-up of 5 June 2026 catalogues continuing assaults and suicide cases across towns in the state/province, indicating that the pattern of attacks recorded in 2025 has not stopped.

The violence documented in the state/province is homophobic rather than trans-specific. The 2025 assault in a city in the state/province targeted gay men, and the 2026 catalogue covers assaults and suicides among local residents; the inventory records no state/province-specific incident aimed at a trans visitor or trans resident. A trans visitor's risk in the state/province therefore rests on the national assessment rather than on a separate regional signal.

The 5 June 2026 local catalogue records suicide cases alongside continuing assaults in towns in the state/province. Those deaths and assaults fall on people living in the state/province rather than on visitors passing through, and they indicate that the hostility documented in 2025 has not receded for residents.

No state/province-specific legal regime, protection body or hate-crime statute was identified in the sources; the state/province's legal position is set by national law.

The 5 June 2026 catalogue is a local outlet's summary and gives no dates, locations or court outcomes for the individual assaults and suicides it lists, so the scale of the pattern in the state/province is not quantified.

Findings on the placement of trans detainees in the prison system and on a dedicated facility for trans prisoners are national in scope and are carried by the national record; they are not specific to the state/province.

This state/province stands under the country's national framework on legal gender recognition, discrimination and asylum. The findings specific to this state/province are judicial and documentary: a regional distribution of recorded anti-LGBT violence, an administrative ruling in its largest city, and a homicide acquittal in one of its university cities.

A civil-society study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, covering 2012 to 2025, ranks six state/provinces at the top by victim count. Two of the six lie within this state/province. The ranking is by raw victim counts, which track population, and the study supplies no per-capita denominator, so it does not establish that any one of these state/provinces carries a higher rate of violence than another.

In the largest city of this state/province, the municipal administration announced on 30 August 2025 that the highest administrative court had upheld the city's 2022 removal of posters attacking "gender" ideology in schools, placed by an anti-trans campaign group. The court found the images discriminatory, one of them showing a boy being handed a red hairbow, and held that public spaces may not be used for messages that generate alarmism, fear or serious disturbance, particularly where minors are concerned. The campaign behind the posters had collected 105,000 online signatures. The outcome confirms that anti-trans public messaging can be restricted in that city.

In a university city of this state/province, the highest court confirmed on 5 March 2026 the appeal acquittal of a trans woman over the death of a man on 27 April 2021. The court held that the death resulted from cardiac arrhythmia caused by accidental compression during a scuffle that the man started, making the acquittal on the homicide charge final. The case was a national anti-trans media flashpoint, and the definitive judicial outcome favoured the trans defendant.

The strongest judicial recognition of a transphobic aggravating motive recorded in this inventory comes from outside this state/province. On 24 January 2025 a first-instance court in a city in a neighbouring state/province found a transphobic motive in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, and awarded damages both to the victim and to the trans-movement association that assists sex workers; the court admitted a trans advocacy organisation as a civil party for the first time. The judgment bears on how courts in the country treat transphobic aggravation, but it is a first-instance decision from another state/province, and no equivalent recognition of a trans association as civil party is recorded for a court within this state/province.

The regional violence figures concern people living in the two state/provinces of this record rather than visitors: those two appear among the six with the highest raw counts of recorded anti-LGBT victims in the 2012 to 2025 study, and the study gives no breakdown below that level.

Residents of the largest city of this state/province are directly affected by the administrative ruling that keeps the city's public spaces closed to anti-trans campaign material; the decision concerns municipal property and messaging aimed at school pupils.

In a university city of this state/province, a trans woman was prosecuted over a death that occurred in the city in April 2021 and was definitively acquitted in March 2026, after the case had become a sustained national media story. Local court practice and local media treatment, rather than any visitor-specific rule, are what the record documents for that city.

The inventory records no rules or practice specific to this state/province on gender-recognition procedures, identity documents, health-care access or police conduct. Those matters are set by the national framework and are not restated here.

The administrative court decision upholding the 2022 removal of the posters is reported through the municipal administration's announcement of 30 August 2025; the inventory does not give the date of the court's own ruling or its reasoning beyond the summary quoted.

The judgment of 24 January 2025 in the neighbouring state/province is a first-instance decision. Whether it was appealed, and whether it stands, is unresolved in this inventory.

The civil-society study is the only regional distribution of violence available here. It gives victim counts by state/province without a population denominator, so per-capita rates of anti-LGBT violence cannot be calculated from it, and the counts should not be read as a severity ranking.

No incident of violence against a trans visitor specifically in this state/province appears in the inventory.

The state/province stands under the national framework. No state/province statute, court ruling or administrative measure specific to this state/province addressing gender identity or sexual orientation was identified, so the assessment rests on documented incidents within the state/province.

An international LGBT federation's annual country review, published in February 2025, records a troubling increase in the number and geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people in 2024, with incidents reported almost monthly. One such incident fell within this state/province: in March 2025 a young man was assaulted by attackers on a scooter in a neighbourhood of the state/province's largest city.

On 13 October 2025 a 63-year-old man was arrested in a town in the state/province after making stabbing threats against a young LGBTQIA+ activist; a local newspaper described it as a grave homophobic episode in the area.

On detention, no dedicated transgender prison facility exists in the country. A 2010 announcement that a prison in another state/province would become one of the world's first facilities for transgender inmates was never realised; as of 2013 it had not been created, and trans detainees remain within the ordinary men's and women's prison circuit, including in this state/province.

The incidents documented in this state/province form part of a national pattern an international LGBT federation describes as increasing in both number and geographic spread during 2024, with reports arriving almost monthly across the country rather than concentrating in any single area.

The 2010 proposal was the country's only documented special-unit initiative for trans prisoners; its non-realisation by 2013 means trans detainees nationwide, including in this state/province, are housed in ordinary facilities with no dedicated unit anywhere in the country.

Residents of this state/province live under the national legal framework, and no state/province-specific protective statute or administrative measure addressing gender identity or sexual orientation was identified in this inventory.

Anti-discrimination statutes exist in several other state/provinces (adopted in 2004, 2009, 2010, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2019, 2020 and 2024), but no equivalent statute for this state/province appears in this inventory.

Whether this state/province has any pending anti-discrimination bill or administrative guidance on gender identity is unresolved in this inventory; the absence of a statute here is a research finding, not a confirmed legislative decision.

The current status of the 2010 trans-prison proposal after 2013 is unresolved; no later reporting appears in this inventory, and the record does not establish whether the plan was formally cancelled or simply lapsed.

The February 2025 review's characterisation of a rise in 2024 violence rests on reported incidents; the inventory does not provide a denominator or reporting-rate context for that increase.

This state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation; the findings below are specific to this region. The region's largest city operates the parent nation's first gender registry, a municipal instrument that allows transgender people to use their chosen name on civic and municipal documents. A national news outlet presents the registry as a milestone for transgender rights in the country and ties it to a 2022 council motion by the country's first elected transgender councillor. A second city in the region runs a parallel alias practice at municipal offices and libraries. Both instruments are city-level, and the inventory documents no region-wide equivalent.

An LGBT rights organisation's breakdown of aggressions by region and city for the period 2012–2025 places two of the state/province's constituent areas among the parent nation's six highest-victim areas for anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence. The ranking is by raw count of victims; the source supplies no population denominator, so it does not measure per-capita risk and does not show that a larger area is more dangerous than a smaller one.

The two documented instruments are municipal in scope. A visitor or resident outside the region's largest city and its second city has no access point to a chosen-name register documented anywhere else in the state/province, and the inventory records no regional body, fund or procedure that extends either practice to the region's other provinces.

The organisational series counts anti-LGBT aggressions as a single category across the parent nation's areas. Its regional placement therefore reflects the volume of reported anti-LGBT incidents in the region as a whole rather than a measure of violence directed specifically at transgender people, and the source provides no per-capita or population-adjusted figure for the region.

The largest city's gender registry lets transgender residents put their chosen name on civic and municipal documents, and the practice originated in a 2022 council motion tabled by the country's first elected transgender councillor. The instrument covers municipal paperwork; the inventory does not state that it alters national identity documents.

Residents of the region's second city can use the alias practice at municipal offices and libraries. Both instruments are municipal provisions, and residents of the region's other provinces have no equivalent documented route to a chosen name on local documents.

For residents of the state/province, the organisation's 2012–2025 series places two of the constituent areas among the parent nation's six highest-victim areas for reported anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence, counted as raw incidents with no population denominator.

The detention material in this inventory does not concern this state/province. A plan announced in January 2010 for a dedicated transgender prison at a facility in another region of the parent nation, intended for about 30 of the country's roughly 60 transgender prisoners and described as an alternative to placement in women's prisons where trans prisoners were held apart for their own safety, was reported abandoned by a national newspaper in 2013. That newspaper's investigation of 28 August 2013 counted 69 trans prisoners across ten facilities nationwide, with placement tracking the sex recorded on the identity card: trans women were held in men's sections, prisoners who had undergone sex-change surgery were sent to women's sections, female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners recorded as men, and isolation was used where cells were lacking. A 2011 court case ordered a local health authority to pay a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity, appealed with a July 2012 appellate decision. Whether any facility in this state/province applies comparable placement, hormone or segregation rules is unresolved in this inventory.

No region-specific legislative text on gender recognition or anti-discrimination appears in this inventory; whether statutes of the region's own governments address gender identity is not sourced here. The organisational breakdown is also not trans-specific: a regional count of violence against transgender people alone is not sourced.

This state/province is a sub-national unit of the parent nation and stands under the national framework: the constitutional equality guarantee, the equality court under the equality legislation, legal gender recognition, the 2024 hate-crime statute and the national correctional rules for transgender inmates apply here as they do elsewhere in the country. No state/provincial law, by-law or state/provincial institution departing from that layer is documented in the sources.

The state/provincial evidence on violence and victimisation is a 2024 masters thesis in criminology at a university in this state/province. It interviewed 15 self-identifying queer participants recruited through a local community organisation in a township in this state/province and reports substantial queerphobic violence and victimisation in that township setting. The study also examines whether the support and interventions available to those residents were adequate, and what safety strategies they used.

The study is small and its participants were purposively recruited, so it records the experiences of that group rather than a measured rate of violence. It does not disaggregate transgender participants from other sexual minorities, and no source gives a state/provincial figure for violence against transgender people. A trans visitor to this state/province has no validated local victimisation figure to work from.

A traditional monarch in this state/province made anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival in January 2012, which drew demands for an apology; a police investigation was opened, and the provincial premier and a traditional-leaders' body intervened over the royal family's account. The remarks concerned gay people rather than transgender people, carried no legal force, and are more than a decade old. No later statement from traditional leadership in this state/province on transgender people appears in the sources.

Traditional authority in the state/province is a social influence on how gay and transgender people are treated locally rather than a source of enforceable rules, and nothing in the sources connects it to a specific enforcement practice against trans visitors.

The township research is resident-facing. It documents queerphobic victimisation among people living in the township and asks whether the interventions and support structures available to them, including through a local community organisation, actually met their needs and what safety strategies residents adopted.

No state/provincial department, state/provincial programme or state/provincial body directed at violence against transgender or LGBTI residents is documented for this state/province; the protection machinery appearing in these sources sits at the national level.

Interview content, specific incidents and participant breakdowns from the township thesis are not reproduced in the inventory, so it is unresolved how many participants were transgender and what incidents they described.

Whether and how the national correctional standards for transgender inmates are applied in state/provincial facilities is not sourced, and no state/provincial correctional complaint or case involving a transgender person appears.

Whether the police investigation opened after the January 2012 remarks by the traditional monarch reached any outcome is not sourced, and no subsequent statement by traditional leadership in this state/province on transgender people is recorded.

Police handling of complaints, identity-document problems when presentation and documents do not match, and gender-segregated facilities in this state/province specifically are not documented; the analyses addressing those points are national in scope.

The state/province stands under the national legal framework. The state/province-specific material in the source inventory concerns the reach of customary law and traditional authority in the rural districts that formed part of the former historic-era homelands.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people living in those former historic-era areas, with no provision allowing anyone to opt out of its jurisdiction. The same report states that rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas.

Mamba Online reported on 18 April 2012, in a piece by Melanie Judge, that the bill was under debate in state/provincial public hearings and would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in those areas through a separate customary system. Lesbians were reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, and those able to do so were expected to leave rural areas. Traditional leaders were also reported to have opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006.

The most recent documented instance in this record dates from 2012; no later instance is documented.

The exposure described here runs through a second, customary justice track rather than through the national courts, which is what distinguishes the rural former historic-era districts from the state/province's urban centres. The reported conduct of traditional leaders, including opposition to the Civil Union Act of 2006, indicates institutional hostility at the level of the authorities operating that track.

The 2012 reports describe a bill under debate, not an enacted instrument, and the record contains no account of its passage or of any later customary-law instrument applying to the state/province.

Rural residents of the state/province's former historic-era districts were reported in 2012 to be subject to chiefs' courts with no mechanism to decline that jurisdiction, and to face poor police cooperation when seeking national protection. The reported practical response of those able to exercise it was to leave rural areas.

The current status of the Traditional Courts Bill is unresolved in this record: whether it was enacted, amended or withdrawn after the 2012 reporting is not sourced here, and no later assessment of customary-court jurisdiction in the state/province is documented.

No state/province-specific material is sourced on identity documents or gender markers, entry and border screening, facility or bathroom access, access to gender-affirming care, hate-crime enforcement, or partner recognition. Those layers sit with the national record.

The 2012 reports concern lesbians and gay and bisexual people; no state/province-specific account of violence or discrimination targeting transgender residents is documented in this inventory.

The state/province sits within the country's national framework, which carries the constitutional discrimination guarantees, the hate-crime statute, gender-recognition rules and corrections standards. What follows is specific to the state/province.

On the night of 14 May 2024, Jo-Ann Isaks, a 27-year-old transgender woman, was found dead in her burning room in a township in one district. She had multiple stab wounds to the upper body. A family member noticed the fire at about 23:00. Police in that district confirmed a murder case had been opened, described the investigation as at a critical stage and reported no arrests; the same statement identified her publicly by a male name. Jenny Sambok, an LGBTIQ+ leader in the district, said the community in the region had been shaken.

Karabelo Pudumo, an 18-year-old transgender Grade 10 learner at a local high school in the capital, was stabbed to death on 1 June 2024. A man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her after realising she was transgender and stabbed her more than 20 times. A suspect was reportedly arrested, a detail the outlet reporting the case could not confirm with the authorities. More than 300 children and community members attended a memorial service at the school. Her death was the second suspected hate-crime murder of a transgender person in the state/province in under a month.

A third LGBTIQ+ resident, Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas, a 50-year-old gay man, was murdered in September 2024. The three deaths are raw counts for one state/province in one year, and the sources provide no per-capita or general homicide rate against which to measure them.

Organised community presence in the state/province is recent. The first Pride event in the state/province was held on 30 November 2024 at a public venue in the capital under the theme 'Pride with a Purpose', with a morning parade, speakers and community activities. A Pride committee member called it a historic moment for the state/province.

The two transgender killings occurred in different districts of the state/province, one around a town in the north-west and one in the capital area, so the documented lethal risk is not confined to a single town or district.

The state/province's first Pride event took place only in November 2024, which indicates that organised LGBTIQ+ infrastructure here is more recent than in state/provinces with long-established Pride events.

The September 2024 killing of a gay man shows that lethal anti-LGBTIQ+ violence in the state/province is not limited to transgender targets, while the two documented transgender deaths share the specific pattern of a victim attacked after her gender identity became known.

More than 300 children and community members attended the memorial service at a local high school in the capital after Karabelo Pudumo's death, and the district LGBTIQ+ leadership in the region publicly registered the shock felt in the town after Jo-Ann Isaks was killed.

Accountability for residents remains open. No arrests had been reported in the Isaks case at the time of reporting, and the reported arrest of a suspect in Pudumo's killing could not be confirmed with the authorities by the outlet that published it.

The inaugural Pride event in the state/province was organised by a local Pride committee as a community event at a public venue in the capital, with a parade, speakers and activities.

Neither the Isaks nor the Pudumo killing has been judicially established as a hate crime. Both are described in the reporting as suspected hate crimes, and the motive in each rests on witness and community accounts rather than on a court finding.

The arrest of a suspect in the Pudumo case is unverified, and no arrest had been reported in the Isaks case at the time of publication. The current status of either investigation is not established by the sources reviewed.

The sources give no per-capita or general homicide rate for the state/province, so the three 2024 LGBTIQ+ killings cannot be compared with the state/province's background rate of lethal violence.

Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas was a gay man, not a transgender person. His killing is recorded as part of the state/province's 2024 LGBTIQ+ violence pattern and not as a transgender-specific incident.

The state/province has no sub-national law or municipal by-law that bars transgender people from gender-segregated facilities; access is decided venue by venue, by the operator's own rules and by the staff enforcing them. On 19 February 2025 a transgender woman was threatened with removal from a publicly owned sports stadium in a metropolitan area after using the women's bathroom. A security guard told her "Look at you, you're a man", directed her to the men's bathroom and said he had the final say. Police were called four times and had not arrived after nearly three hours. The stadium is a public facility operated by the municipal authority; on the day it was rented by a regional athletics body, which was responsible for the security services on site.

The incident records a gap between the absence of any sub-national restriction on facility access and the response a visibly trans person actually received in the state/province's best-resourced metropolitan area. The state/province stands under the national framework of the country; the constitutional guarantees, the criminal-law position, the hate-crime statute, legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are national provisions carried by the national record, and the sub-national layer neither adds to nor subtracts from them.

The security staff involved at the publicly owned stadium were engaged by a regional athletics body that had rented the venue for the day, rather than by the municipal authority directly. The conduct therefore does not by itself establish municipal policy on facility access, and a complaint would run against the renting body as well as the municipal operator.

No other sub-national factor bearing on trans visitors was identified in the source inventory; the state/province's trans-relevant law is the national framework applied locally.

Residents of the state/province face the same venue-by-venue facility rules as visitors, and the same gap in response. The 19 February 2025 incident at the publicly owned stadium involved a local resident who was challenged by a security guard and then waited nearly three hours after four calls to police without a response.

For residents seeking redress, the split between the municipal operator of a public venue and the club or body renting it determines who is answerable for security staff conduct; at that stadium the responsibility sat with the regional athletics body on the day.

The source inventory records no disciplinary, criminal or civil consequence for the security guard or for either body responsible for the stadium on 19 February 2025, and no explanation from the municipal authority or the regional athletics body for the police non-response.

No sub-national statute, sub-national equality body or sub-national hate-crime provision operating independently of the national framework appears in the inventory; whether any exists is not sourced here. No sub-national data on violence against transgender people in the state/province was identified.

Gender-affirming care in the parent nation is concentrated in the major metropolitan centres, and the state/province has no documented concentration of its own. A trans visitor who needs hormone therapy or surgery while in the state/province should expect to travel outside it, paying private prices in the hundreds of thousands of local currency units or waiting on a long public list. No state/province-specific provider, waiting-time or funding data was identified.

No state/province-specific statute, enforcement record, prosecution or documented incident involving a transgender person was identified. Policing, public hospitals, municipal facilities and correctional centres in the state/province operate under the national framework carried by the parent nation's record, and for those matters the national assessment is the one a visitor should rely on.

A national custody ruling heard in one region, in a case brought by a transgender inmate against the national corrections department (judgment 10 November 2025), binds that department nationally, so the remedies it orders for transgender inmates, among them state-funded gender-affirming hormone therapy and enforcement of the department's own standard operating procedures, reach correctional centres in the state/province. The case and its reasoning are carried by the parent nation's record; compliance inside facilities in the state/province is not documented here.
