For residents the practical constraint is distance. Care is concentrated in the metropolitan centres, so people in the state/province travel outside it for hormone therapy and surgery, private treatment is priced in the hundreds of thousands of local currency units, and public waiting lists are long. No state/province-specific gender-affirming provider network, support service or public health policy on trans care was identified.

No state/province-specific protection, ombuds office or programme addressing transgender residents was identified. The safeguards that exist are national instruments available anywhere in the parent nation.

No state/province-specific record of hate-crime prosecutions, police conduct or violence against transgender people was identified. Whether the national justice department's task team, established in 2011, or the 2014 national intervention strategy for LGBTI communities has any implementation in the state/province is not sourced.

Bathroom and facility access: a 2024 academic analysis examines whether gender-segregated bathrooms excluding transgender and non-binary people amount to unfair discrimination under the national equality legislation read with the constitutional equality guarantee, and concludes that trans people do not in practice receive equal protection in facility access. No venue, municipal or state/province policy on gender-segregated facilities was identified, so the position within the state/province is unresolved.

Health provision: whether public hospitals and clinics in the state/province offer gender-affirming hormone therapy, and what waiting times patients face, is not documented in the sources reviewed.

In the state/province, the documented record of violence against transgender people rests on a single recent case. A 23-year-old transgender woman living in a township in the state/province was attacked at about 1:30 am on 26 December 2024 in a tavern in a city in the state/province. A man had been saying that gay and lesbian people 'don't deserve to live'; he smashed a bottle into her face as she lit a cigarette and told her 'I told you I'm gonna kill you'. The cuts to her mouth, lips, nose, cheek and forehead were stitched after treatment at a local clinic. She opened an assault case at a local police station, which had shown no progress when local reporting covered it on 6 January 2025. The incident is the state/province's most recent documented hate crime targeting a transgender person on record.

On 10 November 2025 the high court of the state/province, sitting as an equality court under the national equality legislation, delivered judgment in a case brought by a transgender woman inmate against the head of a correctional centre in the state/province (case number 2024/070075). The court found that the national corrections department had engaged in unfair discrimination and harassment of the inmate by refusing to allow her to express her gender identity and by denying her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy. It held that the right to adequate medical treatment includes gender-affirming hormonal therapy at national expense, and ordered the department to implement the required accommodations and to enforce its own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates. The national human rights commission's preventive mechanism welcomed the ruling on 14 November 2025. The orders are enforceable against the department in the state/province, giving transgender people in the state/province an operational equality-court remedy for discrimination of this kind.

The same judgment records the only documented determination of how transgender prisoners are housed in the state/province. The inmate, a transgender woman serving a life sentence at a correctional centre in the state/province, was initially held in a medium-security section, where she could express her gender identity through long hair, makeup and women's clothing. She was later moved to another medium-security section, and at the time of judgment was held in a segregated unit used for solitary confinement, and was accommodated with cisgender male cellmates despite asking for a single cell; she was first housed with two cisgender gay men and then with one cisgender man, an arrangement the department justified by overcrowding. The court found that its standard operating procedures prescribe accommodation appropriate to gender identity where that is feasible and safe, that no basis existed for refusing her single accommodation, and ordered that she be held in a single cell or with inmates of the same gender identity and that the procedures be enforced.

For a transgender visitor, the risk documented in the state/province concentrates in unprovoked violence against visibly transgender people and in the police response to it, while the courts of the state/province have ordered enforceable protections for a transgender person in custody.

The state/province's own hate-crime evidence base is a research study rather than an enforcement record. A study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people in the state/province was conducted in 2003/04 by a local LGBT rights organisation with a university applied-psychology centre, under a joint research initiative, with partner organisations. It is described as the first representative quantitative provincial hate-crime study in the country.

A 2016 national campaign review, hosted by a local LGBT archive and research organisation and conducted by an LGBT well-being organisation, measures levels of discrimination against LGBT people nationally and records that only three quantitative studies of hate crime against LGBT people have ever been carried out; the 2003/04 study in the state/province is one of them. The state/province's hate-crime baseline therefore rests on a study more than two decades old, drawn from gay and lesbian respondents rather than transgender people.

For transgender people held in correctional facilities in the state/province, the judgment of 10 November 2025 is the operative protection: it converts the national corrections department's own standard operating procedures for transgender inmates into enforceable orders at a correctional centre in the state/province, covering gender-affirming hormone therapy at national expense, clothing and cosmetics expressing gender identity, accommodation and single-cell placement.

Residents who report violence against transgender people to the police face an enforcement gap in the documented case. The assault case opened at a local police station after the 26 December 2024 attack had shown no progress when it was reported on 6 January 2025.

The high court of the state/province sits as an equality court, and it has granted relief in a case of discrimination against a transgender person, which is the mechanism available to residents of the state/province bringing discrimination or harassment complaints.

No statute specific to the state/province on gender recognition, identity documents or facility access appears in the source material; those matters are set at national level, and the state/province's record here is judicial and incident-based.

The date of delivery of the judgment is not fully resolved: the national human rights commission's statement gives 10 November 2025 as the date of the ruling and 14 November 2025 as the date of the statement welcoming it.

The outcome of the assault case opened at a local police station after the 26 December 2024 attack, including whether any arrest resulted in prosecution, is not recorded in the source material.

No rate or count of violence against transgender people specific to the state/province is available in the sources, so no comparison with the state/province's general homicide rate can be made.

This state/province is a sub-national unit of the country and its law sits inside the national framework; the national record carries the constitutional protections, legal gender recognition, marriage law and hate-crime statute. The findings below are those specific to the state/province.

The clearest practical obstacle for a trans visitor who depends on prescribed hormone treatment is the local health system. No public health facility in the state/province provides hormone replacement therapy for transgender people, and the state/province health department confirmed that position to the national human rights commission in response to a complaint lodged by a rights organisation. Residents travel sometimes hundreds of kilometres, most often to a major city in a neighbouring state/province, to obtain treatment. A visitor whose supply runs out cannot expect a public clinic or hospital to fill or continue the prescription.

Institutional enforcement of gendered appearance is documented in the state/province. In March 2016 an 18-year-old was barred from attending school at a village after refusing to wear a skirt; the principal sent her home on the stated ground that she must wear a skirt because she was a girl, and she missed three weeks of classes. The case concerns a pupil rather than a visitor, but it records a local school applying a dress rule against a gender-nonconforming person rather than accommodating her.

The state/province's quantitative evidence on anti-LGBT discrimination rests on a single survey. Conducted during 2009 and 2010 under the auspices of a university applied-psychology centre with local organisations, it surveyed 319 LGBT people, most of them from rural backgrounds in one of the country's poorest and least populated state/provinces, and asked about openness about same-sex sexuality, how LGBT people perceive their environment, and experiences of sexual abuse and discrimination. Campaign research published in 2016 lists that study alongside only two others as the quantitative national studies of anti-LGBT hate crime conducted up to that point.

The state/province's trans health gap pushes patients outward. The documented route for hormone treatment runs to a major city in a neighbouring state/province, so access depends on travel across provincial lines and on services elsewhere rather than on anything available locally.

Published figures for anti-LGBT violence and discrimination are not available for the state/province in the sources reviewed. The only quantitative evidence for it is the 2010 survey of 319 respondents; the 2016 hate-crime campaign study measures the country as a whole and does not report the state/province separately.

The absence of public hormone therapy in the state/province was put on record through a complaint by a rights organisation to the national human rights commission; the state/province health department answered by confirming that it has no facility offering hormone replacement therapy to transgender people.

Local organising around the LGBT population is long-standing but small. The 2010 survey was carried out with local organisations, and it remains the state/province's only quantitative baseline on discrimination and abuse.

For trans pupils the one documented case is the school exclusion at a village in 2016, where a dress requirement was enforced by the principal and the pupil stayed at home for three weeks. No policy response to that case appears in the sources reviewed.

An international human rights organisation reported in May 2012 that a customary-courts bill then before the national parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in areas designated under a historic-era system of separate administration, with no opt-out, that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas. Whether that customary jurisdiction reaches parts of the state/province, the bill's subsequent status, and how any local customary court treats transgender people are not established in the sources reviewed here.

The state/province's evidence base is dated and small: its only quantitative survey of LGBT people was conducted in 2009 and 2010 with 319 respondents, and campaign research published in 2016 lists it as one of only three quantitative hate-crime studies done in the country at that stage. No state/province-specific record of violence against transgender people, or of police action against them, appears in the sources reviewed, and no more recent local discrimination or violence data is present.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation; the constitutional guarantees, the criminal-law position on consensual conduct, the gender-recognition statute, the hate-crime provisions and the national correctional rulings are carried by the national record. The findings below are those specific to the state/province.

Traditional-authority structures have been openly opposed to legal recognition of same-sex relationships. A published letter of June 2010, issued by a national traditional-leadership body together with its state/province-level houses after a meeting held in a town in the state/province, stated that traditional leaders were disappointed that the highest court's marriage judgment had given what the letter called an immoral practice a lifeline, declared that they did not support legalisation of same-sex marriage, warned of ostracism and violence, and committed to a five-year campaign against it. The same structure asked the national legislature in 2016 to review the constitutional clause protecting people against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

Violence against people read as sexuality- or gender-nonconforming has produced both a killing and a mass response inside the state/province. A 25-year-old lesbian resident was found dead near a primary school in a township in a local municipality in the state/province in the early hours of Sunday 29 December 2019; she was half naked and had stab wounds. On 2 January 2020 about 800 people marched in the same municipality in protest, in a demonstration organised by a local LGBTI organisation, a political party's women's league and others. The local mayor called on parents, leaders and churches to stand united against gender-based violence.

Public LGBTIQ+ presence has also drawn official cooperation. The state/province's first Pride march and celebration was held on Saturday 9 August 2014 in the capital of the state/province under the theme 'Moving Forward, Proud, Strong & United'. Around 1,000 participants marched from a broadcaster's offices to a plaza in the capital, followed by a picnic at a park. The organiser said police were visible and supportive and supplied about 20 police and traffic officers; the event launched a state/province-wide LGBTI umbrella body for the state/province's LGBTI organisations.

Police conduct is the most consistently reported grievance. At a Pride flag tour event held at a community club in a township in the state/province on 18 August 2026, LGBTIQ+ community members led by a local LGBTI organisation raised concerns about discrimination and stigmatisation at government institutions, particularly police stations. Participants said they were ridiculed, questioned or treated unfairly when seeking assistance, and one member alleged that after she was sexually assaulted in the township months earlier, an officer at the local police station asked why she had not fought back. Attendees said they fear reporting crimes because of stigmatisation.

The documented pattern is community-level violence and police mistreatment inside a protective national legal framework. Enforcement appears to turn on the individual station, municipality or venue rather than on any state/province-wide practice, and the sources identify no court ruling, policy or facilities rule specific to the state/province.

The state/province's record runs in two directions. In 2014 the police presence at the capital's first Pride was described by the organiser as visible and supportive, with roughly 20 police and traffic officers supplied; in 2026 community members in a township described being ridiculed and questioned at police stations, including by an officer responding to a sexual-assault report. Both accounts come from the state/province and neither cancels the other.

Documented incidents cluster in particular municipalities rather than spreading evenly. The 2019 killing and the 2020 march fall in one local municipality, and the 2026 complaints fall in a township in another. The sources record nothing comparable for the capital or for other districts, which may reflect reporting density as much as the distribution of risk.

The state/province's named LGBTIQ+ organisational infrastructure is small: a state/province-wide umbrella body launched in 2014, a local LGBTI organisation that organised the 2020 march, and a local LGBTI organisation that led the 2026 event. National organisations and national litigation carry the weight of the legal work.

Residents rather than visitors absorb the enforcement record. The grievances raised at the 2026 event concerned ordinary dealings with police stations and other government offices, and attendees said the fear of stigmatisation deters them from reporting crimes at all, which leaves assaults and discrimination unreported and unrecorded.

Local mobilisation has been the main response to violence. The march in January 2020 followed the killing of a resident of the municipality and was organised by a local LGBTI organisation together with a political party's women's league and others, with the municipal mayor publicly calling on parents, leaders and churches to oppose gender-based violence.

In rural parts of the state/province under traditional authority, the 2010 position of a national traditional-leadership body and its state/province-level houses, issued after a meeting in a town in the state/province, and the five-year campaign it announced, describe the local power structure a resident may have to deal with. The sources record no later statement from that structure at state/province level.

No outcome is sourced for the investigation into the December 2019 killing, and no arrest, prosecution or conviction is recorded.

No disciplinary, criminal or other follow-up is sourced for the allegation that an officer at a local police station questioned a sexual-assault complainant about why she had not fought back, or for the wider complaints of discrimination at government offices raised in August 2026.

No prosecution data specific to the state/province under the national hate-crime statute is available in the sources, and no hate-crime or equality-court case from the state/province is identified.

No policy on facilities access specific to the state/province, and no statement from the state/province's health authorities on gender-affirming care or waiting times, appears in the sources. Whether the 2010 traditional-leadership campaign continued past the five years it announced is unresolved.

No statistics at state/province level on violence against transgender people are available; the violence material consists of individual incidents, which carry no rate and cannot be compared with the state/province's general homicide figures.

This state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation. Its trans-relevant law is the national layer: the national constitution's prohibition on unfair discrimination, the national equality legislation and the equality court, the national hate-crimes legislation, and legal gender recognition under the national gender-recognition legislation.

Transgender prisoners held in correctional centres in this state/province are governed by the national placement standard rather than any sub-national rule. Under the regulations to the national correctional services legislation on the accommodation of vulnerable inmates, and the national correctional service's standard operating procedures, inmates are to be housed in cells appropriate to their gender identity where that is feasible and safe, and transgender inmates are to be held in single cells. No case specific to this state/province on transgender placement is on record, so custody practice here is read entirely from the national instruments.

Rural districts under customary jurisdiction carry a risk that does not apply in the metropolitan centres. A customary-courts bill before the national parliament in 2012 would have created a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in areas formerly designated as homelands, with no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. An international human rights organisation reported at the time that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor cooperation from police, and that chiefs' courts punished lesbians in rural areas.

Gender-affirming care in this state/province runs through the public hospital system and is documented as slow. In December 2024 LGBT activists in a city in the state/province delivered a memorandum to a public hospital over year-long delays in transgender healthcare. A trans visitor who depends on the public system should plan for waiting times rather than immediate access.

Police in this state/province arrested four suspects in May 2025 over the killings of two women in a city in the state/province, whose bodies were found at separate locations the previous week. The deaths prompted public outrage and renewed calls to confront gender-based violence in the state/province. The incident is not recorded as trans-specific, and the sources supply no homicide rate for the state/province against which to read it.

Violence data for the state/province is not disaggregated by gender identity, so no rate of violence against transgender people specific to this state/province can be stated. The national protection machinery, including the 2024 hate-crimes legislation and the rapid response arrangements for unsolved cases, applies here without a sub-national counterpart.

Transgender residents of the rural districts of this state/province live under customary-court jurisdiction alongside the national legal system. An international human rights organisation reported in 2012 that rural LGBT people faced discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, and that chiefs' courts punished lesbians; the customary-courts bill then before the national parliament offered no opt-out.

Residents who depend on public gender-affirming care face year-long waits. Activists in a city in the state/province took a memorandum to a public hospital in December 2024 over treatment delays.

Residents held in correctional centres in this state/province are housed under the national placement standard: accommodation consistent with gender identity where feasible and safe, and single-cell accommodation for transgender inmates. No case in this state/province has tested how the standard is applied in its facilities.

The parliamentary fate of the customary-courts bill reported by an international human rights organisation in 2012 is not recorded in the sources, so whether customary jurisdiction currently operates as that bill proposed is unresolved.

No case specific to this state/province on transgender prisoner placement is on record. The operative rule is the national standard, and its application in the state/province's correctional centres has not been tested in the sources.

No data for this state/province disaggregating violence by gender identity is available. The May 2025 killings in a city in the state/province are not recorded as trans-specific, and no homicide rate for the state/province appears in the sources for comparison.

Whether the year-long gender-affirming care delays reported at a public hospital in December 2024 have been resolved is not recorded.

No provision specific to this state/province on identity documents, facilities access or entry appears in the sources; those matters are governed by the national framework.

Four state/provinces carry no state/province-specific law on gender identity, sexual orientation or intersex status. Each stands under the parent country's national framework, which the national record carries; the state/province-specific question is which body of law attaches to each.

One state/province was incorporated into the legislation of one of the parent country's state/provinces from 1 July 2016 under national legislation. A visitor there meets that state/province's law rather than a local enactment.

Two further state/provinces, administered together, are jurisdictions in which the law of another of the parent country's state/provinces applies.

A fourth state/province is governed directly under national law, and the national sex discrimination statute, as amended in 2013, applies throughout the parent country including the state/provinces governed directly under national law. That statute is the anti-discrimination framework a visitor there stands under.

Availability of the 'X' sex descriptor and anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression extend across the state/provinces alongside concurrent national protection. No state/province-specific provision on markers or on discrimination diverges from that position in the four.

No state/province-specific rule on facilities, care access, entry or screening was located for any of the four, and no state/province-specific enforcement action or incident involving a trans visitor was found.

Because the applicable law comes from a state/province rather than a local enactment, the vilification and discrimination coverage a visitor meets in one state/province or in the two administered together follows the regime of the corresponding state/province of the parent country, not a local provision. The same fact means a change in either state/province's law changes the position in the corresponding state/province without any local decision.

The transfer of one state/province to another's legislation in 2016 is the only state/province-level legal change documented; the other three have no comparable transfer on the sources held.

For residents, the practical consequence of the framework mapping is that a discrimination or vilification complaint arising in one state/province runs under the law of one of the parent country's state/provinces, one arising in the two administered together under the law of another, and one arising in the fourth under national law. No local legislature has enacted a separate gender-identity provision.

Residents of the state/provinces governed directly under national law fall within the national sex discrimination statute rather than a local enactment.

No state/province-specific statute, court ruling, enforcement record, care-access rule or facilities rule was located for any of the four. The framework mapping above rests on a single encyclopaedic source and has not been checked against the state/province or national instruments themselves.

Whether the application of the second state/province's law in the two administered together extends to the whole of that state/province's anti-discrimination and vilification statute, or only to part of it, is unresolved on the sources held.

No state/province-level data on trans-directed violence, screening practice or entry processing was found, and nothing indicates a state/province-specific risk distinct from the national position.

This state/province is part of the parent nation and stands under the national framework; the national record carries the national law, and this record covers the state/province layer.

Gender identity has been a protected attribute under the state/province anti-discrimination act since 2002. Amendments that commenced on 29 April 2024 moved serious vilification out of that act and into the criminal code, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment, raised from six months. The same amendments explicitly extend protection to non-binary and gender-diverse people and broaden the definition of gender identity. The state/province human rights commission described the 2024 anti-discrimination bill as a rewrite that modernised the gender identity attribute and revised the vilification provisions.

This state/province was the first jurisdiction in the parent nation to criminalise conversion practices. A health legislation amendment bill passed the legislature on 13 August 2020, making practices including electro-shock, drug and hypnotherapy aimed at changing a person's sexuality or gender identity offences carrying fines and imprisonment for practitioners, with a maximum of 18 months. Survivors report that the ban does not reach conversion practices in informal, non-healthcare settings.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors has been restricted since January 2025. The state/province health minister halted puberty blockers and hormone therapy for new public-system patients under 18 with gender dysphoria, formalised by a health authority directive of 28 January 2025. The restriction remains in force and is legally contested. Patients already enrolled with the state/province children's gender service are exempt, so the practical effect falls on new patients and their families.

Official documents in this state/province have carried an X non-binary option alongside male and female since 1 September 2021, including marriage certificates and official forms. Transgender and intersex residents can update government records and their birth certificate; the requirement to divorce before changing a record was repealed in 2018 and the surgery requirement was repealed in 2024.

State/province law recognises relationships through civil partnership registration or an unregistered de facto relationship, recognised since 2002. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status can register a civil partnership or rely on de facto recognition in the same way as any other couple.

The state/province criminal-law regime has been progressively liberalised. Private consensual sex between men has been legal since 1991, and lesbian sexual acts were never criminalised. The age of consent was equalised at 16 for all sexual acts in 2016, this state/province being the last jurisdiction in the parent nation to do so; the former section 208 carried up to 14 years' imprisonment for anal sex involving a person under 18. The gay panic defence was abolished from the criminal law in 2017.

The conversion-practices offence is confined to health-care settings as described in the reporting. Survivors say informal and non-healthcare practices fall outside it, so the protection is narrower than the ban's scope suggests.

A national advocacy group described this state/province as an outlier among the parent nation's state/provinces for the under-18 care restriction, a characterisation that places the measure against the direction of policy elsewhere in the country.

Residents who change their recorded gender can obtain a new birth certificate and updated government records; the surgery requirement was repealed in 2024 and the divorce requirement in 2018.

Same-sex couples may become parents through adoption, foster care and altruistic surrogacy, and lesbian couples through IVF; eligibility to adopt dates from 11 November 2016.

Convictions for consensual homosexual acts can be expunged under a law passed in 2017 and in effect from 30 June 2018.

Serious vilification sits in the criminal code rather than the anti-discrimination act following the 2024 amendments, so complaints of that kind go through the criminal process.

Under the January 2025 directive, patients already enrolled with the state/province children's gender service keep access to puberty blockers and hormone therapy; new patients under 18 must obtain treatment privately, at costs families report as hundreds of dollars per injection and nearly $2,000 in one case.

The state/province human rights commission's own announcement of the April 2024 changes is no longer reachable, so the account of that rewrite rests on secondary reporting and the record held here.

No enforcement data for the serious vilification offence, whether prosecutions, convictions or sentences, appears in the sources consulted.

The sources do not state whether the under-18 restriction on public-system care affects adult patients, or how it applies to young people visiting this state/province from elsewhere.

Several details of the state/province's legal history rest on a tertiary encyclopaedic source rather than on the instruments themselves.

The scope of the conversion-practices ban outside health-care settings is reported through survivors' accounts and is not resolved by the sources consulted.

This state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation: national law, national courts and national entry rules apply here and are carried by the national assessment. The findings below are the state/province's own.

State/province anti-discrimination law protects gender identity and sexual orientation. The 1984 equal opportunity act was amended in 2016 to add both grounds, giving trans residents and visitors a state/province-level remedy alongside the national one.

Hate-crime sentencing laws that explicitly cover sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex characteristics passed and were implemented in November 2021, so offences motivated by a victim's gender identity fall within the state/province's sentencing aggravation provisions.

The gay-panic defence was abolished on 1 December 2020 and ceased to operate on 1 April 2021. A defendant can no longer rely on a claimed non-heterosexual advance by the victim as a partial defence.

A 2024 conversion practices prohibition act is in legal effect from 1 April 2025, prohibiting conversion practices in the state/province.

Birth certificate changes have been available since 23 May 2017 under a 2016 amendment to the state/province's births, deaths and marriages registration law, which received royal assent on 15 December 2016. A change of sex descriptor requires appropriate clinical treatment but not sex-reassignment surgery, and a marriage does not have to be ended first. Non-binary and indeterminate sex descriptors are also available on state/province birth certificates.

Registered domestic relationships have been available since 1 August 2017. Marriage is recognised under the national act that took effect in December 2017; 62.5% of respondents in the state/province voted Yes in the 2017 national postal survey.

This state/province was the first jurisdiction in the parent nation to decriminalise male homosexual activity, with the change commencing on 2 October 1975. Its 2016 birth-certificate reform placed it, with one other jurisdiction, among the first two to allow a change of the sex recorded on a birth certificate without sex-reassignment surgery.

The state/province's scheme for historical gay convictions is spent rather than expunged, under a 2013 spent-convictions amendment in force from 22 December 2013; it is the only such scheme in the parent nation framed that way.

Same-sex couples have been able to adopt in the state/province since 17 February 2017.

A human rights commission in a neighbouring jurisdiction published a news item on that jurisdiction's discrimination reforms; the page could not be retrieved (HTTP 403) and no finding for this state/province rests on it.

Sources differ on when the 2024 conversion practices prohibition act passed, giving September 2024 and October 2024; both give commencement on 1 April 2025.

No enforcement data for the November 2021 hate-crime sentencing provisions in this state/province was located, so their practical application is not documented in the sources reviewed.

National sex-discrimination law and the national court precedent interpreting it apply in this state/province; the national assessment carries them and they are not restated here.

The state/province issues its own birth certificates and driver licences and runs its own anti-discrimination, conversion-practices and corrections regimes. Marriage and passports are national matters and are carried at the national level.

Discrimination on the basis of transgender status has been prohibited in the state/province since 1996 under its Anti-Discrimination Act 1977, which reaches employment, public education, goods and services, banking, health care, property and nightclubs. A section of the state/province Mental Health Act 2007 states expressly that sexual orientation and gender identity are not mental illnesses.

The Act's exemptions remain significant for a trans visitor. Sport and broadly based religious exemptions in non-public schools permit exclusion on sex and gender grounds, including barring transgender people from female sports categories, and religiously run adoption agencies may refuse same-sex couples.

Sex designations on state/province birth certificates changed on 1 July 2025. Until 30 June 2025 a person had to undergo sexual reassignment surgery and pay $153 to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate; since 1 July 2025 no surgery is required, and the process is an application form, a $73 fee, and a good-faith witness who is an unrelated adult known to the applicant for a year. There is no cap on the number of sex changes, unlike name changes, which are limited to once every 12 months and three in a lifetime; 766 sex changes had been recorded by September 2025. The new certificate does not disclose that a change occurred.

Non-binary and unspecified markers are available. In April 2014 the national high court held that the law permits registration of a change of sex to a non-specific designation, in the case brought by a named plaintiff, and since March 2022 birth certificates listing no gender or sex have been available to people born or adopted in the state/province.

Conversion practices have been a criminal offence in the state/province since 4 April 2025 under legislation passed unamended on 22 March 2024. Practices causing substantial mental or physical harm carry up to five years' imprisonment, and taking a person out of the state/province for conversion therapy carries up to three years. The state/province anti-discrimination body can investigate complaints from 4 April 2025 with civil referral pathways. The Act carries limited religious and parental exemptions, including an exception for religious sermons.

Publicly threatening or inciting violence has been an offence since 13 August 2018 under legislation passed unanimously by both houses in June 2018, with a penalty of up to three years' imprisonment.

Documented fatal violence against a trans woman traveller in the state/province is the 2021 killing of a 25-year-old transgender woman visiting from abroad, in a regional city. The perpetrator's guilty plea to manslaughter drew a 22-month term. The most recent documented case of this kind in this record is from 2021; no later instance is documented.

Corrections practice is governed by state/province prisoner protocols and guidelines in place since 1996, which permit transgender people who have had sexual reassignment surgery to be housed in female prisons for protection. An undisclosed state/province government settlement was granted to a transgender individual held in a male prison in November 2024.

Facilities: the principal city council implemented a gender-neutral bathrooms policy in April 2023.

A judicial inquiry into LGBTIQ hate crimes was announced in November 2021 and began work in November 2022, examining 88 deaths of gay men between 1970 and 2000; the state/province police force were called to give evidence in December 2022. The inquiry's subject matter is gay men's deaths rather than trans-specific violence, and no trans-specific violence statistics for the state/province appear in the sources reviewed.

Other official gestures sit alongside the enforceable provisions. A unanimous, non-binding bipartisan lower-house motion in October 2020 called for human rights, dignity and respect for transgender individuals. A ban on Nazi symbols under the state/province Crimes Act was assented on 19 August 2022 and took effect immediately, with the LGBTIQ community named among those it protects. A government hate-crime bill concerning gay and bisexual men, with penalties up to five years' imprisonment, was before the parliament in March 2026 and had not been debated in either house.

The state/province's decriminalisation of private consensual sex between men in 1984, the equalisation of the age of consent to 16 in May 2003, the 2014 expungement scheme for historical convictions and the June 2024 government apology are matters of the state/province's sexual-orientation history rather than of trans legal status.

Residents seeking a sex change on a state/province birth certificate since 1 July 2025 pay $73 and lodge an application with a good-faith witness who is an unrelated adult known for a year; no surgery is required. Name changes remain capped at once every 12 months and three per lifetime, while sex changes are not capped, and 766 changes had been recorded by September 2025.

A suburban council voted to approve transgender health leave for its staff. The policy has not taken effect because it requires the national-level local government minister's signature.

The state/province operates a registered partnerships scheme for couples, one of the relationship recognition schemes available across most state/provinces in the country.

The state/province anti-discrimination body accepts complaints under the conversion-practices legislation from 4 April 2025 and can refer matters through civil pathways; complaints on gender identity grounds under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 have been available since 1996.

No charging or prosecution data for conversion-practices offences, or for the public threatening and inciting violence offence created in 2018, appears in the sources reviewed. The number of gender-identity complaints received by the state/province anti-discrimination body is likewise not sourced.

The terms of the November 2024 state/province government settlement with a transgender individual held in a male prison are undisclosed, so the precedent it sets for housing decisions is unresolved.

Whether the suburban council transgender health leave policy has since received the ministerial signature it requires is unresolved in these sources.

No trans-specific violence rate for the state/province, with a denominator or against the general homicide rate, is available in the inventory; the record contains a single documented fatal case, from 2021, and no count of incidents over a period.

The 766 figure for sex changes on birth certificates is reported as at September 2025 and has no later data point in these sources.

The Human Rights Act 2004 is in force in the state/province and is the statutory rights framework the state/province's public authorities must operate within. Courts may issue declarations of inconsistency, and section 31 provides that interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. A visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a state/province police officer, public servant or public facility therefore has a review mechanism written into local law. The state/province's legislation register also records uncommenced amendments made by a housing amendment act passed in 2025.

The state/province operates an explicit self-identification policy for housing trans and gender-diverse prisoners. Strip-searching inside its prisons is documented in a 2026 report by a national human-rights law centre produced with two trans-community groups, which records the disproportionate harms of the practice for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners.

Conversion practices are a criminal and civil offence in the state/province. A sexuality and gender identity conversion practices bill passed the local legislature on 27 August 2020 and applied from early 2021, carrying up to 12 months' imprisonment or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties that give the state/province's civil and administrative tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. Practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. The bill was amended before passage after a Christian schools association and the state/province's law society argued that the definition of conversion practice was too broad and vague.

Gender-affirming care in the state/province is constrained by capacity rather than by prohibition. A government health scoping study, reported on 16 April 2022, found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse residents of the capital: a shortage of primary-care professionals including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, producing excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel. The study called the state/province the only jurisdiction in the country without a comprehensive gender-focused health service, in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic.

The state/province's explicit self-identification prison policy places it alongside several other jurisdictions that run comparable stated policies, while a smaller group of jurisdictions are recorded as unclear on the point. A national survey reported on 3 July 2020 estimated up to 400 trans and gender-diverse people held in the country's cells, often inappropriately housed and at elevated risk of physical and sexual violence. That figure is a national estimate with no population denominator, so it indicates scale of exposure rather than a rate.

The local conversion-practice statute was narrowed in response to domestic opposition before passage, with a Christian schools association and the state/province's law society contesting the breadth of the definition. The scope of what now counts as a prohibited conversion practice is therefore the amended text, not the bill as introduced.

Residents needing gender-affirming care face documented queueing. As of April 2022, 20 young transgender people were on the waitlist of the capital's only paediatric endocrinologist, with some patients waiting a year for an appointment, and GP demand rising 20 to 40 per cent a year. The scoping study attributed the shortfall to a lack of primary-care professionals, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, and recorded the cost of interstate and international travel for care that is not available locally.

Residents are protected by local law against conversion practices, with the civil and administrative tribunal able to issue orders and order redress in addition to criminal penalties, and with practices supporting a person undergoing or considering gender transition carved out of the prohibition. Residents also stand under the Human Rights Act 2004 against the conduct of public authorities. The housing amendment act passed in 2025 is recorded on the legislation register as uncommenced, so its housing protections are not yet in operation.

No charging or prosecution data for the local conversion-practice offences appears in the sources reviewed; the enforcement record of the prohibition is unresolved.

The sources do not state how often the self-identification prison policy has been applied, how trans prisoners have been housed in practice, or how frequently trans prisoners have been strip-searched locally. The 2026 strip-searching report is recorded as covering these prisons without local figures in this inventory.

The health-capacity findings date from the scoping study reported in April 2022. No later assessment of local gender-health capacity appears in the sources, so whether waitlists and specialist shortages have since changed is unresolved.

Whether the housing amendment act passed in 2025 has since commenced is unresolved; the legislation register entry available here records it as uncommenced.

The state/province's anti-vilification law, the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958, and repeals the Racial and Religious Tolerance Act. The stated aims are equal participation and public safety. The criminal provisions take effect on 30 June 2026 and cover vilification on the grounds of gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, with a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment. Political, religious and academic exemptions apply, along with a further reported exemption.

Gender identity has been a prohibited discrimination ground in the state/province since 2000, when the Equal Opportunity (Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation) Act 2000 amended the Equal Opportunity Act 1995; the ground was retained in the replacement Equal Opportunity Act 2010. Sex characteristics were added with effect from 2021. The Justice Legislation Amendment (Police and Other Matters) Bill 2022, passed in September 2022, extended protection on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds to on-duty state/province police officers.

Religious exemptions remain in the Equal Opportunity Act 2010. They allow religious organisations, including adoption and fostering agencies and charities that receive no government funding, to discriminate against and reject LGBT employees and clients. The Equal Opportunity (Religious Exceptions) Amendment Bill 2021, passed in December 2021 and effective 15 June 2022, bars religious schools and organisations from discriminating against employees because of sexual orientation, gender identity or marital status, and bars government-funded bodies from refusing services on those grounds except where conformity with doctrine is an inherent requirement, such as hiring a religious studies teacher.

The state/province recognises gender transition. Birth certificates are issued by the state/province births, deaths and marriages registry, and driver licences carry no recorded gender marker. Updated regulations in November 2025 removed all fees and costs for applications to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate. Earlier law required an applicant to be unmarried and to have undergone sexual reassignment surgery. The legislature removed the unmarried requirement early, in May 2018, ahead of its scheduled lapse in December 2018. An August 2016 bill that would have removed both requirements and allowed parents to alter a child's gender descriptor with the child's informed consent did not pass.

Conversion practices are prohibited. The Change or Suppression (Conversion) Practices Prohibition Bill passed the lower house 55-0 in December 2020 and the upper house 27-9 on 5 February 2021, with penalties of up to approximately A$200,000 or up to 10 years' imprisonment, effective February 2022, one year after royal assent. The prohibition was preceded by the Health Complaints Act, from the Health Complaints Bill 2016 and effective 1 February 2017, which empowers the state/province health complaints commissioner to issue warnings and temporary or permanent bans; the commissioner opened an investigation in May 2018.

In August 2024 the state/province supreme court upheld the provision of puberty blockers to transgender children with stress and anxiety. In the same month a state/province coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people. The state/province government says it is reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups will press for their implementation.

The state/province is the only state/province with an LGBTIQA+ commissioner. The inaugural gender and sexuality commissioner was appointed in July 2015 to streamline national and state/province laws so that passports and birth certificates align with affirmed gender and to strengthen workplace protections for transgender workers; the office was later renamed commissioner for LGBTIQ+ communities. A transgender man was appointed on 23 September 2024 for a three-year term to advise government on safe and inclusive policies, services and programmes and to lead implementation of a ten-year LGBTIQA+ equality plan.

Reported funding cuts risk a backlog at the state/province equal opportunity and human rights commission, established in 1975.

The state/province's criminal law history bears on how the current regime was reached. Buggery was a crime in the state/province from 1958 until December 1980, when the government of the day's repeal passed 72-7 and took effect in March 1981. The death penalty remained on the books for sodomy until 1949. The equal age of consent was set at 18 and lowered to 16 by the Crimes (Sexual Offences) Act 1991. A loosely worded soliciting for immoral purposes clause enabled continued police harassment of homosexual men until the late 1980s, including entrapment mass arrests at a beach reported in 1976. Any remaining legislation banning sex between consenting adults in private was removed by royal assent effective 1 March 2022 and in effect by May 2022.

HIV-specific offences were repealed. Intentional HIV transmission was singled out under section 19A of the Crimes Act, carrying up to 25 years' imprisonment against a 20-year maximum for manslaughter; the Crimes Amendment (Repeal of Section 19A) Act 2015 passed on 28 May 2015, received assent on 2 June 2015 and took effect immediately, with such conduct now dealt with as causing serious injury. An April 2022 Act repealed all HIV legislation on mandatory public health notifications, blood donations and human tissue services, effective 15 February 2023.

Sexual orientation has been a protected attribute in the state/province since 2000, retained in the Equal Opportunity Act 2010.

The state/province operates an expungement scheme for historical homosexual offences that are no longer criminal. It passed on 15 October 2014 and took effect on 1 September 2015, allowing the individual or a representative of a deceased person to apply to the secretary of the state/province justice department. On a successful application the person may lawfully claim not to have been convicted, and the conviction does not appear on a police records check, avoiding travel and employment restrictions. The legislature issued a formal apology on 24 May 2016.

Domestic relationships have been registrable in the state/province since 1 December 2008 under the Relationships Act, passed on 10 April 2008.

Residents applying to change the sex recorded on a birth certificate do so through the state/province births, deaths and marriages registry, and since November 2025 no fees or costs apply to those applications.

The August 2016 bill to remove the unmarried and surgery requirements for birth-certificate changes failed. The date on which the surgery requirement was later removed is not established by the source inventory.

The state/province government's response to the coroner's recommendations on health care for trans and gender-diverse people is described as under review; no implementation timeline is sourced.

The scale of the reported funding cuts at the state/province equal opportunity and human rights commission and their effect on complaint handling are not quantified in the sources.

The scope of a further reported exemption in the 2025 anti-vilification Act is not defined in the sources.

Several claims about the state/province's discrimination and vilification framework rest on a reference page rather than a live government or parliamentary document.

The state/province legislates its own anti-discrimination regime beneath the national framework, which carries the national gender-identity protections. The state/province's own layer narrowed in 2025.

The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025) was assented on 30 October 2025, with Part 3 commencing on 27 July 2026. It removes the civil prohibition on conduct that offends, insults, humiliates or intimidates a person in public because of a protected attribute, gender identity among them. From that commencement date a trans visitor or resident cannot found a vilification complaint on that ground before the state/province anti-discrimination commission.

The repeal was announced in March 2025 by the governing party, which framed it as restoring freedom of speech and religious freedom. The government had earlier retreated from scrapping the vilification section outright before the bill passed the legislature on 17 October 2025.

The state/province anti-discrimination commissioner publicly rebuked the change, warning that the government may be opening the doors for a very dangerous stream of hate speech.

The state/province's hate-crime statute does not list sexual orientation or gender identity among the motives it covers. Coverage of those motives in the state/province therefore rests on the national layer alone.

State/province discrimination protections covering gender identity date from 2022, when the vilification provision was added to the anti-discrimination law. That provision is the one now being removed.

Changing the sex marker on a state/province birth certificate has required clinical treatment since 2018.

The state/province government issued a policy directive in December 2025 banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors. In February 2025 it banned rainbow pride flags in public hospitals.

The practical exposure for a trans visitor to the state/province is a shrinking civil remedy rather than a criminal or entry risk: the conduct that will cease to be actionable from 27 July 2026 is harassment and vilification on the ground of gender identity, and no state/province provision replaces it.

Male homosexual activity was decriminalised in the state/province on 1 January 1984 and the age of consent was equalised in 2003. Those provisions regulate sexual conduct and predate any gender-identity protection; they do not themselves address how a trans visitor is treated.

The state/province returned a 60.6% Yes vote in the 2017 national postal survey on marriage, close to the national result.

The state/province's own trajectory runs toward narrower civil protection rather than wider, and the 2025 amendments are the instrument of that narrowing.

Same-sex couples in the state/province have held full adoption rights since 2018.

The 2025 amendments also allow religious schools to prefer staff who share the school's faith when hiring.

Residents can bring discrimination complaints to the state/province anti-discrimination commission on grounds that remain in the law after Part 3 commences; the gender-identity vilification ground is the one being withdrawn.

The terms, scope and enforcement of the December 2025 directive banning gender-affirming healthcare for minors are not detailed in the sources held. Whether it reaches private practice as well as public health services is unresolved.

Whether vilification complaints already lodged with the anti-discrimination commission survive the 27 July 2026 commencement of Part 3 is not sourced.

The state/province timeline, including the 2022 discrimination protections and the 2018 birth-certificate requirement, rests on a Wikipedia article; the underlying primary documents were not retrieved.

The ABC report of 17 October 2025 describes the bill's passage through the legislature; the assent date of 30 October 2025 and the commencement date of 27 July 2026 come from the state/province legislation page for the assented Act.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation, which the parent record carries. Within the state/province, the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998 prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics. A September 2013 amendment extended the Act's reach to transgender and intersex people and made it unlawful to offend, humiliate, intimidate, insult or ridicule a person on the basis of actual or perceived gender, sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2019 amendments to the same Act added gender expression, an express definition of gender identity covering being transgender or transsexual and identifying or living as another gender, and sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics, including as grounds for the prohibition on incitement of hatred.

Gender registration on a birth registered in the state/province is self-declared. Act 2019 No. 7, amending the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 1999, received royal assent on 8 May 2019 and took effect on 5 September 2019: no medical certificate or other medical document is required, and a person aged 16 or over may register male, female, indeterminate gender, non-binary or another self-described gender without parental approval. Parents or guardians may register a gender for a child under 16, supported by the child's own gender declaration where the child is able to give it. Birth sex registration remains male-or-female only and cannot be changed except to correct an initial error, but it ceases upon gender registration. The same laws let parents choose whether a child's gender is recorded, allow a person to remove a gender descriptor entirely, permit parents to change a child's legal gender, and extend the registration period for parents of intersex children to 120 days after birth. The state/province issues 'X' sex descriptors on birth certificates as of 2019.

The 2019 reforms passed the lower house on 10 April 2019 after the lower-house speaker crossed the floor to vote with the opposition, the bill having already passed the upper house. They made gender on birth certificates optional and removed the requirement that transgender people undergo surgery for their gender to be recognised. The government of the state/province opposed the amendments and declined to rule out later repeal; no repeal is recorded in the sources reviewed.

The age of consent in the state/province is 17 years, equal for all forms of sexual activity, a figure shared only with a neighbouring jurisdiction.

A hate crimes bill passed the lower house in September 2025 and explicitly includes gender identity within the 1997 sentencing act. The upper house had not voted on it in the sources reviewed.

Cross-dressing was an offence under section 8(1)(d) of the Police Offences Act 1935 until its repeal on 12 April 2001, the state/province having been the only one in the country to criminalise it. Charges and convictions under that provision as in force before 12 April 2001, including attempts and inciting, instigating, aiding or abetting, are eligible for expungement on application under the Expungement of Historical Offences Act 2017, which received royal assent on 21 November 2017, with expungement available from 9 April 2018 and compensation of up to $75,000 available from 2 August 2026. The expungement scheme followed a parliamentary apology on 13 April 2017.

As of September 2026 conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted within the state/province.

Same-sex couples can enter registered domestic partnerships in the state/province with an optional official ceremony.

No state/province-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or trans-specific violence figure for the state/province appears in the sources reviewed.

The equal-status position on gender recognition was secured against government resistance rather than against any criminalisation or incident series: the government of the state/province opposed the 2019 birth-certificate amendments and did not rule out repeal, and the bill passed only after the lower-house speaker crossed the floor.

The state/province's historical legal regime was among the harshest in the country. Consensual homosexual activity was decriminalised by the Criminal Code Amendment Act 1997, passed 1 May 1997 with assent 13 May 1997 and effect the following day, after penalties of up to 21 years, and the state/province was the final jurisdiction in the country to decriminalise, doing so with effect from 14 May 1997 after a national human-rights statute commenced on 19 December 1994 and in the face of a likely adverse High Court ruling. Cross-dressing remained an offence until 2001.

Equality of adoption rights for same-sex couples applied in every state/province of the country from April 2018, and national law has recognised same-sex couples as de facto relationships since 2009; those layers sit above the state/province's own registered-partnership scheme.

The two pending items in this record are both legislative: the hate crimes bill's upper-house vote, and the unexercised possibility of repeal flagged by the government in 2019.

Legal gender change for a birth registered in the state/province requires only a statutory declaration of identity and lived or seeking-to-live gender. There is no forced divorce, no sex reassignment surgery and no other medical requirement, and the Registrar holds a refusal power limited to terms outside those prescribed.

People aged 16 and over change their registered gender without parental permission. For under-16s the parent or guardian registers, using the child's own declaration where the child can give it, otherwise statements of consistency with the child's will and preference, with optional counselling evidence where the person is under 18.

Historic cross-dressing convictions are expungable on application to the Secretary by the person charged or, where that person is deceased or lacks capacity, by specified representatives. Compensation of up to $75,000 became available on 2 August 2026.

Registered domestic partnerships are available to same-sex couples with an optional official ceremony.

Conversion therapy practices remain legally permitted as of September 2026, so no statutory restriction protects a resident from them.

Discrimination on gender identity, gender expression, sex characteristics and variations of sex characteristics is prohibited by the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998, and the Act also reaches conduct that offends, humiliates, intimidates, insults or ridicules on those bases.

The upper-house vote on the September 2025 hate crimes bill is not sourced, so whether gender identity now sits within the 1997 sentencing act remains unresolved in this record.

No charging, prosecution or complaint data for the Anti-Discrimination Act 1998, including its incitement-of-hatred provision, appears in the sources reviewed; enforcement practice is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence, homicide or victimisation figure for the state/province is sourced, and no incident series is documented. The absence of such data is not evidence of absence.

Whether the government pursued the repeal it declined to rule out in 2019 is not sourced.

Processing times, refusal practice and fee levels under the gender-registration declaration process are not sourced, nor is uptake of the expungement or compensation schemes.

The status of any move to restrict conversion therapy in the state/province after September 2026 is not sourced.

The state/province equal opportunity statute protects one attribute relevant to trans people: "gender history", defined in the statute and in state/province government guidance as living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex. Guidance published by the state/province government and updated on 12 February 2026 states that direct and indirect discrimination on this ground are unlawful, and that treating a person as their former sex is a form of direct discrimination. The attribute is not framed as gender identity, so the protection is worded more narrowly than the gender-identity grounds used in several other jurisdictions in the country.

Eligibility to complain is tied to legal recognition. Gender history is established through a recognition certificate or a recorded change of sex or gender under the births, deaths and marriages framework, which means a trans person who has not amended identity documents in the state/province may sit outside the complaint mechanism even where the treatment described is discriminatory. The state/province equal opportunity commission's fact sheet records that the 2024 recognition reforms amend section 4(1) of the statute to delete the "gender reassigned person" definition and insert one keyed to certificates or registration, that the amendment does not operate retrospectively, and that complaints will have to satisfy the new registration requirements once it commences.

A 2024 births, deaths and marriages registration amendment statute was assented to on 26 September 2024 and took effect on 30 May 2025. It repeals the state/province gender reassignment statute and abolishes the state/province gender reassignment board, which the head of the state/province government and the minister responsible for justice described at introduction on 16 April 2024 as the last body of its kind in the country. Medical and surgical reassignment are no longer prerequisites; a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling, replaces the board process. Male, female, indeterminate/intersex and non-binary descriptors are available, a change may be made once a year, the fee is A$195 and non-refundable, and processing takes up to four weeks. Applicants under 18 need parental consent or the permission of the state/province family court. The statute carries a statutory review clause after three years.

The removal of surgical prerequisites has a longer history in the state/province. Sterilisation was required before 2012, until the High Court held on 6 October 2011 that two trans men who had undergone bilateral mastectomies and androgen therapy were entitled to male recognition certificates without hysterectomy, oophorectomy or genital reconstructive surgery. The requirement that an applicant be unmarried was repealed by legislation that passed both chambers in early 2019 and commenced on 19 March 2019.

Complaints go to the state/province equal opportunity commissioner, with a 12-month lodgement window, acknowledgment of receipt within one week and a free conciliation conference as the next step. A complainant may instead use the national route to the national human rights commission under national sex discrimination law within 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters, but only one route may be chosen. Trans-specific support organisations in the state/province, one of them for people under 26, provide assistance.

Prison policy reported in November 2020 allows transgender prisoners to be housed according to their gender identity for health and safety reasons, provided their criminal record carries no sexual offences. Placement turns on that record check rather than operating as an unconditional entitlement.

No law in the state/province prohibits conversion practices. The government said a bill would be introduced only after the March 2025 state/province election; as of September 2026 the state/province and one neighbouring jurisdiction were the only places in the country without an explicit criminal prohibition, leaving the state/province the only mainland state/province where the practices remain lawful. A public order bill that would criminally ban harassment on grounds of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics passed the lower house but had not passed the upper house. Announced reforms to the equal opportunity statute would add gender identity and sex characteristics as protected attributes and repeal the exemption allowing religious schools to discriminate; neither change had been enacted.

In October 2021 the state/province supreme court removed a transgender child from parental custody entirely over continuing abuse, the first order of its kind in the country, following the April 2021 death of a 15-year-old trans teenager in the capital that prompted calls to reform the birth-certificate law.

The recognition reform was announced on 16 April 2024 as one part of a wider package: a replacement equal opportunity statute and a ban on conversion practices were both signalled for 2025. Only the recognition statute has passed, so the state/province anti-discrimination law still uses the older "gender history" formulation and still contains the religious-schools exemption.

The 2024 statute's three-year statutory review clause means the annual-change limit, the A$195 non-refundable fee and the clinical-statement requirement are all revisitable, but no review body or terms of reference are set out in the material available.

The protected attribute is narrower than the gender-identity grounds used in several other jurisdictions in the country, and the announced equal opportunity rewrite is the mechanism by which that gap would close. Until it passes, a trans visitor relying on state/province law is working with a definition drafted around transition and certification rather than around identity as such.

The public order bill's progress is a live variable: lower-house passage has been recorded, upper-house passage has not, and the criminal harassment protection it would create on gender-identity grounds therefore does not yet exist.

Residents pursuing a state/province complaint file with the equal opportunity commissioner within 12 months of the conduct, receive acknowledgment within a week, and are offered a free conciliation conference. The national alternative at the national human rights commission runs to 24 months, or 12 months for employment matters, and the two routes are mutually exclusive, so the choice is made once.

Changing a birth certificate now runs through the births, deaths and marriages registry rather than a board: a supporting statement from a doctor, nurse or psychologist, A$195 non-refundable, up to four weeks, one change per year, and male, female, indeterminate/intersex or non-binary descriptors. Under-18 applicants need parental consent or state/province family court permission.

Because complaint eligibility under the equal opportunity statute is keyed to a recognition certificate or a registered change, residents who have not completed that process may find their discrimination claim limited, and the 2024 amendment to section 4(1) will require complaints to meet the new registration requirements once it commences.

Trans-specific support organisations in the state/province provide assistance, one of them for people under 26. Prisoners may be housed according to gender identity where their record carries no sexual offences. Conversion practices remain lawful in the state/province, and the announced ban had not been introduced at the time of the source material.

Commencement of the 2024 recognition statute is described inconsistently across the sources: the equal opportunity commission fact sheet treats it as passed with commencement still to be proclaimed, while other material records it taking effect on 30 May 2025. The proclamation instrument itself was not reviewed, and the interim handling of gender-history complaints before commencement is not sourced.

The High Court decision on surgical prerequisites is dated 6 October 2011 in one source and 2012 in another. The 2011 date matches the reported judgment; the 2012 reference is unresolved.

Whether the replacement equal opportunity statute and the conversion practices bill were introduced after the March 2025 state/province election is not established by the sources, and the upper-house fate of the public order bill remains open.

The practical operation of the prison housing policy, including how the sexual-offence record check is applied and whether placement decisions are reviewable, is not documented in the material available.

The state/province stands under the national human-rights and criminal law framework of the country, supplemented by its own statute. The state/province's human rights act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression: members of the legislature voted unanimously on third and final reading of a bill on 13 March 2017, and the justice minister stated that the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At the time of that vote it was the first sub-national jurisdiction in the country to list gender identity or expression among the protected grounds in its human-rights law.

Birth certificates issued in the state/province carry a third, non-binary sex designation. On 18 September 2025 members of the legislature voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore that option through amendments to the vital statistics act, after the standing committee had struck it from the health minister's May 2025 bill, and the bill was then approved on third reading. The bill's sponsor said the state/province government now joins the rest of the country in recognising non-binary and transgender individuals.

The state/province government funds transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents. Reporting of 22 March 2022 records that the health department began funding such care, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty named among the procedures, under a partnership with a surgical centre in a large city elsewhere in the country. A local LGBTQ group called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside the capital.

No trans-specific violent incident, hate-crime count or victimisation figure for the state/province itself is documented in this record, and no dated instance of anti-trans violence there appears in it.

National police-reported hate-crime data supplies the only quantified turbulence signal available, and it carries no breakdown for the state/province. The national statistics agency's release on police-reported hate crime in 2024, published 30 March 2026, counts 4,882 police-reported hate crimes, up 1% over the year and 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or gender expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and a 184% rise since 2020; sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, with June 2024 alone recording 113 against a monthly average of roughly 50. The same release reports rates about 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a distribution that matters for a state/province with no metropolitan reporting hub of its own.

A national LGBTQ organisation's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an NGO analysis of police-reported data including gender identity and expression motivations, supplies national victimisation context rather than figures for the state/province.

Residents of the state/province may request the non-binary sex designation on a birth certificate issued there under the amended vital statistics act as approved on 18 September 2025; the record does not specify an effective date for the change or the procedure for applying.

Residents have a state/province statutory route against discrimination: the human rights act, as amended in 2017, names gender identity and gender expression among protected grounds in employment, housing and services within the state/province's responsibility.

Transition-related care is funded for residents through the health department under the surgical partnership reported from 22 March 2022.
