A local LGBTQ group flagged at that time that information about the service does not reach residents outside the capital, which remains an access gap for people living in the communities.

No hate-crime statistics, trans-specific violence counts or survey figures for the state/province are sourced here; the national statistics and the national NGO analysis are country-wide and report no breakdown for the state/province, so its own rate is unresolved rather than low.

Whether a visitor or newcomer can access the funded surgical pathway, and on what terms, is not sourced; the reporting describes funding for residents.

National-layer material, including national hate-crime statistics, national criminal-law amendments and the laws of other state/provinces, belongs to the parent record and is not restated here.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the country. No statute of the state/province restricts trans people's access to restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, to gender-affirming care, or to gender-related name use in schools, and it has enacted no hostile legislation of its own in these areas.

The state/province's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds across employment, housing, and public and private accommodations. Complaints against private businesses proceed under that statute, since charter equality guarantees do not bind the private sector directly.

Section 15 of the country's charter of rights applies in the state/province. The highest court has interpreted the concepts of sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality, and section 15 reaches all laws and government institutions in the state/province, including law enforcement authorities. Those guarantees remain subject to reasonable limits under section 1 and to the notwithstanding clause in section 33.

Vital statistics, including birth certificates and other identity documents, fall under the state/province's own jurisdiction, so a gender-marker change on a local birth certificate is governed by the state/province rather than nationally.

The state/province has no counterpart to the school and health restrictions adopted elsewhere in the country. One state/province passed a 2023 education amendment act invoking the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who request use of a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting calls for repeal and legal action. Another state/province passed three statutes in 2024 covering health, education and sport; the resulting legal challenges were blocked when its government passed a further statute amendment act in 2025 using the notwithstanding clause.

The national statistics agency reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in the country in 2024, up 1% on 2023 after a 34% rise in 2023 over 2022, and 169% above the 2018 total. The national rate fell 2% to 11.9 per 100,000 population. Incidents targeting sexual orientation declined 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. These are national figures released on 30 March 2026 and they carry no state/provincial breakdown.

A national baseline near the top of the source's jurisdictional comparison rests on charter equality protection, nationwide criminalisation of conversion therapy, and legal gender change available in every state/province including this one.

A 2020 national public-opinion survey found that 87.6% of respondents said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person. The figure covers the country as a whole, is four years old at the time of the survey's publication, and says nothing about opinion within the state/province specifically.

Same-sex adoption has been legal in the state/province since 1996, the first state/province in the country to permit it, and the state/province grants parental status to three or more intentional parents.

Residents seeking to change the gender marker on a birth certificate or another vital statistics record deal with the state/province's own vital statistics process, because those records sit under its jurisdiction rather than a national one.

The statistics agency release of 30 March 2026 covering 2024 police-reported hate crime reports national totals only. No state/provincial breakdown appears anywhere in the inventory, so this state/province's own hate-crime level is unresolved rather than established at any figure.

A national 2024 analysis by a 2SLGBTQI advocacy organisation of police-reported hate-crime incidents is a national report; the inventory records no state/provincial findings from it, and its distribution across state/provinces is unresolved here.

The inventory documents no trans-specific killing or violence incident in the state/province with a date and outcome, and no prevalence figure for it is sourced. That is a gap in the sourcing, not evidence that no such incident has occurred.

The specific evidence, forms and waiting periods the state/province requires for a gender-marker change on a birth certificate are not documented in the inventory. Only its jurisdiction over vital statistics is established; the procedure itself is unresolved.

No region-specific border, airport or security-screening practice affecting trans or gender-nonconforming travellers is documented in the inventory for the state/province, and the inventory does not address any provincial-level use of the charter's notwithstanding clause.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the country. Its own instruments govern gender-marker changes on provincial documents and driver's licences.

In April 2016 the provincial government tabled a bill amending the vital statistics act so that a resident can change the gender recorded on official provincial documents by declaring the gender they identify with and providing a letter from a doctor. Sex-reassignment surgery ceased to be required, and the province's gender-marker change has operated without a surgery requirement since that amendment.

Since 4 December 2018 residents identifying gender on a driver's licence may select 'gender not listed', shown on the licence as X, or 'prefer not to say', shown as a blank, alongside male and female. The state/province government states this made it the first jurisdiction in the country to offer the 'prefer not to say' blank option; provincial photo ID issued at provincial service counters can therefore carry an X or a blank gender marker.

Under the province's published process, an adult may apply for a change of gender designation if born in the state/province and resident in it for at least three months and not in the lawful custody of another person. The application requires completed forms including a physician statement and a written statement by the applicant, with signatures arranged before a commissioner of oaths at the provincial vital statistics office.

The source inventory records no state/province-specific hate-crime rate or incident count. The national statistics agency's release of 30 March 2026 on police-reported hate crime for 2024 gives national figures only, and no provincially deviating pattern for this state/province is documented.

Advocacy for a third gender category has been voiced from within the state/province but is not law: a provincial Pride board member welcomed the 2016 amendment while calling for a future third gender category, noting that many people he knew in the provincial capital identify outside the binary.

The change-of-gender-designation route is resident-facing: it requires at least three months of provincial residence and, for a person born elsewhere, is not available on the terms published by the province as captured on 1 July 2022.

For a minor under 18 born in the state/province and resident in it for at least three months, a legal custodian may apply, with written consent of any other custodian or parent and of the child if aged 12 or older.

A linked item on a national broadcaster's article page of 18 April 2016 reports that the provincial health authority would cover the costs of three surgeries for transgender patients. The record does not state whether that coverage has continued, been expanded, or ended.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no state/province-specific hate-crime figure, no trans-specific violence count for the province, and no documented enforcement or complaint outcome under the province's gender-marker rules. The absence of a provincial figure in the national release is not evidence of a low or high rate.

Not sourced: whether provincial service counters or other provincial facilities have documented practices for handling gender-marker discrepancies between a visitor's national passport and provincial photo ID, and whether any provincial facility policy governs sex-segregated spaces, is not addressed anywhere in the inventory.

Not sourced: the current status of the third gender category advocated in 2016. No later provincial instrument creating a non-binary marker on birth records or other vital documents appears in the record; the X and blank options documented here apply to driver's licences and provincial photo ID.

The state/province sets its own schools policy on sexual orientation and gender identity inside the national legal framework. The policy, issued by the state/province education department, has been in force since 17 August 2020 and was revised on 1 July 2023, 23 August 2023 and 1 January 2025.

In the version effective 1 January 2025, students of any age may choose the names and pronouns used for them in informal school settings; parental consent is encouraged but not required. Formal records for students under 16 still require parental consent. The revision went further than the recommendations of a child advocate.

The policy's application clause covers the school environment and names all students together with school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers and visitors, so its rules reach adults present in classrooms who do not live in the state/province.

From 1 July 2023 until the January 2025 revision, the policy barred teachers from using the chosen name and pronouns of a student under 16 without parental consent, reversing a three-year-old rule that required teachers to obtain the student's informed consent before discussing names and pronouns with parents. The 1 July 2023 change also dropped explicit wording letting students take part in extracurricular activities, including sports teams, reflecting their gender identity. The premier's governing party made the change without a legislative vote, citing complaints from parents and teachers; two ministers resigned in protest and two were removed, and eight party members including six cabinet ministers sat out question period in June 2023 to protest the lack of process. Dissidents called for a leadership review. The head of government of the parent nation said trans kids in the state/province "need to feel safe, not targeted by politicians".

The proposed changes drew public opposition before they took effect: about 350 people rallied at the state/province legislature on 14 May 2023 to protest the review, and the education minister confirmed the review was under way. An official from a teachers' advocacy group who helped write the policy told the rally that "we know it saves lives" and warned that "with this policy changed or removed, we're going to lose kids".

The policy as adopted in 2020 requires schools to respect students' chosen names and pronouns and to provide gender-neutral bathrooms. A national civil-liberties group mounted a constitutional challenge to the 2023 parental-consent rule.

The state/province's parental-consent dispute was settled by executive policy rather than by statute: the governing party amended the schools policy without a legislative vote, and no notwithstanding clause was invoked. Two other state/provinces took the legislative route. One passed a 2023 parents' bill of rights education act invoking the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask schools to use their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and that act drew legal action by human rights groups. Another passed health and education amendments and a sport fairness act in 2024, which were challenged in its courts and then shielded from those challenges by a 2025 statute also using the notwithstanding clause.

The dispute produced sustained intra-party and intergovernmental turbulence: two cabinet ministers quit over the 2023 changes, two were pushed out, party dissidents demanded a leadership review, and the head of government of the parent nation publicly intervened on the safety of trans children in the state/province. The administration's 1 January 2025 revision reversed the 2023 consent rule and drew coverage framing it as going beyond the child advocate's recommendations.

For state/province families, the operative split in the schools policy is between informal and formal records. A student of any age may set the name and pronouns used informally at school without parental consent under the version effective 1 January 2025, while any change to formal records for a student under 16 requires parental consent.

The policy binds school personnel, contract and casual employees, visiting professionals, student teachers, parents and volunteers as well as students, so the naming, pronoun and bathroom provisions govern the conduct of adults working in or visiting state/province schools, not only teachers.

The 2023 parental-consent rule is the subject of a constitutional challenge brought by a national civil-liberties group; the record does not state how that challenge was decided.

The outcome of the national civil-liberties group's constitutional challenge to the 2023 parental-consent rule is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Whether the 1 July 2023 removal of explicit wording on taking part in extracurricular activities and sports teams reflecting a student's gender identity was restored by the 1 January 2025 revision is not documented in this inventory.

No state/province jail placement rule for transgender detainees is documented here; rules for people held in national institutions are carried by the parent record. Provincial correctional policies vary across the country and this state/province's own is not sourced.

No state/province-specific rules on changing a gender marker on provincial documents, and no state/province human rights complaint procedure, appear in this inventory; the general provincial human rights framework is carried at the national level.

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence, homicide or survey data for the state/province, and no dated incident record for it.

The state/province's Human Rights Code prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and accommodation. On 18 March 2025 the provincial government introduced a bill to add gender expression as a protected ground; the justice minister stated the change would bring the state/province into line with most other state/provinces and would cover preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing. The bill was before the legislature for debate later in 2025, and a provincial trans advocacy organisation's executive director welcomed it.

The national statistics agency reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, a 1% increase over 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. The state/province recorded the joint-lowest rate among state/provinces at 5.3 per 100,000 alongside a neighbouring jurisdiction, with no increase in 2024; it was among the eight state/provinces whose rates were stable or declining. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations in that data was published by a national LGBTIQ+ organisation. Police-reported figures capture only incidents reported to police.

On 30 May 2024 the state/province's legislature passed a bill recognising 31 March as Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility, brought forward by a backbench legislator for a named riding who is transgender. The legislator said the day would show transgender, two-spirit and non-binary residents that they are supported.

On 20 November 2023 the state/province again raised the transgender flag in a park in the capital city for the Transgender Day of Remembrance, an observance first marked eight years earlier. The flag was raised by the same legislator, the first openly trans man elected to the state/province's legislature. The families minister and health minister stated that the government supports and upholds the life-saving work of trans, two-spirit and gender-diverse residents. A local advocate said the day memorialises people murdered as a result of transphobia, violence she said shows no sign of slowing.

Changing the gender marker on vital statistics documents, including birth certificates, falls under provincial jurisdiction in the country; transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all state/provinces under varying rules. Section 15(1) of the national charter of rights has been interpreted to include transsexuality and applies to all laws and government institutions, including law enforcement, with courts required to interpret human rights statutes consistently with the charter.

Provincial legislative activity on trans rights in the country has moved in both directions. One state/province passed an education act in 2023 invoking the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, prompting human rights calls for repeal and legal action. Another state/province passed health, education and sport statutes in 2024, then passed a further statute in 2025 using the notwithstanding clause to prevent court challenges. The state/province covered by this record has moved in the opposite direction, with the 31 March visibility day and the pending gender-expression amendment.

In December 2020 the national association of police chiefs apologised for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities, stated police must stand together against homophobia, transphobia and marginalisation, and created an internal committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and discrimination in practices and policies.

A 2020 poll commissioned by the national cabinet office reported that 87.6% said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person; 91.8% said they would be comfortable if a next-door neighbour was gay, lesbian or bisexual. The country ranked first in an international LGBTQ+ danger index in 2023, first in a gay travel index in 2024, and ninth in an equality index in 2024.

The state/province's Human Rights Code already prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and accommodation, giving residents a provincial complaint route on that ground. The 18 March 2025 bill to add gender expression would extend that protection to preferred pronouns and outward appearance such as clothing; as of that reporting it was in the legislature awaiting debate later in 2025, and its final status is not documented in this record.

Residents can change the gender marker on provincial vital statistics documents, including birth certificates, under provincial rules; the specific procedure and evidentiary requirements are not detailed in this inventory.

The openly trans legislator who represents a named riding brought forward the Two-Spirit and Transgender Day of Visibility bill passed on 30 May 2024. A provincial trans advocacy organisation with a named executive director is active in the state/province.

The final status of the gender-expression amendment bill introduced on 18 March 2025 is unresolved in this record; whether it passed, was amended, or remained pending after the 2025 debate is not sourced here.

The state/province's specific rules and evidentiary requirements for changing a gender marker on birth certificates and other vital statistics documents are not sourced in this inventory; only the general provincial jurisdiction over vital statistics is documented.

The national hate-crime figures for 2024 are not broken down by motivation category in this inventory for this state/province specifically, so the province's rate cannot be attributed to gender-identity-motivated incidents. Police-reported data capture only incidents reported to police.

No incident of violence against a trans person in this state/province, with date and outcome, is documented in this inventory; the 20 November 2023 Remembrance Day statements describe transphobic violence generally without a local case.

The country is a state/province of the country and stands under the country's national framework: national criminal law and the national human-rights regime apply in the state/province as in every other state/province. Provincially, the state/province's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has prohibited discrimination because of gender identity and gender expression since 2016, reaching employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Provincial enforcement machinery has produced a documented win for a trans visitor or resident. On 10 June 2024 the state/province's Human Rights Tribunal found that a bar in the provincial capital had discriminated against a trans woman in hiring because of her gender identity, ordering the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training.

The state/province's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial with 29 witnesses, the state/province's Superior Court (2021 QCCS 191) declared provisions of the Civil Code invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people; the Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision (2024 QCCA 348), and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code.

Correctional placement in the state/province now turns on anatomy rather than gender identity. On 19 June 2025 the state/province's public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the state/province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety priorities; the directive was issued just after a trans woman convicted of murdering her partner and children sought a transfer to a women's prison. Advocates say the policy violates the state/province's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This is a dated, province-specific reversal of the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.

The national statistics agency's police-reported hate crime release of 30 March 2026 reports 4,882 hate crimes nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, with rates across state/provinces ranging from 5.3 per 100,000 in two jurisdictions to 16.0 in another. No figure specific to this state/province appears in that release, so the record's assessment of this state/province at national parity rests on the absence of a divergent figure rather than on a measured number. The underlying analysis of national police hate-crime data, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations, was published by an LGBTIQ+ organisation.

Consensual sexual activity between adults was decriminalised nationally in 1969, and effective 21 June 2019 the Criminal Code provision on that conduct was repealed, barring conviction for any historical sexual offence unless the act would constitute an offence if committed on the day the charge was laid; that repeal removed that consensual-sex criminal liability in this state/province.

The state/province created civil unions by amending the Civil Code in 2002, giving couples regardless of gender or sexual orientation the same effects as marriage in respect of family direction, parental authority, expenses, family residence, family patrimony and compensatory allowance, valid only within this state/province. Same-sex adoption was legalised here in 2002.

2021 census data cited by a provincial legal-information service indicates that 0.14% of residents aged 15 and older, and 0.27% of those aged 15 to 34, identify as transgender.

This state/province sits within a national picture in which police-reported hate crime rose 142% between 2018 and 2024 to a rate of 12.1 per 100,000, with eight state/provinces stable or declining in 2024; the release does not break out this state/province.

Other state/provinces have moved in the opposite direction on trans-related rules: one neighbouring jurisdiction's 2023 education act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who request use of a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, and another passed a package of health, education and sport statutes in 2024, then blocked court challenges with a further 2025 statute also using the notwithstanding clause. A visitor moving between state/provinces should not assume this state/province's framework travels with them.

The national association of police chiefs apologised in December 2020 for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities and created an equity, diversity and inclusion committee to address implicit bias and systemic barriers.

The country statutorily banned conversion therapy nationwide in 2022, for minors and adults, and made subjecting anyone to it a crime under the Criminal Code.

Rankings of the country's LGBT-friendliness are framed around gay-friendliness and sexuality rather than transgender people specifically: first (least dangerous) in one LGBTQ+ danger index in 2023, first in one gay travel index in 2024, and ninth in one equality index in 2024.

A 2020 poll commissioned by the national cabinet office found 87.6% of respondents said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour. Separate sexuality-attitude figures, not transgender-specific, showed 2020 support for social acceptance of homosexuality at 85% of the general population and 92% among ages 18-29, up from 80% in 2013.

The provincial capital maintains an established gay area, with Pride celebrated every summer in major cities with national, provincial and municipal political participation.

Transgender residents can change their legal gender under provincial rules; the Civil Code provisions governing sex designation were declared invalid in 2021 and largely upheld on appeal in 2024, prompting legislative reform.

Discrimination complaints on gender identity or expression in areas of provincial responsibility run through the state/province's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms and its Human Rights Tribunal, which has awarded damages in a trans hiring case.

Transgender inmates in provincial custody are placed according to anatomical sex under the directive announced by the public security minister on 19 June 2025, reversing prior practice; advocates contend this breaches the state/province's Charter.

The state/province's 2002 civil union regime is valid only within this state/province and does not travel to other state/provinces.

The national statistics release of 30 March 2026 contains no hate-crime rate specific to this state/province, so the province's position relative to the 5.3 to 16.0 per 100,000 range is unresolved in this record; the parity assessment rests on the absence of a divergent figure rather than a measured one.

Whether the 19 June 2025 correctional placement directive has been challenged in court, and with what outcome, is not sourced here; only the advocates' position that it violates the state/province's Charter is documented.

The specific Civil Code provisions invalidated in 2021 QCCS 191 and the terms of the resulting legislative reform are not set out in this inventory; the current wording of this state/province's sex-designation rules is unresolved.

The 0.14% and 0.27% transgender identification figures derive from 2021 census data as cited by a provincial legal-information service and are not a current prevalence measure.

The country's trans-specific lawmaking is a package of three statutes that passed final legislative stage on 4 December 2024. The Education Amendment Act, 2024 introduced parental opt-in for classroom instruction on sexuality and rules governing students' preferred names and pronouns and their participation in school sport. The Health Statutes Amendment Act, 2024 bars certain gender-affirming care for minors. The Fairness and Safety in Sport Act bars trans women from women's sport.

Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting and invokes the Charter's notwithstanding clause to shield the three trans-youth laws from legal challenge for years. Two national LGBT organisations and five families announced constitutional litigation, calling the package discriminatory, and state that their court challenge continues regardless; the laws are in force with constitutional litigation pending.

The head of government's 12 February 2024 announcement of the package stated the bans would not include a ban on women's shelters, women's prisons or women's changing rooms, and the statutory trans package deliberately excluded jail and prison settings. No provincial placement-by-birth-sex rule for trans prisoners was enacted, and no specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented in this record.

Provincial correctional policies vary and no specific rule is documented. National corrections operations inside the country accommodate offenders based on gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth: since 2018 a national corrections agency permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex/gender marker on identity documents, with requests refused only where the agency finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 the agency reported 90 self-identified transgender women in national institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. The national correctional oversight office called the agency's 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the lack of clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse.

Provincial human rights commissions handle discrimination complaints in areas of provincial responsibility, and gender identity and gender expression are prohibited grounds in employment, housing and public and private accommodations across all jurisdictions as of 2017. Section 15 of the Charter applies to all laws and government institutions including law enforcement authorities, and Supreme Court jurisprudence has interpreted sex and physical disability in section 15 to include transsexuality. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender under provincial vital statistics rules governing identity documents such as birth certificates.

Since 2022 the Criminal Code statutorily bans conversion therapy nationwide for both minors and adults, making it a crime to subject anyone to it as defined by statutory law. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 20 July 2005 under the national Civil Marriage Act; the province's 2000 Marriage Act defining marriage as between a man and a woman and invoking the notwithstanding clause was invalid because capacity to marry is exclusive national jurisdiction and its five-year exemption expired in 2005.

In a poll commissioned for the national cabinet office reported for 2020, 87.6% of those surveyed said they would be comfortable if a neighbour was a transgender person. This figure is a general-population attitude finding from 2020, not a measure of current risk or of violence.

In December 2020 the national police chiefs' association apologized for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer Communities, acknowledged contribution to institutional bias, intolerance and violation of human rights, and created an equity and diversity committee to identify, mitigate and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers.

On 28 November 2017 the head of government issued a formal parliamentary apology for oppression of lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and two-spirit communities, and on 21 June 2018 an expungement of historically unjust convictions act received royal assent allowing records of pre-1969 homosexual acts or section 159 convictions to be destroyed or removed.

In 2023 a neighbouring jurisdiction passed an education parents' bill of rights act invoking the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 requesting use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity, a comparable provincial measure to this package.

The province legalized stepchild adoption in 1999 and joint adoption in 2007. Rankings such as a 2023 LGBTQ+ danger index (first), a 2024 gay travel index (first) and a 2024 equality index (ninth) are general LGBTQ rankings not disaggregated for transgender people.

Residents seeking to change the gender marker on birth certificates and other vital statistics documents do so under provincial vital statistics rules; the specific current procedure and evidentiary requirements are not documented in this inventory.

The Education Amendment Act, 2024 governs students' preferred names and pronouns in schools and their participation in school sport, with parental opt-in for classroom instruction on sexuality; these rules bind school authorities and residents rather than visitors.

Provincial correctional facilities operate under provincial correctional policy, for which no specific trans placement rule is documented; transgender people in national custody fall under national corrections agency policy permitting placement aligned with gender identity.

The inventory does not document the current evidentiary standard or processing time for changing a gender marker on a provincial birth certificate; this remains unresolved in these sources.

No specific trans-prisoner placement, special unit or segregation case is documented in this inventory, and provincial correctional policy on gender-diverse placement is described only as varying without a specific rule being sourced.

The outcome of the constitutional litigation by two national LGBT organisations and five families against Bill 9 and the underlying statutes is not documented; the record shows the laws in force with litigation pending.

No trans-specific violence or killing rate with a denominator and period is present in this inventory, so no such figure is stated.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the country; this assessment covers its own layer: its human rights code, the commission that administers it, the province's published policy, and the state/province's recorded hate-crime figures.

The state/province human rights commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the state/province human rights code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. The policy defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. It is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in the state/province's workplaces, housing and services.

The national statistics agency reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate crimes in the country in 2024, 1% more than in 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. The state/province recorded the highest rate among state/provinces at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population. The figure covers all reported motivations and does not isolate gender-identity motivation. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting levels are shaped by awareness and community trust.

On 28 August 2023 the state/province education minister said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school. He said teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child. The state/province had not adopted parental-consent legislation of the kind some other state/provinces were enacting at that time, and no later legislative instance on this question is documented in this record.

The education minister's August 2023 remarks were made amid legislative activity on student name and pronoun changes in several other state/provinces; the contrast matters for a visitor with school-age children, because the position at that date rested on ministerial direction and school-board practice rather than statute.

The state/province's 16.0 incidents per 100,000 for 2024 is a per-capita rate, so its first-place ranking among the country's state/provinces is not a population artefact. It measures police-reported hate crime of all motivations combined and therefore indicates the reporting and enforcement environment a trans visitor would enter, not a trans-specific rate.

Residents discriminated against on gender identity or gender expression grounds raise complaints under the state/province human rights code, which the state/province human rights commission administers and whose protections the commission sets out in its published policy on gender identity and gender expression.

For families, the documented provincial position as of 28 August 2023 is that parents are to be fully involved and fully aware when a student decides to use a different name or pronoun at school, with teachers and school boards directed to weigh exceptional circumstances and potential harm to the child.

No trans-specific killing or violent incident in the state/province is documented in this inventory, and no trans-specific figure with a stated period is available, so no trans-specific rate can be stated for the state/province.

The 2024 hate-crime figure covers all reported motivations and does not break out gender-identity motivation for the state/province. A national LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of 2024 police-reported data covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations exists but is national in scope and is not broken down to the state/province here.

Whether the state/province legislated parental consent for student name or pronoun changes after the 28 August 2023 statement is unresolved in this record; the most recent dated item on that question is 28 August 2023, and no later instance is documented.

No state/province-specific public-opinion survey on acceptance of transgender people is sourced here, so no local prevalence figure for attitudes can be given.

The state/province stands under the national framework, which the parent record carries. Within state/provincial competence, the state/province operates no restrictive trans-specific legislation and instead maintains an explicit inclusion framework.

The state/provincial government released the state/province's first 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan on 8 January 2026, developed under a Dismantling Racism and Hate Act passed in 2022, described by the state/province as the first law of its kind in the country to explicitly acknowledge 2SLGBTQIA+ people. The plan was informed by more than 600 community members through surveys, virtual meetings and consultations, and maps actions to improve programs and policies supporting full inclusion of 2SLGBTQIA+ people.

On 10 June 2026 the state/province announced more than $176,000 through the first round of its 2SLGBTQIA+ Community Impact Grant program, including $12,067 to a local sexual health centre for queer and trans outreach, $25,000 to a employment programme for queer people, $25,000 to a regional Pride organisation, and $50,000 to a Pride organisation to host the state/province's first provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ conference. Per-project grants are capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing and accommodation is prohibited in the state/province as in all state/provinces and the national level; as of 2017 all state/provinces and the national level explicitly include gender identity as a prohibited ground in their human rights acts. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in the state/province under state/provincial rules.

The documented correctional case concerns a transgender woman from the state/province's largest metropolitan area held in a men's prison while serving a two-year robbery sentence. On 18 March 2025 a national-level judge granted her more time to file her application for judicial review of that placement, citing a lack of transparency and clear, timely communication in the institutional decision-making and systemic barriers restricting her access to her lawyer. No later instance of this case is documented in the record.

The national statistics agency reported on 30 March 2026 that 4,882 police-reported hate crimes were recorded nationally in 2024, a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018; eight state/provinces recorded stable or declining rates. The release carries no state/province-specific rate or incident count. The underlying analysis of sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations comes from an LGBTIQ+ organisation's 2024 hate-crime analysis report.

In a 2024 international travel index, the country including this state/province shared first place with four other countries among 213 countries and regions as a travel destination covering lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex people.

A 2020 poll commissioned by the national cabinet office found 87.6% of respondents said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person, while 91.8% said the same of a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour. The figure measures comfort with a neighbour, not law, enforcement or protection outcomes, and no state/province-specific tolerance, enforcement or facility-access data appears in the record.

Other state/provinces in the country have moved in a restrictive direction on trans-related matters: one state/province's Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act 2023 requires parental consent for students under 16 using a gender-related preferred name or gender identity, passed invoking the notwithstanding clause; another state/province's 2024 health and education amendments and sport act faced legal challenges which that state/province government sought to block through a 2025 statute also using the notwithstanding clause. This state/province has enacted no comparable measure.

The national chiefs-of-police association apologised in December 2020 for harm to Two-Spirit, Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer communities and created an Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Committee to identify and eliminate implicit bias and systemic barriers.

Residents of the state/province can change their legal gender under state/provincial rules, and gender identity and expression are protected grounds in employment, housing and public and private accommodation under the state/provincial human rights framework applicable to all state/provinces and the national level as of 2017.

The state/provincial 2SLGBTQIA+ Action Plan released 8 January 2026 commits the government to mapping actions across programs and policies for full inclusion, developed under a 2022 Dismantling Racism and Hate Act with input from more than 600 community members.

The Community Impact Grant program's first round distributed more than $176,000 on 10 June 2026 to local organisations including Pride groups, an employment programme and a sexual health centre, with per-project grants capped at $25,000 from the 2025-26 fiscal year.

A transgender woman from the state/province's largest metropolitan area is pursuing judicial review of a decision to hold her in a men's prison during a two-year robbery sentence; a national-level judge on 18 March 2025 extended her filing deadline, citing institutional opacity and systemic barriers to her access to counsel. The record documents no later development in this case.

The national statistics release of 30 March 2026 provides no state/province-specific hate-crime rate or incident count; whether the state/province's rate tracks, exceeds or falls below the national figure of 12.1 per 100,000 is unresolved in this record.

No trans-specific violence or killing figure for the state/province appears in the inventory, so no comparison against a general homicide rate can be drawn; the magnitude of any such harm in the state/province is not sourced here.

The record contains no state/province-specific data on airport or border screening treatment of trans travellers, document-marker practice at points of entry, or facility-access outcomes; these remain not sourced.

The outcome of the judicial review of a trans woman's correctional placement is not documented beyond the 18 March 2025 scheduling decision.

The state/province's human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, giving a visitor or resident a provincial complaints route.

Change of legal gender is a provincial function and is available in the state/province under its own rules.

On 22 August 2023 the provincial education ministry announced parental inclusion and consent policies. Schools must seek parent or guardian permission before changing the preferred name and pronouns of students under 16, parents must be informed about the sexual-health curriculum, and third-party school programs were paused. That release initiated the court challenge.

A 2023 education amendment act was passed with the provincial government invoking the notwithstanding clause, a five-year override of the national charter. It requires schools to obtain parental consent for students under 16 who request use of their gender-related preferred name or gender identity. Human rights groups called for repeal, and the invocation of the clause may prevent legal action from succeeding on charter grounds.

In August 2025 the state/province's Court of Appeal set aside the 2023 chambers decision, so the pronoun-notice policy stands. The appeal court held that charter breaches under sections 1 and 15 cannot be tested where section 33 has been invoked. Reporting on the same judgment states that the appeal was granted in part, that a judge has jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits charter rights, and that a provincial LGBTQ+ organisation's litigation may continue in the provincial trial court.

An international human-rights organisation participated as an intervenor in the appeal and welcomed the August 2025 decision as a meaningful victory for the protection of human rights in the country. It argued that courts can still determine whether the provincial anti-trans pronoun law violates the charter and issue a declaration to that effect even where the notwithstanding clause shields the law from being struck down, and that use of the clause must align with the country's international-law obligation to provide an effective remedy.

A national LGBTQ+ organisation's co-counsel said the local Pride centre will continue the litigation, noting that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.

On 6 November 2025 the country's highest court said it will hear the appeals in the challenge to the school pronoun law. Both the provincial government and the local LGBTQ+ organisation appealed the Court of Appeal decision and asked for the hearing to be expedited alongside the challenge to another province's separate legislation. No merits ruling has changed the policy, and the constitutionality of the shielded consent rule is now before the country's highest court.

The provincial government argued that its use of the notwithstanding clause should end the challenge entirely. The Court of Appeal granted that appeal in part in August 2025 while allowing litigation to continue, and both sides then appealed to the country's highest court, so the dispute is unresolved at the date of the latest source, 6 November 2025.

The request to expedite this case was made together with the challenge to another province's separate legislation, placing the province's pronoun-notice measure among the constitutional matters the highest court was asked to take up on an accelerated schedule.

The pronoun-notice policy has been in force since 2023 while the litigation runs; counsel for the respondents stated in August 2025 that students had been living under the reality of the law for two years.

Residents are covered by the provincial human rights complaints route for discrimination based on gender identity or gender expression in employment, housing, and public and private accommodations, and legal gender change is handled under the state/province's own rules.

For residents with school-age children, the parental inclusion and consent policies and the 2023 education amendment act require parental consent before a student under 16 uses a gender-related preferred name or gender identity at school, and require parents to be informed about the sexual-health curriculum.

The state/province is one of three state/provinces, with two others, that will grant parental status to three or more intentional parents, allowing a wider range of queer and trans families.

Human rights groups have called for repeal of the 2023 measure, and the legal action they supported continues in the provincial trial court pending the highest court's hearing.

The two sources describing the August 2025 judgment differ in emphasis and are not fully reconcilable from the inventory: one reports that courts lack jurisdiction to test section 1 and section 15 charter breaches where section 33 was invoked and that the policy stands, the other reports the appeal granted in part with a judge retaining jurisdiction to determine whether the law limits charter rights. This is unresolved.

No state/province-specific correctional placement rule or case is documented in the inventory; provincial correctional policies are described only as varying. The placement policy and custody statistics available are national in scope and are not carried here.

No trans-specific violence, homicide or assault figure for the state/province is sourced, and no dated incident of violence against a trans person in the province appears in the inventory. Nothing about present violence levels can be stated either way.

The procedural detail of legal gender change in the state/province, including evidence requirements, waiting periods and processing times, is not sourced. Entry, visa, identity-document marker and airport-screening rules are national matters and are not documented for this province.

Beyond the 6 November 2025 announcement that the country's highest court will hear the appeals, no hearing date, no merits ruling and no outcome is documented; the policy's constitutionality was undecided at that date.

The available public-opinion figures on transgender tolerance are national, were collected in 2020, and are not specific to this province, so they are not carried in this record.

This state/province is a sub-national unit of the parent nation. Criminal law, human rights protections and entry rules are set nationally rather than by the state/province, and its own legislative activity on transgender issues concerns vital statistics and name change.

In June 2026 the state/provincial legislature was taking feedback from police and from a local advocacy organisation on proposed amendments to the vital statistics legislation and the change of name legislation intended to make the legislation more inclusive for transgender, non-binary, gender-diverse and two-spirit people. The proposals include an option for trans and non-binary people to request that a name change not be published in the official gazette. This is the first on-record state/provincial legislation specifically addressing transgender and non-binary people. The amendments were under consultation and had not been enacted.

The national police service has taken a position against part of the proposal. A senior officer asked members of the legislature to remove or amend the registrar general's option not to notify authorities, arguing that criminal records are tied to a person's legal name and that officers may put themselves in danger if records are not transferred to a new name. A member of the legislature pressed the police on how officers would verify legal names without identification. The police service is therefore on record opposing a measure designed to keep a trans person's former name out of public view.

Organised community support for trans and Two-Spirit young people is documented in the state/province. In June 2023 a regional education authority bused seventeen regional students into a regional centre for pride events centred on feeling comfortable in one's own gender and sexuality, with workshops led by a Two-Spirit musician, a documentary screening and a pride parade. The gathering included a moment of silence at a community greenhouse for a local LGBTQ2S community member missing since 2023.

A small hamlet on a river in one region held its first Pride celebration on 28 June 2025, organised jointly by a local school, the hamlet administration and the local police detachment. A local officer counted more than 50 attendees and described the day as creating a safe and welcoming space for the 2SLGBTQI+ community. The police detachment covered food and paint while the hamlet and school supplied volunteers, firewood and the venue.

The national police service's position at the legislature and the local detachment's role in the 2025 Pride celebration are both on the record, and they run in opposite directions. The force argued at the legislature against a measure that would keep a trans person's former name out of the gazette and away from automatic notification, while a detachment in one region helped fund and staff a Pride event whose officer described the day as welcoming the 2SLGBTQI+ community.

The two documented community events are separated by two years and by geography: a regional centre gathering in 2023 that drew students from across one region, and a first-ever hamlet Pride in 2025. Both were organised with public institutions, the education authority in the first case and the school, hamlet administration and police detachment in the second.

A name change in this state/province is published in the official gazette, and the registrar general holds an option to notify authorities. Both provisions are the subject of the current review, so a resident who needs a name change kept out of public view is relying on an amendment that has not been enacted.

In one small hamlet, organisers planned monthly inclusive school events from September 2025, run through the school and the hamlet administration with the local police detachment.

The proposed amendments to the vital statistics legislation and the change of name legislation were still under consultation in June 2026. Whether the registrar general's option not to notify authorities survives, and whether the gazette non-publication option is enacted, is unresolved.

No state/provincial breakdown of national hate-crime statistics is published, and reporting infrastructure in this state/province is thin relative to metropolitan areas, so no state/provincial rate can be derived from the national series. A national advocacy organisation's analysis of police-reported hate-crime data contains no state/provincial data.

The disappearance of a local community member from a remote community in 2023 remains unresolved. No anti-trans motive has been documented, and the case is not evidence of trans-specific targeting in the state/province.

The state/province is a state/province of the country. Its human rights legislation lists gender identity and gender expression among prohibited grounds of discrimination, covering employment, housing, and public and private accommodation.

Legal change of gender is available in the state/province. Vital statistics and identity documents such as birth certificates fall under state/province jurisdiction; the sources reviewed do not set out the state/province's own requirements for amending a marker.

On 30 March 2026 the state/province legislature marked International Transgender Day of Visibility, with members rising to speak across party lines. A state/province legislator praised the courage, resilience, contributions and accomplishments of transgender, two-spirited and gender-diverse residents, acknowledged that too many people have experienced discrimination, harassment and hate for far too long, and cited a national study showing transgender 15-17-year-olds face 7.6 times the risk of suicide attempt. This is the state/province's own cross-party, in-legislature acknowledgement of trans residents on record.

On 13 June 2024 a local news outlet reported that a Pride flag was allegedly vandalized and stolen from an elementary school in the state/province capital over a weekend in June 2024, with a replacement flag promptly put up. In a statement issued 12 June, the state/province education minister reaffirmed her commitment to the state/province's sexual orientation and gender identity policy.

A national statistical release (published 30 March 2026) reports that police reported 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, up 1% on 2023 and up 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Hate crimes targeting gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive yearly increase and up 184% since 2020. These are national figures; the release does not report state/province-level victimisation. Police-reported hate crime rates are about 2.5 times higher in large metropolitan areas (13.9 per 100,000) than in smaller towns (5.5), which bears on sparsely-populated state/provinces where reporting infrastructure is thinner.

A national LGBT organisation's 2024 hate-crime analysis examines police-reported hate-crime data with gender identity or expression and sexual-orientation motivations; its figures are national and do not report state/province-level victimisation.

The national hate-crime statistics cited above are national aggregates and do not measure the state/province specifically; the metropolitan-versus-smaller-town gap in reporting rates suggests that police-reported figures for a sparsely-populated state/province may understate incidence.

A 2020 government-commissioned poll found 87.6% of respondents said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% for a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour — a national attitudinal snapshot, not a state/province-specific measure.

The national association of police chiefs apologised in December 2020 for institutional bias and pledged to stand against transphobia through an internal equity committee; this is a national policing commitment rather than a state/province-specific one.

Adoption by same-sex couples was legalised in the state/province in 2003 as part of nationwide legalisation.

The state/province's SOGI 123 policy governs sexual orientation and gender identity in state/province schools; the education minister publicly reaffirmed it in June 2024.

The sources reviewed do not set out the state/province's own requirements for amending a gender marker on a birth certificate or other vital-statistics document; this remains unresolved in this record.

No state/province-specific hate-crime or victimisation figures are available in the sources; the statistical and advocacy-organisation data are national.

No documented instance of trans-specific violence in the state/province appears in the sources; the most recent documented incident in this record is the June 2024 Pride flag vandalism at a school, and no later instance is documented.

The state/province stands under the parent nation's national framework on gender identity and gender expression; that national layer is carried on the parent record and is not restated here. The findings below concern state/provincial documents, services and enforcement of state/provincial responsibility.

Provincial law has not required sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing the gender marker on a birth or marriage registration since an amendment to the vital statistics legislation received assent on 13 April 2016. The amendment brought the statute into compliance with an order of a Board of Inquiry under the state/province's human rights commission, issued in December 2015 on complaints brought by two trans women.

Since 23 June 2021, when further amendments to the same legislation received assent, a person born outside the state/province who has lived there at least three months has been able to obtain a change of sex designation. The change certificate costs $25, counts as official state/provincial identification, and is described by the government as a document that can be leveraged to update records in other jurisdictions. The amendments align with the earlier addition of a non-binary option on provincial birth certificates; the bill received second reading on 17 June 2021.

Under the current application rules, applicants must be 16 or older, or be represented by a parent or legal guardian, with the consent of the other parent or guardian and the written consent of applicants aged 12 to 15. Applicants must be born in the state/province or have resided there at least three months. The application itself carries no fee; charges apply only to official copies of the updated documents, at $35 for a new birth certificate or $30 online.

The province states that it cannot guarantee a birth certificate bearing an 'X' gender marker will be accepted by authorities in other organisations. That is the documented cross-border caveat for carrying state/provincial records elsewhere.

Police-reported hate crime in the state/province was recorded at 5.3 per 100,000 for 2024, the joint-lowest rate in the country alongside one other state/province. The figure rests on 29 incidents, up from 19 in 2023, which makes the 51 per cent rise statistically fragile at that volume. Police counts capture only incidents reported to and recorded by police. The national statistics agency published the data on 30 March 2026.

Nationally, police reported 4,882 hate crimes in 2024, a 1 per cent increase on 2023 after a 34 per cent jump the previous year, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000. One state/province recorded the highest rate at 16.0 per 100,000, about three times the figure for this state/province. The comparison spans jurisdictions of very different size and composition, and raw rates at these volumes move on a handful of incidents.

An LGBTIQ+ organisation publishes an analysis of national police-reported hate-crime data that includes offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. Its 2024 report is national in scope.

Residents apply for a change of sex designation through the state/provincial vital statistics process. The application is free of charge; a replacement birth certificate costs $35, or $30 if ordered online, and those charges are the only fees attached to the change itself.

Applicants under 16 are handled through a parent or legal guardian, with the consent of the other parent or guardian and the written consent of the young person where they are aged 12 to 15. The three-month residency threshold applies to residents born elsewhere, and the resulting certificate serves as state/provincial identification for people born outside the country.

Provincial birth certificates carry a non-binary 'X' option alongside the male and female markers, and the surgery requirement was removed from the statute in 2016 rather than being replaced by any other medical condition.

Same-sex adoption has been legal in this state/province since 2002.

The national statistics agency series cited here counts all police-reported hate crime. The inventory does not break out offences motivated by gender identity for this state/province, so no trans-specific rate can be stated, and the 5.3 per 100,000 figure should not be read as one.

No state/province-specific count or rate of killings or violence against trans people appears in the sources, and none is asserted here.

Whether authorities elsewhere will accept a birth certificate carrying an 'X' marker is unresolved. The state/provincial government itself declines to guarantee acceptance, and no source in the inventory records how other jurisdictions treat the document.

The LGBTIQ+ organisation's report is national in scope; no finding specific to this state/province from it is carried into this record.

A 2020 national opinion poll measuring comfort with a transgender neighbour is not attributed to this state/province.

Aruba is a constituent state/province within the state and stands under that framework; the state/province's own Criminal Code, enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources.

Partner recognition is established at two levels. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per a news agency account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the supreme court of the state upheld the appeals court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the supreme court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the state and in other state/provinces of the state. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all governments of the state endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba and two neighbouring jurisdictions. Aruba's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the state/province, who were stigmatized as disordered.

Harassment has been documented. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other constituent state/provinces to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the state/province's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period; no later instance is documented.

Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including two named local equality organisations and a third whose spokesperson is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'

The official tourism board markets the state/province as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

A cultural report edited in January 2017 describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open, with a smaller and quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than a neighbouring jurisdiction, and identifies Catholic influence as the main brake on further change. The same report notes that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the state.

Religious and cultural opposition was strong enough in 2016 that the registered-partnership bill passed only after a 2.5-year campaign, and a same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 failed on tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.

Same-sex adoption is legal in Aruba, per the cultural report edited in January 2017.

The registered-partnership campaign ran 2.5 years, with an openly-gay MP as sponsor, introducing the bill in August 2016, and a local equality organisation's petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

Resident-facing organisations include two named local equality organisations and a third, alongside several gay bars and clubs in the capital city.

Whether gender identity or gender expression is recognised anywhere in Aruban law is unresolved in these sources: the Criminal Code grounds enumerated in Article 1:221 cover sexual orientation only, and no transgender-specific provision is cited. Whether any separate instrument addresses gender markers, identity documents or legal gender recognition is not sourced here.

No findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources; the age of consent of 16 is the only youth-specific threshold given.

No trans-specific violence or killing statistics for Aruba appear in this inventory, and no per-capita or population denominator is available for any figure, so no comparative risk ranking can be drawn.

The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record dates from the 2004–2007 court challenge; no later instance is documented, and the absence of a later documented case is not evidence that none occurs.

The tourism board's safety claims are self-description by the destination's marketer and are not independent verification.

The state/province is governed by local law, and the parent nation's legislation reaches it only where an order extends it, so no parent-nation anti-discrimination floor applies of its own force.

Private consensual same-sex conduct was decriminalised by an order of the parent nation's highest judicial body on 5 January 2001, in a decision that also covered four other jurisdictions in the region. The order was issued unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. The state/province had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other jurisdictions.

Local law provides no protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The constitution's anti-discrimination clause reaches race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin, so gender identity sits outside the protected categories and a trans visitor has no statutory non-discrimination footing.

The age of consent is 18 for same-sex conduct and 16 for different-sex conduct. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship therefore carries legal exposure that a different-sex couple does not face.

The marriage statute defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal, and the state/province is among those that have not legislated for civil partnerships. A commercial destination-wedding service marketing ceremonies there states that same-sex marriage is not recognised under local law, so a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has access only to a symbolic, non-legal ceremony. Non-legal ceremonies of same-sex couples have taken place.

Public LGBT life is highly constrained. A subdued and subtle climate of homophobia has pushed local LGBT people toward secrecy. There are no pride events, gay organisations, venues, bars or clubs and no community infrastructure, which the source attributes to a small population. The only recorded public event is a small protest on 17 May 2011 in the capital marking an international day against homophobia, transphobia and biphobia.

Visiting same-sex couples have described the state/province as gay-friendly and reported that nobody was discriminatory in any way, though the same source cautions that the position of local people may differ. A 2023 first-person account by a queer family found same-sex conduct legal under the order but the scene muted rather than openly visible, an outcome that account attributes to decriminalisation imposed from outside rather than to local initiative.

The 2001 decriminalisation came from the parent nation's highest judicial body rather than from the state/province's own legislature, and it covered five jurisdictions at once. The state/province's position on civil partnerships places it alongside other jurisdictions that have not legislated for them, so the absence of partnership recognition is a pattern across the subregion rather than a measure confined to one jurisdiction.

The state/province is small and about 100 miles east of a neighbouring jurisdiction. The 2012 country report and the 2023 travel account both tie the absence of any LGBT venue, organisation or pride event to that small scale at least as much as to enforcement or legal prohibition.

Accounts written for visitors describe a relaxed reception for visiting same-sex couples while the material on residents describes secrecy and a subdued climate of homophobia. The two bodies of evidence describe different populations, and the visitor material was produced by couples on holiday rather than by residents.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The constitution's protected grounds are race, political opinions, colour, creed, sex and place of origin.

The age of consent for same-sex conduct is 18, against 16 for different-sex conduct, a differential that applies to residents as well as to visitors.

Marriage under the marriage statute is the union of a man and a woman as husband and wife. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and civil partnerships are not available, and couples can hold only symbolic ceremonies.

Local LGBT people are described as pushed toward secrecy by a subdued and subtle climate of homophobia. There are no pride events, gay organisations, bars, clubs or venues and no community infrastructure, which the sources attribute to a small population. No trans-specific organisation, support service or venue appears in the sources either. The one recorded public event is a small protest in the capital on 17 May 2011 marking an international day against homophobia, transphobia and biphobia.

Decriminalisation was imposed by order of the parent nation's highest judicial body after the local legislature declined to repeal the prohibition, and it drew protest from religious leaders.

No source in the inventory sets out the state/province's rules on gender markers on identity documents, on entry or immigration screening, or on access to sex-segregated facilities. Those questions are unresolved here.

No trans-specific violence data and no hate-crime enforcement data were identified, and the inventory contains no general homicide denominator, so no risk magnitude for anti-trans violence can be stated.

Sources give different years for decriminalisation: the 2023 travel account states 2000, while the order of the parent nation's highest judicial body is dated 5 January 2001 and the encyclopaedic coverage gives 2001. The 2001 date is the documented one.

Whether any order of the parent nation has extended parent-nation anti-discrimination legislation to the state/province is not established in the inventory. The sources identify the mechanism but name no such order.

The favourable accounts of how visiting same-sex couples were treated describe a different population from the residents covered by the material on secrecy and lack of protection, and the sources themselves caution that local conditions may differ from the visitor experience. No source reports how a visibly trans visitor, as distinct from a same-sex couple, was received.

The state/province's own criminal code does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, covered male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct; the legislature's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the Senate rejected a bill introduced by a legislator that would have outlawed it, after the House Judiciary Committee recommended the bill be killed; at the committee hearing a fa'afafine resident testified that fa'afafine do not seek marriage with men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In July 2015 the national justice department was reviewing whether the national supreme court's 2015 marriage-equality ruling reached the state/province and said he did not know, while the governor stated that it did not apply, citing the state/province's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in the state/province records that none has applied since.
