In January 2016 the Senate unanimously confirmed a former head of the national justice department as a district court judge after he told confirming senators, including a senator who was a retired associate judge of the state/province's highest court, that he had not read the 2015 ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

In July 2024 a local survey by a constitutional and comparative law professor at a university tested whether the state/province's ban would survive a challenge under the parent nation's equal-protection guarantee. As of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question. The 2026 article reaches the opposite conclusion on the law, holding that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements and that the state/province would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation path through the state/province's highest court first, with the registrar as defendant, then the national interior department. Since 13 December 2022 the state/province has been obliged to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples.

The state/province's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties. It refers to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'.

Gender markers on local documents are changeable within limits. The state/province's highest court has held that birth certificates may be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the vital records office reads that ruling as covering applications from transgender people: it changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Documented trans-specific legal matters in the state/province concern employment and criminal proceedings. In June 2023 a national civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the state/province government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the national justice department secured a settlement with the state/province government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated.

Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in local scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional culture, and a fa'afafine organisation formed in 2010 campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in a settlement in the state/province, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. A 2009 travel column described reserved public behaviour as expected of people of all orientations in the state/province.

In July 2015 the state/province was the only outlying jurisdiction of the parent nation that had not settled whether the national marriage-equality ruling applied to it, while several other outlying jurisdictions moved to apply it; the national justice department said applicability was still under review and that he did not know. That comparison is dated 10 July 2015 and describes the position at that time.

The 2003 bill's defeat means the state/province deliberately declined to enact a formal same-sex marriage ban before the 2015 ruling, and the committee record preserves contemporaneous fa'afafine testimony opposing such a ban on religious grounds rather than on grounds of marriage rights.

A 2009 travel column contrasted the state/province with a neighbouring jurisdiction, describing homosexuality as widely accepted in local culture while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected, and reported that hotels in the main town skew toward business travel. The column is a publication's own framing and is now more than fifteen years old.

The 2026 law-review article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative here, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality of an untested statute book. No court in the state/province has decided the question.

The local fa'afafine organisation was formed in 2010 by merging a local queens association and a sports association, and re-anchored its identity to cultural pride. It campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival took place in August 2016 in a settlement in the state/province with pageant, song, dance and poetry competitions, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support in numbers.

Residents have obtained relief in the employment sphere: a June 2023 national civil action alleged a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the state/province government, and in September 2023 the national justice department settled an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee with the state/province government.

Residents seeking to amend a birth certificate deal with the vital records office, which changes the name when presented with a name change order and may change the gender marker on medical documentation of the sex change, reading the highest court's ruling to cover transgender applications even though the ruling itself addresses only erroneous information and adoption-related name changes.

The state/province's own legislative and academic record is active on the marriage question: the legislature rejected a ban in 2003, a constitutional law professor surveyed the community in July 2024, and local attorneys published the 2026 analysis. Fa'afafine are described in local scholarship as an integral part of traditional culture, and a long-standing practice of raising some boys to fill a domestic role is documented, alongside a highly religious society in which conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate.

Whether the 2015 national marriage-equality ruling applies to the state/province is unresolved in this record. The 2026 law-review article says it does and that a certificate would have to be issued; the governor and the judiciary have acted on the premise that it does not. No court has ruled, and no same-sex couple is documented as having applied for a licence at any point.

No outcome is stated for the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a 16-year-old transgender teenager, and no later instance of violence against a trans person is documented in this inventory. Whether further incidents occurred and were not recorded is not sourced either way.

No source in this inventory reports a refusal by the vital records office to change a gender marker, or any appeal from such a refusal, so the practical limits of the medical-documentation requirement are not sourced.

National passport policy and the 2025 executive orders on sex definition, healthcare funding and sports are not restated here; they are carried at the national level of the parent record. This summary covers only the state/province's own laws, institutions and documented events.

No figure is available for the prevalence of discrimination complaints, police reporting, or public attitudes toward trans people in the state/province; the 2024 survey tested constitutional durability, not incidence.

The jurisdiction consists of three special municipalities within the parent nation and stands under the national framework: the parent nation's civil-status and anti-discrimination law, as in force in the historic-era core of the state, applies here in the same form, with no separate local legislation on marriage or discrimination operating alongside it.

No source in the inventory describes a provision that addresses trans visitors directly. The protection that exists on this state/province is carried by marriage registration and general anti-discrimination law, not by text naming gender identity, gender markers or facilities.

The local census office in Saba registered the region's first same-sex union on 4 December 2012: a visitor aged 26 wed a visitor aged 27, both visiting residents. Same-sex unions have therefore been registrable in this state/province since 2012, and the state/province registry has performed one for visitors. This 2012 registration is the only dated union event in the sources; no later instance is documented.

For a trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex, that registration evidences a working route rather than a paper right. Civil ceremonies on Saba run through the state/province registry, with the Court Room in the Administrative Building recorded as the simplest venue for an efficient ceremony and the registrar of record documented as flexible about couples' wishes. Full destination-wedding suppliers, including caterers, florists and accommodation, operate in the state/province.

A travel publication (14 December 2022, updated 1 September 2023) places the jurisdiction at #5 in a "Top 10 destinations that celebrate marriage equality in one subregion" list, stating that as a state/province of the parent nation its citizens and visitors are protected by strict anti-discrimination laws and that same-sex couples are warmly welcomed. This is a publication's editorial ranking of destinations, not a measurement of risk, enforcement or trans-specific conditions, and it makes no finding about gender identity, markers or facilities.

The inventory contains no comparative figure for this state/province against other jurisdictions in the subregion on trans-specific violence, screening practice or legal recognition, so no ranking of the state/province's relative safety can be drawn from it.

Residents of the jurisdiction are covered by the national anti-discrimination law as applied in the state/province, with no local equality statute of their own operating beside it. Protection therefore runs through the general statute rather than through any provision naming gender identity.

The state/province registry on Saba performs civil ceremonies as a routine public function, documented through its official tourism service, and it registered a union for two visiting residents on 4 December 2012. Residents seeking recognition of a relationship classed locally as same-sex use the same registry route.

No source in the inventory addresses airport or seaport screening, document or marker rules, gendered facilities, healthcare access, hate-crime enforcement or violence data for this state/province. Whether the anti-discrimination law has been invoked on gender-identity grounds here, and how it has been enforced, is not sourced.

The 4 December 2012 union is the only dated registration event in the sources; no later instance is documented, and the absence of later records is not evidence either way about current practice.

The destination ranking is editorial framing by a travel publication and is not a risk assessment; it is carried here as evidence of how the state/province presents itself, not as a finding about conditions on the ground.

The state/province stands under the national framework of the parent nation: its criminal law, identity documents, anti-discrimination statute and marriage regime apply here as they do in the parent nation's home state/province.

Medical capacity is the sharpest practical constraint. The state/province covers a small land area and holds a small population, and the single red flag recorded against it in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access. Prescriptions and ongoing gender-affirming treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally, and a visitor who depends on either should carry supplies and confirm provision before arrival.

The same aggregate index rates the state/province 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against the one healthcare red flag.

Anyone detained in the state/province falls under the parent nation's prison administration, whose placement policy recognises only biological sex; trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex. The national detention oversight body, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, with recommendations that also cover intersex and non-binary persons.

Socially the state/province is discreet rather than permissive. It has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene; same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low, and the sources record no hostility toward gay or trans visitors. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples, and hospitality staff are described as trained for a diverse clientele.

Politically, the state/province's joint deputy with a neighbouring jurisdiction was among 11 deputies representing outlying jurisdictions who voted against the 2013 law opening marriage to same-sex couples.

Among the jurisdictions of the region, the state/province's standing as an international celebrity destination is credited with a more open and relaxed social climate for LGBTQ people than neighbouring jurisdictions.

The state/province's small size and its reliance on a luxury-tourism economy shape both the absence of an organised scene and the discretion expected of visitors, in contrast to the larger jurisdictions of the region.

Residents who need ongoing gender-affirming care face the same capacity limit that constrains visitors: the state/province's small size and population support only limited medical services, and specialist provision is not assured locally.

The state/province's representation in the national legislature voted against the 2013 marriage law, and the state/province has no LGBTQ venue, Pride event or visible organising of its own.

No government LGBT+ travel advice specific to the state/province exists, and a national travel advisory records no warnings for it. No trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted to the aggregate index.

The aggregate rating of 7.7 out of 10, with nine positive rights and one red flag, is a composite score rather than a legal finding, and its components are not itemised in the source.

Accounts of the state/province's LGBTQ infrastructure conflict: one source lists gay bars, discos, saunas and beaches among the jurisdictions of the region including the state/province, while jurisdiction-level guides report no LGBTQ venue or scene. The discrepancy is unresolved.

The state/province stands under the parent nation as a historic-era state/province in which local legislation governs; the parent nation's statutes do not extend automatically. The state/province has no legal recognition of transgender people. Its human rights statute has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the upper house passed an amendment that also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not a protected ground, so trans people have no statutory protection against discrimination. Proposals to extend that protection were failed or dropped in 2004–2006 and again in 2009.

The sources identify no state/province-specific provisions on identity documents or gender markers, border or airport screening, restroom and facility access, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery for transgender people. The absence of gender identity as a protected ground is the only trans-specific legal finding the record carries.

The record describes expression of gender identity as often difficult and documents one instance of official interference: in 2006 the local government attempted to bar a drag performer, known by a royal-themed stage title, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The most recent documented instance of this kind in the record is from 2006; no later instance is documented.

Same-sex marriage has been unavailable since 2022. The supreme court legalised it in May 2017 in a marriage-licence case; a domestic partnership law, given assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, replaced marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making the state/province the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The supreme court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the court of appeal on 23 November 2018, but the parent nation's highest court of appeal banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no marital recognition.

Consensual sex between adult men was decriminalised in 1994 when the legislature voted 22–16 to remove two criminal code sections, replacing prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex; lesbian activity was never illegal. As of 2022 the age of consent stands unequal at 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 against 16 for other sexual activity, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

Organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples is documented: one major denomination and other churches protested a gay cruise ship visit on 12 July as "incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre". Such hostility is aimed at couples read locally as same-sex, which would reach a trans visitor whose relationship is read that way.

The 1994 decriminalisation debate split the state/province: religious leaders were divided and a Christian coalition staged marches against the change, evidence of an organised constituency for the conduct-based restrictions that remained in the criminal code.

In November 2020 reporting, the local government spent approximately £150,000 to appeal an unconstitutional case against a man charged and threatened with jail under an obscenity provision for importing DVDs of gay porn, an expenditure of public funds defending a prosecution of same-sex material.

A prior higher age of consent of 18 for gay male conduct was found in violation of a regional human-rights convention, which produced the equalised-but-still-split consent structure in force from 1 November 2019: 18 for anal intercourse, 16 for other sexual activity.

Same-sex couples may adopt equally under the state/province's adoption statute following the February 2015 supreme court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and the supreme court granted binational same-sex partners equal employment and benefits in November 2015.

The local regiment, formed by random lottery-style conscription, officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers and does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation, though such conduct has been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent that one conscript described the regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists".

Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the local hospitals board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise applied to women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men.

Protection on the ground of sexual orientation arrived only after failed and dropped proposals in 2004–2006 and 2009; gender identity was not added at any point in that sequence.

Whether local authorities recognise a changed gender marker on a foreign passport or identity document is not sourced; the record contains no provision either way, and this remains unresolved rather than permissive or restrictive.

The record contains no trans-specific violence or homicide figures for the state/province, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made, and no incident involving a transgender person after the 2006 parade episode is documented. An undocumented present is not evidence of an absent risk.

The year of the cruise protest is not given in the source, which dates it only to 12 July; the year remains unresolved.

Whether the human rights statute's sexual-orientation protection has ever been applied to conduct or presentation read as gender-nonconforming is not sourced, and no reported enforcement or complaint machinery specific to transgender people is identified.

The state/province is an autonomous constituent part of the parent nation, with full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the parent nation's highest court.

Both male and female same-sex sexual activity is legal, with an equal age of consent of 16 for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. A trans visitor in a relationship read locally as same-sex faces no conduct offence on that basis.

Same-sex marriage has been legal in the state/province since 12 July 2024, when the parent nation's highest court upheld an Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation. Before that ruling, the state/province recognised as valid same-sex marriages registered in the parent nation and in other state/provinces of the parent nation, but offered no marriage, civil union or other form of recognition within the state/province itself.

Recognition arrived by court order rather than by statute. A limited-rights proposal was put to the legislature in 2017, and a marriage bill submitted on 4 June 2019 was withdrawn in September 2020 for lack of support. In April 2015 representatives of all governments of the parent nation agreed that LGBT people in the state/province and in neighbouring jurisdictions should receive equal rights quickly, and the August 2015 judgment of a regional human rights court, applicable to the state/province, required legal recognition.

The Criminal Code enacted in 2011 prohibits unfair discrimination and incitement to hatred and violence on grounds that include heterosexual or homosexual orientation. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any distinction affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights in political, economic, social, cultural or other social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The protected grounds named in the source material do not include gender identity, and no authority specific to the state/province on gender-identity coverage was identified.

Official rhetoric has not consistently governed practice. In April 2015 a commissioner of a political party publicly backed equal rights for everyone in the local press, while a colleague in the same party opposed the rights push fiercely and used a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement to force a 2013 Pride event to relocate to a hotel premises. Public LGBT assembly in the state/province can be obstructed through administrative permitting at short notice.

The state/province opened an LGBT community centre in 2010, and alongside neighbouring jurisdictions has acted as a driver of equal-rights moves across the parent nation. A Pride organiser cites an industry award naming the state/province the most gay welcoming in the region, and a rights wishes-package was delivered to ministers at the parent nation's seat of government.

No sourcing specific to the state/province was found on gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry or border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, or the designation of facilities. Those areas are unassessed rather than cleared.

A neighbouring jurisdiction in the same parent nation passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That is comparator context and not the law of the state/province.

The April 2015 agreement covered several jurisdictions jointly, so the direction of travel was parent-nation-wide rather than specific to the state/province.

The industry award cited by a Pride organiser is a promotional characterisation by a local organiser, not an independent assessment of conditions for trans visitors.

Recognition of same-sex marriage in the state/province rests on the 12 July 2024 ruling of the parent nation's highest court rather than on an act of the legislature; the 2017 limited-rights proposal and the 2019 marriage bill withdrawn in September 2020 both failed in the legislature.

The Criminal Code's discrimination provisions name heterosexual or homosexual orientation as protected grounds and do not name gender identity, so a resident seeking to bring a discrimination complaint on gender-identity grounds has no provision identified in the source material.

Local organisers face administrative permitting as a practical constraint: the 2013 Pride event was forced to relocate to a hotel premises by a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement.

An LGBT community centre opened in 2010.

Gender markers in locally issued identity documents, entry and border screening triggered by gender presentation, access to gender-affirming care, and facility designation are unassessed for the state/province; no sourcing specific to it was identified.

Whether the Criminal Code's discrimination provisions have been applied to gender-identity complaints is not sourced.

The industry award and the delivery of a rights wishes-package to ministers at the parent nation's seat of government are recorded as claims by the organisations involved; no outcome from the wishes-package is documented in the source material.

The state/province's constitutional discrimination grounds were drafted in 2009 without sexual-orientation protection. The omission drew criticism from a committee of the parent nation's legislature, which called it deplorable and warned that local courts could afford less protection than a regional human-rights convention's non-discrimination provision requires; the parent nation's foreign ministry answered that the list of grounds was open-ended. No enumerated constitutional ground anchors a discrimination claim, and no trans-specific ground is listed.

No domestic route to marriage exists. In March 2019 the senior court's chief justice struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the appellate court overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban. Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration: in December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the marriage of two residents who had wed in another jurisdiction, and the appellate court held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. For a trans visitor whose relationship would be locally classed as same-sex, a marriage in another jurisdiction therefore carries immigration effects even though the state/province offers no domestic route to marry.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, among them the head of the local government, the representative of the administering state, ministers and elected legislators, joined a local LGBT organisation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation.

No trans-specific legal provision is documented for the state/province. Nothing in the available sources addresses gender recognition, identity documents, single-sex facilities, healthcare access or hate-crime protection, and no trans-specific incident or enforcement action is recorded.

Public expression is arranged rather than free-standing. Organisers of the 2021 Pride parade asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection as a condition of the public-space route, so the broad official participation came with negotiated limits on visible intimacy.

Partner recognition rests on an immigration decision and an appellate equality holding rather than on a marriage statute: the statutory ban on same-sex marriage was restored on appeal in August 2019, while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived. The protection therefore sits in administrative practice and case law rather than in legislation.

The 2009 constitutional drafting episode is the clearest documented instance of the administering state and the state/province disagreeing in public over LGBT protections, with a committee of the parent nation's legislature invoking a regional human-rights convention as an external benchmark the local framework might not meet.

Residents have no domestic route to marry. The senior court struck the statutory ban down in March 2019 and the appellate court restored it in August 2019, so a couple must marry abroad for the marriage to have any local effect.

Where they do, immigration authorities recognise the marriage in another jurisdiction. The December 2020 recognition of two residents' marriage in another jurisdiction, resting on the appellate holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds, gives couples an immigration route that the marriage statute does not provide.

The constitution's discrimination grounds do not expressly cover sexual orientation, so residents have no enumerated constitutional ground on which to challenge discriminatory treatment.

No trans-specific legal provision for the state/province appears in the available sources. Gender-recognition procedures, identity-document and marker rules, single-sex facilities, healthcare access and hate-crime provisions are all unsourced, and no trans-specific incident or enforcement action is recorded.

The final text of the 2009 constitution, and whether the open-ended list of discrimination grounds has since been read to cover gender identity, is unresolved.

Whether the condition organisers placed on displays of affection at the 2021 Pride parade was enforced, and by whom, is not sourced.

The state/province is disputed, with no single legal order running through it. The administering authority controls most of the ground and its security services, courts and detention facilities operate there; a rival claimant authority asserts sovereignty and governs through exile institutions and refugee camps in a neighbouring jurisdiction. Which framework a visitor stands under depends on which part of the state/province they are in.

The administering authority's jurisdiction reaches into the state/province in practice. On 9 December 2005 an international human-rights organisation reported the trial of seven human-rights defenders from the part under the administering authority's control on charges of fomenting illegal protests, called the charges dubious and demanded a fair trial. The case shows the administering authority's courts and detention operating on local political cases, not only on paper.

Same-sex intimacy is criminalised under both frameworks. The administering authority's law carries six months to three years of imprisonment. For the rival claimant authority, international monitoring organisations record same-sex sexual activity as illegal for both men and women, punishable by up to three years, and a July 2017 international media roundup listed that authority among jurisdictions where homosexuality is illegal for men and women and had been for decades. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status therefore stands inside a criminal prohibition in either part of the state/province.

The rival claimant authority's own position is contested. In 2010 its diplomatic representative in another country said the Constitution 'does not refer to homosexuality or any other sexual practice... it does not punish it'. A refugee-assistance organisation reads the same silence as leaving LGBTQ people with no legal protection against discrimination or violence. Constitutional silence is not decriminalisation, and no statute in the inventory decriminalises anything.

The only documented account of the local authorities applying such charges comes from a 2009 report by a refugee-assistance organisation: officials running the refugee camps in a neighbouring jurisdiction said they were holding some prisoners on 'homosexuality' charges while alleging facts that would more fittingly describe rape. The charge sits in the hands of camp administration rather than a court.

Social exposure is high. Most residents are Muslim, and relationships between people of the same sex are widely read as a foreign phenomenon.

The state/province is a dependent state/province of a larger country, with its own local legislature that legislates locally; the administering state is responsible for its defence. The anti-discrimination provision in force since 1 January 2007 makes anyone who publicly makes a statement threatening, insulting or degrading a group on account of race, colour, national or ethnic origin, religion or sexual orientation liable to a fine or up to two years' imprisonment. Gender identity is not among the listed grounds. On the sourced account this made the state/province the last jurisdiction in the region to prohibit discrimination and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation.

Before that provision took effect, homophobic conduct was legally unaddressed. In 2006 an openly gay singer, songwriter and radio host was severely beaten by five men in the capital and hospitalised shortly after coming out; he and his family then received threatening telephone calls, and police refused to handle the case because no local law banned discrimination against sexual minorities at the time. He was later moved to a psychiatric hospital with severe depression exacerbated by the beating, never recovered, and died by suicide in 2012. The most recent documented assault in this record is that 2006 attack; no later instance is documented.

A second documented attack dates from 2005, when a visiting drag group had to run from a gang of young men intent on physically assaulting them in the capital; the group was not attacked anywhere else on its tour.

Hostility from elected office is documented across a decade. In September 2010 the leader of a centre party refused to attend a state banquet for a visiting neighbouring country's prime minister and her partner, citing his religion. In June 2015 the Speaker of the national legislature published a letter attacking the national broadcaster for the space it gave the local LGBT organisation and condemning a drag show at the national cultural centre as 'non-culture', asking whether 'these people do not feel any shame'. The same year the party leader demanded that Pride be banned and repeatedly compared the local LGBT organisation to anti-whaling protesters, and his party remains formally opposed to homosexuality. A singer publicly urged people to ignore him, documenting organised public pushback alongside the hostility.

Public expression has been contested since the first gay pride march in 2005, which provoked substantial controversy; in 2015 the party leader also suggested the capital's pride parade be moved out of the city centre.

Partner recognition is unresolved in this record. No later sourced statement establishes the current status of partnership or marriage registration here.

Public petitioning has run in both directions. An internet petition after the 2006 assault collected 20,000 signatures, and eight women in the capital gathered a further 2,000 by email and in shops, tourist centres and gas stations. A petition against same-sex marriage gathered 1,262 signatures.

The record documents hostility to LGBT public expression alongside organised counter-mobilisation: a singer publicly urged people to ignore a party leader's call to ban Pride in 2015.

This state/province's own law governs legal gender recognition, and it requires surgery. To amend a birth certificate, a transgender person must give the vital records office a sworn statement from a physician confirming sex reassignment surgery, after which the office amends the certificate. The motor vehicle authority issues an amended driver's licence on receipt of a sworn physician statement that the applicant's sex has been surgically changed.

A 2018 attempt to remove the surgery requirement failed. A legislator introduced a bill in May 2018 to permit legal gender change on judicial permission with a letter confirming gender identity supported by documentation from a certified psychologist, social worker, therapist or other licensed professional, with no surgery required. The legislature postponed a vote on 13 December 2018 pending medical and law enforcement process issues, and the bill failed on 17 December 2018 by a 6 to 7 vote. Surgery remains the condition for both documents.

Marriage recognition for a trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship rests on the 2015 ruling. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making the state/province the first in the parent nation to recognise same-sex marriage.

Private consensual adult non-commercial sexual conduct has been lawful since the 1978 reform of the Criminal Code; the penal code in force before that, ordained in 1933, had criminalised sodomy, fellatio and cunnilingus with between one and ten years' imprisonment.

The state/province hosts a large permanent national military presence, so national policy on transgender service members bears directly on personnel stationed there.

The state/province's contemporary reputation for tolerance rests on general LGBTQ findings rather than transgender-specific evidence. The available material describes the indigenous population as historically accepting of homosexuality and transgender people, with homosexuality taken for granted as part of life rather than treated as taboo, and characterises the state/province as tolerant and accepting of LGBTQ people with very few reports of societal discrimination or harassment. A visible LGBTQ social scene has existed since the 1990s, with a handful of nightclubs and social functions and an annual pride event held since 2017 attracting a few hundred people. The state/province is a member of an international travel association and has begun marketing itself as a tourist destination for LGBTQ people.

Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression is prohibited under the state/province's law. In August 2015 the legislature passed a bill unanimously, banning discrimination in private employment on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, and separately forbidding discrimination against government employees on grounds of sexuality or identity.

Hate-crime coverage based on gender identity and sexual orientation derives from national law rather than the state/province's statute, and national military service policy is likewise national in scope.

The state/province is a self-legislating state/province of the parent nation. Its parliament enacts its own statutes on gender recognition, equality and criminal law, and national legislation reaches it only when extended by special national instrument rather than automatically.

The 2009 gender recognition statute allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have the new gender recognised. The 2017 equality act, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 and largely in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited.

A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the upper chamber and took effect in 2024. In 2024 the state/province became the first state/province in the state, and the first part of the state's state/provinces, to prohibit the practice.

In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. The bill's status after that consultation is not sourced.

Sexual offences law applies gender-neutrally. Private consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of twenty-one, lowered to eighteen by a 2001 criminal justice statute, then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by a 2006 amendment statute. Until 2021, a section of the 1992 sexual offences statute retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral under the 2021 sexual offences and obscene publications statute, which received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation.

On partner recognition, same-sex couples have held civil partnerships since 6 April 2011 under the 2011 civil partnership statute, and marriage has been available since 22 July 2016 following royal assent on 19 July 2016. Existing civil partnerships could be converted without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex enters a jurisdiction that recognises the union.

Family law has not kept pace with that recognition. Under the 2011 civil partnership statute, same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates in cases of IVF and surrogacy, and no law on the state/province acknowledges surrogacy.

The primary legislative record of the marriage-equality debate is the parliament's official proceedings of 26 April 2016, covering the upper chamber's third reading of the 2016 marriage and civil partnership amendment bill and consideration of the equality bill.

The reform sequence is documented: the head of government publicly backed same-sex marriage on 9 June 2015 and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the marriage prohibition, the political commitment that preceded the marriage and civil partnership statute in force from 22 July 2016.

The 2024 conversion-therapy prohibition places the state/province ahead of every other state/province in the state and of any other part of the state's state/provinces on that measure, a comparison the sources explicitly note rather than a ranking derived from incident counts.

Employment protection on sexual orientation predates the 2017 equality act: the lower chamber adopted an employment bill amendment on 30 November 2005 protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds, tabled by one of its members, and the 2006 employment statute made dismissal on those grounds unlawful with effect from 1 September 2006.

The 2017 equality act lists sexual orientation as a protected characteristic and defines it to include attraction to the same, opposite or either sex and lack of attraction to either sex.

The 2021 sexual offences and obscene publications statute pardoned historical gay sex offences committed before 1992, explicitly modelled on a 2017 pardon law in a neighbouring jurisdiction. The head of government issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022, on the thirtieth anniversary of decriminalisation, the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992.

The state/province's only prison, a facility fully operational since 14 August 2008 and run by the prison service, holds separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No birth-sex-versus-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice are documented; the prison-housing axis therefore yields no usable finding.

The status of the hate crime bill after the July 2022 community consultation is unresolved in the sources, as is any update to the birth-certificate position for IVF and surrogacy after the August 2023 consultation.

The state/province is a dependent jurisdiction. Travel documents, immigration and airport screening are governed by the parent nation's national rules rather than by local law, and the national layer of this assessment sits with the parent nation's record.
